ars-chemica-quod-sit-licita-recte-exerce: Ars chemica, 1566. The lawful chemical art. This book preserves that work. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
arxiv-2510-00066:
Iver Brevik, with Moshe Chaichian and Mikhail Katsnelson, wrote this 2025 comment paper in theoretical physics. It answers a bold claim by Chyba and Hand about making electric power from Earth's spin. Their idea used a magnetic shell moving through Earth's own magnetic field. Brevik and his co-authors rechecked the theory behind that claim and found it wanting.

The authors focus on a boundary rule for moving materials that the earlier work left out. Under that rule, the claimed current does not appear at all. They also show that moving the shell sideways takes no outside work. With no work going in, the steady power output the claim needs would break energy conservation. The paper is a careful rebuttal, and it shows how one missed condition can undo a striking claim.
arxiv-2510-00266:
Paul Parsons of Purdue University wrote this 2025 essay rethinking what visualization research should study. Most work in the field asks how charts spark insight or guide decisions. In real workplaces, though, successful visualizations often sink into the background of daily routine. Parsons argues that this quiet, trusted presence deserves study in its own right.

He draws on joint cognitive systems, naturalistic decision making, and infrastructure studies for theory. His running example is mission control at NASA, where displays saturate the room yet rarely draw comment. There, visualizations scaffold attention, coordination, and judgment rather than starring in dramatic discoveries. Treating invisibility as design failure misses how expert practice actually works, Parsons contends. He calls for new concepts and methods aimed at visualization-in-use, even when nobody notices it anymore.
arxiv-2510-00366:
Andreas Stavrou wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on symmetries of surfaces and the algebra they leave untouched. The mapping class group collects all the ways a surface can be twisted and deformed into itself. It acts on the surface's rational group ring, cut off at powers of the augmentation ideal. Stavrou computes exactly which part of that ring the whole group leaves invariant.

The surface in question is compact and oriented, with a single boundary component. The computation holds in a range that grows with the surface's genus. Results of this type feed group cohomology, the algebra that measures a group's hidden structure. The author notes this is the first such computation with non-symplectic coefficients since work by Kawazumi and Soulie. Pinning down invariants is a basic step toward understanding how surface symmetries organize algebraic data.
arxiv-2510-00866:
Nait Saada and five co-authors, several at Apple, dissect classifier-based quality filtering for language model pretraining in this 2025 arXiv paper. The recipe trains a classifier to tell web text from a curated set, then keeps the web documents the classifier scores highest. Models trained that way do better on tasks, so the method sits inside most training pipelines. The authors ask whether the filter selects for quality.

Their analysis says the mechanism is different. Filtering does not pull data closer to the high-quality set in language modelling terms. Instead, the classifier implicitly filters the high-quality set, emphasizing examples that sit far from the web bulk. Synthetic experiments with permuted text showed different trends from filtering. The authors conclude the method removes the bad rather than imitating the good. It should be read as alignment with downstream evaluations, not a universal quality measure.
arxiv-2510-01266:
Inuwa-Dutse red-teams an open-weight language model in Hausa and finds its safety training largely stays in English. Guardrails that hold in major languages can quietly dissolve in low-resource ones. Polite or grateful phrasing further relaxed the model's defenses, a reward-hacking pattern the author documents.

With minimal prompting, the model produced harmful and culturally insensitive content. It even treated common local poisons as safe for people to consume, a potentially lethal error. A small community survey confirmed how widespread those substances are. The study presses builders to audit safety where users actually live. Hausa serves millions, yet counts as low-resource in model training terms. The exercise responded to a public red-teaming competition for the model. Insecticide and rodenticide errors show factual and safety failures intertwining. Underrepresented communities bear the risk that audits skip. Politeness should never unlock harm.
arxiv-2510-01366:
Chau and co-authors unify two kinds of ideal powers in algebra under one function and bound their complexity combinatorially. Symbolic powers of monomial ideals track geometry, while squarefree variants have proliferated separately. A new squarefree-power-like abstraction covers both sequences at once.

A vanishing criterion for certain homological groups drives the main bounds. The key quantity is an admissible set read off an associated hypergraph. For edge ideals of special graph families, the lower bound sharpens into an exact formula. Block graphs get formulas for every power, a first for this corner of algebra. Castelnuovo-Mumford regularity is the complexity measure being bounded. Mixed sums of ideals supply the vanishing tests used throughout. Chordal graphs contribute the second exact family at power two. Computations on small graphs verify the conjectured wider formula. Combinatorics ends up governing algebra's invariants once again.
arxiv-2510-01766:
Camacho, Gonçalves-Dosantos, and Sánchez-Soriano propose a practical way to estimate the core of a cooperative game in this 2025 paper. In such games, the core collects payoffs that no group of players can beat by breaking away. Finding the full core is computationally hard for large games. Their method samples its extreme points instead of solving for the whole set at once.

The algorithm solves randomized linear programs again and again with carefully chosen objectives. Every extreme point it returns is a genuine core allocation, never an infeasible guess. The authors analyze how the method converges and what it costs to run. Extensive simulations on several game models showed high accuracy in rebuilding the core's shape. The approach scales to games where exact core computation would be far too slow.
arxiv-2510-02166:
Mbodji and five co-authors propose verifiable quality certificates for public code datasets in this 2025 paper. Code agents and software research train on shared datasets whose quality is asserted, not proven. Static dataset cards describe properties in prose, but nobody can audit them. Each team rebuilds its own cleaning pipeline, fragmenting effort and raising costs.

Their framework, SIEVE, converts per-property checks into Confidence Cards. These machine-readable certificates carry anytime-valid statistical bounds on each checked property. Anytime validity means the guarantee holds whenever a user inspects it, not just at publication. The paper outlines a research plan to mature the framework with community participation. Replacing narrative cards with verifiable certification should lower assurance costs across the field. Trust in a dataset becomes something one can compute rather than assume. The proposal targets the data layer that modern code intelligence stands on.
arxiv-2510-03066:
Farabi and co-authors present InsideOut, a framework for reading faces. Emotion recognition from faces serves teaching tools, clinics, and driver safety. The task stays hard in the wild. Occlusion, odd light, and tilted heads all blur the cues. Rare emotions also suffer from skewed training data. Their system builds on EfficientNetV2-S, a lean modern network. Transfer learning adapts it to the FER2013 benchmark.

Careful image cleanup and balanced splits came first. Strong augmentation then stretched the training set further. A small new head was tuned with a class-weighted loss. Rare classes thus pull their fair share of attention. The system reached a solid accuracy level on the test set. Its macro F1 score showed the balance held across classes. Plain convolutional baselines were matched or beaten. The authors stress openness over raw novelty. Full code ships with the paper for checking.
arxiv-2510-03166:
González-Sanz, Hallin, and Yao extend quantile forecasting from single series to whole vectors at once. A point forecast hides the spread of what may come next. Quantile methods recover that whole spread for one variable. Multivariate quantiles, though, lacked an agreed definition for years. Measure transportation ideas recently supplied such a definition. This paper builds autoregression on that foundation.

Their vector quantile autoregression is fully nonparametric. It handles nonlinear dynamics as readily as linear ones. The whole future distribution, given the past, is the target. Forecast regions at any probability level follow from it. That beats a bundle of separate one-variable forecasts. Joint extremes, like twin market crashes, become visible. Finance and biology both track many series jointly. Risk managers need joint tails, not marginal guesses. The work gives multivariate prediction a quantile language at last.
arxiv-2510-03266:
Sharma and Kumar teach an autoencoder to flag extreme swings in plant productivity inside a climate model. Gross primary productivity tracks how much carbon plants absorb. Climate anomalies can crash that uptake in extreme events. The team applied variational autoencoders to Earth system output. The Community Earth System Model supplied the simulated data. Four United States regions and three eras were compared. A traditional spectral method served as the benchmark technique.

The autoencoder learned normal seasonal patterns from twelve-month windows. Reconstruction errors then marked the anomalous periods. Both methods agreed on where extremes cluster spatially. The learned method set somewhat higher event thresholds overall. The autoencoder discovered periodic structure on its own. Both methods project worse extremes by mid-century. Western and central North America face the sharpest increases. Negative carbon events grow in size and frequency together.
arxiv-2510-03366:
Fartale and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper that asks whether language models recall facts and reason through problems using separate inner parts. The team probes transformer models layer by layer, head by head, and neuron by neuron. Controlled puzzles let them switch single parts off and watch what breaks. Two model families, Qwen and LLaMA, went through the same causal tests, which strengthens the claims beyond one design.

Turning off the parts tied to recall cut fact retrieval by up to fifteen percent in the tests. Reasoning scores stayed nearly untouched during those same cuts. Flipping the test hurt multi-step reasoning while leaving recall largely intact. About a third of the neurons studied fired mainly for one task type. Recall layers spread widely through the models, while reasoning layers clustered in fewer spots. Separable circuits mean safety fixes might one day tune one skill without damaging the other.
arxiv-2510-03766:
Askar, Vergara, and Ali present a 2025 arXiv paper simulating how intermediate mass black holes form in star clusters. Such black holes, hundreds to hundreds of thousands of times the Sun, bridge stellar and supermassive ones, and their birthplace is unsettled. In compact clusters, massive stars sink to the center and collide, building a massive star that can collapse into a black hole. The authors ran N-body and Monte Carlo simulations across cluster densities and masses.

Runaway collisions produced black holes of a thousand to ten thousand masses within five million years. Formation happened only in compact clusters, above a core density threshold. Both simulation methods agreed, though collision counts and collapse timing differed. After birth, the black holes grew by merging with stars and remnants. Gravitational wave observatories and transient surveys can test these predictions. Knowing which clusters can forge black holes tells observers where to point telescope time.
arxiv-2510-03866:
Zhang and Gao wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on using a new optimizer, called Muon, for federated learning. In federated learning, many devices train a shared model without pooling private data. Muon has recently beaten standard optimizers in several settings because it orthonormalizes its update direction. Its behavior in the federated setting, where data differs across devices, was still untested.

The authors propose FedMuon, a federated version of the optimizer, and prove a convergence rate for it on nonconvex problems. Their analysis shows the learning rate need not depend on problem-specific constants, a practical convenience. The method also tolerates heavy-tailed noise, which often appears in real training data. In image experiments, FedMuon beat strong baselines, including methods that use extra control variables to fight data differences. The gap grew when devices communicated less often. The results make Muon promising for distributed training.
arxiv-2510-04366:
Klugmann and Kondermann wrote this 2025 paper on how to score how unclear a labeling task is. People sort each item into one box from a fixed set. When people split their picks, the split is often not just error. Some items are so hard to tell apart that honest people keep picking in more than one way. The authors turn the spread of picks into one such score.

It builds on older spread scores, but treats one pick in a new way. A can't-solve pick counts apart, so two kinds of doubt stay split. One kind is classes that blur together; the other is items no one can solve. It also adds ways to guess the score from few picks, with a check on how unsure the guess is. Teams can drop hopeless items and send real splits for a second look.
arxiv-2510-04766:
Beterov, Kozenko, Peng Xu, and Ryabtsev wrote this 2025 physics paper on making a quantum gate faster. Neutral atom computers entangle atoms by lifting them to Rydberg states, which interact strongly. A controlled Z gate built from gentle adiabatic pulses is reliable but slow. Slow gates waste the lives of Rydberg states and cap fidelity. The team adds counterdiabatic driving, a control that cancels unwanted transitions. Pulses are applied in mirror order to atoms at once.

The speedup is at least fivefold over earlier adiabatic schemes. The authors designed analytic pulse shapes for one, two, and three photon excitation routes. They covered both rubidium and cesium atoms in the analysis. Bell state fidelity, counting lifetimes and imperfect blockade, reaches the top of the scale today. The upper limit sits near ninety nine point nine nine percent at room temperature. Faster gates with fidelity serve the push toward error corrected atom computers.
arxiv-2510-04866:
Ryotaro Honma and Tan Van Vu wrote this 2025 physics paper on how sharply currents can flow in quantum systems. A rule, the thermodynamic uncertainty relation, ties current steadiness to entropy cost. In classical two part systems, information flowing between the parts can steady the current. Quantum systems add coherence and simultaneous change, which rewrite the trade off. The authors derive a quantum version of the rule for multi part systems.

Their bound weighs current fluctuations against three resources. Local dissipation is one, information exchange is the second, and quantum coherence is the third. All three can suppress fluctuations in their analysis. They checked the bound on two model systems in simulation. One is an autonomous quantum Maxwell demon, and the other is a quantum clock. The results matter for quantum heat engines, sensors, and clocks that promise precision. Designers now know information and coherence are currencies for steadiness, not dissipation.
arxiv-2510-04966:
Anna Chistyakova and Mikhail Pautov address theft of valuable AI models in this 2025 arXiv paper. Large vision models cost a fortune to train, so owners license them under strict terms. A dishonest customer can resell a copy and claim it as their own work. The authors build a watermark that exposes such copies.

Their method, ActiveMark, fine-tunes a few expressive layers of the model on a hidden set of images. A small encoder-decoder pair plants the mark inside the model's internal responses. The mark survives later fine-tuning for tasks like classification and segmentation. Theory and experiments show low rates of both false alarms and missed detections. Honest, independent models are not mistaken for marked copies.
arxiv-2510-05066:
Dushmanta Sahu imports a century-old magnetism effect into nuclear physics in this 2025 arXiv paper. The Barnett effect says a spinning ferromagnetic material magnetizes itself. Heavy-ion collisions create matter that spins extremely fast. Physicists usually credit the collision's magnetic field to fast spectator protons flying past.

Using a hadron resonance gas model under rigid rotation, Sahu computes the Barnett magnetization of that spinning matter. The induced field turns out comparable to the spectator field at low collision energies. Magnetization grows with temperature, density, and spin rate. The result adds a previously overlooked source to models of spin dynamics. It also matters for anomalous transport in the quark-gluon matter these collisions create.
arxiv-2510-05266:
Christina Thrainer and six co-authors spot sewer and culvert defects with very little training data in this 2025 arXiv paper. Infrastructure inspectors label defect images by hand, which is slow and expensive. New defect types appear with almost no examples available. Few-shot segmentation promises to learn categories from a handful of support images.

Their framework pairs an enhanced feature pyramid encoder with prototypical learning. Masked pooling builds a prototype for each defect class from the support set. Global, local, and cross-attention sharpen the feature matching. The best setup reached an F1 score near 83 percent with strong overlap accuracy in two-way tests. Self-attention alone added about 2.6 points of F1 over the baseline. Bidirectional prototypical learning brought even larger gains.
arxiv-2510-05366:
Yassine Kebbati and four co-authors give a race car a learning predictive controller in this 2025 arXiv paper. Autonomous racing pushes vehicles to their physical limits on tight circuits. The controller must plan the fastest line while respecting tire, track, and vehicle constraints. It also needs accurate state estimates in real time.

Their scheme couples nonlinear model predictive control with a moving horizon estimator. An offline planner computes the best trajectory under the car's limits and circuit rules. Gaussian process regression learns the model's errors and improves its predictions online. The estimator reconstructs the car's state from noisy measurements as it runs. Tests on two different race tracks validated the combined planning, estimation, and control design.
arxiv-2510-05566:
Lin and colleagues make uncertainty estimates for language models hold up when topics shift. Conformal prediction wraps a model's answers in a set that should contain the truth. That promise relies on test data matching the calibration data closely. Real deployments break the match, since users drift to new subjects and styles.

Their framework, DS-CP, reweights calibration examples by closeness to the test prompt. Nearby examples count more, so the answer set adapts to the new domain. Theory in the paper bounds the coverage from above and below. On the MMLU benchmark, the method restored coverage where standard conformal prediction fell short. The fix costs only a modest growth in set size, keeping answers usable. The authors present the method as a practical step toward trustworthy deployment. It needs no retraining of the underlying language model at all.
arxiv-2510-05666:
Nguyen and colleagues build intersecting set families from small generating collections. A family is intersecting when every two of its sets share an element. Left-compressed families, closed under shifting elements leftward, anchor extremal set theory. Their 2025 paper constructs such families from a chosen collection of generators.

The construction grows a full family from the generating sets by downward closure. The authors identify conditions on the generators that guarantee an intersecting family. Those conditions yield a convenient method to build new examples. The same machinery extends an existing left-compressed intersecting family. They compare their criterion with a theorem of Bond on the same theme. Strong intersection between generators does the heavy lifting in the proofs. Compression techniques underlie classics like the Erdős–Ko–Rado theorem. A handy construction kit matters because intersecting families are otherwise built case by case.
arxiv-2510-05766:
Kumar and colleagues count special diffusion matrices used inside ciphers. MDS matrices spread input changes optimally across outputs, giving strong diffusion. Involutory and orthogonal versions let encryption and decryption share circuitry. Their 2025 paper studies generalized semi- variants of both families.

The authors prove structural bridges between the semi- and classical families. Counts of semi-involutory matrices follow directly from counts of involutory ones, and back. The same two-way correspondence holds for semi-orthogonal matrices. Matrices enjoying both semi- properties are characterized completely. A generic structure for orthogonal matrices of arbitrary order underlies the counts. For three-by-three matrices, that double class matches the semi-involutory count exactly. Closed forms enumerate the three-by-three orthogonal and semi-orthogonal cases. All enumeration happens over binary extension fields used in real ciphers. Structural shortcuts beat brute-force searches for new diffusion layers.
arxiv-2510-05866:
De Ara and colleagues measure quantum capacitance between two approaching metal electrodes. Capacitance normally looks purely classical, set by geometry and field flux. A quantum contribution from the Pauli principle usually hides inside metals' huge density of states. Their 2025 experiment pushes platinum and gold electrodes toward contact.

As the gap shrinks, capacitance first climbs classically as expected. Then the increase saturates at the quantum capacitance limit. Closer still, quantum tunneling produces a measurable capacitance leakage. The quantum and classical parts act like capacitors in series. Because quantum capacitance tracks surface density of states, it becomes a probe. Adsorbed toluene molecules change that density, and the setup detects it. Surface chemistry sensing is a plausible application beyond the physics. Atomic-scale junctions are where the effect matters most practically. Neglected quantum corrections thus become measurable before contact forms.
arxiv-2510-05966:
Hirvensalo studies a medical imaging method in a 2025 paper on inverse problems. The method sends current through a body and reads voltages at the skin. From those readings, doctors hope to infer how well tissue conducts inside. He studies a ball shaped domain and small changes that depend only on radius. The work treats the linear step used to rebuild an image from data.

He shows that the response patterns for such changes are spherical harmonics. He also writes each strength value in closed form from the radial profile. Those strengths shrink at a shared rate as the pattern degree grows. Hence short sums of patterns can stand in for the full response map. The result extends the theory to rougher changes in any dimension. Such finite sums should make computer solvers for the scan faster and safer.
arxiv-2510-06166:
Desai and three co-authors tackle the synthesizability gap in perovskites in a 2025 materials science paper. Halide and chalcogenide perovskites are prized for cheap, abundant ingredients and tunable properties. Density functional theory scans their vast composition space for strong optoelectronic behavior. Yet few screened candidates are ever made in a lab, because calculations say nothing about synthesizability.

They combine high-throughput screening with labels mined from past lab reports. Their classifiers use positive and unlabeled learning, built for data where only successes are recorded. The models estimate synthesis probability from their energies and similar compounds already synthesized. Several feature sets feed the classifiers, compared across feature choices. The data and models ship as a public nanoHUB tool following FAIR principles. The framework promises fewer wasted synthesis attempts and a faster path from computation to real crystal.
arxiv-2510-06366:
Santos-Sanz and twenty-seven co-authors report JWST observations of a stellar occultation by the Centaur Chariklo in a 2025 planetary science paper. Chariklo hosts the first known small-body ring system, a double ring revealed by occultations. Almost nothing is known about how such rings originate or survive.

The near-infrared measurements show a system in flux. The inner dense ring has become significantly more opaque than before. That points to ongoing replenishment or dynamical restructuring. The outer ring tells the opposite story. Its signature is far weaker in the near-infrared than in earlier visible-light detections. Material loss could make the outer ring transient, or its opacity may depend on wavelength. Either way, the two rings are evolving differently. Occultation timing remains the only tool sharp enough to probe such tiny, distant rings. The authors stress an unprecedented complexity among small-body rings.
arxiv-2510-06466:
Xue and Ye combine a Dirichlet policy with attention for reinforcement-learning portfolio management in a 2025 finance paper. Portfolio agents must output weights that sum to one and respect trading constraints. Standard reinforcement learning often breaks the rules or wanders at random.

Their Dirichlet policy yields feasible weightings by design. It handles tradability constraints smoothly and explores stably. Per-asset encoders track each asset's recent history. A global attention layer captures cross-asset structure, including sector links and factor spillovers. The reward charges transaction costs and punishes portfolio variance. That ties learning to the classic mean-variance trade-off investors care about. In tests, attention-based Dirichlet policies beat equal-weight and standard reinforcement learning benchmarks. They won on terminal wealth and Sharpe ratio, with plausible turnover and drawdowns. Principled action design plus attention makes agents steadier and easier to read.
arxiv-2510-07266:
Bechavod, Lu, and Roth present the first algorithm for a shared prediction problem with long-term limits. Their 2025 paper studies omniprediction, where one learner broadcasts predictions to many decision makers. Each maker has its own goals and constraint functions, and all act as if the shared prediction were correct. The learner wants every maker to fare well, even against an opponent who changes the world each round. Regret here is dynamic, measured against action sequences that themselves change over time.

The algorithm gives all makers their regret guarantees at once. Constraint violations shrink toward zero for every maker as rounds accumulate. Remarkably, the makers need no memory of their own. Each round, they only solve a single one-round constrained problem based on the fresh prediction. The work extends online learning toward settings where one forecast serves many agents with long-run limits.
arxiv-2510-07366:
Agrawal, Hook, Loladze, and Reig offer a simple cure for the axion quality problem. Their 2025 paper concerns the QCD axion, a favored candidate particle that would solve a puzzle about matter and antimatter and might form dark matter. Gravity is expected to spoil the delicate symmetry behind the axion. That spoilage is the quality problem. The authors make the axion the leftover ripple of a broken baryon-number symmetry. The breaking happens inside a new composite sector when it confines, like quarks binding into protons.

Because the baryon operator has high dimension, dangerous symmetry-breaking terms arise only at very high order. Quality then grows rapidly as the number of colors in the new sector rises. A minimal neat version uses ten colors and ten flavors. In that version the known forces sit inside a grand flavor symmetry in a natural way.
arxiv-2510-07966:
Hess and thirteen coauthors wrote this 2025 astronomy paper on galaxy gas at intermediate redshift. Their sample comes from the CHILES survey, which detects atomic hydrogen beyond the local universe. Fourteen hydrogen-detected galaxies sit in a cosmic overdensity at redshift near zero point one two. ALMA mapped their carbon monoxide, the tracer of cold molecular gas. It is the largest resolved dataset of its kind at such distances.

Carbon monoxide appeared only in the most massive galaxies. It traced a rotating disk matching the atomic gas. Stacking the silent galaxies still revealed a modest average molecular reservoir. Molecular gas sat inside a wider atomic envelope. The redder colors of detected galaxies point to dusty, obscured star birth. Mild signs of evolution in gas ratios appear, though scatter blocks firm claims. Satellite radio interference may block similar detections for years to come.
arxiv-2510-08066:
Gill and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on switching graphene's valleys with light despite graphene having no band gap. Valleytronics encodes information in which of two momentum valleys electrons occupy. Circular light normally selects valleys only in gapped materials, which excludes graphene and its gapless relatives. The authors design a two-color light pulse instead. A deep ultraviolet pulse excites electrons at the saddle points of graphene's band structure. A terahertz envelope then pushes that excitation into one low-energy valley.

Simulations with tight-binding models and time-dependent density functional theory confirmed the scheme. The combined pulse produced a nearly perfectly valley-polarized excitation. The route works because it detours through the saddle point rather than fighting the missing gap. The idea should extend to graphene's gapless Xene cousins. Lightwave valleytronics could eventually write information at ultrafast speeds. The paper gives experimentalists a concrete pulse recipe.
arxiv-2510-08166:
Kristmann, Wimmer, and Schütz wrote this 2025 computer graphics paper showing that JPEG, long dismissed for real-time rendering, can compress game textures on modern graphics cards. Rendering needs random access to individual texels, which variable-rate formats deny. Their system uses a deferred pipeline to identify which image blocks a frame needs. A compact indexing table restores random access, and mipmaps plus a cache cut decoding work.

The indexing overhead adds a small fraction of a bit per pixel. Even so, total size stayed well below the standard fixed-rate formats, with better quality than BC1 and results competing with ASTC. The pipeline added well under a millisecond per frame on a high-end card, and their demo scene rendered at over a thousand frames per second. The authors expect friendlier successors like JPEG XL to make variable-rate textures genuinely attractive.
arxiv-2510-08466:
Ying Wang, Mengye Ren, and Andrew Gordon Wilson cluster data with language models in a 2025 arXiv paper. Classic clustering needs a fixed similarity measure chosen in advance. Their method, In-Context Clustering, lets a pretrained model infer groupings through its attention mechanism instead. Attention patterns inside the model turn out to carry clear cluster signals.

Pretrained models already cluster text-encoded numeric data well with no training at all, they show. Running spectral clustering on the model's attention matrices gives surprisingly competitive results. Fine-tuning with a next-token prediction loss sharpens clustering on numeric and image data further. Prompting also enables text-conditioned image clustering, where words steer what counts as similar. Classical methods cannot do that trick, the authors note. The work extends in-context learning, usually a supervised skill, into unsupervised territory.
arxiv-2510-08566:
Meixi Song and co-authors stabilize 3D scene reconstruction from very few photos in a 2025 arXiv paper. 3D Gaussian Splatting renders new views in real time from explicit 3D blobs, but sparse views degrade it badly. The team identifies two failure modes. Gaussians pile up near the camera and overfit, while distant areas get too little coverage and underfit.

Their framework, D2GS, attacks both problems with depth and density guidance. A dropout strategy adaptively masks redundant Gaussians based on their density and depth, curbing overfitting. A distance-aware fidelity module adds targeted supervision to far-field regions that are usually neglected. They also introduce a new metric quantifying the stability of learned Gaussian distributions. Extensive experiments across data sets showed better visual quality and robustness under sparse views. The method keeps reconstruction usable with only a handful of input images.
arxiv-2510-08766:
Trehan, Knuth, and Way describe early work on predicting the light signatures of distant planets, in this 2025 arXiv paper. When starlight passes through a planet's atmosphere, gases absorb specific colors, and that pattern hints at the planet's climate. The team wants a model that predicts the pattern from traits such as size and temperature. Such a model, run in reverse, could later reveal a planet's traits from a measured spectrum.

This first stage fits smooth curves to simulated spectra from a NASA climate model of rocky planets. The curves show how each slice of the spectrum changes as one planet trait varies. A Bayesian search method, which weighs evidence as it explores, then flags the regions where more data would help most. The authors present the study as work in progress toward judging which far-off planets could support habitable conditions.
arxiv-2510-08866:
Gordina and Sarkar work out the spectrum of noise-driven motion on a class of curved spaces, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their spaces are step-two Carnot groups, geometries where movement is allowed freely in some directions and only indirectly in others. They perturb the natural diffusion on such a space with jumps that act along the restricted directions. The resulting processes are Lévy-type, mixing steady drift with sudden leaps.

Using harmonic analysis, the mathematics of waves on groups, the pair link their operators to simpler semigroups on flat Euclidean space. That intertwining exposes the full spectrum of the perturbed operator. They then build matching equilibrium-seeking processes, called Lévy-Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroups, and prove these settle into balance over time. Strangely, every such generator shares the same spectrum. The paper also describes the pattern spaces exactly and gives formulas for partner eigenfunctions.
arxiv-2510-09166:
Blanco, Laborda, and Martínez-Antón ask when an easy substitute problem secretly solves a hard scheduling-style problem exactly, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Ordered optimization covers decisions where sorting is part of the job, like placing facilities so the worst-served customer is protected. Such problems are attacked by relaxing them: drop the whole-number requirements, solve the smooth version, and hope the answer comes out whole. The authors study when that hope is justified.

They identify input properties that decide whether the relaxation returns the true optimum. Adding ordered components, they show, adds complexity that breaks the exactness familiar from classical problems. For the min-max case, where the largest cost is minimized, the relaxation never recovers the true whole-number solution at all. Strength tracks closeness to the classical problem: near ones relax tightly, distant ones weakly. Experiments on location benchmarks confirmed this.
arxiv-2510-09466:
Alma Cavallin, Oliver Thim, and Christian Forssén connect nuclear symmetries with quantum entanglement in a 2025 arXiv paper. They study how two nucleons, the protons and neutrons inside atomic nuclei, scatter off each other. The interaction between them shows accidental symmetries, patterns not forced by deeper laws, including the Wigner SU(4) symmetry and Serber symmetry.

The authors build potentials from chiral effective field theory, the standard low-energy theory of nuclear forces, at several levels of these symmetries. Computing the full scattering matrix, they show how neutron-proton spin entanglement tracks the symmetry content, plus which operators and partial waves are present. They also follow the entanglement order by order in the theory's expansion. Neutron-neutron scattering shows no entanglement suppression, which they attribute to the Pauli principle, with no accidental symmetries present there. Entanglement, they conclude, usefully guides the study of nuclear power counting.
arxiv-2510-09566:
Ilia Revin, Leon Strelkov, Vadim Potemkin, Ivan Kireev, and Andrey Savchenko present an automated optimisation framework in a 2025 arXiv paper. Training neural networks efficiently involves tangled choices about architecture, compression, and training strategy. Their framework, PETRA, applies evolutionary optimisation, which breeds and selects design variants, to both the model architecture and how it is trained.

PETRA combines pruning, which removes unneeded connections, quantisation, which stores numbers more cheaply, and loss regularisation. The team tested it on real-world financial event sequences and on image and time-series benchmarks. The framework shrank model size by up to seventy-five percent and latency by up to a third. Throughput rose by thirteen percent, with no noticeable loss in the target metric. The authors present PETRA as a step toward neural models that stay accurate while demanding far fewer resources to train and run.
arxiv-2510-09666:
Aditya Chakravarty, the sole author, maps uncertainty in wildfire forecasts in a 2025 arXiv paper. Climate change is intensifying fire risk, and learning models now often predict wildfire spread from Earth observation data. Yet forecasts without uncertainty estimates leave emergency planners guessing how much to trust each predicted fireline.

Chakravarty presents the first full analysis of how spatial uncertainty behaves in wildfire spread forecasting from multimodal satellite inputs. Predictive uncertainty turns out to have coherent spatial structure, concentrated near the fire perimeter. A new distance metric shows the high-uncertainty regions form steady buffer zones twenty to sixty metres wide around the predicted firelines. That width is of direct use for escape and supply planning. Tracing the drivers shows plant health and fire activity drive most of the uncertainty. The author frames the work as a step toward wildfire systems robust enough for towns facing growing fire risk.
arxiv-2510-09766:
Mehdi Rezaei, Supriya Pan, Weiqiang Yang, and David Mota ask whether dark energy changes with time in a 2025 arXiv paper. Dark energy drives the accelerating expansion of the universe, and its equation of state may sit at exactly minus one, a constant, or drift. The authors test that question with a broad set of present-day probes plus simulated future gravitational wave distances from the Einstein Telescope.

Their framework is the Padé approximation, a flexible family containing several known dark energy models. They examine three forms of it in both flat and curved universes, fitting supernovae, baryon acoustic oscillations, nucleosynthesis, expansion rate data, and the cosmic microwave background. One form, Padé-II, repeatedly prefers a time-varying equation of state. The preference reaches roughly four to six standard deviations depending on the dataset combination, and it persists, somewhat weakened, when the gravitational wave data are added.
arxiv-2510-09866:
Santoni, Stefano Bolognesi, and Andrea Luzio study baryons and solitons in gauge theories in this 2025 arXiv paper in theoretical physics. They consider SU(N) gauge theories, a family of force theories, in both chiral and vector-like forms. The matter sits in mixed one-index and two-index representations, two ways fields can transform under the force.

The authors focus on the color-flavor locked phase, a dense state where color and flavor symmetries lock together. In that phase they compute the topology of the coset, the space of distinct states, of the low-energy effective theory. That topology decides which solitons, stable lumps of field, can exist. The work connects baryon structure to a theta-periodicity anomaly, a subtle clash between symmetries.
arxiv-2510-10066:
Jiang, Chenguang Zhu, and Sarfraz Khurshid test JavaScript obfuscators in this 2025 arXiv paper on software verification. Obfuscators scramble code to protect intellectual property and fight reverse engineering. Their evaluations usually measure how hard the output is to read, not whether the scrambled code still behaves the same.

That correctness question is the paper's focus. OBsmith uses a large language model to generate test programs and check whether obfuscation preserves program semantics, the actual behavior of the code. An obfuscator that changes behavior silently breaks the software it protects. The authors argue that semantic preservation deserves the same scrutiny as resilience, and they automate the hunt for violations.
arxiv-2510-10166:
Gupta, Muhammed Tawfiqul Islam, and Rajkumar Buyya survey autoscaling for edge computing in this 2025 arXiv review paper. Edge computing moves computation near users through micro-service designs that demand low latency. Service level agreements set strict targets for performance, reliability, and availability.

Autoscaling adds or removes resources as demand shifts. Proactive methods predict load and scale ahead of time, while reactive methods respond after load changes. The authors compare both families for edge settings, where resources are thin and the cloud must back up peaks. A hybrid cloud and edge design is often required to meet the agreements. The review maps which strategy fits which workload pattern.
arxiv-2510-10266:
Jaiswal, Ivar S. Haugerud, Hidde D. Vuijk, and Christoph A. Weber study chemical power from cyclic environments in this 2025 arXiv paper on the physics of life. Living cells run molecular machinery that spends high-energy molecules to build complex structures. At life's origin no such machinery existed, so simple physical mechanisms must have harvested energy first.

The authors examine environments that cycle, such as day-night or tidal rhythms, as an energy source. They ask how such cycles can drive chemical work or produce chemical power without enzymes. A robust prebiotic mechanism would show how chemistry could bootstrap toward metabolism. The work treats environmental cycles as a battery that early molecular systems could tap.
arxiv-2510-10466:
Jinjin Cao and five co-authors address a failure mode of vision language models in this 2025 arXiv paper: the models invent fluent answers that ignore the image in front of them. They trace much of this hallucination to language bias, where the model leans on word patterns instead of visual evidence. Their remedy is Cross-Modal Guidance, a decoding method that needs no extra training.

The method works by contrast. It deliberately degrades the model's visual perception, by masking the attention paid to the most influential image tokens in chosen layers. It then compares the normal output with the degraded one. Steering the final answer away from the degraded output strengthens the visual signal and weakens the pull of language habits. In their experiments, the method improved scores on hallucination benchmarks across several models, with no added training cost.
arxiv-2510-10566:
Naoki Maruyama, Masayuki Ohzeki, and Kazuyuki Tanaka examine a mismatch between quantum annealing and its classical simulation, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Quantum annealing searches for ground states, the lowest energy configurations of a problem. It often samples among equally good ground states unfairly, which matters when diverse optimal solutions are wanted. Quantum Monte Carlo is widely used to simulate annealing, but whether it reproduces that unfair sampling was unclear.

The team compares final ground state distributions from the Monte Carlo master equation against true Schrödinger dynamics. They find Monte Carlo tends to produce uniform probabilities across ground states, unlike annealing's biased output, and the bias grows as annealing proceeds. Their analysis traces the bias to replica alignment: setups where all replicas coincide dominate, because mismatched kink setups are suppressed in energy. They flag this as a basic limit of discrete time Monte Carlo for simulating annealing.
arxiv-2510-10766:
Ahmad Mohammadi and seven co-authors detect GPS spoofing attacks on autonomous vehicles with an adaptive clustering method, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Spoofed signals can feed a vehicle false positions. Their approach tunes a density based clustering algorithm, DBSCAN, in real time. The detection threshold updates from the running mean and spread of errors between GPS and the vehicle's own sensors, but only using moments judged non anomalous, so attacks cannot quietly retrain it.

An initial threshold comes from 120,000 clean data samples, letting the system catch even subtle, gradual spoofing from the start. The team tested it on five subsets of a real world driving dataset from the Honda Research Institute, simulating large and small attacks. It identified turn by turn, stop, overshoot, and multiple small biased attacks, with detection accuracies ranging from about 98.4 to 99.9 percent across the attack types in their tests.
arxiv-2510-10866:
Shudong Sun, Hao Helen Zhang, and Joseph C Watkins measure how similar two datasets are by how well models cross between them, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Similarity matters for transfer learning and domain adaptation. Most measures compare only input feature distributions, ignoring labels and how features map to responses. Their Cross-Learning Score instead uses two way generalization: train a decision rule on one dataset and test it on the other, in both directions.

They ground the score theoretically, linking it to the cosine similarity between decision boundaries under standard linear models, which gives it a geometric meaning. A robust ensemble based estimator is easy to implement and avoids high dimensional density estimation. For transfer learning, they add a zones framework that sorts source datasets into positive, ambiguous, and negative transfer regions. Extensions handle deep learning's encoder head designs. Experiments validate the score for similarity and transfer assessment.
arxiv-2510-10966:
Santanu S Dey, Frédéric Meunier, and Diego Moran Ramirez probe the limits of a classic optimization theorem, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Geoffrion's theorem assesses how good Lagrangian relaxation is, a standard technique for bounding integer programs. The theorem quietly assumes the feasible set is finite, or describable by rational linear constraints. The authors ask whether the theorem survives when those assumptions are dropped, allowing infinite feasible sets that no finite list of linear constraints can describe.

It does not, in general. Through concrete examples, they show the theorem's conclusion can fail once finiteness and rationality are removed. The paper then rebuilds the result, giving sufficient conditions under which Geoffrion's conclusion remains valid even for infinite feasible sets beyond finite linear description. Knowing exactly when a trusted quality guarantee holds, and when it silently breaks, protects both theory and practice. Relaxation bounds guide solvers everywhere, so the boundary matters.
arxiv-2510-11466:
Alexis Bouthier and Eric Vasserot prove a long-sought result in geometric representation theory. Their 2025 arXiv paper extends the geometric Satake equivalence to affine Kac-Moody groups. The classical equivalence links geometry on a space called the affine Grassmannian with the representations of a dual group. Kac-Moody groups are infinite-dimensional generalizations, and their infinite size had blocked the usual methods for twenty years.

The authors build a well-behaved category of sheaves on the relevant quotient stack and equip it with a t-structure, a tool for slicing the category into layers. They prove a version of Braden's hyperbolic localization theorem for this stack. Using size estimates for special cycles, they show the constant term functor respects those layers exactly. The resulting equivalence matches special geometric objects, called IC complexes, with the dual group's irreducible highest-weight representations.
arxiv-2510-12166:
Kenneth Weiss and five co-authors make standard how to compare supercomputers fairly. High-performance architectures keep diversifying, and everyone wants to know how a code performs across platforms. Yet guidance on designing such studies barely exists. Their 2025 arXiv paper argues the natural base unit is one compute node per platform, and builds its method around node-to-node scaling.

The authors give practical guidance for setting up, running, and analyzing these studies, plus templates for presenting the scaling results. Several case studies demonstrate the approach's benefits. Node-level comparison sidesteps a common apples-to-oranges trap: whole machines differ wildly in node counts and budgets, while nodes are what codes actually inhabit. For procurement committees and porting teams alike, the framework converts marketing claims and anecdotes into a repeatable measurement discipline. Its contribution is comparability itself.
arxiv-2510-12566:
Kirkeby and Lagermann check the simplified energy models behind sustainability reports for web services against real readings, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Reporting frameworks in Denmark and the United Kingdom estimate the energy used on end user devices when people browse sites. Such models are widely adopted, but their accuracy and precision were little explored.

The authors measured actual energy use during realistic interactions with shopping, booking, navigation, and news sites. Set user flows ran on four laptop platforms, and measured energy was compared with model predictions. The commonly used constant power approximation, power multiplied by time, diverged greatly from measurements. The gaps depended on website category, device type, and task. The deviations were systematic rather than random. The authors argue that sound sustainability reporting needs category aware, device reflective power parameters, instead of one constant for every session.
arxiv-2511-00066:
Tue Le, Linh Ngo Van, and Trung Le improve group relative policy optimization for training language models with verifiable rewards, by guiding it with sharpness. Generalization during such training is usually left uncontrolled. A robustness view bounds generalization loss by empirical loss plus a sharpness surrogate measured by gradient norm, suggesting flatter solutions should transfer better.

Their token-weighted variant, GRPO-SG, shapes probabilities using that sharpness guidance. Machine learning readers get a simple modification aimed at reasoning models that generalize beyond their training problems. Verifiable reward training is now a main route to better reasoning, so controlling its generalization is timely.
arxiv-2511-00366:
Shridhar Vashishtha, Krishna Prasath Logakannan, Jacob Hochhalter, Shandian Zhe, and Robert Kirby build a digital twin part for aircraft structures. A twin needs a fast surrogate model that forecasts the real part's future state and updates as service data arrives. Their surrogate is a Gaussian process enriched with derivative data, which sharpens accuracy but inflates the covariance matrix until updates become far too costly.

A modified streaming sparse Cholesky solver removes that bottleneck, letting the model absorb fresh data dynamically. Experiments show accuracy improves as new data streams in, beating earlier surrogate variants. The team then runs the algorithm inside a full twin setup that models fatigue crack growth in an aircraft part. The run shows how the pieces of twin methods fit as one system in practice.
arxiv-2511-00466:
Ayan Kumar Nai and G K Samanta demonstrate a free-space quantum network that serves six users from a single source of entangled light. Quantum key distribution promises secure keys, but classic setups link only two parties at a time. Sharing entanglement among many users, called multiplexing, had been shown in fiber networks, while free-space versions stalled on active switching hardware.

Their design uses spatial multiplexing and stays fully passive, with no active switches in the path. Twelve channels form a fully connected network, and any pair of nodes shares record coincidence rates, yielding sifted key rates above four hundred kilobits per second in their report. The approach scales to more nodes and can join fiber links, sketching a practical route to city-scale quantum networks.
arxiv-2511-00566: Tara Macalister Brough, Marianne Johnson, Mark Kambites, and Carl-Fredrik Nyberg-Brodda prove a theorem about free inverse monoids, algebraic structures built from partial symmetries. Their word problem, deciding when two expressions name the same element, turns out to be co-context-free for every finite rank: the set of unequal pairs is a context-free language. The proof works through grammars, linking algebra with formal language theory.
arxiv-2511-00866:
D. S. Delion and A. Pencu systematize proton emission, the rare decay in which a nucleus ejects a proton, focusing on nuclei near the proton drip line. They cover both spontaneous emission and the beta delayed kind, organizing the data by Coulomb strength, reduced radius, and angular momentum.

Three ways of estimating the decay width of a resonant state are compared. One uses a continuity equation for outgoing states. Another uses phase shift analysis of scattering states. The third uses direct numerical integration in the complex plane. The methods agree where comparison is possible. The authors also show a universal decay law, linking the reduced width to penetrability and a fragmentation potential, holds for beta delayed emission too. It describes all measured cases within about a factor of three.
arxiv-2511-01066:
Stephan Oepen and a very large team present HPLT 3.0, an open collection of text data for training language and translation models in almost two hundred languages. At thirty trillion tokens, they describe it as likely the largest multilingual pretraining collection available to all.

The data come from web crawls, processed by a fully open pipeline that selects documents, extracts text, identifies languages, removes duplicates, and annotates register, quality, and personal information. Quality is probed by statistics, by hand inspection in twenty four languages, and by training models end to end. The release also adds test benchmarks for nine European languages and a family of fifty seven monolingual encoder decoder models, plus a large parallel corpus for translation.
arxiv-2511-01466:
Changyuan Zhao and colleagues defend semantic communication against physical layer attacks. Deep joint source channel coding sends meaning rather than bits. It beats standard separate coding. But pilot spoofing and subcarrier jamming can corrupt the shared channel knowledge it depends on, damaging the reconstructed content.

Their framework, SecDiff, plugs a diffusion model into the decoder. Pseudoinverse guided sampling keeps reconstruction fast, with guidance that adapts. Jamming is fought by masking the attacked subcarriers by power and treating recovery as an inpainting problem the diffusion model solves. Spoofing is treated as a blind inverse problem. An expectation minimization routine alternately refines the pilot signal and the channel estimate. Both the reconstruction loss and the channel operator guide it.
arxiv-2511-20166:
Schehr and Yılmaz measure how wildly focused light intensity fluctuates through messy media. Their 2025 paper studies wavefront shaping in complex, scattering materials. Shaping an incoming wave can focus it onto target points. The brightness gain is called the enhancement factor. Experiments need that gain reproducible, not random.

Experiments, simulations, and exact theory were combined here. Random matrix theory supplies the analytical backbone. Multi-point focusing distributions were derived in full. The classic Marčenko-Pastur law covers only many-channel limits. Their results predict mean enhancement for finite channels too. Fluctuations are captured when long-range correlations are absent. Weakly scattering media fit that calm regime well. Strong scattering broke the pattern dramatically. Giant fluctuations appeared in experiments and simulations alike. Long-range mesoscopic correlations cause those wild swings. Enhancement statistics thus double as a correlation probe. Biomedical imaging and optical trapping depend on such control.
arxiv-2511-20466:
Boulin and Haufs predict extreme rainfall by deliberately simplifying the problem. Their 2025 statistics paper estimates exceedance chances for environmental extremes. Floods depend on rain accumulated over space and time together. Multivariate extreme value theory is notoriously heavy machinery to use. The authors project such problems onto a single-variable version instead.

Their estimator minimizes the squared distance between data and model curves. It fits a Pareto law to peaks over a threshold. Limit theory for the estimator is derived in the paper. Simulations validated how the estimator behaves. Honest comparison found maximum likelihood slightly better in Monte Carlo tests. The method still shone in the EVA 2025 Data Challenge. Team Bochum's entry used weather ensemble data near Asheville. The grid covered five by five locations in North Carolina. Their submission won the overall preliminary challenge against ten teams. It also took top-three finishes in two of six categories.
arxiv-2511-20666:
Arief Anbiya tackles in 2025 an unstable wave equation, the two-dimensional 'bad' Boussinesq equation, a wave equation from water-wave theory. The nickname comes from its linearised form, which is ill-posed: at high frequencies, tiny changes in the starting state grow explosively, so naive computer solutions blow up. Anbiya asks which wave components can be kept, using Fourier analysis to split the wave into frequency modes.

The analysis yields a bound each kept mode must obey. Anbiya builds it into two solvers: the fourth-order Runge-Kutta method, and Strang operator splitting, which advances the equation in alternating half-steps. Keeping only modes inside the bound gave stable, accurate solutions, checked against an exact soliton wave. Adding even a few modes outside the bound made solutions blow up. Runge-Kutta edged out splitting by a small margin, and a final run showed boundary reflections behaving as expected.
arxiv-2511-20766:
Karen Ullrich and colleagues show in 2025 that AI agents which ace an app can collapse when the app changes its look. Benchmarks freeze one clone of an app, but real apps vary in design and content. Their OpenApps ecosystem ships six configurable apps, messenger, calendar, maps and others, and runs on a single CPU, so thousands of variants can be generated cheaply.

The team ran more than 10,000 independent evaluations across seven multimodal agents, including Claude, OpenAI, and Qwen-VL models. Within one fixed variant, reliability looked stable. Across variants, task success swung by more than 50 percentage points for many agents. Kimi-VL-3B's average success ranged from 63 percent down to just 4 percent depending on the app version. Failure styles shifted too: UI-TARS was five times more likely to hallucinate actions under some configurations than others. The authors argue app variation is a missing axis of reliability.
arxiv-2511-20866:
Alexey Fakhrutdinov and Oleg R. Musin revisit in 2025 the pancake theorem, a classic result in discrete geometry. For any finite set of points in the plane, two perpendicular lines split the set into four equal parts. The authors design an algorithm that finds the two lines in time proportional to the number of points.

That linear running time is provably the best possible, since every point has to be inspected anyway. The result sits beside the older ham-sandwich theorem, which bisects several point sets with one cut and also admits linear-time algorithms in the plane. The authors also treat generalisations, showing that orthogonal hyperplanes, their higher-dimensional analogues, can be found in polynomial time. They note the harder equipartition question behind it all, posed by Grünbaum in 1960: splitting one measure into equal parts with hyperplanes remains open in dimension four.
arxiv-2511-21266:
Lotta Meijerink and eight coauthors clarify a shortcut for judging new medical treatments in a 2025 methodology paper. Trials are the gold standard, but new radiotherapy techniques often enter clinics before trial results exist. The shortcut predicts each patient's outcome under the old standard care with a model built earlier, then compares those predictions with the outcomes actually observed under the new treatment.

Meijerink and her coauthors use the potential outcomes framework to state exactly when this comparison yields a valid average treatment effect. The approach, known in radiotherapy as model-based clinical evaluation, is a form of model-based standardization related to the g-formula. A practical case study in radiotherapy, the setting where the method gauges tools like proton therapy, shows how the conditions bite in practice. The authors close with practices that make such estimates more credible and transparent.
arxiv-2511-21366:
Dmitri Kovalenko builds in 2025 an autonomous robot system that tightens nuts, a manipulation task harder than pick-and-place because it is dominated by contact. Threaded fastening appears everywhere from heavy industry to home repair, yet the robot must seat the nut on the bolt and turn it without crushing anything. Kovalenko's system uses a serial arm with a parallel gripper, guided by a hierarchical planner built from motion primitives.

Its controller switches between position control, for moving through free space, and force control, for the delicate contact phases, as each primitive demands. Extensive simulations show the system tolerates wide variation in initial conditions, so the nut need not start in a perfect pose. Against the baseline controller, the proposed system tightened threaded screws 14 percent faster. It also applied 40 times less contact force to the parts, a margin that protects fragile pieces. The implementation is open-sourced.
arxiv-2511-21466:
William De Deyn, Michael Herty, and Giovanni Samaey train small neural networks by committee vote instead of by gradient, in a 2025 applied mathematics paper. Consensus-Based Optimization lets a swarm of candidate parameter sets drift toward their weighted consensus, a derivative-free training method with an elegant limit theory. When infinitely many particles interact, the swarm's motion lives on a space of distributions stacked on distributions, and its variance shrinks monotonically.

De Deyn and his coauthors couple that limit with the mean-field limit of the network itself, recasting the optimizer in optimal transport language. In experiments, plain consensus training matched Adam's final error on a smooth regression task. A hybrid, consensus plus Adam, proved more robust than Adam on MNIST digit classification and converged faster than consensus alone. For multi-task learning, their reformulation recycles particles across tasks, keeping accuracy high with minimal extra memory.
arxiv-2511-21566:
Ali Amirahmadi and five coauthors predict whether ring-shaped drug candidates can slip through cell membranes, in 2025. Cyclic peptides can reach targets inside cells that ordinary drugs cannot, but only if they cross the membrane, and public permeability data are scarce. Rather than a data-hungry deep network, the team built a chemically informed similarity measure and paired it with Gaussian processes, models that report honest uncertainty with each prediction.

Their monomer-aware decoupled alignment kernel compares peptides residue by residue, using chemical similarity for local matches while decoupling those matches from gap penalties. A variant adds a positional prior and tightens the error bars further. Across extensive experiments the simple kernels beat leading transformer models on every metric, most clearly under the harder split that separates chemical families. Mixing in a fingerprint-based model recovered top accuracy scores as well, showing sequence context and local substructures complement each other.
arxiv-2511-21966:
García Muñoz and colleagues explain a missing signal on warm Neptune-sized exoplanets, where hydrogen absorption is extreme on three planets. So the helium triplet line should also be strong, yet appears on only two, weakly.

The team identifies a chemical culprit: vibrationally excited hydrogen molecules, H2 in an energized state, destroy the helium ions that are the direct precursor of the absorbing helium state. At the temperatures of the atmospheric layers probed, this reaction runs notably fast. Their simulations show the process severely mutes the line on GJ 3470 b and wipes it out entirely on GJ 436 b, explaining the nondetection there in their models. The effect strengthens where the molecule-to-atom transition sits high, set by high-energy radiation received. Weak helium absorption, they warn, does not mean a planet lacks a primordial hydrogen-helium atmosphere.
arxiv-2511-22566:
da Costa-Luis and colleagues report PETRIC, the first organised challenge for PET image reconstruction. Positron emission tomography builds medical images from detected photon pairs. Turning raw data into pictures is an inverse problem whose iterative algorithms are slow, a growing problem as long-scanner designs produce far more data. The challenge gave participants open-source software, an objective function, gold-standard reference images, metrics, and curated phantom datasets from different scanners and tracers, split into training and evaluation sets.

Four teams entered nine algorithms in total, drawing on optimisation tools such as preconditioning and stochastic gradients, plus artificial intelligence. Approaches that looked similar on paper performed quite differently in practice, showing how much implementation matters for reconstruction speed. Because the automated framework is open source, researchers can reuse it to benchmark new or existing methods on new scanners, tracers, and phantoms, and variant editions are already launching.
arxiv-2511-22666:
Bonanno, Haridev, and Narain examine how nonlocal interactions reshape a scalar field theory's long-distance behaviour. Adding an inverse-derivative term makes the field interact across distances, a toy model for nonlocal gravity extensions and condensed matter with long-range forces. Using the functional renormalisation group, tracking the theory at progressively lower energies, they map the infrared fixed points where the flow settles, through approximation schemes of increasing sophistication.

In the simplest local potential approximation, nonlocality shifts fixed points and can induce symmetry breaking. The flow turns singular before the deep infrared when the nonlocal coupling is positive. With derivative corrections, the infrared-stable fixed point is the nonlocal Gaussian one, and critical exponents ignore the nonlocal parameter. Generalising the interaction's power, infrared behaviour is unchanged up to a threshold, then follows Sak's prediction up to the local limit, while the highest-derivative case matches known Lifshitz results.
arxiv-2511-23066:
Matsuoka and colleagues test whether a generative image model can safely clean up medical scans before other AI tools read them. Children's hand X-rays used to estimate bone age often carry non-anatomical markers. And the team asked the foundation model gpt-image-1 to erase those markers by inpainting, filling the spots with plausible-looking tissue, guided only by written prompts.

From 200 original radiographs in the RSNA Bone Age Challenge dataset they generated 600 inpainted versions, then ran established deep learning ensembles on both sets. The cleanup badly hurt performance: bone age error rose from 6.26 months to 30.11 months on average, and gender classification accuracy, measured by AUC, fell from 0.955 to 0.704 in the same runs, with pixel-level shifts showing the model had quietly altered real anatomy, a warning against using such edits in clinical pipelines without task-specific validation.
arxiv-2511-23166:
Amanzhol and Park argue that picking a vision transformer for an edge device by accuracy or operation counts alone is misleading. Real energy use depends on how an architecture interacts with specific hardware. Their two-stage pipeline first screens 13 models with the device-agnostic NetScore metric. It then measures actual time and power on target hardware and ranks the survivors with a Sustainable Accuracy Metric for deployment.

The hybrid LeViT_Conv_192 was benchmarked on ImageNet-1K and CIFAR-10 using a Jetson TX2 edge board and an RTX 3050 mobile GPU. It cut energy use by up to 53 percent on the TX2 against a standard transformer baseline. The distilled TinyViT-11M led on the mobile GPU. Theory alone would have misranked them, since one rival with fewer operations and parameters still ran about 10 percent slower on the TX2 in their head-to-head test in practice.
arxiv-2511-23366:
Syed and colleagues propose an agentic artificial intelligence framework that runs retail inventory replenishment autonomously. Watching stock levels, forecasting demand, choosing suppliers, negotiating orders, and scanning for trending high-margin products to add. Retailers handle thousands of varied products with volatile demand. And the authors note global losses above 1.8 trillion dollars a year from poor demand prediction and inventory mismatch, which fixed reorder rules handle badly in stores.

They build a prototype for a mid-scale mart and test it on three conventional and synthetic datasets against baseline heuristics. Reporting fewer stockouts, lower inventory holding costs, and better product-mix turnover than the baselines. The system combines demand forecasting, supplier-selection optimization, multi-agent negotiation, and continuous learning, and the authors discuss limits honestly. Pointing to scalability to very large catalogs and real-world field deployment as the next steps before wider adoption.
arxiv-2512-00166:
Ultralight dark matter, if it exists, would push gently on ordinary objects with tiny oscillating forces. Louis Hamaide, Hannah Banks, Peter Barker, and Andrew Geraci propose a new sensor to detect those forces in 2025. Their design uses optically levitated objects held in place by light.

Optically trapped sensors are known for high force sensitivity but have been little explored for dark matter searches. The proposed tabletop experiment, called MOLeQuTE, is tunable to different force patterns. A positive signal would be a major discovery, and even a null result narrows the space of allowed dark matter models. Tabletop experiments are far cheaper than collider or space missions, which adds to the appeal.
arxiv-2512-00366:
Forecasting data that moves through space and time, like traffic or weather, usually needs heavy models. Wenshuo Wang, Yaomin Shen, Yingjie Tan, and Yihao Chen present a knowledge distillation method for it in 2025. Distillation trains a small student model to copy a large teacher.

Their method, named in the title with semantic and spectral parts, preserves both meaning and frequency structure. Recent frequency-aware distillation already showed that keeping high-frequency details and low-frequency trends matters. A faithful lightweight student could bring strong spatiotemporal forecasts to devices and services that cannot run the full teacher model. Spectral preservation keeps both the sudden spikes and the slow drifts of the data.
arxiv-2512-00566:
Shape-free regression lets the data choose the curve, but that freedom creates bias that ruins naive confidence ranges. Giuseppe Cavaliere and co-authors improve inference for nonparametric regression in 2025. Such estimators are central to the economist's toolkit, including regression-discontinuity designs.

Large-sample bias throws off the true coverage of standard intervals, so reported confidence is often false confidence. Existing robust bias-corrected intervals help, yet the authors push the theory further. Credible ranges matter wherever policy is judged by estimated effects at a cutoff, from education funding to health eligibility rules. Regression discontinuity is where these intervals are most often used in policy work. Improved inference means narrower honest intervals, not just corrected ones. For folks who judge aid or school rules by a line in the sand, the gain is trust. The spread they quote is the spread the data can back up in full.
arxiv-2512-00666:
L Voigt wrote a 2025 cosmology paper on weak lensing, the slight bending of light from far galaxies by matter in between. Measuring that bend, called shear, helps map dark matter and test models of the universe. New Stage IV surveys will measure shear with great care and detail.

Voigt focuses on a sneaky source of error. Galaxies too faint to be detected still add their light and can bias the shear values. Using a machine learning method built to avoid noise bias, the author measures that effect for a survey like Euclid. The results help planners keep faint galaxies from skewing their maps.
arxiv-2512-01166:
Lily Stelling and five coauthors evaluate the safety frameworks of frontier AI companies in a 2025 paper. After the AI Seoul Summit in 2024, twelve AI companies published frontier safety frameworks. These documents outline how each firm plans to manage catastrophic risks from advanced AI systems.

New laws increasingly treat the frameworks as accountability mechanisms and fold them into reporting duties. The authors ask what the frameworks actually commit each company to do. Comparing promises across firms shows where commitments are concrete and where they are vague. That clarity helps regulators and the public judge whether self-governance is real.
arxiv-2512-02066:
Sorting breast tumor images into benign and malignant is a high-stakes classification task where better feature extraction could help. Ece Yurtseven's 2025 paper builds a hybrid quantum-classical convolutional network for the job, running several quantum circuits in parallel and fusing their features.

The network is tested on BreastMNIST, a standard benchmark of breast tumor images prepared for machine learning. Quantum machine learning promises richer ways to pull signal from high-dimensional medical data, though the hardware remains young. Testing parallel quantum circuits on a real diagnostic benchmark shows where the approach stands and what it might add to classical networks.
arxiv-2512-02366:
Quantum sensors measure temperature, fields, and time with precision bounded by a quantity called the quantum Fisher information. Rui Zhang and three co-authors derive in 2025 a universal upper bound on that quantity for probes in thermal equilibrium with their surroundings.

The work unifies the equilibrium and non-equilibrium frameworks of quantum metrology for many-body systems, under dynamic sensing schemes. A universal bound tells experimentalists the best any thermal probe could ever do, before they build it. Such limits discipline the search for quantum sensors that beat classical instruments in real, warm conditions.
arxiv-2512-02566:
Kun Yuan and nine co-authors train AI models that read medical figures and text together. Biomedical vision language models learn from web scale scientific papers. Most training, though, pairs a whole figure with its caption and drops the fine links between small regions and words.

Clinicians rely on exactly those fine links when they zoom into local structures. The team's zoom in pretraining keeps panel level detail, matching small figure regions with the text that describes them. Models trained this way could support diagnosis and research tools that point to the right spot, not just the right page. Fine links like these are what let a tool point to a spot, not just a page, when it counts.
arxiv-2512-02666:
Ashkan Abedi, Vittorio Giovannetti, and Dario De Santis simulate a classic model of electrons on a square lattice. The two dimensional Hubbard model captures how electrons hop and repel, a core puzzle in condensed matter. Tensor network methods must first flatten the square into a chain.

The team maps the lattice with a Hilbert curve, a space filling path that keeps nearby sites close. That compact mapping yields a smaller matrix product state than the usual snake path. Cheaper simulations let physicists probe larger systems in the search for new phases of matter. Flat maps that keep near sites near are a cheap win, and cheap wins stack up in long runs fast.
arxiv-2512-02766:
Yichao Huang, Jinglin Wang, and Xiaolin Zeng refine a lattice model used to probe disordered quantum systems. The model, known by its H 2|2 label, lives on a hierarchical lattice with a tree like structure. Earlier work by Disertori, Merkl, and Rolles gave an exact coarse graining for its random field.

The authors extend that result to the model's random Schrödinger operator form. They also build fine graining, the reverse move, and prove an exponential martingale property for it. Two way scaling tools help connect small scale randomness with large scale behavior in disordered media. Two way scale moves let a proof climb from the small to the large and back, a round trip few tools can make.
arxiv-2512-02966:
Isha Chaudhary and five co-authors build Lumos, a system for certifying language model systems against stated properties. As these systems spread into more applications, alignment with human ethics grows crucial. Recent works certify properties like fairness, correct answering, and safety, but each method is ad hoc.

Ad hoc certificates are hard to generalize from one property or model to the next. Lumos aims at certification as a reusable system, not a one off proof. Portable certification could give regulators and buyers a common way to check AI claims before deployment. One stamp for many traits beats ten stamps for ten traits. Shops must ship a tool that firms and boards can trust at scale in the field.
arxiv-2512-03166:
Robot soccer is a tough test for teams of AI agents. Aya Taourirte and Md Sohag Mia study learning methods for that test in this 2025 work. Agents must decide in real time, work as a team, and cope with rivals in a virtual field.
