Reinforcement learning is a promising route, but it strains under split tasks. Long-term plans and split-second moves need different handling, and many agents add complexity. The authors work on methods that scale better. Progress here could transfer to warehouse robots, rescue teams, and other real multi-agent jobs. Virtual soccer gives a safe, cheap arena to test team tactics before real robots play.
arxiv-2512-03366:
Judging an A/B test method is hard when true effects are unknown. Ryan Kessler, James McQueen, and Miikka Rokkanen offer a way around that in this 2025 work. They split each test's data into two parts to measure method performance.

Their framework shows sample-split estimators are generally biased for full-sample performance. Yet those estimators consistently estimate the sample-split analogues of it. Knowing that gap helps firms judge testing methods honestly. Better method checks lead to better product and policy decisions from experiments. Sample splits are cheap, since they reuse data that testing teams already collect.
arxiv-2512-03466:
Two agents with half the facts each must cooperate to win. Xavier Cadet, Edward Koh, and Peter Chin present AsymPuzl in this 2025 work. Most multi-agent setups use open-ended role-play, which is hard to evaluate in a controlled way.

AsymPuzl is a minimal two-agent puzzle with information asymmetry. Each agent sees a partial, complementary view of a symbolic puzzle. They must exchange messages to solve it together. The setup isolates communication skill, a clean target for testing language model teamwork. Minimal puzzles strip away role-play noise, leaving pure communication skill exposed.
arxiv-2512-03666:
Qi'ao Xu and colleagues build the first benchmark that asks AI to find objects by what they are for, in first-person video. An embodied agent hears a task, not a description, and must locate the tools it implies. Their 2025 ToG-Bench assembles one hundred egocentric clips from ScanNet scenes.

Over two thousand seven hundred instructions demand explicit finds and context-inferred ones alike. A single instruction may also map to several objects the task needs. A semi-automated pipeline drafted annotations with foundation models, then human reviewers refined them. Seven leading multimodal models were benchmarked with task-level metrics, exposing how far task-oriented grounding still has to go.
arxiv-2512-03766:
Step-free stations decide whether many riders can use a transit system at all, yet accessibility is rarely studied as a network property. Katherine Betz examines that question in a 2025 preprint on social and information networks. She builds models of two large systems, London's Underground and the subway network of New York City, keeping only stations with infrastructure such as elevators and step-free access.

In these models, stations are nodes and line connections are edges, letting network tools reveal how the accessible skeleton is shaped. Betz measures clustering, maps where accessible stations sit, and uses centrality scores to find the hubs of the accessible network. She then compares neighbourhood wealth and tourism popularity against the supply of accessible stations. Strong disparities appear in both cities. The work shows how network mathematics can guide fairer upgrades to modern transit infrastructure.
arxiv-2512-03966:
A biological neuron fires only when input crosses a threshold, then rests before firing again. Steven Louis and colleagues build an electronic version in a 2025 applied physics preprint. Their spiking neuron pairs a transistor with a magnetic tunnel junction, adding novel devices to standard chip technology.

Simulated in industry-standard circuit software, the combined unit reproduces the neuron's repertoire: firing past a threshold, resting through a refractory period, integrating synaptic inputs, and accepting inhibition. Those behaviours come from the junction's magnetisation dynamics, so no extra control circuitry is needed. Wired together, the units form an analogue multi-layer network. It updates its weights by a spike-timing rule derived from gradient descent. Training and inference both run in the analogue domain. The network propagated spikes and learned the classic XOR task, a proof of concept for on-chip learning with magnetic devices.
arxiv-2512-04066:
Open quantum systems leak energy into their surroundings, and the mathematics of that leakage can be brutal in infinite dimensions. Pablo Costa Rico, Paul Gondolf, and Tim Möbus study dissipative bosonic systems in a 2025 mathematical physics preprint. For a class of these evolutions, they prove a smoothing property: the dynamics instantly regularises starting states.

The setting is quantum Markov semigroups on bosonic Fock space, with Lindblad operators built as polynomials in the creation and annihilation operators. The team shows such dynamics immediately produce states with finite expectation in every power of the number operator. The headline application is the bosonic cat code, a design for error-resistant quantum computing hardware. There, they obtain trace-norm estimates for convergence speed, sharpening perturbative bounds at short and long times. A generation theorem for multi-mode systems supplies the domain care the arguments need.
arxiv-2512-04266:
Inflation, the early universe's burst of expansion, should have left a three-point fingerprint in how galaxies cluster. Anton Chudaykin, Mikhail M. Ivanov, and Oliver H. E. Philcox search for it in the first data release from the DESI survey, in a 2025 cosmology preprint. The fingerprint's shapes, local, equilateral, and orthogonal, point back to different inflationary physics.

Their analysis models the galaxy power spectrum and bispectrum within effective field theory at one-loop order, keeping scales where that description is trustworthy. The local amplitude comes out consistent with zero, with an uncertainty competitive with the cosmic microwave background's. Adding high-redshift DESI data and BOSS data, plus simulation-based priors on bias parameters, yields the strongest large-scale structure constraints on the non-local shapes. Combined, the local bound tightens by nearly a fifth over the microwave background alone: the strongest limit on multi-field inflation.
arxiv-2512-04366:
Fernando Zampieri explains a family of tests for watching clinical trials as they run, built on betting rather than fixed formulas. Standard trial monitoring leans on assumptions about data shape or on large-sample approximations. Those can mislead when a trial must be checked again and again. His 2025 arXiv paper presents the e-RT approach, which draws its validity from the random assignment of patients itself.

Each test works like a wager. Before each new outcome counts, the method bets on the next random assignment or event label, growing a pool of test wealth. If the treatment does nothing, that wealth cannot grow on average. This gives error control that holds at any stopping point, with no need to state an expected effect size first. Variants cover yes-no outcomes, event timing, and continuous measures. Trial teams can watch results live without spending their error budget.
arxiv-2512-05266:
Loris Di Cairano builds a quantum field theory, for the free-electron laser, that works out of equilibrium — the device turns a relativistic electron beam into coherent light. He starts from a microscopic description of the beam coupled to a single radiation mode. He applies the Keldysh formalism — the standard machinery for systems driven out of equilibrium — and integrates the electrons out of the problem entirely.

What remains is an effective action for the light mode alone. In it, dispersion, gain, and noise all flow from one object: the electronic self-energy built from the beam's current fluctuations. For a steady Gaussian beam he obtains formulas for frequency pulling, gain loss from energy spread, and the noise the field feels. At low frequency the theory shrinks to a Landau-Ginzburg form, and the laser threshold appears as a non-equilibrium phase transition, with the coherent amplitude as its order parameter.
arxiv-2512-05566:
I. Stergakis, Th. Diakonidis, and Ch. Moustakidis use machine learning to read the equation of state of dense matter out of the stars it builds. What matter does at densities beyond nuclear — inside neutron stars and hypothetical quark stars — is a central open problem of nuclear physics. The standard attack is theory checked against collisions and telescope data. The authors instead train machine and deep learning regressors on the mass-radius relations of compact objects, aiming to infer the underlying equation of state from the observable curve.

Their training ground is a library of physically consistent equations of state for neutron stars and quark stars, each satisfying established constraints. Learned models map between the stellar observables and the matter properties in both directions. The results show data-driven methods can refine insight into matter at supranuclear densities and complement classical modelling, relevant as multimessenger astronomy sharpens the observations.
arxiv-2512-05866:
Md Mahbub Hasan Akash, Aria Tasnim Mridula, Sheekar Banerjee, and Ishtiak Al Mamoon restore underwater photographs with a generative network whose eyes are transformers. Water washes colors toward green and blue, fades contrast, and adds haze. Convolutional networks see only small patches at a time, so they struggle to fix a color cast that spans the whole scene. The team's generator arranges Swin Transformer blocks inside a U-Net.

A PatchGAN discriminator judges the output patch by patch, pressing the generator to keep high frequency detail honest rather than smoothing it away. Trained and tested on the EUVP collection of paired underwater images, the system set state of the art scores on the standard quality measures. Visually, colors rebalanced, contrast returned, and haze thinned. An ablation study confirmed the transformer design beats convolutional stand-ins. Clearer pictures mean decisions made on what is actually there.
arxiv-2512-05966:
Waleed Qaisar lifts a classical construction into the world of categories. Isomonodromic deformation slides a flat connection along a path while keeping its monodromy, the data of how solutions wind around singularities, unchanged. The connections here may have logarithmic singularities along a chosen divisor. Qaisar upgrades the slide from an operation on individual connections to a functor between whole categories of them, one functor for each path, and the assignment itself respects how paths compose.

The machinery is the theory of Lie groupoids. Three applications follow. Isomonodromy becomes a map between moduli stacks. Higher information appears, as an action of the fundamental two-groupoid of the base on the connection categories. And the functors themselves are born from something more basic: Morita equivalences, from which the functors can be drawn by passing to representations. It records coherence data the old picture discards.
arxiv-2512-06066:
John Monnier and nineteen co-authors present two decades of watching two massive stars tear each other's winds apart. WR 112 is a binary pairing a carbon rich Wolf-Rayet star with an O star; their supersonic winds collide. Their winds collide in bright shocks, making a dust pinwheel. The team reports first X-ray detections beside twenty seven years of radio monitoring. Seen nearly edge on, the collision zone hides and shows with the twenty year orbit.

Single speed dust models cannot fit the data together. The data demand an accelerating post-shock flow, climbing from near rest to over a thousand kilometers per second within one orbit, which reproduces the spiral and the radio brightening's timing. WR 112 becomes a benchmark for future simulations.
arxiv-2512-06266:
Chen Yang and a large team introduce Nanbeige4-3B, a compact language model built to punch above its size. Small models are cheap to run, yet they usually trail large ones on hard tasks. The team trained their model on a vast set of high grade text, then fine tuned it on tens of millions of varied prompts.

Training came in stages. A warm up plan shifted the data mix step by step, and the fine tuning data was cleaned by a loop that rewrote drafts and rebuilt chains of thought. Later, a top reasoning model taught the small one through a dual preference method, and a final round of reward based training sharpened both reasoning and tone. On many tests the small model beat peers of its size and matched much larger ones. The team released the model weights for public use.
arxiv-2512-06466:
Le Thanh Dung Nguyen and Pawel Parys prove a theorem about logic queries run over strings. The queries are written in the formal languages known as MSO and first order logic. One case shows the idea. Suppose a query over binary strings returns few answers, at most a count tied to the zeros times the ones. Then each answer can be pinned down inside the same logic. Naming a zero position, a one position, and a small piece of fixed data is enough.

The proofs also cover the first order case, tied to aperiodic monoids in algebra. As a payoff, they settle a piece of folklore: that dimension can always be cut down for string to string readings given in first order logic. Theorems of this kind tell language designers exactly how much data a query answer really needs.
arxiv-2512-06666:
Urav Maniar asks whether two fast time series classifiers, teamed well, can rival a champion ensemble that takes weeks to train. Sorting time series into classes, from sensor traces to signals, trades accuracy against computing cost. The champion system is accurate but needed hundreds of hours on a standard benchmark, which bars it from large data. Maniar pairs Hydra, which races convolutional kernels against each other, with Quant, which reads quantile features over nested intervals.

Six ways of joining the pair were tested on ten large data sets. The best pairing nudged average accuracy above either method alone and won on most data sets. Yet prediction level blends captured only a small share of what an oracle join could give, while joining at the feature level beat the oracle by learning new boundaries. The lesson: the hard part is no longer making methods different, but learning how to combine them.
arxiv-2512-07166:
Siyuan Xu and co-authors study the forgotten second half of privacy protection for image-editing models: getting the real content back. Tools that swap private details in a photo for safe surrogates let people use multimodal editors without leaking themselves. But nobody had measured how well the protected content can later be restored, or whether the restored version keeps the edits. That recovery quality is what their work puts under the microscope.

They contribute SPPE, a data set spanning many privacy categories and user instructions, holding protected surrogates beside their edited versions so recovery can be scored directly. Framing recovery as guided generation driven by complementary signals from both versions, their unified method rebuilds the private content while preserving the editor's changes. Tests on SPPE and on a standard editing benchmark show the approach transfers across varied content and tasks.
arxiv-2512-07366:
Alexander Saccani and Paolo Tiso shrink the cost of simulating structures that bend so far their geometry changes the physics. Full finite element runs of such geometrically nonlinear systems are too slow when engineers must sweep many shapes. Their reduced-order framework builds small surrogate models from vibration modes and their modal derivatives. Reading the needed nonlinear pieces straight out of standard simulation outputs, without ever opening the solver's code.

A library of these small models is computed at sampled shapes, and every ingredient, stiffness. The quadratic and cubic coupling pieces, damping values, and the reduction basis itself, is interpolated across shapes with radial basis functions. A two-stage compression yields one global basis, with a reordering step that keeps the interpolation smooth.
arxiv-2512-07466:
A. Karakonstantakis and W. Kluźniak wrote this 2025 astrophysics paper on telling wormholes from black holes. A spinning wormhole might imitate a Kerr black hole in X-ray binaries and galactic centers. Sharper instruments could expose the impostor if a clear difference in accretion exists.

The authors compare how matter orbits and heats up around each object. Using a standard Lagrangian method, they derive the orbital traits of test particles. Thin disk theory then turns those orbits into a disk surface temperature. For circular orbits at the same radius, the two objects match exactly. Speed, energy, angular momentum, and frame-dragging precession are identical. One hard difference remains: a wormhole has no orbits smaller than its throat. Its disk is smaller in area than a black hole's disk. That smaller disk runs visibly cooler when the throat is wide enough. Temperature, they conclude, tests wide-throated wormholes.
arxiv-2512-07766:
Matteo Cipollina, Michail Karatarakis, and Freek Wiedijk wrote this 2025 paper on proving neural network behavior. Networks are everywhere, yet checking what they will do remains hard. The authors formalize two classic network families inside the Lean proof assistant.

Hopfield networks come first in their formal development. These recurrent networks store patterns as stable states they settle into. The team proves the networks converge to those states as claimed. They also prove Hebbian learning correct, the rule that writes patterns in. Boltzmann machines, the stochastic cousins, come second in the work. Their random updates should settle into one unique stationary distribution. Proving that ergodicity needs the Perron-Frobenius theorem about matrices. The authors formalize that theorem fresh along the way. Learning dynamics for the Boltzmann machine are formalized as well. Machine-checked proofs turn folklore about these networks into certainty. The work points toward verified machine learning as a practical craft.
arxiv-2512-07966:
Zhiyi Wu, Xuandong Sun, Songlei Wang, and eight co-authors wrote this 2025 quantum physics paper. Quantum computers must measure qubits mid-calculation to correct errors as they go. Feeding those results back fast enough has limited what experiments can attempt.

Their team built a superconducting processor around that loop. Global mid-circuit checks run with high quantum non-demolition fidelity. Feedback then fires with a decision lag of mere hundreds of nanoseconds. On this platform, two distinct phase changes appear in one adaptive circuit. Single quantum paths show a measurement-induced entanglement transition. The averaged channel shows an absorbing-state shift of its own. Key exponents at the second shift are measured head-on. They match the directed percolation class closely. The two transitions sit at different tuning values. Such circuits thus become a test bed for nonequilibrium quantum matter.
arxiv-2512-08566:
Yorgo Chamoun and Samuel Mimram work in category theory, a branch of math that studies structure in very general terms. They look at relational presheaves, which extend the usual notion by using relations instead of functions and by allowing looser maps. That extra freedom helps model objects with no boundary or with several boundaries at once.

The authors show that these presheaves form models of a cartesian theory, which gives them strong general properties. They then build realization functors that turn abstract presheaves into geometric objects in a suitable setting. A key use is in the study of concurrency, where the method links syntactic and geometric views. It also gives a syntactic form for the blowup operation on directed spaces.
arxiv-2512-08666:
Wang Wei Yu and Bruce Allen combine public data from five pulsar timing arrays to search for a faint background of gravitational waves. Pulsar timing arrays track the arrival times of pulses from many pulsars and look for a shared pattern. The combined set covers more than a hundred pulsars, about four times larger than any single array alone.

For pulsars seen by more than one array, the authors use a new direct method to merge models and data without forcing one best timing model. They estimate the strength and slope of a possible background spectrum. The results fit a nonzero background, but the evidence stays below the standard level for a firm claim. The pattern of correlations across pulsar pairs does match the expected curve for gravitational waves.
arxiv-2512-08766:
Vladimir Parfenyev studies the fastest route for a self propelled agent moving in a two dimensional fluid flow. The classic Zermelo navigation problem asks for the path with the least travel time between two points. Here the agent is carried by the flow, moves at a fixed own speed, and can steer its heading freely.

Flows range from steady rotation and a time dependent sink vortex to a periodic flow and to turbulence. Optimal control theory gives time minimizing paths, but those paths become unstable when the flow is chaotic. The author therefore tests reinforcement learning, comparing a value based method with an actor critic method. Both reach near optimal travel times in regular flows. In turbulent flows the gap grows larger, yet learning still succeeds. Agents trained on coarse grained turbulence also transfer to the full flow, a key point for real ocean and air use.
arxiv-2512-09066:
Simon Sedlacek and coauthors present ORCA, a model based method to judge the correctness of open ended answers from large audio language models. Reliable assessment is essential as audio benchmarks grow more complex and subjective, requiring free form responses rather than fixed choices. Human rating is costly, so a trustworthy automatic judge is needed.

The team builds a three stage annotation pipeline that joins human judgment, structured feedback, and human artificial intelligence correction. That yields thousands of annotations over question answer pairs from many audio models and three benchmarks, with strong inter rater agreement. Training with curriculum learning, their judge matches average human correctness ratings closely on seen benchmarks. It also generalizes well to unseen benchmarks, beating several large model judge baselines. Predicted variance from the judge tracks human disagreement strongly. That signal can flag problematic benchmark items where even humans cannot agree on a single correct answer.
arxiv-2512-09266:
Ryosuke Nagumo and Hironori Fujisawa study density ratio estimation, a statistical task that compares two probability distributions through the ratio of their densities. The task underlies methods for detecting shifts in data. Their focus is robustness: what happens when the data are heavily contaminated with outliers.

They examine weighted density ratio estimation, a method earlier work had shown to be doubly strongly robust in the long-run, asymptotic sense. Nagumo and Fujisawa prove the finite-sample version: even under heavy contamination, the weighted method stays sparse and consistent. Their analysis rests on assuming the weighted ratio is bounded, and on at least one of two conditions holding: contamination is limited, or outliers carry small weights. The paper gives the first non-asymptotic analysis of strong robustness under heavy contamination, a step toward guarantees that hold for real dataset sizes.
arxiv-2512-09866:
Hanyu Cheng, Supriya Pan, and Eleonora Di Valentino test whether today's cosmic data can pin down a dark energy model with four free parameters. Richer models are often dismissed as excessive, since constraining many parameters is hard. But surveys have improved fast, and the authors ask whether combined observations are now up to the task. Their model describes dark energy through its present equation of state, its early value, the time of transition between them, and the steepness of that transition.

They fit the model with cosmic microwave background data from Planck, baryon acoustic oscillation data from DESI, and three separate supernova compilations. The verdict is mixed. The transition time is not constrained by any dataset, the early value and steepness only weakly, while the present value is well measured throughout. For some data combinations the model is mildly preferred over simpler rivals, though not strongly.
arxiv-2512-09966:
Ishan Swamy and Deobrat Singh study a black hole tied to a cosmic string. Rotating black holes with strong magnetic fields launch jets through the Blandford-Znajek mechanism, which extracts spin energy. A cosmic string attached to the hole extracts rotational energy too, spinning the hole down further. The authors ask how that reduced spin changes the jet, and how the answer depends on the string's tension. 

They find the jet energy flux falls as the inverse square of the string tension, and its rate also varies with time through the tension. They then track the hole's total angular momentum under four effects: accretion, the jets, the string, and the Bardeen-Petterson effect from the disk. Spin down turns out possible for both small and large tensions, more likely for large ones. Jets may also align with the string. The authors suggest these effects could help detect cosmic strings.
arxiv-2512-10066:
Yongkai Chen, Samuel WK Wong, and SC Kou hunt for metamorphic proteins, shape shifters that fold into several distinct structures. AlphaFold2 predicts one structure per sequence brilliantly, but that one to one picture fits only single fold proteins. The authors repurpose AlphaFold2 itself: by sampling its sequence alignments, they coax it into generating an ensemble of conformations for one protein. Features describing the ensemble's shape and spread then feed a random forest classifier.

Trained on a curated benchmark of known cases, the classifier separated metamorphic from single fold proteins well in cross validation. The team then screened six hundred proteins sampled from the Protein Data Bank. Several candidates emerged, including a ribosomal protein whose shape change serves a second job in antimicrobial defense. The approach turns the field's flagship predictor into a discovery tool for the very proteins that break its core assumption.
arxiv-2512-10266:
Chia-Hsiu Hsu leads a team explaining why one celebrated topological material gives clashing experimental answers, and how to fix it. Zirconium pentatelluride is highly tunable and hosts rich quantum phenomena, making it a favorite platform for quantum technology. Yet labs keep reporting conflicting electronic and topological states. The culprit, the authors argue from first principles math, is defects. They study every intrinsic point defect in the crystal, one by one. Two dominate: zirconium atoms wedged into gaps act as donors, and missing tellurium atoms act as acceptors, and their competition sets the Fermi level.

Raising the tellurium ratio during growth suppresses the defects and, as tests confirm, steadies an ideal weak topological insulator state. The guidance is concrete enough to act on: control the ratio, control the defects, and the topological state becomes reliable.
arxiv-2512-10466:
Siarhei Finski extends geometric quantisation to big line bundles, a broader class of bundles over complex spaces where many classical results were proved only under stronger positivity. Quantisation links a bundle's geometry to the spaces of its holomorphic sections. And the bridge is a map from metrics on the bundle to norms on those section spaces.

He proves that this map is asymptotically an isometry, so the two sides agree ever more closely for high powers of the bundle. From that, submultiplicative norms on the section ring turn out to match sup-norms in the limit. As an application, any bounded submultiplicative filtration on the section ring produces a Mabuchi geodesic ray, a path in the space of metrics, and the ray's speed records the filtration's statistical invariants. The study runs to fifty-seven pages.
arxiv-2512-10666:
Marina Afonina, Anton Biryukov, and Sergei Popov ask whether lonely neutron stars that feed on interstellar gas could ever be seen. Most neutron stars are born in supernovae and race through the galaxy; a few slow down enough to start swallowing the thin medium around them. Earlier population studies gave rough counts, but with simpler pictures of the interstellar medium and of how the stars' spin and magnetism evolve.

Their synthesis model follows isolated neutron stars across the Milky Way's whole lifetime with the more detailed physics included. Everything hinges on the propeller stage, when a spinning magnetosphere flings incoming gas away. If that stage ends soon enough and accretion runs efficiently, the eROSITA survey could hold a few thousand such objects. If not, the number collapses. Wide low-mass binaries with neutron stars, recently found by Gaia, may settle the question.
arxiv-2512-10866:
Ruslan Gokhman reports a humbling result from the UrbanAI 2025 Challenge: for forecasting indoor temperature far ahead using nothing but the temperature's own past, simple linear models beat fashionable transformers. The setting is deliberately hard, a single series, no outside weather or occupancy signals. And a long horizon over which errors compound.

Six models were compared under standardised training, validation, and test splits: three linear designs, plain Linear, NLinear. And DLinear, against the Transformer, Informer, and Autoformer architectures. The linear family won consistently across all splits, and DLinear, which splits a series into trend and remainder before extrapolating each, took the best overall accuracy. The finding is a reminder that in constrained forecasting settings, a carefully designed linear baseline is not a straw man but often the model to beat.
arxiv-2512-10966:
Farica Zhuang and colleagues present a model for diagnosing Alzheimer's disease that combines several kinds of brain data. Standard methods often just stack features from scans together, which cannot weigh each source well for a given person or brain region. Their system, called MREF-AD, treats regions within each scan type as separate experts.

A gating network learns person-specific weights for those experts, using imaging and background data from a major Alzheimer's study cohort. The model matches strong classic and deep learning baselines on accuracy. More importantly, it shows which regions and which scan types drove a diagnosis, giving doctors an interpretable view of how structure and molecular signals work together.
arxiv-2512-11266:
Ashutosh Tripathi, Paul Wiita, and Krista Lynne Smith search for rhythmic flickering in blazars, galaxies whose jets point almost straight at Earth. They examined light curves from the TESS space telescope for blazars already catalogued in a long running hard X ray survey. Four sources showed candidate quasi periodic oscillations repeating over at least five cycles.

Two independent rhythm finding techniques agreed on the signals, and a time series model that fills gaps stochastically supported them. Correcting for how many frequencies and sources were examined lowered the confidence, leaving the strongest case at moderate significance. The periods correspond to cycles of roughly one to two days. Possible causes inside the relativistic jet include a kink instability in its plasma currents or precessing substructures and mini jets. The authors present the detections as probable rather than certain, a useful target list for follow up monitoring.
arxiv-2512-11666:
Graham L Giller solves a money placement puzzle for a cautious investor with a hard floor. His investor uses a budget threshold utility: gains count in a straight line way, but the plan must respect set position caps and a budget line. Returns are assumed fat tailed, with more extreme moves than a bell curve allows.

Giller finds an exact formula for the best single period placement. The answer has a strikingly simple shape. It reads as plain trading plus a clear risk cost term. That simple form makes the rule easy to explain and to code. It also shows how hard caps reshape trades even before risk views enter.
arxiv-2512-11766:
Xavier R Advincula, Christoph Schran, and Angelos Michaelides draw the line between water at a surface and water truly confined. Water acts oddly both near walls and in gaps under a nanometer wide, and the two regimes blur in most accounts. The team used learning based simulations with first principles accuracy.

They placed water at graphene walls with gaps from open to angstrom scale. When three or more water layers fit, the wall layer looked just like water at an open surface, in density, bonding, and tilt. Below that, the whole liquid reorganized: order grew, bonds rewired, and tilts changed. The three layer rule gives a clear guide for nanofluid device design.
arxiv-2512-11866:
Ibrahim Talha Ersoy, Andrés Fernando Cardozo Licha, and Karoline Wiesner tie three puzzles of neural network training into one story. The puzzles are sudden phase shifts during training, the many saddle points in the loss landscape, and mode connectivity, the fact that good solutions link by low loss paths.

The team proves that phase shifts in learning are governed by saddle points in the loss shape. They then give a fast probe that uses the size penalty knob to map the error landscape. On MNIST it finds paths joining top solutions with ease. Saddle points also mark the borders between solutions that encode different digit classes. The picture gives trained networks a layered, phase like order.
arxiv-2512-12066:
Erik Larsen shows that large language model safety refusals wobble from run to run. Standard safety tests ask once and treat the answer as the model character. Larsen tests four tuned models from three families on 876 harmful prompts, each run 20 ways across temperatures and random seeds.

Depending on the model, 18 to 28 percent of prompts flipped labels between refuse, partial, and comply. A Safety Stability Index falls as temperature rises, from 0.977 at zero to 0.942 at one. Borderline prompts wobble most. For Llama 3.1 8B, one shot grading matched the pooled truth only 92.5 percent of the time. The paper urges sample counts that grow with temperature.
arxiv-2512-12166:
Jane Hsieh, Emmie Regan, Jose Elizalde, and Haiyi Zhu study rideshare work in a 2025 paper. Riders get cheap, quick trips, but drivers carry most of the cost and risk alone. Rules and rider support for drivers stay weak, in part because riders rarely see the work behind a trip.

The team ran nine workshops with 19 drivers and 15 passengers, using game-like tasks during rides. Games showed riders what they did not know about driver costs and effort, and shifted how they saw their own power as buyers. Drivers shared what kinds of contact they welcome. The paper ends with design guidelines for safer, fairer ride apps.
arxiv-2512-12266:
Leonid Prokhorov and many co-authors report trapping highly charged xenon ions in a 2025 physics paper. Such ions are atoms stripped of many electrons, prized for precision tests. The team made them in a compact electron beam trap, picked the charge they wanted, slowed the ions, and sent them into a cold Paul trap.

Inside, laser cooled calcium ions form crystals that cool the xenon ions by contact. The xenon ions sit as dark voids in the glowing calcium crystal, in patterns the team can control. They checked charge states and lifetimes, and studied joint motion. The setup suits precise frequency work, searches for new physics, and quantum information.
arxiv-2512-12566:
Ling-Qi Huang and nine co-authors present a plane-convex microcavity for room temperature polaritons in a 2025 paper. Polaritons are hybrids of light and matter excitations, usually studied in cooled setups. Their open cavity uses one flat and one curved mirror, and its effective length is calibrated directly from the free spectral range, with piezo tuning at near normal incidence.

With a spin coated quasi-2D perovskite film, they saw clear anti-crossings in reflection, with vacuum Rabi splittings up to 71 meV in reflection and 87 in photoluminescence near 3 micrometers length. After linewidth correction, the coupling rate g scaled with length to the minus one half. Shortening the cavity is thus a reliable lever to strengthen coupling.
arxiv-2512-12766:
Yihan Guo and Lek-Heng Lim work out the distributions of vector sets from random matrix decompositions in a 2025 math paper. Random matrix ensembles are families of random matrices used across physics and statistics. Their eigenvectors, singular vectors, and related vector sets have distributions that the authors pin down exactly for the best known ensembles.

Eigenvectors of the Gaussian, Laguerre, and Jacobi ensembles follow the uniform distribution on the complete flag manifold. Singular vectors of Ginibre ensembles are uniform on a product of a flag manifold with a Stiefel manifold. Circular ensembles split by type: cosine-sine vectors land on products of flag manifolds with classical groups, while Autonne-Takagi vectors land on Lagrangian Grassmannians. Uniformity is the unifying theme.
arxiv-2512-13366:
Simonetta Abenda and co-authors connect the KP equation, a central equation of integrable systems, to the geometry of banana curves. These curves are built from rational pieces and arise as a degeneration of hyperelliptic curves. Their multi-soliton solutions of the KP equation form the paper's focus.

The authors relate the soliton family to the combinatorics of the curve's tropical theta divisor. Its Delaunay polytopes turn out to match uniform matroid polytopes, so the matroid and Grassmannian structures behind the solutions are encoded in the divisor. They define a Hirota variety for the graph and give an explicit parametrization of its tau functions as multi-solitons.
arxiv-2512-13766:
Michiel Min and a large team of contributing authors set out the science case for directly imaging cool gas giant planets with the Habitable Worlds Observatory. Cool giants like Jupiter and Saturn are poorly characterized beyond our solar system. The planned observatory would image and take spectra of such planets below 400 K.

Using reflected light spectroscopy and polarimetry, HWO could measure molecular composition, clouds and haze, and temperature structure. Targets span varied sizes and orbits around solar-type and M-dwarf stars. That would bridge the gap between hot exoplanets and solar system giants, and test ideas on planet formation and cloud physics. The authors give observing requirements and survey strategies for that program.
arxiv-2512-14066:
Saiyang Zhang, Boyuan Liu, Volker Bromm, and Florian Kühnel test primordial black holes as seeds for the extreme galaxies JWST has found. One such system, Abell 2744-QSO1 at redshift near 7, is a compact, metal-poor galaxy dominated by its black hole. Its extreme mass ratio and low metallicity challenge standard seeding models.

Their high-resolution simulations plant a primordial black hole seed of 50 million solar masses, with fully coupled accretion, feedback, and early star formation. Strong thermal feedback delays star formation to redshift below 10, giving short, bursty episodes. Outflows expel enriched gas while pristine inflows replenish it, yielding low metallicities and extreme mass ratios in agreement with JWST data. Accretion runs at about 1 to 10% of the Eddington rate.
arxiv-2512-14366:
Julian McGinnis and seven coauthors challenge a common belief about implicit neural representations in a 2025 paper. Such models store a signal, like an image, inside a neural network. Plain multilayer perceptrons were thought unable to represent high frequency content, pushing work toward special embeddings and activations.

The authors argue the real problem is stable rank degradation during training, not the architecture itself. Regulating network rank during training greatly improves fidelity, even for simple ReLU networks. Optimizers like Muon, which give high rank, near orthogonal updates, help across architectures. Gains reach up to plus 9 dB PSNR over the same architecture. Tests cover natural and medical images and novel view synthesis.
arxiv-2512-14866:
Christian Hornhuber and nine coauthors describe a custom radio transmitter built to help catch the most energetic neutrinos in nature. Such neutrinos are hunted with radio antennas buried in polar ice, which listen for the pulse made when a neutrino hits the ice. To read those signals well, the antennas must be calibrated with a known source.

Their device pairs a battery powered kilovolt pulser with an antenna named SPUNK that can stand pressures of 200 atmospheres. The team lowered it into a borehole at the South Pole to a depth of 1740 meters. It sent clear signals picked up 5 kilometers away, with a strong signal to noise ratio. That reach shows the tool can map antenna response across the full range of angles a real neutrino could take.
arxiv-2512-15166:
Kazuyuki Yoshida develops a unified framework for sequences of quantum measurements, where the order of questions changes the answers. The study treats composite instruments in serial and parallel arrangements. It proves a tight bound on bipartite order effects, with the exact equality cases pinned down on a classic two subspace block.

Four results anchor the work. Doeblin type minorization is upgraded to composite instruments, with a product lower bound that yields data driven exponential mixing rates. A diamond norm commutator bound measures how rearrangements shift observable outcomes. A monitored Lindblad limit links discrete look and return loops to continuous time GKLS dynamics. Finite sample certificates, built from exact binomial intervals, turn the constants into numbers users can estimate from data. A small qubit toy model and scripts make the results fully reproducible.
arxiv-2512-15266:
Fan Zhang and four coauthors replace a cosmological bottleneck with a neural network that answers in milliseconds. Big Bang nucleosynthesis predicts the primordial amounts of light elements, a sharp probe of the early universe. Full calculations run a complex nuclear network and have grown too slow for large inference campaigns.

Their emulator, BBNet, trains on outputs from two public codes, PArthENoPE and AlterBBN, extended to cover dark radiation and a stiff equation of state. A residual multi head network learns the convoluted physics. BBNet then predicts helium-4 and deuterium abundances with negligible error, up to ten thousand times faster than first principles solvers, and stays unbiased over wide parameter ranges. The authors argue it can retire the simplified prescriptions that trade accuracy for speed, serving precision cosmology and new physics searches.
arxiv-2512-15566:
Lewis Cole and Ben Hoare construct two dimensional field theories with holomorphic integrability from a four dimensional theory in a 2025 paper. Integrable theories can be solved exactly, and many higher dimensional examples show partial holomorphic features. The authors use defect setups inside 4d holomorphic BF theory as the starting point.

In a simple example they build the 2d theory explicitly and carry out a first classical analysis. Using its symmetries, they write down an infinite family of solutions to the equations of motion. They then explain how 2d holomorphic integrability sits between standard integrability in one and two dimensions. Closing remarks cover higher dimensional prospects and quantization.
arxiv-2512-15666:
Gongjun Choi and Tony Gherghetta study a QCD axion arising in a five dimensional warped grand unified theory in a 2025 paper. The axion is a candidate particle tied to a long standing puzzle about the strong force. Here it comes from the fifth component of a bulk gauge field in a warped orbifold setup.

In flat extra dimensions, gauge couplings run too fast above the Kaluza Klein scale, forcing a large axion decay constant. Warped geometry slows that running to a logarithm, allowing smaller values. Bulk contributions still set a lower bound. The familiar axion window, from ten to the ninth to ten to the twelfth giga electron volts, fits naturally if the curvature sits near the Planck scale.
arxiv-2512-15766:
Yijie Zhi and co authors present LOOPRAG, a retrieval augmented framework that guides language models in loop transformation optimization, in a 2025 paper, dated December 12. Loop transformations reorder code loops to gain speed or parallelism without changing meaning. Picking the best mix is hard, and language models alone often produce errors or weak optimizations.

LOOPRAG retrieves legal example codes chosen by a loop aware algorithm that balances similarity and diversity. A feedback loop then feeds compilation, testing, and timing results back to the model, with mutation and differential testing to check equivalence. On PolyBench, TSVC, and LORE suites, speedups over base compilers pass 11, 14, and 9 times on the three suites.
arxiv-2512-15866:
Renato M Fonseca and two co-authors put this physics paper on arXiv in 2025. It deals with effective field theories, which are tools that describe particle physics at low energies without tracking every detail. The team works out how one class of building blocks in these theories, the fermionic operators, changes as the energy scale shifts.

The authors supply the beta functions for these operators up to mass dimension six. Beta functions are the formulas that tell how strongly each term runs with energy. With an earlier companion paper, the results let anyone renormalize any effective theory at one loop using only a group theory calculation. That completes a general recipe researchers can reuse across many models.
arxiv-2512-16066:
Syed Salauddin Mohammad Tariq and three co-authors study slow software starts in a 2025 arXiv paper. Serverless computing lets code run on demand, but the first run after idle time is slow, a problem called cold start. Rather than treating fixes as a black box, the team treats cold starts as a design flaw developers can see and fix.

From 81 settled issue reports in open-source serverless projects, they built taxonomies of bad design patterns, fixes, and diagnostic hurdles. They then created SCABENCH, a shared benchmark, and INITSCOPE, a tool linking loaded code with executed code. On the benchmark, INITSCOPE located problems up to 40 percent more accurately and cut diagnostic effort by 64 percent. A developer study showed faster, more accurate diagnosis with the tool.
arxiv-2512-16366:
Omar Namnakani and four co-authors improve eye-typing in work posted to arXiv in 2025. Dwell input lets users select targets by holding their gaze, useful on phones when hands are busy. Fixed target sizes fail in mobile life because posture changes alter viewing distance, which changes how big targets look.

Their interface, GAUI, resizes gaze targets on the fly to suit the current viewing distance. In a two-phase study with 24 participants, GAUI beat a large static interface on task time and made fewer errors than a small static one. Participants rated it the most preferred option overall and reflected on using it in six postures. The authors distill design guidelines for context-aware adaptive interfaces for handheld dwell input.
arxiv-2512-16466:
Pietro Baratella and Joan Elias Miro revisit a classic formalism in a paper released on arXiv in 2025. Dashen, Ma, and Bernstein showed long ago that a system's thermal free energy can be written through its scattering matrix, the S-matrix, rather than by summing states directly. The trick works beautifully at low orders of perturbation theory.

At higher orders, trouble appears: the free energy develops infrared divergences, infinities from very soft particles. In ordinary treatments a screening scale, the Debye mass, cures them. But the S-matrix formula is built from vacuum scattering, so where would a thermal mass come from? The authors answer that question, showing how the thermal mass emerges inside the formalism. Their resolution clears the way for higher-order thermal calculations in quantum chromodynamics and other relativistic field theories.
arxiv-2512-16666:
William T. Emond, Christian Käding, and Peter Millington give a concrete case of a known flaw. The flaw sits in quantum field theory on curved spacetime. States on one time slice cannot always be linked to states on another slice. No proper unitary map may exist for the link.

Working with a free scalar field in de Sitter space, they quantize the field in the standard way. De Sitter space is the expanding model used for the early universe. They then show plainly that the vacuum on one slice is unitarily apart from the vacuum on any other slice. The gap holds even for tiny time steps. It holds once both the background change and the field dynamics are counted, not just in far limits.
arxiv-2512-17566:
Mathilde Gajda Faanes and coauthors train a single model that outlines bright regions on FLAIR brain scans across many tumor types and scan times. FLAIR images guide diagnosis, treatment planning, and follow up for brain tumors, and the bright volume often measures the tumor itself or the swelling around it.

The team trained an Attention U Net on about 5,000 FLAIR images from several centers and checked it against models trained on one dataset each. Its Dice scores reach 88.65 percent for meningiomas before surgery and 90.92 percent for gliomas in the BraTS benchmark before surgery, though scores drop after surgery, to 61.27 percent for lower grade gliomas. One general model thus matches the specialists closely enough for clinic use, and it ships inside Raidionics, an open source tool for tumor analysis.
arxiv-2512-17766:
Zhiwei Gao sharpens a statistical trick for simulating events so rare that plain simulation almost never sees them. A diffusing particle, say a stock price or a molecule, may take a freak path once in a million runs. Importance sampling steers the simulation toward those freak paths and corrects the bookkeeping afterward, but a bad steering wastes every run.

Gao derives the ideal steering from large-deviation theory, recast as an optimal control problem with its Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation. A spectral formula approximates that steering, and the cross-entropy method fits its settings by least squares. The proof shows the estimator is log-efficient, the gold standard for rare-event work. A numerical example confirms the steered sampler finds the rare event with far fewer runs.
arxiv-2512-18066:
Annie S. Booth strengthens deep Gaussian process models, a layered stand in used when a simulation is too costly to run often. Such stand ins warp their input space until patterns look smooth, then fit the warped data. Slope data, which tells how fast an output changes, can sharpen a fit a lot, but slopes had not been worked into the deep form.

Booth's framework folds slopes in for both fitting and forecasting, with full accounting of doubt. On wavy test surfaces and on real quantum chemistry runs for molecule energy and forces, the slope fed deep models beat rivals on both counts. The code ships in an open R package, with a speed option for big data.
arxiv-2512-18166:
Jayani P. Gamage and coauthors introduce quollr, an R package for judging the 2D maps that nonlinear dimension reduction methods draw from high dimensional data. Different methods and settings can produce wildly different maps of the same data, and users have had little way to tell which map is faithful.

quollr builds a model from a 2D layout and lifts it back into the high dimensional space as a wireframe, so distortion becomes visible. Analysts can then see which method and which settings keep the true structure and which ones tear or fold it. The package's built in scurve data shows how the method works. Single cell RNA sequencing data from mouse limb muscle shows it in real use.
arxiv-2512-18266:
Lizhi Ma leads an eight author team cutting cloud bills on the Databricks data platform. Big data jobs there are costly, and fixed machine settings waste money when loads swing. LeJOT instead forecasts how long each job will run, then solves for the cheapest machine mix that still meets its deadline.

The system plans ahead rather than reacting after the fact, and reshuffles resources in near real time. On real Databricks workloads it cut cloud costs by an average of 20 percent, within a scheduling window of minutes. Static settings, the usual practice, could not match that pace. The design suits the lakehouse style of data work now common in large firms.
arxiv-2512-18566:
Ruiqi Chen and three colleagues at Washington University in St. Louis tackle a comparison problem in neuroscience modeling. Recurrent neural networks trained on brain data can learn similar mechanisms while using completely different internal coordinates. That makes their dynamics hard to compare directly. Their framework, DFORM, posted to arXiv in December 2025 and published in Neural Computation, learns a smooth change of coordinates between two systems.

Once aligned, the systems' paths can be checked for topological equivalence: the same mechanism in different clothing. Tests on textbook systems and trained networks confirm DFORM recovers known transformations. It also scores similarity between genuinely different systems. As a byproduct, it locates hidden motifs like invariant sets and saddle cycles. On networks trained on human fMRI data, it finds limit cycles that match earlier numerical work.
arxiv-2512-18766:
Guohui Zhang and five co-authors bring reinforcement learning to masked image generators, models that build pictures by unmasking patches step by step. Tuning such models with RL is awkward: every step's probability matters, so full trajectories are costly, yet optimizing random steps works poorly. Their framework, MaskFocus, posted to arXiv in December 2025, grades each step by how much it matters.

They score a step's information gain by comparing its intermediate image with the final one, then concentrate policy updates on the most critical steps. An entropy-based routing scheme also steers sampling toward mask patterns worth exploring on low-entropy samples. Across several text-to-image benchmarks, MaskFocus validates the approach. The lesson for generative modeling is simple: spend the training budget where the picture is actually decided.
arxiv-2512-18866:
Yong-Kang Huang and four co-authors sharpen predictions for how B mesons decay into pions, a process that helps measure the CKM matrix governing quark mixing. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, pushes light-cone sum rule calculations of the B-to-pi form factors to next-to-next-to-leading order in the large-recoil region.

The new correction term adds about 6.1 percent over the tree-level result. Merging their large-recoil predictions with lattice QCD results at small recoil, they fit the form factors across the whole kinematic range. From measured decay rates they then extract the CKM element |V_ub| as 3.73(14) times ten to the minus three. They also compute branching ratios, the lepton-flavor ratio R_pi, and several asymmetries for muon and tau decay channels, quantities experiments can test.
arxiv-2512-19066:
K. S. Kavya, T. Vinutha, B. Revathi, and Kazuharu Bamba test a modified theory of gravity against fresh sky data. The theory is exponential teleparallel gravity, which rebuilds cosmic expansion from torsion rather than curvature. They reconstruct the expansion history the theory predicts.

The check uses Hubble measurements, DESI baryon acoustic oscillation data, gravitational-wave standard sirens, and two supernova sets. Standard model-comparison scores judge how well the theory fits. The authors also check the theory's stability and how matter clumps grow. On all these grounds, they find the model stays consistent with current observations.
arxiv-2512-19166:
Luca Reggiani and Arnaldo Spalvieri spend signal energy wisely when tracking a moving target by arrival times. Fixed anchors at known spots listen for, or send, signals of known symbols. Longer or louder signals locate better but drain more power, and anchors may differ in both.

The goal is the least total energy that still meets a set accuracy bound, given by the posterior Cramér-Rao bound. Their main advance is a closed-form formula for how that bound shifts when total energy changes at each tracking step. Two algorithms put the formula to work, covering the case where signal amplitude is held fixed.
arxiv-2512-19266:
M. G. van der Schans, W. P. M. de Kleijne, M. A. Brozius, and B. Koopmans switch single magnetic skyrmions with single flashes of light, and no magnetic field at all. Skyrmions are tiny, stable swirls of magnetization that could carry data in future memory. Earlier light work created random crowds of them, not chosen individuals.

Femtosecond laser pulses now write or erase one bubble at a time, as small as one hundred seventy-five nanometers across, with fixed handedness. The team engineered cobalt-gadolinium multilayers to tame the contest between random and controlled creation. On-demand control of single skyrmions opens the door to studying richer textures and building skyrmion devices.
arxiv-2512-19366:
Simon Ståhlberg, Blai Bonet, and Hector Geffner ask when policy gradient learning can produce policies that truly generalize. Deep reinforcement learning wins many games yet often fails on new instances of the same domain. Classical planning, by contrast, has learned provably correct general policies by combinatorial means, at the cost of flexibility.

The authors model a policy as a classifier over state transitions, since ground actions change from instance to instance. Graph neural networks built for relational structure carry the value and policy functions. Lessons from both traditions shape the setup. The goal is to state the conditions under which gradient methods can match the systematic reach of combinatorial learners.
arxiv-2512-19466:
Walter Quattrociocchi, Valerio Capraro, and Matjaž Perc argue that language models and humans know things in deeply unlike ways. Surface agreement between their answers hides a structural mismatch in how judgments get made. The authors trace the path from symbolic AI and filtering systems to today's generative transformers to make the gap precise.

Seven fault lines are mapped: grounding, parsing, experience, motivation, causal reasoning, self-monitoring, and value. Models, on their account, complete patterns by walking a vast graph of language transitions, rather than forming beliefs. They name the result Epistemia, where fluent plausibility stands in for real evaluation. Consequences for testing, governance, and literacy follow.
arxiv-2512-19566:
Bartosz Bieganowski, Norihisa Ikoma, and Jarosław Mederski prove that the nonlinear Born-Infeld equation admits ground state solutions, its lowest-energy nontrivial states. The equation, a relativistic cousin of the minimal surface equation, resists standard methods because its gradient term saturates. Older proofs leaned on approximations or assumed symmetry, and could miss the true ground level.

The team builds a direct variational attack: minimization over a Pohožaev manifold, joined with profile decomposition to recover compactness. Both zero-mass and positive-mass cases are covered. A fresh proof of the matching Sobolev-type inequality comes with them, including the sharp constant. Nonradial solutions appear from dimension four on.
arxiv-2512-19866:
Samuel Jacob Chacko leads a six-author team building an advising early-warning system for computer science students. Departments teach hundreds of students per counselor, well beyond recommended ratios, so struggling students surface late. CS-Guide instead collects weekly self-reported grades and reflective journal entries, then uses large language models to read both the numbers and the words.

From those structured and unstructured signals the system extracts features and triggers tailored interventions, from academic support to health and wellness referrals. Evaluated on a four-year longitudinal dataset of roughly twenty thousand entries, it reached up to 97 percent F1 in recommending interventions for first-year students. The authors position CS-Guide as a way to give every student frequent, consistent, domain-specific monitoring feedback that human advising cannot scale to alone.
arxiv-2512-20066:
Arijit Paul studies the fine distribution of zeros of a family of L-functions, the Γ1(q) family, under the assumption of the generalized Riemann hypothesis. One-level density calculations compare those zeros against predictions from random matrix theory, and the reachable range depends on how far the test function's Fourier transform support can be pushed. Paul extends that support further than before for this family.

With the wider support, the Katz-Sarnak prediction for this unitary family is verified. The headline application concerns central values: at least 62.5 percent of forms in the family do not vanish at the central point, the highest such proportion known for any unitary-group family, still assuming the generalized Riemann hypothesis. Paul notes the L-functions' structural properties mattered more to the extension than the symmetry group itself.
arxiv-2512-20266:
Z Q Qu, R Y Zhou, H Su, and Y Liang report a new scattering source low in the Sun's corona. During the total solar eclipse of April 8, 2024, observed from Oden, Arkansas, their spectrograph recorded Fraunhofer lines below one solar radius above the limb. Maps at sample lines show light scattered by tenuous, cool neutral atoms and a smaller number of singly ionized ions.

The scattering pattern differs sharply from the familiar dust-driven F-corona seen farther out, so the authors name it the inner F-corona. Its existence means the corona contains a non-negligible population of neutral atoms alongside electrons and ions. They argue that collisions between outflowing neutrals and ions in coronal loops could make anomalous resistance the leading coronal heating mechanism.
arxiv-2512-20466:
Samuel Nyckees, Pratyay Ghosh, and Frédéric Mila chart the ground state of a Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the maple-leaf lattice. This lattice, a decorated cousin of the triangular grid, hosts competing interactions. The team uses infinite projected entangled pair states, a tensor-network method, with a corner transfer scheme respecting the lattice's threefold symmetry.

Varying the dimer coupling produces just two phases. One is magnetically ordered, with moments arranged in a canted pattern of one hundred twenty degrees. The other is an exact product of dimer singlets with no order at all. The transition between them is first order. Inside the ordered phase, quantum effects shrink the moments and shift the canting angle away from classic predictions almost everywhere.
arxiv-2512-20566:
Caio Peixoto, Daniel Csillag, Bernardo F P da Costa, and Yuri F Saporito optimize functions of variables without limit without ever computing a full gradient. Such tuning is usually tamed by using something finite as a stand-in, like a neural network. Their method stays functional, asking only for slopes along chosen directions.

The approach needs a pre-basis, a linearly independent set whose span is dense, which is far easier to obtain than tidy bases or kernels that may not exist. Those slopes come from automatic differentiation in practice. Guarantees of settling come along, which stand-in approaches rarely offer. As a showcase, the method solves partial differential equations in the style of physics-informed neural networks, now with provable convergence attached.
arxiv-2512-20766:
Rose Ranson and co-authors build a watt-class ultraviolet laser for atomic physics from a modest seed. Their wavelength, three hundred ninety-nine nanometres, serves ytterbium experiments. The system injection-locks a powerful multimode diode laser to five milliwatts from a single-mode external-cavity diode laser, and the big diode obediently inherits the seed's agility and narrow linewidth.

Up to one watt of output emerges, with well over half the power in the locked fraction and only kilohertz-level broadening. Active stabilization keeps the lock alive for more than a day. Spectroscopy on an ytterbium atomic beam verifies the system does real atomic physics, not just bench tricks. High-power, frequency-agile ultraviolet light is a recurring bottleneck in cold-atom laboratories, and diode-based watt-class sources are prized.
arxiv-2512-21766:
Jing Gao, Linfeng Zhang, Junchi Yan, and a large team present UniLabOS, an operating system for self-driving labs. Self-driving labs promise faster discovery by pairing learning algorithms with robotic experiments. In practice, adoption stalls on fragmented software: planning tools do not talk cleanly to the instruments that pipette, heat, and measure.

UniLabOS unifies the lab through typed, stateful building blocks. Every device and material is modeled under an action and resource scheme, and the lab's structure is represented twice, as logical ownership and as physical connectivity. A transaction protocol keeps the digital record reconciled with material motion, so the software's picture of the lab cannot drift from reality. The system runs on an edge-cloud architecture, allowing protocols to move across rearranged lab layouts. Human oversight is built in as governance. The team demonstrates UniLabOS in four real settings, from liquid handling to a distributed electrolyte foundry.
arxiv-2512-21866:
Yiming Qian, David Hardoon, and their co-authors let banks fight fraud together without pooling their customers' raw transactions. Their framework distills a trained random forest into a compact synthetic dataset that institutions can share. The forest's decision rules become transparent rectangular regions in feature space, and synthetic transactions are sampled uniformly inside each region.

The distilled data shrink volume by eighty-five to ninety-three percent while keeping detection precision and F1 scores competitive, with only a modest drop in area under the curve. Sharing the synthetic sets across three institution-like clusters of the IEEE-CIS fraud dataset improved precision, recall, and detection quality for everyone. Privacy held up under testing: membership-inference attacks performed at chance level, suggesting the synthetic records do not memorize real ones. Each flagged case carries a human-readable rationale and an uncertainty estimate from tree disagreement.
arxiv-2512-22366:
Aziz El Ghazouani and three co-authors deliver a verdict on the conformable derivative: it is not a fractional derivative at all. The operator has been marketed in many papers as a new fractional calculus tool. The authors show it is classic differentiation in disguise. It equals usual calculus after a nonlinear change of the time variable. That makes it useful for power-law time scaling, but it carries no genuine fractional memory effects.

Problems posed with the conformable derivative can be transformed into classic ones, solved, and transformed back, which exposes the absence of nonlocal behavior. Numerical simulations compare conformable, classic, and truly fractional Caputo models side by side. The authors also discuss why the misconception persists, urging classic or established fractional tools for memory-dependent phenomena.
arxiv-2512-22566:
Raahul Singh and Ashutosh Pandey present Starkindler, a training objective for working out photometric redshifts, the distances to galaxies inferred from their brightness in a few color bands. Such estimates are critical for astronomy, but machine learning methods often ignore the errors baked into the data itself, the aleatoric uncertainty. Starkindler builds those data errors directly into what the model is trained to hit.

The team trained a simple CNN on Sloan Digital Sky Survey data and compared it with the survey's own redshift estimates. Scores and calibration improved, and the predicted outlier rate fell. A knockout study confirmed the reason: removing data errors from the goal made performance much worse. The authors also argue their uncertainty estimates are more readable than purely epistemic ones.
arxiv-2512-22666:
Mert Ikinci and eight co-authors present INTERACT-CMIL, a deep learning system for grading precancerous pigmented lesions of the conjunctiva, the eye's clear surface tissue. Grading these melanocytic lesions guides treatment and melanoma prediction, but the cues are subtle and the diagnostic criteria interlock. The system predicts five grading axes at once, following two World Health Organization schemes plus horizontal spread, vertical spread, and cytologic atypia.

Shared feature learning with combinatorial partial supervision lets the model train despite incomplete labels, and an inter-dependence loss forces the five predictions to stay consistent with each other. The dataset holds 486 expert-annotated biopsy patches from three university hospitals. The system beat convolutional and foundation-model baselines, with the largest relative gains on the WHO4 axis and on vertical spread.
arxiv-2512-23066:
Houcine Cherief and co-authors built GLiSE, a tool for harvesting grey literature in software engineering research. Blog posts, Q&A threads, and project pages record real practice and decisions that journals rarely capture, but gathering them reproducibly is painful because sources, formats, and interfaces all differ. GLiSE starts from a plain research topic prompt and does the legwork automatically.

The tool expands the prompt into platform-specific queries, collects results from GitHub, Stack Overflow, and Google Search, then filters and ranks them with embedding-based semantic classifiers judging relevance to the original intent. Every setting is configuration-based and every query is visible, which keeps searches reproducible. Alongside the tool, the authors release a curated dataset of grey-literature results labeled by semantic relevance, and they report an empirical usability study. The package targets researchers who synthesize practitioner knowledge at scale.
arxiv-2512-23466:
Kai-Heng Xiao and ten co-authors address a speed limit in topological pumping, a method for moving energy or information through a material in a protected way. Pumping is usually run very slowly, because the standard adiabatic rule demands gentle changes at every moment. The team replaces that moment-by-moment rule with a global criterion that bounds the overall error instead.

Working with photonic waveguide arrays written by femtosecond lasers, they add a second rule that smooths out unevenness along the device. The accelerated pumping reached fidelity above ninety-five percent while using a device five times shorter than standard designs, and it stayed robust across a wide range of wavelengths. The result offers a general design rule for fast, compact adiabatic devices.
arxiv-2512-23566:
Dimitra Maoutsa asks how to learn the rules that drive a noisy system when we see it only now and then. Most ways to learn such rules need dense, fast records of the path. Or they need the system to save energy, which many do not. Her target is the overdamped Langevin class. These describe small bits of matter that drift and shake in a force field.

She turns the task into a control task. The system's long-run density shows its shape. That shape guides a step that fills in likely paths in the gaps. The rules are then read off those paths, with no fixed form forced on them. On test cases made in a lab of math, the way worked well even with very sparse records. It beat the best known ways. The paper was accepted at ICML 2026.
arxiv-2512-23666:
Saurav Goyal, Sven-Olaf Moch, Vaibhav Pathak, and V. Ravindran compute two key ingredients of high-precision particle physics at four loops in quantum chromodynamics. Soft-collinear effective theory organizes the large logarithms that plague high-energy reaction calculations by factorizing cross sections into hard, jet, soft, and beam functions. The jet and soft functions are universal, shared across processes from deep-inelastic scattering to Higgs production.

Building on recent four-loop results for eikonal and collinear anomalous dimensions for quarks and gluons, plus all lower-order information, the authors present the four-loop quark and gluon soft and jet functions. These results are an essential component of the N-jettiness subtraction method at next-to-next-to-next-to-next-to-leading order, a step toward fully differential cross sections at that accuracy for collider experiments.
arxiv-2512-23766:
Karim Salta, Michael Kirby, and Chris Peterson cluster data that live as subspaces rather than as points. In many tasks each item, an image set, a spectrum, a video clip, is best summarized by a subspace. A cluster then needs a representative subspace of its own, analogous to a mean. Distances between subspaces come from their principal angles on the Grassmann manifold.

Their representative is a Schubert Variety of Best Fit: a trainable prototype subspace chosen to come as close as possible to intersecting every cluster member in at least one fixed direction. Plugged into the classic Linde-Buzo-Gray clustering pipeline, the scheme improved cluster purity on synthetic, image, spectral, and video action data. Because the prototype is a genuine geometric object on the manifold, the mathematical structure needed for later analysis is preserved.
arxiv-2512-24166:
Boya Sun and four colleagues design a smarter signal from car to pedestrian. Self-driving cars cannot wave or make eye contact. External interfaces fill the gap with lights or sounds. Fixed displays cannot adapt, though. They ignore what the pedestrian intends to do.

Their interface adds intent recognition. It reads the intentions of both sides. Pedestrian and vehicle cooperation states are identified. Signals then adjust to speed agreement between them. The system was built on a virtual reality platform. Statistical tests measured its effect. Crossing efficiency improved significantly. Pedestrians' gaze wandered less during crossings. Interaction safety stayed at least as good as a fixed-distance design. The authors frame this as a new pattern for vehicle-pedestrian cooperation.
arxiv-2512-24266:
Alexey Talambutsa proves results about the word problem for just infinite groups. Such a group has almost no quotients: every proper one is finite. The word problem asks whether a product of generators equals the identity. Whether an algorithm can always answer that question is the theme.

For finitely generated groups, the answer is yes in a uniform way. The relations of the presentation must be listable by a program. The proof avoids the known structure theorem for such groups. It works directly from the definition. Classic ideas from Kuznetsov and from McKinsey and Maltsev guide it. Countably generated presentations come next. There the word problem can be decided except in one corner case. That case is locally finite groups with no computable bound on subgroup sizes. Talambutsa even builds such groups with an undecidable word problem under one presentation and a decidable one under another.
arxiv-2512-24366:
Ben Kabongo and Vincent Guigue test whether recommendation explanations tell the truth. Text-based explainable recommenders justify suggestions in natural language. Language models now write those justifications fluently. Fluency is not factuality, though. The explanations may drift from the evidence in reviews. That question had gone largely unmeasured.

Their framework builds ground truth from the reviews themselves. A prompting pipeline extracts atomic statements from review text. Those statements isolate the factual content. Five Amazon categories supply augmented benchmarks. Statement-level metrics then score generated explanations. Language-model and inference-based scorers combine. Six leading explainable models were tested. Semantic similarity scores looked high across them. Factual precision told another story. It stayed alarmingly low for every model. The authors call for factuality-aware evaluation of explanation systems.
arxiv-2512-24466:
Mustafa Bakr reframes quantum measurement as a boundary problem. In circuit QED, a transmon qubit ends a transmission line. The qubit's state changes the line's ringing frequency. That shift is the readout used across superconducting quantum computing. Bakr derives the effect from first principles, starting at the circuit Lagrangian.

The boundary condition depends on frequency. Its poles encode the qubit's transition frequencies. Two approximations simplify the boundary function near resonance. An extended space from Fulton-Walter spectral theory then frames the mode problem. The dressed modes depend on the qubit state. The readout shift and the vacuum Rabi splitting emerge from one equation. A repulsion result guarantees no dressed mode hits a qubit transition. Two-qubit parity measurement is analyzed as well. True parity-only readout needs built-in suppression of the linear terms.
arxiv-2512-24666:
Dong Hao Ou Yang computes the momentum distribution of an electron gas on a three-dimensional torus in the mean-field regime. The trial state comes from the random phase approximation, a standard way to include collective screening. The goal is the occupation number of Fourier modes, which says how electrons spread across momenta.

Mean-field versions are obtained of classic formulas for high density and for metallic density, following work by Daniel and Voskov, Lam, and more recent analysis by Christiansen, Hainzl, and Nam. Mathematical physics readers get a rigorous analogue of textbook electron gas results. Momentum distribution shapes how conductivity and other bulk properties are understood.
arxiv-2601-06866:
Research by Li Bai and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with united we defend. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. Membership inference attacks (MIAs), which determine whether a specific data point was included in the training set of a target model. Have posed severe threats in federated learning (FL).

Unfortunately, existing MIA defenses, typically applied independently to each client in FL. Are ineffective against powerful trajectory-based MIAs that exploit temporal information throughout the training process to infer membership status. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07066:
Lyubov Vladimirova and Vesselin Drensky wrote a paper on groups of algebras that obey a rule of third degree. The work first came out in 1986 in Pliska Stud. Math. Bulgar., volume 8, pages 144 to 157. A copy was posted on arXiv in 2026. The algebras here are associative, which means the way terms are grouped does not change the result.

The authors give a full account of all such groups over a field of characteristic zero. In such a field, no prime count of ones sums to zero. Each group in view obeys a polynomial identity of third degree. That is, one fixed rule of degree three holds for all its members. A core task in the theory of PI-algebras is to list all groups of algebras with a set trait. The paper solves that task for this one trait.
arxiv-2601-07166: Research by Jun Wang # and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with dynamic Water-Wave tweezers. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. Following a recent show of stable trapping of floating particles by stationary (monochromatic) structured water waves [ Nature 638 , 394 ].
