The file shows why. The church in El Salvador had paid for its witness with its own martyrs. Its word on abuses was hard for any government to wave away.
cia-0000045166:
A statement on the Zona Rosa killings was clarified, in a CIA record dated August 4, 1985. Clarifications follow statements that landed badly or caused confusion. The killings had taken place in San Salvador's Zona Rosa district.

Inside, the corrected official wording on the attack is preserved. Governments clarify when the first version costs them too much. Each new version invites readers to compare it, line by line, with the old one it replaced in the public record. The file holds the second draft of the official story, and with it a small lesson in how states manage the news of a massacre.
cia-0000049066: Captain Carlos Alfonso Morales Figueroa was detained in El Salvador in 1983. A CIA item from that year preserves the record, kept with the Truth Commission files. The title gives the fact without the charge, which the document's pages would carry. Detentions of officers thread through these records as the war's slow grind toward accountability.
cia-0000049166: House intelligence committee members were briefed in 1990 in connection with Congressman Moakley's delegation, in a partly blacked-out CIA item. Moakley led the House task force on the Jesuit murders, and his delegations went to San Salvador to press the case. The briefing prepared the members for what the agency would say, and would not.
cia-0000049266: A Senate intelligence committee staffer was briefed in 1990 on El Salvador and Honduras, and a CIA item preserves the session. Honduras was the war's back yard: American bases, Salvadoran refugees, and the contra war next door. Briefing the two together showed how the committee's map joined them, country to country.
cia-0000049366: Dated November 2, 1983, declassified CIA document 0000049366 is a Central American threat assessment marked for the Truth Commission. The paper weighs threats across the region rather than in one country. It survives as a short declassified assessment whose title states its purpose. It belongs to the agency's regular regional reporting. Its job was to sum up dangers in Central America for its readers.
cia-0000075166: Briefing of a redacted person to load drop for a redacted recipient is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000075166, dated April 3, 1961. Both key names appear as blanks in the catalog heading. The file is a brief declassified briefing record whose redactions are its defining feature, showing the limits of what the released record actually reveals.
cia-0000096666: Sixth Report to the President by the President's Board of Consultants on Foreign Intelligence Activities is declassified CIA document 0000096666, dated January 1, 1961. The heading is cut short in the catalog. The brief file is a later board report in the same series as the third reports, showing the board still reporting at a new decade's start.
cia-0000100166: Soviet Union Urals town contaminated by radioactive waste, to be evacuated, is declassified CIA document 0000100166, dated January 2, 1991. The heading joins the pollution to a planned evacuation. Readers find a short declassified contamination record from the Soviet Union's final year, its title carrying both the problem and the intended response in one line.
cia-0000102966: Alleged use of forced labor on the Siberian pipeline is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000102966, dated July 5, 1982. The word alleged is part of the heading, so the record presents a claim, not a settled finding. The brief file ties prison labor to a major Soviet gas project. It was filed while that pipeline drew wide outside attention.
cia-0000109066: Status of Cuban-soviet Trade Relations; Soviet Gift of Atomic Reactor to Cuba is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000109066, dated November 2, 1967. The title pairs a trade status report with a striking gift: an atomic reactor for Cuba. A semicolon joins the two items in one heading. The brief record is a trade and reactor item from 1967.
cia-0000119766: As of 9 a.m. on November 1, 1956, this CIA report gives the situation in Hungary on the morning after Nagy declared the country neutral. Hope stood at its highest that day, and the Soviet answer was still two days off. The paper captures the peak of that optimism. Neutrality, declared November 1, was the revolution's boldest act, and a morning report from that date catches the country holding its breath in hope.
cia-0000126866: A March 1964 CIA document reports Babu's agreement to a union with Tanganyika. Abdulrahman Babu, a leading figure in Zanzibar, was helping broker the joining of island and mainland that formed Tanzania. The paper records the agreement as the agency understood it. The union took effect in April 1964, creating Tanzania, and this March paper catches the deal in its final stage of bargaining between island and mainland.
cia-0000126966: A September 1968 CIA situation report covers Panama a month before the National Guard's October coup. That takeover would bring Omar Torrijos to power for years. The paper captures the country on the edge of the change, as the agency reported it. The October coup that followed made this September paper the last of the old order's file, a baseline against which the Torrijos years would later be measured.
cia-0000132266: Situation report 573, from January 1991, covers political developments and reaction to an Iraqi act the heading leaves unfinished. By that number, the daily crisis watch was running at full tempo. The report collects the responses as they came in. Reaction items near a series' end tend to gather the world's second thoughts. This one's cut-off heading leaves the provoking act to be found in the text.
cia-0000132566: Arms aid planned by the Castro regime for Guatemalan leftists fills item 5 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated October 5, 1960. Guatemala had been the agency's own success story in 1954, when a coup it backed took power. Now Havana was treating the country as a target for exported revolution. The short item tracks the aid plans.
cia-0000132666: Cuba getting ready to mark the anniversary of Castro's victory fills a CIA paper dated November 5, 1960. The date ahead was January 1, 1961, two years since Batista fled the island. The second anniversary was planned as a showcase of the revolution's gains. The short paper covers the plans for parades, speeches, and displays that winter.
cia-0000132766:
Seizures of American property drive this CIA briefing on Cuba, dated June 4, 1960. Castro's government was taking over U.S. firms on the island. Washington watched with growing alarm as the revolution turned hard left.

Property fights mattered because they turned ideology into losses that businesses and newspapers could count. Each takeover pushed the two governments further apart that summer. The briefing, one of two Cuba papers dated June 4, tracks the early-summer radicalization that made a break hard to avoid. It survives through the CIA Reading Room, mirrored online by the Internet Archive.
cia-0000134266: Trade missions between China and Cuba being set up fill item 1 of a CIA general series dated February 2, 1960. Trade missions were the plumbing of the new bond between the two states. Beijing and Havana were building the machinery for regular commerce that winter. The short item reports the arrangement and the first visits planned under it.
cia-0000135866: From 4 August 1952 comes a CIA document, since declassified, on links between Calligeris and General Trujillo of Santo Domingo, a tie with a fellow strongman. The paper sits inside the CIA drive against President Arbenz, run under the code name PBSUCCESS and crowned by the June 1954 coup. Later books on the coup rest on stacks of paper exactly like this, dated, coded, and only partly opened.
cia-0000136166: From the CIA files comes a cable dated 5 April 1954, long since declassified, on an urgent message from SEMANTIC for passage onward. The name Lincoln marks the forward station of PBSUCCESS, the CIA campaign that brought down President Arbenz in June 1954. A reader gets the unpolished version here, complete with code names, short titles, and gaps left by the censors.
cia-0000136266: The CIA cable of 1 May 1954 is about a request that authorization for bombings come from Lincoln, and it survives in declassified form. Lincoln was where PBSUCCESS staff worked the Guatemala operation day to day, under code names, in 1953 and 1954. The file rewards slow reading, since its short heading is often the only summary the agency ever gave it.
cia-0000136566: This Spanish text, dated 5 November 1960, belongs to the 2506 Brigade papers in the CIA's declassified release. The brigade was then a secret exile unit in training. The catalog record states no subject for the document. It joins the cluster of brigade items from the first week of November 1960, all in Spanish. Dated and placed, it is left to speak for itself in the full text held here.
cia-0000136766: An estimated 1961 date, given only as the year, heads this Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade collection. The brigade was the CIA-trained exile force whose story peaked at the Bay of Pigs that April. The catalog record flags the date as estimated and names no subject for the item. It survives in Spanish in the declassified release, a loosely dated piece of the brigade's final-year paperwork.
cia-0000136866: Tone down the propaganda, headquarters tells LINCOLN in this March 1954 cable. It went to Dunbar and Notting from Whiting. All agree an abortive coup has propaganda value. But bigger points come first. For now, efforts should focus on intelligence work. The event must be fully documented. Evidence tying Guatemala in matters most of all. A strong record could support charges before the OAS. Sloppy claims could be disproved. That would waste the incident's impact.
cia-0000136966: Propaganda for the SHERWOOD broadcast is drawn from a Guatemala City cable. The cable is dated 19 June 1954. A propaganda chief sent a warning telegram. He worked for the National Agrarian Department. He warned Arbenz and the armed forces chief. He warned the police chief and labor leaders too. One hundred Hondurans were in Champona, he said. Five thousand local men backed them. Little word had come from that area since. The item could encourage internal resistance. It could also hurt enemy morale. False sourcing would need care.
cia-0000138966: Islamic fundamentalism is the newest and most dynamic force on the Lebanese political scene, this May 1987 CIA assessment opens, but an Islamic republic is only a distant possibility. Major opposition comes from key militias including moderate Shias and Sunnis, Christians, and Druze, and from Lebanon's neighbors Syria and Israel. Barring a full-scale Syrian move, the excerpt begins, before the text cuts off. Dated during Lebanon's civil war, the report weighs Hezbollah-era fundamentalism against the country's fractured militia politics.
cia-0000139366: Terms of reference for National Intelligence Estimate 11-3-61, Sino-Soviet Air Defense Capabilities Through Mid-1966, are forwarded in this 30 December 1960 memorandum from Deputy Assistant Director Chester Cooper. Representatives are asked to meet on 6 January in the Administration Building to discuss the draft terms, which state the problem the estimate will answer. The sample contains the framing paperwork only, not the air defense judgments. It documents how the community scoped its forecast of Soviet and Chinese air defenses at the U-2 era's end.
cia-0000139466: Document 0000139466, dated 1988, is one of the SUN STREAK files: the remote viewing program in which the United States paid people to try to see far-off targets with the mind alone. Sessions under the program produced typed reports, sketches, and scores, and files like this one held them. The catalog gives no hint that this item differs from its neighbors. It survives as evidence of a real, funded program that later reviews judged to have produced no usable intelligence.
cia-0000141166:
CIA historian Jack Pfeiffer sat down with James A. Cunningham on 11 October 1977 and taped his account of the Bay of Pigs air war. Cunningham had run office work for the Development Projects Division, the unit behind the U-2 and the Cuba air effort. The excerpt kept here centers on a dry but sharp dispute: what time did the bombers really take off?

Cunningham walks through rival mission logs. One shows pilot Herrera leaving alone at 0700Z. A later fix by Gar Thorsrud moves Doug Price's takeoff beside Connie Seigrist's. A book on the landing had stirred the fight, and the Taylor Committee had used one version. The talk shows how hard the basic facts were to pin down.
cia-06701366: DETENTION OF ARGENTINE SOCIALIST LEADER CAUSING SECURITY AND HUMAN RIGHTS PROB, a CIA document. The detained leader. This file preserves that declassified paper. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
cia-06862566: MOZAMBIQUE-SOUTH AFRICA: NEW IMPETUS TO CAHORA BASSA TALKS, a CIA document. The dam negotiations. This file preserves that declassified paper. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Scholars prize such firsthand sources from long ago.
davis-death-after-life-1866:
Death and the After-Life, from 1866, gathers three discourses by Andrew Jackson Davis. Davis, the Poughkeepsie Seer, taught that death is a birth into a higher sphere. His name for the spirit world was the Summer Land. The discourses give his core statement of the spiritualist afterlife.

He describes the process of dying as his clairvoyant sight reported it. The spirit leaves the body by stages, then wakes among scenes of the after life. Friends and guides greet the new arrival in his telling. Comfort for mourners runs through every page. The small book carried his teaching to a wide audience. It stays a key spiritualist text.
drake-witchcraft-delusion-vol1-1866:
Samuel Gardner Drake, a Boston antiquarian and bookseller, built his Witchcraft Delusion in New England around two famous Salem-era books. Volume one, issued in 1866, reprints Cotton Mather's Wonders of the Invisible World in full. Mather first published that defense of the trials in 1693, while the Salem hangings were still fresh.

Mather, a leading Boston minister, wrote to prove the trials were just and the threat was real. Drake adds his own preface, opening essay, and notes to set the scene. Readers get the case for the prosecution in its own strong words. The volume pairs a key source with a guide to its world.
drake-witchcraft-delusion-vol2-1866:
Volume two of Drake's Witchcraft Delusion in New England answers volume one. Where the first volume gave Cotton Mather's case for the Salem trials, this 1866 volume reprints the reply. Its author was Robert Calef, a Boston merchant with no love for the Mathers.

Calef's More Wonders of the Invisible World, first printed in 1700, charges that ministers and judges fed the Salem panic. He retells cases, prints letters, and questions the proof used to hang men and women. Drake's notes frame the feud for later readers. The book stands as the first close, on-the-spot attack on the trials.
drake-witchcraft-delusion-vol3-1866:
Volume three closes Samuel Drake's three-volume Witchcraft Delusion in New England, printed in 1866. The set reprints the great books of the Salem era with Drake's prefaces and notes. This last volume carries the story past Mather's defense and into the long argument that followed.

Its pages hold further tracts and records from the New England witchcraft years. Read with the first two volumes, it fills in names, cases, and charges the famous books leave out. Drake meant the set to serve as a working archive, not a tale retold. Together the three volumes give the trials and their fallout in full.
duncan-masonic-ritual-1866:
Malcolm C. Duncan put out his Masonic Ritual and Monitor in 1866. The book prints the rites of the craft lodge in full. It runs from the first grade, Entered Apprentice, up to Royal Arch. Duncan wrote for Masons and for the keen man in the street.

Signs, grips, oaths, and floor work stand in plain print, grade by grade. Cuts show the lodge room, the tools, and the dress of each rank. Past books had hid the rites; Duncan sold them to all. The work is still the stock guide to the craft rites of its age.
espositione-di-giovanbattista-agnello-ve: Espositione di Giovanbattista Agnello Venetiano, 1566. The Venetian exposition. This book preserves that work. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc10957466:
Marin and a large team tested a ready-made cell therapy for blood cancers in this 2024 trial report. Natural killer cells are immune cells that kill infected or cancerous cells. The team fitted such cells, taken from donated cord blood, with a sensor that targets a marker called CD19 on B cell tumours. The cells also carried a growth signal called interleukin-15. Thirty-seven patients with B cell cancers took part.

No severe side effects such as cytokine release syndrome or graft-versus-host disease appeared, the team reports. Half the patients, 48.6 percent, had responded by day 30, and the rate held at day 100. One year after treatment, 68 percent were alive. Responses were strongest when the cord blood had few red cell precursors and was frozen within 24 hours of collection. Those best units yielded cells rich in attack genes.
europmc-pmc10958066:
Deng and colleagues give a full account of one key growth signal in health and disease in this 2024 review. TGF-beta is a signal protein made by nearly every tissue and cell type. Its signals guide embryo growth, wound healing, and the day-to-day balance of tissues and the immune system. When the signal goes wrong, it can drive disease instead.

The review retraces the field's history and explains how the protein is made, switched on, and passed into cells. It then details what the signal does in healthy states and in illness. Therapies that target the signal are highlighted, since they have brought new options for linked diseases. The authors aim to give readers one systematic map of the whole topic. They also flag where fresh work is most needed.
europmc-pmc11405266:
Argentieri and a large team build a blood protein clock that estimates biological age in this 2024 study. Plasma proteins can potentially measure how fast a person is ageing, beyond years lived. The team developed the clock in the UK Biobank with 45,441 people, using a platform that measures 2,897 plasma proteins. They then tested its use for predicting disease and death in diverse populations.

A set of 204 proteins predicted chronological age with a correlation of 0.94, they report. Faster proteomic ageing tracked with 18 major chronic diseases, including heart, liver, kidney, and lung diseases, diabetes, brain degeneration, and cancer. It also tracked with having several diseases at once and with all-cause mortality. Links appeared with telomere length, frailty, and reaction time. Top clock proteins act in matrix structure, immunity, inflammation, and hormone pathways.
europmc-pmc11880366:
Xiao and co-authors surveyed peptide drugs in a 2025 review. Peptides are short chains of amino acids, the building blocks of proteins. They can act as precise drugs for many diseases. Weak points include fast breakdown in the body.

New design methods and smart delivery systems now ease those faults. Peptides treat diabetes, weight gain, cancer, and rare diseases. They also serve as vaccine parts and as guided carriers. Xiao tracks market growth and trials in progress. Artificial intelligence now speeds the search for useful peptides. It appeared in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy.
europmc-pmc1247566:
Bornehag and colleagues linked house dust phthalates to child allergy symptoms in 2004. Allergy and asthma rates in children had climbed for three decades. Dust was sampled in homes of 198 symptomatic children. A matched set of 202 symptom-free children served as controls.

One phthalate, BBzP, ran higher in case homes, at 0.15 versus 0.12 milligrams per gram. BBzP tied to runny nose and eczema symptoms. Another, DEHP, tied to asthma instead. Each child got clinical and home technical checks. Bornehag shows indoor chemical dust may track with lasting allergy. Cases and controls came from a wider cohort of 10,852 children in Sweden.
europmc-pmc1253666:
Nash and colleagues exposed zebrafish to a potent hormone drug across generations in 2004. Ethynylestradiol is a birth control drug found in waterways. It acts at very low concentrations in fish. Breeding groups were kept on realistic water levels for life.

Lifelong exposure at 5 nanograms per liter cut egg output by 56 percent. That generation then failed fully, with no fertilization at all. Males lacked working testes and showed disturbed sex development. By contrast, 40 days of exposure in adult parents caused no harm. Nash proves life-stage timing decides the damage. The harm thus skipped the first group and struck the next generation in full.
europmc-pmc1318466:
Akins, Tolson, and Cole tested expert panel stability with bootstrap methods in 2005. Delphi surveys poll experts in rounds to reach consensus. No rule fixed how many experts a panel needs. The test case was a first-round survey of 23 health quality experts.

Responses covered 54 survey items on hospital excellence criteria. Bootstrap sampling expanded the data to two larger fake panels. Means, trimmed means, spread, and confidence ranges were compared. First-round data were chosen for their widest diversity. Akins checks whether small panel results hold up when virtually enlarged. In the end, the small panel's answers stayed stable under both larger fake panels.
europmc-pmc1564166:
When SARS struck in 2002, doctors had no tested treatments. Stockman, Bellamy, and Garner reviewed all treatment studies in 2006 for the World Health Organization. They covered ribavirin, steroids, two HIV drugs, interferon, antibodies, and patient plasma.

In lab dishes, ribavirin, lopinavir, and interferon slowed the virus. In patients, proof was far weaker. Of 26 ribavirin studies, all were inconclusive or flagged possible harm. Of 29 steroid studies, four suggested harm. Plasma and antibody studies were also inconclusive. Stockman concludes no treatment had proven benefit, a stark brief for future outbreaks. Strong trial proof was missing throughout.
europmc-pmc2000966:
Conenello and colleagues pinpointed in 2007 a single change that makes influenza A far more deadly. The viral protein PB1-F2 helps trigger cell death and worsens disease in mice. Comparing H5N1 viruses from the 1997 Hong Kong outbreak revealed one amino acid difference linked to harm. That same change appears in the 1918 pandemic virus.

Swapping in the serine form at position 66 raised virus growth in mouse lungs 100-fold. Infected mice lost more weight and died more often. Reversing the change in the rebuilt 1918 virus weakened it greatly. Its lethal dose rose about 1,000-fold, and lung virus levels fell. Both harmful forms also raised inflammatory signals called cytokines in the lungs.
europmc-pmc2022666:
Cohn and colleagues asked in 2007 whether DDT exposure early in life predicts later breast cancer. Earlier studies measured exposure late, after DDT had faded from the body and been banned. This team used stored blood from young women in Oakland, California, taken in 1959 to 1967 just after childbirth. Cases were 129 women who developed breast cancer before age 50.

Controls were 129 women matched on birth year, and follow-up averaged 17 years. High blood levels of p,p'-DDT, the active ingredient, predicted a five-fold higher cancer risk. That link appeared only in women exposed before age 14, as DDT use peaked. Women first exposed later showed no association. The authors warn many heavily exposed girls had not yet reached the age of highest risk.
europmc-pmc2124966: A medical paper on the relation of the spleen to blood destruction and regeneration. The spleen's work. This article preserves that hematology. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2125966: A medical paper with further studies on pure vaccine virus cultivated in vivo. The vaccine, grown. This article preserves that virology. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2126266: A medical paper on experimental trypanosomiasis applied in chemotherapeutic investigation. The sleeping sickness model. This article preserves that pharmacology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2128466: A medical paper on a reaction product in Trypanosoma lewisi infections which inhibits reproduction. The parasite blocker. This article preserves that parasitology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2131266: A medical paper with studies on pathogenic B. coli from bovine sources, the pathogenic action. The cattle E. coli's harm. This article preserves that veterinary bacteriology. Later readers can locate it. It retains its place in time.
europmc-pmc2140366: A biology paper on influence of a slight modification of the collodion membrane on the sign of charge. The membrane's charge. This article preserves that biophysics. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2140566: A biology paper on the adhesiveness of leucocytes to solid surfaces. The sticky white cells. This article preserves that cell biology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2248166:
Sidney and colleagues derived binding motifs in 2008 for 19 MHC class I molecules from humans and mice. These molecules display protein fragments to T cells, and each variant prefers particular fragment patterns. Knowing those motifs helps find vaccine targets. The team used positional scanning combinatorial peptide libraries, mixtures where each position is varied systematically, to measure binding preferences quantitatively and without bias.

All 19 alleles, fifteen human and four mouse, yielded distinct binding patterns under one uniform approach. The team introduced a method to convert the data into classical anchor positions, the key slots in the fragment, with their preferred building blocks. The matrices successfully identified candidate binding peptides and T-cell epitopes in vaccinia and influenza viruses. Motifs are provided for several alleles lacking detailed descriptions before, including HLA A*3001 and B*1501.
europmc-pmc2361666:
Illing and colleagues reported early Western trials of focused ultrasound for liver and kidney tumors in 2005. The method, HIFU, beams high-intensity sound from outside the body to cook a small zone of tumor, with no cut at all. The device used was a Chinese system already in use in Asia since 1997.

Thirty patients had one treatment session under general anaesthesia, then scans 12 days later. Among 27 patients who could be assessed, 25 showed a clear killed zone in the tumor. Liver tumors responded every time, while kidney tumors succeeded in 67% of cases, a gap the authors reported plainly. Side effects compared well with more invasive methods. Some patients later had tumors removed, letting doctors confirm the scan findings in real tissue.
europmc-pmc2375266:
Pérez-Tenorio and Stål, working with the Southeast Sweden Breast Cancer Group, tested a survival protein in breast cancer in 2002. The protein, Akt, helps cancer cells stay alive and keep growing, and it sits below the erbB-2 growth receptor in the cell's signal chain. All 93 patients were under 50 and received hormone-based treatment.

The team measured both the protein and its switched-on form, called pAkt, in tumors. Patients whose tumors showed pAkt were far more prone to the cancer spreading to distant sites. That link held after accounting for growth rate and lymph node spread, with a significance value of 0.004 in the adjusted analysis. The on-form also came with a lower share of cells in the copying phase. The authors said Akt activation may flag patients whose hormone treatment will fail.
europmc-pmc2519166:
Deco, Jirsa, Robinson, Breakspear, and Friston reviewed in 2008 how computer models capture the living brain's activity at every scale. The cortex, the brain's outer layer, supports perception, language, and thought. Its moment-to-moment dynamics are far less mapped than its wiring. The authors set out to unify modelling work from single neurons up to the whole brain.

They show how models at each level answer different questions, from how single neurons exchange signals to how large regions interact. Mean-field models, which track average activity across cell groups, link the levels and can be fitted directly to brain recordings such as EEG and fMRI scans. The authors argue that such principled models are a prerequisite for grounding brain data in real theory.
europmc-pmc2568866:
Fullerton, Bruce, and Gordon reviewed in 2008 the health toll of indoor smoke from biomass fuels such as wood, dung, and charcoal. About a third of the world's people burn such fuels for cooking, heating, and lighting, mostly in the developing world. The smoke fills homes with high levels of pollutants, and the authors summarised what is known about the damage.

Biomass smoke is linked to more respiratory infections, including pneumonia and tuberculosis, and to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. It is also associated with low birthweight, cataracts, cardiovascular events, and higher death rates for adults and for children. Why these links arise is not fully understood. The review highlights where the evidence is solid and where knowledge gaps remain.
europmc-pmc2627866:
Knowlton and colleagues assessed the health impact of the 2006 California heat wave in 2009, focusing on illness rather than deaths. Heat waves are projected to grow more frequent and severe, yet few studies had measured the hospital burden. The team counted hospitalisations and emergency department visits across six California regions during the 18-day event and compared them with a reference period.

The heat wave produced 16,166 excess emergency visits and 1,182 excess hospitalisations statewide. Visits for heat-related causes rose 6.30-fold, and hospitalisations for heat illness rose 10.15-fold on the rate ratio measure. Kidney failure, electrolyte imbalance, diabetes, and cardiovascular problems also climbed significantly. Children under five and adults over 65 were at greatest risk. Even modest-temperature regions like the Central Coast suffered. Acclimatisation seems to shape vulnerability.
europmc-pmc2658866:
van Dam and colleagues followed 77,782 American nurses for 24 years to measure how five daily habits, combined, shape the risk of death. The study, published in 2008, scored smoking, body weight, exercise, alcohol use, and diet quality. The women were 34 to 59 years old and free of heart disease and cancer at the start in 1980.

Over the follow-up, 8,882 women died. Each habit on its own predicted death, and the effects stacked. Women with all five risk habits faced over four times the death risk of women with none. For heart deaths the gap was eight-fold. The team estimates smoking alone accounted for 28 percent of all deaths. Smoking, excess weight, inactivity, and poor diet together accounted for over half, a share alcohol barely changed.
europmc-pmc2683166:
Kelly and co-authors tackled in 2009 a measurement problem in synthetic biology: gene switches called promoters have no shared unit of strength. Labs building with standard DNA parts, called BioBricks, reported promoter strength in raw instrument numbers. Those numbers shift with growth conditions and machines, so one lab's strong promoter was another's weak one.

The team chose one promoter as a living reference standard, measured in the same sample beside every test promoter. Reporting strengths relative to that standard cut the scatter from differing conditions and instruments by about half. They named the ratio the Relative Promoter Unit and built a kit so any lab could adopt it. Sending test promoters to several labs confirmed the fix: relative values agreed far better than raw ones. Shared units, they argue, turn scattered part descriptions into engineering data.
europmc-pmc2698066:
Jensen and colleagues found in 2009 a marker, Lrig1, that picks out a distinct reservoir of stem cells in mouse skin. Skin renews itself from several stem cell pools whose borders were fuzzy. In humans, Lrig1 already marked one quiet stem cell type, and it helps keep those cells resting rather than dividing.

In mice, Lrig1 marked the junctional zone of the hair follicle, the neck region beside the oil glands. Cells from that zone could rebuild every skin lineage in grafting tests, proving their potency. In daily life they fed only two: the oil gland and the surface skin between follicles. Removing Lrig1 made stem cells divide more eagerly and thickened the skin. Boosting a growth signal expanded the zone, while losing Lrig1 let that signal sprout stray follicles. The zone, the authors conclude, is a stem cell niche hiding in plain sight.
europmc-pmc2745766:
Dick and co-authors used genome sequence signatures in 2009 to sort DNA fragments from an acid biofilm microbial community without growing the microbes first. Metagenomic data, DNA taken straight from an environment, mixes many species, including rare ones that are hard to assign. Composition patterns in a genome, such as letter frequencies, are fairly constant within a species and can act as a fingerprint.

Applying signature clustering to the acid mine community, they identified and grouped fragments de novo, recovering information about low-abundance members that standard methods miss. The approach helps trace fragment origins and reveals population diversity and gene exchange inside a community. It offers a culture-free window on microbes that drive chemical cycles in extreme environments.
europmc-pmc2762766:
Eysenbach framed in 2009 infodemiology and infoveillance, public health methods that analyze how health information spreads and is sought on the Internet. Search queries can predict flu outbreaks, social media posts can support syndromic surveillance, and web content can reveal gaps in health information or the reach of anti-vaccination sites. Seven years after coining the concept, he revisits and expands the framework.

The framework separates supply-based work, studying what is published online, from demand-based work, studying search and navigation behavior, and passive from active surveillance. New metrics include information prevalence, concept occurrence ratios, and information incidence, all measurable in near real time. Such measures can follow or even predict health events, and need standardization for public health use.
europmc-pmc2814866:
Ortega and colleagues profiled tiny gene regulators called microRNAs in human fat tissue and fat cells in 2010. MicroRNAs are short RNA pieces that fine-tune gene activity, and they had been tied to body weight in mice but never mapped across human fat cell growth. The team screened more than seven hundred microRNAs in belly fat from lean and obese women, some with type 2 diabetes.

Fifty microRNAs showed different levels in fat cells taken from lean versus obese donors. Seventy swung up or down as young fat cells matured, showing a near mirror-image pattern between the two states. Eleven differed in fat from obese women, and most of those also shifted during cell growth. The authors flag them as candidate markers and drug targets for obesity.
europmc-pmc2815666:
Kabsch laid out the working principles in 2010 behind key steps of his XDS program for processing crystal diffraction data. The four steps covered are modeling where spots should fall, adding up spot strengths, correcting and scaling the data, and assigning the crystal's symmetry group, called its space group.

Spot positions depend on a small set of values that the program refines until predicted and seen spots agree. The same principles hold whether each rotation image spans a thin slice or a wide angle. Much of the theory dates back about thirty years to film methods, later extended for fast electronic detectors at synchrotron beamlines, machines that make intense X-ray beams. The article explains the methods as XDS applies them.
europmc-pmc2831066:
Soscia, Kirby, Washicosky, and a large team reported in 2010 that the amyloid beta protein, long blamed as mere waste in Alzheimer disease, actually kills germs. The protein builds the plaques found in Alzheimer brains and was thought to have no normal job. Its traits, though, mirror a family of natural antibiotics called antimicrobial peptides.

In lab tests the protein fought eight common disease germs as strongly as, and sometimes more strongly than, a benchmark human defense peptide called LL-37. Brain tissue from Alzheimer patients killed germs better than tissue from matched healthy donors, and the strength rose with amyloid levels. Stripping the protein out with antibodies erased the extra killing, tying the effect to amyloid itself.
europmc-pmc2851566:
Cunnington, Santibanez Koref, Mayosi, Burn, and Keavney asked in 2010 how one stretch of chromosome 9 gained links to heart disease, diabetes, stroke, and several cancers. The risk variants there sit outside genes, so the team suspected they tune the output of nearby genes instead. They measured gene activity in blood from nearly five hundred healthy volunteers in Britain and South Africa, using both total and allele-specific readouts.

Variants tracked most strongly with ANRIL, a non-coding RNA beside the two cell-cycle brake genes in the region. Risk variants for coronary disease, stroke, diabetes, melanoma, and brain tumors all tied to ANRIL's allelic balance, sometimes shifting expression twofold. The authors argue that dialing ANRIL up or down mediates much of this hot spot's disease reach.
europmc-pmc2897766:
Pincus and colleagues used in 2010 a mix of computer modeling and yeast experiments to show how a helper protein fine-tunes the cell's protein-folding alarm. When misfolded proteins pile up in the cell's folding compartment, a sensor called Ire1 triggers the unfolded protein response, which expands folding capacity. The helper, BiP, binds the sensor, and its grip was thought to be the alarm's main switch.

Simulations predicted that BiP binding instead sets how sensitive the sensor is and how quickly the response shuts back off once stress eases. Experiments with altered BiP and sensor matched those predictions, shifting response timing without abolishing it. The alarm behaves less like a simple on-off switch and more like a tuned thermostat, with BiP as the calibration dial.
europmc-pmc2911766:
Benes and colleagues tested in 2010 whether guiding fluids during major abdominal surgery by the heartbeat's own variation improves recovery for high-risk patients. The measure, stroke volume variation, tracks how much each heartbeat's output swings with breathing and predicts who will respond to extra fluid. Sixty patients got variation-guided care with a bedside monitor, and sixty got routine care, assigned by chance.

The guided group received fluid in measured boluses whenever variation crossed the target line, rather than by habit or blood pressure alone. Guided patients developed fewer infectious and organ complications in the month after surgery, and markers of tissue under-perfusion ran lower. Intensive care and hospital stays also trended shorter. The trial supports physiology-guided fluids over fixed recipes for fragile patients facing big operations.
europmc-pmc3013466:
Curtis, de Barra, and Aunger presented disgust as an evolved disease avoidance system in a 2011 article. The feeling, they argue, works like a behavioural immune system, steering people away from things likely to carry germs.

Its basic triggers look universal, yet sensitivity varies with personality and with states such as pregnancy and infancy. Learning tunes it through paired tastes, copying common habits in a group, and rules of purity that harden into manners and social boundaries. Shared hygiene efforts such as sanitation cut germ levels for everyone. The model links psychology, culture, and epidemiology.
europmc-pmc3111466:
Audrey Neyrinck and colleagues reported a 2011 mouse study in PLoS ONE on a wheat fibre that feeds gut bacteria. Fat-rich diets disturb gut microbes and drive weight gain, so the team tested whether a water-soluble wheat extract could reverse that pattern. Obese mice on a fatty diet got the fibre for four weeks.

Fibre-fed mice regained bacterial groups the fatty diet had cut, and one helpful group rose well above normal levels. Their gut barrier worked better, a blood marker of inflammation fell, and fat cells shrank. The mice also gained less weight, stored less cholesterol, and handled insulin better. The authors link the gains to the shifted microbes and propose the wheat fibre as a candidate for preventing obesity.
europmc-pmc3136466:
David Baltrus and colleagues sequenced nineteen strains of a plant-infecting bacterium in a 2011 paper in PLoS Pathogens. Close relatives of this germ attack very different crops, and injected proteins that disable plant defences were thought to set that range. The team screened strains for new injected proteins and read full genomes from diseased plants of many kinds.

Injected protein sets differed hugely between strains, with only a handful shared by all, likely the bare kit needed to cause disease. Small changes in one shared protein flipped how harmful a strain was. Toxin-making routes varied just as widely. One cucumber-attacking group had recently picked up a giant extra DNA ring carrying many unknown genes. Host range, the study shows, is a fast-moving trait.
europmc-pmc3156766:
Victoria Hall and colleagues reviewed diabetes across sub-Saharan Africa in a 2011 paper in BMC Public Health. The region still battles heavy infectious disease while diabetes climbs fast, and planners lacked a current picture. The review gathered studies from 1999 to early 2011 on rates, complications, care access, and costs.

Type two diabetes dominates, ranging from rare in rural areas to more than one adult in ten in some cities. Complication rates for eyes, nerves, and kidneys were often strikingly high, and death within five years varied enormously between settings. Over two fifths of cases found in surveys had never been diagnosed, and diagnosed patients often lacked testing supplies and affordable treatment. The authors urge integrated care that handles infections and chronic disease together.
europmc-pmc3185266:
Willeke Westendorp and colleagues pooled nearly ninety studies on infections after stroke in a 2011 paper in BMC Neurology. Stroke patients are prone to infection in the first days, but reported rates swung wildly between studies. The review, covering well over a hundred thousand patients, aimed for a trustworthy overall figure and its effect on survival.

About three patients in ten developed an infection, with pneumonia and urinary infections each striking about one in ten. Intensive care patients fared far worse on every count. Studies that hunted infections deliberately, and those with older or more female patients, reported more. Pneumonia stood out as deadly, tied to several-fold higher odds of death. The authors press for prevention as a core part of stroke care.
europmc-pmc3218866:
Christian Kubicek and a large consortium compared the genomes of three Trichoderma fungi in this 2011 study in Genome Biology. Trichoderma species are used to protect crops because some attack other fungi, a lifestyle called mycoparasitism. The team sequenced two of these fungus-eating species and compared them with a relative that does not prey on fungi.

Gene order was strongly conserved across the three genomes, and mobile DNA elements were largely inactive. The two predatory species shared expanded gene families, often in regions where gene order breaks down. Family-tree analysis showed the non-predatory species descended from predatory ancestors and lost the trait. Genes specific to mycoparasitism thus arose once, in a common ancestor. The findings should help breeders design better biocontrol strains.
europmc-pmc3267166:
Carlos Mas-Moruno, Florian Rechenmacher, and Horst Kessler told the development story of cilengitide, the first anti-angiogenic small molecule drug candidate, in this 2010 review. The drug is a small ring-shaped peptide that blocks integrin receptors tumors use to grow new blood vessels. At the time of writing it was in late-stage trials for the brain cancer glioblastoma and mid-stage trials for other tumors.

The authors developed it in the early nineteen-nineties with a strategy they call spatial screening. That produced a ring peptide far more potent than straight versions. It was also selective against a platelet receptor that had to be avoided. One further chemical tweak, methylating a single bond, boosted activity again and yielded cilengitide itself. The review covers the biochemical background and the ongoing trials, noting that combinations with classical cancer therapies may strengthen its effects.
europmc-pmc3314666:
Nohynek led a Finnish study linking a swine flu vaccine to a sudden rise in childhood narcolepsy, reporting in 2012. Narcolepsy is a lifelong sleep disorder causing overwhelming daytime sleepiness and sudden muscle weakness. Cases in Finnish children jumped soon after the 2009 pandemic and the national campaign using the Pandemrix vaccine, which contained a strong immune boosting additive.

Following every child in the country through health records, the team confirmed sixty seven new cases in the study window. Narcolepsy appeared far more often in vaccinated children than in unvaccinated ones, at roughly thirteen times the rate. The extra risk worked out to about one case for every sixteen thousand vaccinated children and teens. Adults showed no such rise, and the authors urge research into how the vaccine and its booster ingredient may have triggered the disorder.
europmc-pmc3384466:
Barouki and co-authors argued in a 2012 white paper that many chronic diseases begin with conditions before birth and in early childhood. Early life is a flexible phase when the body adjusts to its surroundings. That flexibility peaks before birth and in the first years, exactly when tissues are forming.

Nutrition, chemicals, drugs, infections, and stress during those windows can set lasting patterns in body function. The authors link part of the forty-year rise in major diseases to such early nutritional imbalance and chemical exposure. Their concept, called developmental origins of health and disease, has held up across species. They call for research and prevention to aim at the earliest stages of life.
