frus-1861-d166:
Horace Perry wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 19 June 1861. The dispatch is document 166 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Two Perry reports in one week mark a busy stretch at the Madrid legation. Spain's court was weighing its stance as the war hardened. His letters fed Washington the small facts by which such weighing could be judged from afar. Spain's queen, Isabella, ruled a court where access turned on form and favor. Form and favor decided much in Madrid, and Perry learned their rules fast. Fast learning served him well in Madrid.
frus-1861-d266:
One more voice from abroad reached Washington on 6 November 1861: James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands writing to Seward. It was printed as Document 266 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. By then, in the autumn of the war's first year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d66:
On 6 August 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams about the long work ahead in London. The letter is document 66 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward's August letters turn to the long haul: blockade law, trade claims, and watch on the yards. The glamour of the first months was gone. This note shows the Secretary settling into the grind of a war he now knew would not end soon. The grind he describes became the pattern of the London post for the next three years. Three years of such grind kept Britain neutral, which was half the war won.
frus-1862-d166:
On 21 October 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, in a letter printed as Document 166 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The exchange between the two men fills much of the volume's British section.

Autumn 1862 was the high-water mark of European talk about stepping into the war. Once Antietam and the emancipation plan landed, that talk cooled but did not die. Seward's frequent letters kept Adams pressing the Union case while London made up its mind, one cabinet meeting at a time. Earl Russell, the British foreign secretary, was the minister Adams dealt with most in London.
frus-1862-d266:
On 15 April 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent William L. Dayton a dispatch printed as Document 266 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Dayton held the Paris post as American minister to France.

Mid-April found Union forces closing on New Orleans and Corinth while McClellan crept toward Richmond. From Paris, the war could look either endless or nearly won, and French policy hung on the reading. Seward's steady letters gave Dayton the administration's version to press on the French foreign ministry, week after week. A steamer's sailing day set the legation's week, and Dayton wrote against that clock.
frus-1862-d366:
William H. Seward, as Secretary of State, addressed Henri Mercier again on 26 May 1862. In a letter printed as Document 366 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The two letters of that month show the channel in regular use.

Late May 1862 found the war's armies closing on Richmond and Corinth, while France reinforced its army in Mexico. Mercier, back from his Richmond trip, remained Seward's daily problem and partner in the French file. Letters like this one handled the steady business between them, case by case, in a formal and watchful tone. Mercier had served in Washington since 1860 and knew the capital's politics at close range.
frus-1862-d466:
On 8 October 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to George Perkins Marsh, the American minister in Turin. The dispatch is Document 466 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

With Antietam fought and the emancipation order published, Seward's October instructions carried a new confidence to friendly courts. Italy's government read the American war as a fellow struggle for national unity, and Marsh was the right man to press that parallel. The order belongs to the autumn campaign of paper fought by the Union that year. By it, a drawn battle in Maryland became diplomatic gains across Europe. The gains came one legation at a time.
frus-1862-d566:
On 3 April 1862 Henry Shelton Sanford sent this report from Brussels to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is Document 566 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

Sanford wrote two days before the battle of Shiloh opened the war's bloodiest spring. From Brussels he surveyed the European scene for Seward: the courts' tempers, the press's tone, and the movements of Confederate emissaries. Belgium's King Leopold was a confidant of Queen Victoria, which made gossip from Brussels unusually well sourced. A report of this kind had value out of proportion to the size of the post. The letter is part of the spring file in which Sanford established himself as one of Seward's most useful eyes in Europe.
frus-1862-d66:
Seward wrote again on 19 May 1862, this time to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It was printed as Document 66 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. It was written in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d666:
Washington spoke straight to Japan's court in this formal note from Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 5 March 1862. The note went from Washington to the shogun's court without passing through the American legation's hands as a report. It is document 666 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Formal notes of this kind fixed the terms on which two governments dealt with each other. Seward had written to the same ministers the summer before, and this letter kept that direct line warm. In a file full of one envoy's reports, such notes stand apart. They show the United States speaking in its own name to a court it had known for less than ten years.
frus-1863p1-d166:
On 23 April 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward for the second time that day. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 166 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The second sheet of Adams's pair held the rest of the day's London news, split off for clean filing at home. His April mail is a close chart of Britain's turn on the ship question. This letter is the mate to document 165. Together the pair closes the legation's mail for the week, in the split-sheet habit that marks the whole file.
frus-1863p1-d266:
A dispatch dated 21 August 1863 carried news from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It is document 266 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers. It was one of 4 letters between the same men dated that day.

Union wins at Gettysburg and Vicksburg in early July 1863 weakened the case for aiding the South. British leaders grew more careful, and Adams's post grew a little less tense. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d366:
One of Lord Lyons's regular notes to the State Department, this paper to Secretary of State William H. Seward is dated 20 January 1863. It appears as document 366 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Taken as a run, these notes chart Britain slowly accepting that the Union would not collapse. That judgment, formed in Washington, helped keep Britain out of the war. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d466:
A dispatch dated 17 April 1863 went from Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington to Secretary William H. Seward. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d566:
From Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington: a letter dated 10 June 1863. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d66:
On 29 January 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward for the second time that day. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 66 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Paired sheets let Adams keep one point per page, so Seward's clerks could file each part cleanly. The pair of 29 January closed the legation's mail for the month. This letter is the second of them. Read with its mate, it shows the tight back-and-forth that bound the Union's cause in Britain to two men's pens. The orders it would soon draw back complete the loop.
frus-1863p1-d666:
The 17 November 1863 mail between Washington and London included a letter from William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. Mail between London and Washington crossed the Atlantic by steamer, so each reply took weeks to complete the round trip.

Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d166: British members of the Moscow Conference's committee on Iran wrote a memorandum dated October 25, 1943, preserved as Document 166 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Iran, crossed by Allied supply lines to Russia, had its own committee at Moscow, and this paper states the British members' hand. The American committee members answered in kind the next day. The memorandum is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d266:
The foreign callers who visited President Roosevelt at Cairo on the afternoon of 24 November 1943 are listed in an editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume. The names come from the President's Log, with additions from Admiral Leahy's account, and the calls appear to have been brief and mainly courteous in nature.

Egyptian leaders came first, then King George II of Greece with Prince Paul, British commanders from Egypt, and King Peter II of Yugoslavia with his prime minister. Leahy adds Turkey's prime minister and Britain's ambassador to Turkey. No memoranda were made of any of the talks. King Peter's own book later described his conversation, which ranged over reconciling Tito and Mihailović and the case for Allied landings on a fixed date.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d366:
Charles Bohlen's minutes record the second plenary session at Tehran, on 29 November 1943 at four in the afternoon. With no set agenda, Roosevelt calls for reports from the military staffs who had met that morning, and Brooke, Marshall, and Voroshilov speak in turn.

Brooke reports the committee ranged over Italy, Yugoslav aid, Turkey and the Dardanelles, a southern France operation alongside Overlord, and the bombing of Germany, without finishing its work. Marshall stresses that landing craft, above all those carrying forty tanks, are the choke point, while a million tons of supplies already sit in England on schedule. Then Stalin asks who will command Overlord. Told it is undecided, he warns that nothing will come of the operation unless one man is made responsible for both its preparation and its execution.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d466:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull cabled President Roosevelt on December 2, 1943, while the President was traveling between the Tehran and Cairo conferences. Hull had stayed in Washington, so the State Department's part in the summit season ran through messages like this one. The cable appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

Hull was the administration's senior diplomat, fresh from the Moscow foreign ministers' meeting that had prepared the way for Tehran. His cables kept the traveling President tied to the department and to the questions waiting at home. For readers, the message shows how much of wartime diplomacy was done by wire, across thousands of miles.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d566:
Harry Dexter White wrote this third memorandum on September 13, 1944, while the Second Quebec Conference was meeting. White's Treasury work fed directly into that conference, where the treatment of postwar Germany was fiercely debated. The memorandum appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

A White paper dated during Quebec sits close to one of the war's most argued episodes: the Morgenthau Plan for Germany's economy, which the Treasury championed and others resisted. Readers should treat the date and desk as the story here. The memorandum shows staff work arriving at a summit in real time, as the economic peace was fought over.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d66: Edward Stettinius, the Acting Secretary of State, wrote to President Roosevelt on October 28, 1943, while Hull was still abroad. The letter is Document 66 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Stettinius minded the State Department at home during the secretary's Moscow trip, and his letters kept the president current. The record names the parties and the date. Its business is stated only in the printed Foreign Relations text.
frus-1944-quebec-d166:
Operations for the defeat of Japan in 1944–45 are scheduled in C.C.S. 417/8, issued by the United States Chiefs of Staff on September 9, 1944. The agreed objective was Japan's unconditional surrender, forced by blockade and bombardment and by invading her industrial heart. The paper lays out a dated course of action for planning across the Pacific.

The schedule runs from Talaud in October 1944 through Leyte that December, then Formosa or Luzon in early 1945. The Bonins, Ryukyus, and the China coast follow, with southern Kyushu in October 1945 and the Tokyo Plain in December. Every effort, it adds, should bring the Soviet Union into the war at the earliest practicable date. Events overtook several target dates during the conference itself.
frus-1944-quebec-d266:
C.C.S. 676, presented September 12, 1944, compiles the area commanders' reports on Pacific operations from November 1943 to September 1944. In the Central Pacific, amphibious forces had successively taken the Gilberts, including hard-defended Tarawa, then the Marshalls, then Saipan, Tinian, and Guam in the Marianas. The Palaus operation was scheduled for September 15.

The report records the Philippine Sea engagement, where carrier aircraft inflicted severe damage on the Japanese fleet during the Marianas operation. It praises the submarine campaign's heavy toll on Japanese shipping. The Marianas, it notes, offered bases for very-long-range bombers against Japan proper, with preparations underway at full speed. Northern Pacific operations were limited to raids on the Kuriles.
frus-1944-quebec-d66:
President Roosevelt addressed this message to Secretary of the Treasury Henry Morgenthau on September 12, 1944, the opening day of the Quebec Conference. Morgenthau had come to Quebec with the plan for Germany that bears his name. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Morgenthau proposed stripping Germany's industry to keep it harmless, a plan that split the American government and startled the British. A presidential message to him on day one sits at the center of the conference's most famous controversy. For readers, it is a direct thread to the Morgenthau Plan episode, told from inside the President's own party.
frus-1945-50-intel-d166:
On 26 August 1946 the Seventh Meeting of the Intelligence Advisory Board sat, and the minutes of the session survive here. It stands as document 166 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. Central intelligence then sat with the National Intelligence Authority, a board of top officials served by the Central Intelligence Group.

Minutes trade color for proof: they may skip the tone of a talk, but they pin down its outcome. Staff in other offices then worked from this record, treating its lines as the settled word. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d266:
On 2 April 1948, staff wrote up the discussion at the 9th Meeting of the National Security Council for the President. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 266 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. With the Soviet threat in mind, the Council was deciding what secret work the United States should do abroad.

Where no stenographer sat in, a memcon is the meeting. It holds the talk in the words of the man who wrote it up. The note's date matters: made within days of the talk, it stands close to the event itself. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d366: On 14 February 1949, the Office of Reports and Estimates, Central Intelligence Agency put a memorandum into the files. It survives in print as document 366 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. It was a season of stock-taking: the CIA was a year old, and its friends and critics were both writing things down. A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top.
frus-1945-50-intel-d66:
Acting Secretary of War Kenneth Royall and Secretary of the Navy Forrestal wrote jointly to Secretary Byrnes on 6 January 1946. Two service secretaries signing together again signal a settled military front. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

In January the question was no longer whether a central intelligence body would exist, but on what terms the departments would join it. A joint letter from War and Navy to State set those terms from a position of unity. Readers can compare this letter with the joint letter of the previous September. The autumn letter opened a negotiation; the January letter nearly closes it, sixteen days before the president acted.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d166:
Rebuilding Poland and the Balkans gets a cool cost-and-politics survey in this briefing book paper. Prepared for the President's trip, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Its summary weighs American interests against the Soviet attitude, and finds one of the two easy to state.

American trade interests are general: an early return to many-sided trade, and a stable, thriving Europe. In politics, Washington probably would not fight a chief Soviet influence in the area, but it would not want its own voice wiped out. The needs are plain: better farm methods, rebuilt railways, new rolling stock, mended roads and bridges. American help would flow through Export-Import Bank credits, farm experts, and the proposed International Bank.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d266:
“Operations for the Defeat of Japan” states the allied design in a United States Chiefs of Staff paper of 22 January 1945. Numbered C. C. S. 417/11, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It was written for the combined staff talks at Malta.

The agreed aim is Japan's unconditional surrender. It is to be forced two ways. First, her ability and will to resist are to be lowered by blockade and heavy air bombardment. Her air and naval strength is to be destroyed. Second, allied forces are to invade and seize ground in the industrial heart of Japan itself. The American sequence runs through Okinawa, then further positions to tighten the blockade. Next comes an assault on Kyushu. Last comes the decisive invasion through the Tokyo Plain.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d366: General Antonov answered Admiral Leahy's invitation the same day, February 7, 1945, writing from the Crimea. He said he would be glad to meet the American chiefs on February 8 at three in the afternoon. The place would be the headquarters of the Russian staff. Antonov asked Leahy to name the persons who would attend with him. The reply is short and formal, given here in translation. Behind its courtesies sits a milestone: the first full staff meeting between the two armies on the Pacific war.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d466:
A joint announcement on the world body takes shape in this American draft of February 11, 1945. The Dumbarton Oaks proposals, it says, have been considered. Agreed proposals have been worked out on the major points left open there. The agreed views are going to the governments of China and France for their consideration.

Once those consultations finish, the proposals will be made public. Invitations will follow to a United Nations conference in the United States about April 15. That conference will prepare the charter of the general international organization. The draft, an unsigned carbon, still carries the earlier April date — ten days before the final one.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d66:
Harry Hopkins, the President's special assistant, sent this light personal report from London on 24 January 1945. It is printed in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences. Hopkins was traveling ahead of Roosevelt and had just met Churchill.

Hopkins calls his London visit very satisfactory and says he leaves for Paris the next day. He passes on Churchill's joke that ten years of research could not have found a worse place than Yalta. Churchill planned to survive it with plenty of whisky, which he claimed was good for typhus and deadly on lice. Hopkins ends with word that Watson was seasick as usual.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d166:
The State Department answered the British on the Turkish Straits in a memorandum extract dated June 23, 1945. The extract is document 166 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. London had urged a quick, firm joint protest to Moscow over Soviet demands on Turkey.

Washington declines to move that fast. Under the Yalta understanding, the Department says, it stands ready to discuss the Straits at the coming meeting, where the Soviet government will presumably present its wishes. Talks between Molotov and the Turkish ambassador seem to have been friendly and exploratory, so a protest now would be premature. Above all, the United States does not wish to appear to have decided the question before the heads of government meet. The full text is printed later in the volume.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d266:
The State Department set its Danube policy in a memorandum dated July 10, 1945. The memo is document 266 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It responds to SHAEF's telegram urging an interim arrangement for running the river, which had seemed urgent enough to raise at the Big Three meeting.

Before the surrender, Danube shipping under German control was moved into the American area. The Soviets claim some vessels never arrived and demand their delivery, the memo notes, while restitution is a question for the governments. Soviet commanders nearby have no power to strike local deals on shipping that mostly belongs to Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, and other river states. The attached recommendation backs SHAEF's plan: an interim Danube navigation agency, starting with the United States, Britain, and Russia, and expanding later to all interested states.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d366:
France divides Pauley from his own instructions in his cable from Moscow of July 5, 1945. Reading Washington's July 2 message, he finds agreement in principle on all main points but two. The sharpest is France. The Department urged that any new three-power percentage formula for reparations include a fixed share for France now.

France, though, had no seat at the Moscow conference. Maisky insisted the talks stay three-power, as the Crimea Protocol provided. Pauley, Harriman, Ambassador Clark Kerr, and Sir Walter Monckton had all pressed Moscow to admit France, to no avail. Following Washington's suggestion, Pauley warns, would leave him in an impossible position.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d466:
Italy policy is put to President Truman in Grew's memorandum of June 18, 1945, on the principal questions in the treatment of Italy. In the twenty months since Italy became a co-belligerent, Grew writes, the United States has sought to promote Italian political and economic well-being. It did so in acknowledgment of Italy's very real contributions to the war.

A soundly democratic Italy, the memorandum argues, matters for general European security and stability. The program's purposes enjoy wide support in American public opinion, but the measures taken have been inadequate to serve them. Grew asks approval for more vigorous, realistic planning, in politics and economics alike, with detailed recommendations to follow.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d566:
Ambassador Alexander Kirk sent a long secret report from Caserta on June 22, 1945. Extracts of it form document 566 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It describes General Morgan's return with the signed Duino deal on Venezia Giulia.

Morgan wanted a meeting to explain the text before handing over a copy. He said the talks were hard and took give and take to get General Jovanovic to sign. Kirk told him the deal would get a cold welcome in Washington. It must not be let to weaken the Belgrade agreement, Kirk warned. He foresaw only trouble in Trieste and urged firmness, top staff, and more security forces in the zone.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d66:
Robert Murphy, the political adviser for German affairs, reported to H. Freeman Matthews in Washington on June 15, 1945. His secret telegram from Paris is document 66 in the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. It carries early news of how the physical setup for the Berlin conference would be worked out with the Russians.

Murphy relays that Eisenhower is sending a group of officers and men to Berlin on June 17 for a first meeting with Marshal Zhukov's representatives. They will plan housing, communications, the entry of American troops and supplies as U.S. forces pull out of the Russian zone, and security. General Deane in Moscow is asked to find out if Zhukov will name people to take part. Summit logistics, the telegram shows, began on the ground weeks ahead.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d666:
London ambassador Winant sent a brief secret update on Tangier on July 5, 1945. It is document 666 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Washington had just explained its July 2 answer to Moscow's demand for a seat at the talks.

The Foreign Office's offhand reaction, Winant reports, was blunt. The Soviet Union would probably have to be brought into the Tangier discussions after all. One awkward feature stood out for London. Other signatories of the 1923 statute had not been invited either. Winant names the Dutch, the Belgians, and the Portuguese. The short wire captures a plan unraveling in real time. A three-power talk meant to move fast was turning into a wider negotiation no one had planned.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1066:
Prime Minister Churchill circulated this secret memorandum on Greece at Potsdam on July 22, 1945. A Soviet memorandum had raised the Greek question, and Churchill answers it with two attached reports. One comes from Field Marshal Alexander. The other records a visit to Greece by a British trades union delegation, led by Sir Walter Citrine.

Churchill says the union report gives a true picture of the rights and wrongs in Greece. He takes issue with the Soviet phrase representatives of Greek democracy. The EAM-ELAS elements, he argues, in no way speak for most Greeks. Their attempt to seize Athens last winter opened a gulf with the Greek people that will last for years.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1166:
Assistant Secretary Dunn wrote to Novikov, secretary of the Soviet team, on 27 July 1945. Four days earlier Novikov had written to him. The exchange shows routine business flowing between the two staffs through their secretaries' channel.

Such notes arranged the talks' daily life: papers passed, times fixed, points clarified. They are the answered mail that summits run on. This reply completes a pair in the record, Soviet note and American answer. It is a small proof that, mid-bargaining, the staffs still kept the courtesies and the machinery in working order.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1266:
The Secretariat of the Combined Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum on 23 July 1945. The Combined Chiefs were the joint British-American body that directed the Western war effort. Their secretariat kept its papers, minutes, and flow of work in order.

A secretariat note put shared analysis on paper so the combined chiefs could decide. It speaks for the joint machine rather than one nation. This memorandum dates from the summit's second week, when the combined staff was planning the war's last phase. It is the alliance's joint staff thinking aloud, in the form its own clerks gave it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1366:
George Allen sent another paper to Assistant Secretary James Dunn on 19 July 1945. It comes early in the run of Allen and Dunn exchanges printed in the volume. Allen's office covered the Near East and Africa. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Dunn chaired the committee that joined State, War, and Navy, so he read regional papers with an eye to the whole government. Allen's note reached him two days into the Potsdam talks. For readers, this early paper helps set the terms of the longer exchange that follows in the volume. What the Near East desk wanted. What the center was willing to hear, as the summit began.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-166:
Charles Yost, executive secretary of the conference's Central Secretariat, wrote this memorandum on August 7, 1945. The Potsdam Conference had closed five days earlier. The Central Secretariat had run the meeting's paper flow: texts, records, and copies for three governments. Yost's memo belongs to the wrap-up work printed in the second Potsdam volume.

After-action papers have their own worth. They tie loose ends while memory is fresh. Yost wrote as the man who had watched every document pass. Readers get a view of the conference as a working system, not just a stage. The memo helps explain how so much paper became an orderly record.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-66:
Benjamin Cohen's notes on the plenary session of July 22, 1945, run in compressed parallel to Thompson's minutes. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Cohen catches the opening exchange and the long report debate that followed.

Stalin announces that the withdrawal of Soviet troops from Vienna's northern zones has begun. It should be completed in a few days, he says. Churchill answers that the British government is pleased at the prompt action, and Truman adds that the American government is too. Eden then reads the foreign secretaries' report. On the U.S. paper for southeastern Europe, Cohen notes, the British agreed but the Soviets could not. The provisions on reorganizing governments and on elections were the sticking points. Press access and control commission practice went to a subcommittee, and the German economic principles were accepted save for one paragraph's wording.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d766:
The Economic Subcommittee issued its report on July 24, 1945, as document 766. The report gathered the group's work for the conference's senior levels. Economic officers had spent a week on the settlement's material base. Their findings now moved upward. The report joined the second Potsdam volume.

A subcommittee report marks the point where detail meets power. Experts state what they could agree and what they could not. Leaders then choose. Readers see both halves of that act in one text. The document stands as a key piece of Potsdam's economic record, the ground on which the political deals rested.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d866: William Clayton and Emilio Collado sent this short secret telegram from Babelsberg to Washington on July 21, 1945. Clayton was Assistant Secretary of State, and Collado headed financial policy work. They report that the British and Americans were pressing for joint financing of German imports, with imports ranked as a first charge. Soviet officials balked at that ranking, so the question went to the foreign ministers.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d966:
The United States restated its reparations proposal in the paper of July 31, 1945. It may have lain before the eleventh plenary meeting that day. Russian and Polish claims would be met from the Russian zone, plus two shares from the Ruhr.

The first share is 25 percent of surplus factory equipment, traded for equal value in Soviet food, coal, potash, and other goods. A further 15 percent would pass free. Removals must end by May 10, 1947, and the exchange goods by May 10, 1951. The Ruhr is defined by an attached map. The Reparations Commission, with France added, would judge what equipment is surplus.
frus-1947v05-d66: A third 1947 FRUS document from the Near East and Africa volume. The Acting Secretary's papers continued. This document holds that record. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
frus-1952-54v13p1-d666: A 1952-1954 FRUS memorandum by the Joint Chiefs on Indochina. The Pentagon weighed deeper involvement. This document preserves that memo. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
gao-gaoreports-b-295866: Satellite Services doubled its April 2005 protest — two dockets, one space fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Paired filings get one careful answer.
gao-gaoreports-b-296366: Dynamic Corporation took its June 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298266: Serco took its August 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Global firms get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-298766: R&D Dynamics Corporation took its December 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Research firms get the same fair hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-299266: Solec Corporation took its March 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Solar names get the same full hearing as everyone.
gao-gaoreports-b-299766: Lockheed Martin's maritime arm took its August 2007 contract fight to GAO — two case numbers, one sea-systems prize. The combined ruling sorts the defense giant's claims against procurement law. Naval tech deals draw the fiercest bid wars, and GAO's call is the harbor master.
gao-gaoreports-b-306666: The Forest Service's water fees got a fiscal ruling in this June 2006 GAO call, which tests the surface water management charges. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the fees were legal. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-b-310066: A 2007 ruling from GAO, the office that settles fights over federal contracts. Eggs & Bacon, Inc. said an agency picked the wrong winner, and this ruling lays out both sides plus the final call. Like all GAO protest rulings, it follows the rules Congress set for fair bidding — and it stands as a guide for future contract fights.
gao-gaoreports-b-310766: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by IVI Corp. The January 23, 2008 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts. The library keeps it as part of the public record.
gao-gaoreports-b-311266: This 2008 GAO ruling is about designated Employee Agent at Gloria Kortum. The decision answers a legal question about spending public funds. The library keeps it in the public record of federal fiscal decisions. The full text sits with this description in the library.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-166: Hemispheric trade talks stalled in 2005, and GAO's report says a missed deadline prompted efforts to restart the negotiations. The review tracks the diplomacy. The Americas' markets deserved the second chance. The efforts had to restart. The Americas' markets deserved the second chance.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-266: The FAA's tech blueprint was too flimsy in 2005, and GAO's report says a stronger architecture program had to guide the modernization. The report calls for a sturdier map. The skies' software deserved the planning. The architecture had to be strong.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-366: Medicare rehab labels needed sharper lines in 2005, and GAO's report says the sorting rules had to be clear. The review demands the precision. The patients deserved the fair labels. The criteria had to be specific. The patients deserved the fair labels.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-566: The IRS's 2006 budget ask got graded in 2005, and GAO's report assesses the request. The review puts the tax collector's wish list under the lamp. The dollars for chasing dollars were weighed. The assessment was delivered. The dollars for chasing dollars were weighed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-666: Military groundwater cleanup got a GAO review in 2005, and the report says the Pentagon used a range of remediation technologies. The findings take the measure. The report shows the tainted bases were being cleaned. The technologies had to be understood.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-866: Government data mining needed privacy compliance in 2005, and GAO's report says agencies took key steps, though significant issues remained. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the citizens' data deserved protection. The issues had to be resolved.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-966: Pay-for-results supply deals needed proof in 2005, and GAO's report says the Pentagon had to show the promised gains. The findings demand the evidence. The report warns that the supply deals deserved honest results. The benefits had to be shown.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-166: Private airport screeners were getting set up in 2006, and GAO's report says progress had been made, though more work remained. The findings balance credit and caution. The report warns that the privatized checkpoints needed finishing. The work had to continue.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-566: Grant paperwork was still a burden in 2006, and GAO's report says grantees had concerns with the streamlining efforts. The findings hear the complaints. The report warns that the simplification should actually simplify. The processes had to ease. The easing had to be real.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-66: The Pentagon paid billions in bonuses regardless of results in 2006, and GAO's report says award and incentive fees flowed despite acquisition outcomes. The findings follow the waste. The report warns that the rewards should follow the results. The fees had to be earned.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-666: Cheyenne Mountain's modernization needed better management in 2006, and GAO's report says more oversight changes were required for the effort. The findings demand the discipline. The report warns that the mountain fortress's upgrade could not drift. The modernization had to be managed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-766: Tracking sex offenders got a new data lead in 2006, and GAO's report says new-hire records had potential for updating convicts' addresses. The findings spot the tool. The report warns that the registry's addresses should not go stale. The data had to be used.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-966: The Army Corps' continuing contracts needed watching in 2006, and GAO's report says better monitoring and clear guidance would improve their use. The findings demand the oversight. The report warns that the water projects' deals needed daylight. The contracts had to be clean.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-166: Closing bases left toxic cleanup bills in 2007, and GAO's report says the cost reporting could improve and the land transfers should speed up. The findings press for action. The report warns that the shuttered forts should not stay fenced forever. The dirt had to be cleaned and conveyed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-466: Doctor pay had a geography problem in 2007 — GAO's report says Medicare's cost-of-practice map needed redrawing. The findings show the payment zones no longer matched reality. The report argues that where a doctor heals should not warp what healing pays.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-66: Veterans' mental health money fell short in 2007, and GAO's report says spending on the strategic plan's initiatives lagged far behind. The findings document the gap. The report warns that the invisible wounds needed visible funding. The dollars had to reach the distressed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-866: The Navy's floating giant was busting its budget in 2007 — GAO's report says building the carrier Gerald R. Ford on budget looked grim. New tech and rosy estimates collided on the biggest ship ever attempted. The findings are a case study in how defense megaprojects drift from the dock of affordability.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-166: This 2007 GAO report audits the tax collector itself — the IRS's own books for 2007 and 2006. An outside audit team dug into its accounts, cash controls, and money reports. The report hands down a formal grade plus any big flaws found: a yearly physical for the agency that touches every paycheck in America.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-266: From the Government Accountability Office's 2007 series, this report analyzes how the IRS uses third-party information returns — the W-2s, 1099s, and similar forms filed by employers and banks. It tallies what it costs to collect and match those forms against tax returns, and measures how much revenue that matching recovers. The findings weigh the efficiency of one of the tax system's most powerful compliance tools.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-366: The Government Accountability Office dug into chemical and Biological Defense: DOD and VA Need to Improve Efforts to Identify and Notify Individuals Potentially Exposed during Chemical and Biological Tests in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-466: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands: Pending Legislation Would Apply US Immigration Law to the CNMI with a Transition Period. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-566: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on value-Added Taxes: Lessons Learned from Other Countries on Compliance Risks, Administrative Costs, Compliance Burden, and Transition. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.

Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-966: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on rebuilding Iraq: DOD and State Department Have Improved Oversight and Coordination of Private Security Contractors in Iraq, but Further Actions Are Needed to Su. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
ghayat-al-surur-fi-sharh-diwan-al-shudhu: Ghayat al-surur fi sharh Diwan al-shudhur, 1766. The Arabic commentary. This book preserves that manuscript. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Coming generations can find it. The paper lived through the years and remains here.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ClarkRamseyExec:
On October 31, 1966, Attorney General Ramsey Clark issued this order on the physical evidence of the Kennedy assassination. Acting under Public Law 89-318, it provides for the United States to acquire and preserve the items of evidence pertaining to the assassination.

The order was the legal hinge on which the autopsy materials and other exhibits passed into the National Archives under controlled custody. Preservation sounded simple; in practice it set off decades of argument over access, since the same law that saved the evidence also fenced it. The order is preserved as the founding document of the assassination archive's custody.
hiram-grand-master-key-1766:
Hiram, or the Grand Master-Key, appeared in London in 1766 under the byline of a member of the Royal Arch. The exposé covers both Antient and Modern masonry. That double coverage makes it a pivotal witness to the rival rituals of the Masonic schism, the great split that divided the English Craft in the eighteenth century.

Two competing Masonries stand weighed in a single key. Their words, signs, and charges differ in ways the pamphlet sets side by side. Readers of 1766 could compare what the lodges kept apart. Historians still use Hiram to date and distinguish the two workings. The Grand Master-Key unlocks less a door than a quarrel, and preserves both sides of it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lubelski-philip:
Philipp Lubelski (1788–1879) was a Polish physician born at Zamosc, and a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Herman Rosenthal and Max Rosenthal gives his life. He began as an army surgeon under Napoleon I, who made him an officer of the Legion of Honor. After the war he became chief physician of the military hospital at Zamosc.

From 1826 Lubelski lived in Warsaw and worked in private practice until his death there. The second half of the article turns to his son Wilhelm (1832–1890), also a physician in Warsaw. Wilhelm studied at Dorpat, Vienna, and Paris, served a children’s hospital in Warsaw, and published four medical works between 1861 and 1869. The entry thus records two generations of one medical family, the father honored by Napoleon and the son trained across Europe.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-manna-10366:
Manna, the food that fed Israel in the wilderness, is described in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. The name is said to come from the question the Israelites asked on first seeing it: what is it? Ebers instead derived it from an Egyptian word for food. The Psalms call it the corn of heaven.

The article gathers the Bible's details and wonders. Manna fell at night like coriander seed, and the ground looked frosted by morning. It was ground into flour and baked into cakes tasting of honey wafers. It melted in the sun, so it was gathered early. Each person ended with exactly one omer, however much he picked. Friday's portion was double, and it alone kept fresh over the Sabbath. Leftover manna on other days bred worms. The supply lasted forty years and stopped at Gilgal. The entry also notes Sinai's tamarisk sap, still sold as manna.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-massachusetts-1:
Massachusetts and its early Jews are surveyed in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906 by Cyrus Adler and Godfrey Morse. The record begins on May 3, 1649, with an allowance paid to Solomon Franco while he waited to return to Holland. Puritan intolerance kept numbers tiny for a century. The article notes a few names in Boston records and a baptism at Charlestown in 1702. It also notes Judah Monis, who taught Hebrew at Harvard from 1723 to 1760 after his own baptism.

Real settlement came with the Revolution. In 1777 Aaron Lopez, Jacob Rivera, and fifty-nine other Jews fled the British occupation of Newport. They planted a colony at Leicester and kept their customs strictly. The article also follows Moses Michael Hays, a Newport merchant who moved to Boston. He prospered in insurance and served four years as grand master of the Massachusetts Masons.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meir-of-clisson:
Meir of Clisson was a French Talmudist of the first half of the thirteenth century. Solomon Schechter and A. Peiginsky give him a few lines in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He appears in an extract from the “Pa'neah Raza,” preserved in a Halberstam manuscript. There he comments on a verse of Genesis. That is enough to class him as a Bible commentator of his generation.

Beyond that the entry offers an identification rather than a life. Gross, in the Revue des Études Juives and in his “Gallia Judaica,” takes this Meir to be the same man as Meir ben Baruch. That Meir emigrated to Jerusalem in 1211 in the famous company of French rabbis. His brother, the tosafist Joseph of Clisson, went with him. If Gross is right, his story ends in the Holy Land; the entry leaves the proof to the two works it cites.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mendes-mendez-1:
Mendes, also spelled Mendez, was a Netherlandish family carried from Spain to Portugal to Holland and England. Gotthard Deutsch and Meyer Kayserling trace it in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. It was one of thirty prominent families that left Spain under the aged Isaac Aboab and received Oporto from King John II. Driven out by the Inquisition, its members reappear. One is an Amsterdam synagogue-builder, one a Dutch consul in Barbary. Others are poets and a string of physicians.

The star is Fernando Mendes. He was professor of medicine at Coimbra and physician to King John IV of Portugal. Sent to attend Catherine of Braganza, Charles II's queen, on her journey to England, he stayed as her physician. In London he openly professed Judaism under the name Moses, and his daughter was born in the royal palace with the queen as godmother. In 1687 he entered the Royal College of Physicians.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-minz-10866:
Minz is a rabbinic family that carries Mayence in its name to Italy, charted in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board. Judah ben Eliezer ha-Levi Minz, settled or born in Italy in the fifteenth century, founded its most prominent branch; his cousin Moses was a rabbi back in Germany. Others bore the name without close kinship.

One namesake branch decamped from Milan to dodge its share of a 13,000-gold-piece levy owed the duke — a detail from Joseph Colon's responsa. Judah's line ran four generations of direct male descent, and at the start of the sixteenth century the Padua Minzes married into the Katzenellenbogens, Abraham Minz's daughter wedding Meïr Katzenellenbogen. The entry's family tree does the rest.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-b-benjami:
Moses ben Benjamin Wolf was a Polish physician who worked at Kalisz in the second half of the seventeenth century. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He is known not for his practice but for two medical books.

Both books were written in Yiddish, the everyday language of Polish Jews. The first, Yerushat Mosheh, appeared at Frankfort on the Main in 1677. The second, Yarim Mosheh, followed in 1679 as a continuation, printed at Frankfort and Amsterdam. The entry is a small marker of how practical medicine reached Yiddish readers in that age.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-najara-najar-ni:
Najara is an Oriental Jewish family from Najera in Navarre, found later at Algiers, Tunis, Damascus, and Gaza. The Jewish Encyclopedia article, by many hands, centers on Israel ben Moses Najara. Born at Damascus in the sixteenth century, he died as rabbi of Gaza. He was poet, liturgist, cabalist, preacher, and commentator at once.

Israel set his hymns to Arabic and Turkish tunes to draw Jewish youth from profane songs. His Zemirot Yisrael, printed at Safed in 1587, put hundreds of his hymns into the prayer books of many lands. His Aramaic 'Yah Ribbon Olam' is still sung on the Sabbath everywhere. Hayyim Vital attacked his bold imagery, but Isaac Luria defended the hymns.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathan-ben-meir:
Nathan ben Meïr taught Talmud in southern France. Herman Rosenthal and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in Trinquetaille in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. He also wrote notes on the Bible. His pupils and kin carried his name far.

Nathan taught both Nahmanides and Samuel ha-Sardi. Samuel later wrote the book Sefer ha-Terumot. Nathan was grandfather to Estori ha-Parhi, the famed traveler. Later teachers quoted Nathan as an authority on Talmud. His grandson cites a Pentateuch study from his hand. He also wrote Sha'are Tefisah, on goods seized against the law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neumann-abraham:
Abraham Neumann was a Russian rabbi of two capitals' reach. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Gerolzhofen in 1809. He died at St. Petersburg on Aug. 22, 1875. He studied Talmud at Fürth from 1822.

Neumann read theology at Würzburg and at Giessen. In 1843 he succeeded Lilienthal as rabbi of Riga. He served there for twenty full years. Prince Suvorov's friendship helped him reform district schools. He also drew plans for settling Russian Jews on land. In 1856 rabbis chose him to head a committee. Its memorandum sought better conditions for Russia's Jews. In 1863 St. Petersburg called him as its rabbi.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nittel-11566:
Nittel is the Judæo-German word for Christmas. Gotthard Deutsch wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It comes from the Latin Natale Domini. The French Noël springs from the same root. Moses Isserles notes a custom tied to the season.

Jews sent presents on the eighth day after Nittel. That day itself was called New Year in the custom. Card playing was also common on Nittel night. Some explained it as defiance of Christian solemnity that evening. The entry gives a plainer source for the games. They survive, it says, from old German merrymaking. The feast night simply kept its games among Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ofan-ofannim-11: Ofan is a part of the morning prayer of the Jews. Gotthard Deutsch wrote its short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The passage tells of praise sung by the hosts of heaven. Its first words name the ofannim, or wheels, and holy beasts. They rise with a great noise to praise the Lord. The thought comes from the first chapter of Ezekiel, where the prophet saw wheels by the throne of God.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-palestine-11866:
Palestine is the old land of the Israelites in Syria. Joseph Jacobs, Immanuel Benzinger, and Judah David Eisenstein wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It holds the land between the Jordan and the sea. It holds land just east of that river as well. The word is the Greek form of a Hebrew name.

In the Old Testament that name names the Philistine coast alone. It names the shore land south of Phoenicia, in short. The Greeks were the first to spread the name wide. They used it for the inland parts of the land too. Herodotus used the phrase for coast and inland as one. In time the short term took the place of the long one. Vespasian set the name on coins for the whole land.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-peace-offering-:
The peace-offering was a sacrifice that ended in a shared meal. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Louis Grossman wrote the article. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The offering came in three kinds, each with its own motive.

The thank-offering answered a clear act of God's kindness. The votive offering paid a vow after a prayer was granted. The free-will offering sprang from plain piety, with no vow behind it. Most peace-offerings were private, and guests shared the meat. Leftovers faced strict time limits before they were burned.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pestilence-1206:
Pestilence was the dread sickness of ancient Israel. Emil G. Hirsch and Schulim Ochser wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It was most likely the bubonic plague. In most cases the disease ended in death.

Moses warned the people that plague would punish rebellion. One plague under David killed seventy thousand in three days. The Mishnah set a clear test for the name. Three deaths in three days mark a small city. Nine deaths in three days mark a larger one. A stricken city must fast and pray.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pinhas-jacob-12:
Jacob Pinhas was a German Jewish editor at Cassel. Gotthard Deutsch wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in 1788 and died there in 1861. His father had been court painter to the Elector. The government trusted his moderate, honest counsel.

Pinhas trained as an artist, then turned to news. He joined the staff of Westphalia's official Moniteur. After Waterloo he founded the Kassel'sche Allgemeine Zeitung. He edited that paper until his death. He shaped the 1823 law organizing Hesse's Jews. An 1833 law he backed offered Jews full citizenship.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ponte-lorenzo-d:
Lorenzo Da Ponte was born Jeremiah Conegliano at Ceneda, Italy, in 1749. Cyrus Adler and Max J. Kohler wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He came from a known Jewish family of Italy. At fourteen he was baptized with his parents and brothers. His new name honored a bishop who protected him.

Da Ponte taught fine writing at Treviso and then at Venice. A sharp poem of his led to exile from Venice. He went to Austria and won the favor of Emperor Joseph the Second. The emperor made him poet to the court theaters in Vienna. There he met Mozart and wrote words for his operas. His libretti for Figaro and Don Giovanni made him famous. Favor at court ended when the emperor died.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pringsheim-nath:
Nathaniel Pringsheim was a German student of plants, born in 1823. Isidore Singer and Max Cohen wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was schooled at Breslau and studied at Leipzig. At Berlin he took his doctorate in 1848. In Paris he gave himself to the study of plants. He died at Berlin in 1894.

From 1851 Pringsheim taught botany at Berlin as a private lecturer. His first known work came out that same year. It traces the growth of a small water plant. A larger work on the ground plan of plants followed. His studies dealt with algae and fungi most of all. The entry lists the books that made his name in science.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rameses-12466:
Rameses was an Egyptian city named in the Book of Exodus. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and W. Max Muller wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Exodus calls it a treasure city built by Israelite slaves. The Israelites also began the Exodus journey from there.

The article also treats the wider land of Rameses in Genesis. That land overlaps Goshen, where Jacob's family settled. The writers link the name to King Rameses II. They weigh canal work, new towns, and likely ruin sites. No stone record yet proved the city's exact place, they note. The entry shows scholars testing Bible geography against Egyptian remains.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ransom-12566:
Ransom of captives ranked among the highest duties in Jewish law. Wilhelm Bacher and Julius H. Greenstone wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The rabbis called captivity worse than hunger or death. Freeing a captive came before feeding or clothing the poor.

The article piles up Bible verses behind that duty. It warns that delay makes a person like a murderer. Even money saved for a synagogue could be used instead. Building goods for a synagogue could be sold for ransom. The entry then turns to hard cases with several captives. It shows a community rule where one duty outranks almost all others.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reinowitz-jacob:
Jacob Reinowitz, called Reb Yankele, was a member of London's bet din. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Wilkowisk, Poland, in 1818. He died in London on May 17, 1893.

The article says he became rabbi of his native town at twenty eight. He held that office for thirty years. In 1876 he became preacher to London's Talmud Torah. Chief Rabbi Adler noticed his learning and East End work. Adler then brought him onto the London bet din. That court decides questions of Jewish law. Reinowitz is believed to be Zangwill's Reb Shemuel. That figure appears in the novel Children of the Ghetto. The entry links a real rabbi to a famous book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ring-max-12766:
Max Ring was a German novelist, poet, and dramatist born on August 4, 1817. Isidore Singer and Joseph Sohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Zauditz in Silesia. He died at Berlin on March 28, 1901.

The article says he revealed poetic gifts at age eight. His school poem was called Der Judenkirchhof. He studied medicine at Breslau and Berlin. He took his medical degree in 1840. During a typhoid epidemic he treated Silesia's poor. He also described their misery in effective verse. Most of his writings were suppressed by the censor. In 1848 he moved to Breslau for literature. His first novel inspired Gutzkow's famous masterpiece, they say. He won stage success with a comedy and a drama.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenthal-harry: Harry Louis Rosenthal was an English Bible commentator born about 1860 at Vladislavov, in Poland. Joseph Jacobs wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Brought to Manchester as a boy in 1869, he returned to Vladislavov in 1878 to study Hebrew, then went into business. His one named work is Sod Kedoshim, a commentary on the prophecies of Daniel, printed at Manchester in 1895.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sabbath-and-sun:
Sabbath and Sunday asks why Christians stopped keeping the seventh day as Sabbath. Joseph Jacobs and Emil G. Hirsch wrote the entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Jesus and his disciples, it notes, kept the seventh day themselves.

The question grew sharp under Paul, as non-Jewish Christian communities rose. The party of Peter insisted on strict Jewish law for converts from outside. Paul protested against judging believers over feast days or Sabbath days. He called day observance a matter each person must decide alone. Meanwhile the first day gained longer worship and collections in Gentile circles.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samelsohn-juliu:
Julius Samelsohn was a German ophthalmologist born at Marienburg on April 14, 1841. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He took his medical degree in 1864 and settled at Cologne in 1867.

Samelsohn wrote weighty essays on the eye for leading German journals. His study of testing the light sense in eye practice appeared in 1885. That work earned him the Gräfe prize in ophthalmology for the year. Other essays treat eye disease in spinal ailments of patients. One more examines the incongruence of the two retinas in sight.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schiff-13266:
Joseph Jacobs, Cyrus Adler, Schulim Ochser, Isidore Singer, Frederick T. Haneman, and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on the Schiff family. The Schiffs belong to Frankfort-on-the-Main. Their line reaches back to Jacob Kohen Ẓedeḳ Schiff, born about 1370. Few Jewish families can be traced so early with certainty. The name came from a house sign in the Judengasse.

Family rabbis include Maharam Schiff, who died in 1644, and Tebele Schiff of London. The entry's modern giant is Jacob Henry Schiff. Born at Frankfort on January 10, 1847, he emigrated to America in 1865. In 1875 he joined Kuhn, Loeb & Co. in New York. He soon led the firm in practice. His German ties drew German capital into American railways. The entry presents him as banker and philanthropist.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sebag-solomon-1:
Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Solomon Sebag. He was an English teacher and Hebrew writer. Sebag was born in 1828. He died at London on April 30, 1892. His father was Rabbi Isaac Sebag. Solomon was educated in the orphan school of London's Portuguese congregation. He later became master of the Sha'are Tiḳwah School.

When Ḥazzan De Sola died, Sebag filled in as reader at Bevis Marks Synagogue. In 1852 he published a Hebrew primer. For a long time it was the chief textbook for Jewish children in England. His Hebrew poems and odes for special occasions were also printed. The entry rests on the Jewish Chronicle of May 6, 1892.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shabbat-ha-gado:
Shabbat ha-Gadol, the Great Sabbath, falls just before Passover each year. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Rashi already used the name Great in the eleventh century. The name recalls a wonder tied to the first Passover in Egypt.

God told Israel to take a lamb on the tenth of Nisan. The lamb was a god to Egypt, so Israel feared revenge. Tales say Egyptians fainted, froze, or urged Israel's release instead. That tenth of Nisan fell on a Sabbath. The entry gathers those tales and explains why one Sabbath each year carries a special name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sherira-b-hanin:
Sherira ben Hanina, known as Sherira Gaon, led the academy of Pumbedita in Babylon. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. Born about 900, he came from gaonic families on both sides. His family seal was a lion, emblem of Judah's kings.

Sherira first served as chief judge of his academy. In 968 he was elected gaon, its head. He then placed his own son as chief judge. His responsa, his formal legal answers, spread his fame widely. His famous letter traces the chain of Jewish tradition. He boasted a lineage reaching back before the exilarch Bostanai. He died about 1000, and the entry presents Babylonian Jewry's great spokesman.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-silva-joao-mend:
João Mendes da Silva was a Brazilian poet and attorney born at Rio de Janeiro in 1656. Isidore Singer and George Alexander Kohut wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He took his law degree at Coimbra in Portugal. Back in Brazil he married Lourenca Coutinho there.

The Inquisition repeatedly charged his wife with relapsing into Judaism. She was reconciled at an auto in 1713. A later auto condemned her to prison at its pleasure. She died, it is said, three months after her son's execution. That son was Antonio José, the martyred poet. After his wife's arrest, João followed her to Portugal. He practiced law there jointly with Antonio for years. The Inquisition seized Antonio in 1726, ending their partnership. João died at Lisbon in 1736, his own poems now lost.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sin-11766:
Sin, in Jewish teaching, means willful disregard of God's commands. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Those commands came through Moses and were explained by the rabbis. Sin here covers wrongs against God above all. It can also cover wrongs against society or a single person.

The article sorts sin into three grades of weight. The lightest is a fault done in ignorance of a rule. Next comes a breach done with full knowledge of the rule. The gravest is a bold, rebellious act against God. The high priest confessed sins in that same order on Yom Kippur. Sin, the article argues, harms man himself most of all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sinai-mount-137:
Mount Sinai is the mountain linked with the giving of the Law through Moses. Joseph Jacobs, M Seligsohn, and Wilhelm Bacher wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It stood in the desert of Sinai. Scholars think its name comes from Sin, the Babylonian moon god. The Bible also calls it Horeb and the mountain of God.

At Horeb, God spoke to Moses from the burning bush. Moses later struck water from a rock there. Israel camped before the mountain to receive the commandments. For three days the people prepared for that solemn hour. Then cloud, smoke, lightning, and trumpet blasts covered the peak. The article traces each of these events in turn.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-ben-jos:
Solomon ben Joseph ibn Ayyub of Granada was a Spanish physician. Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He lived at Béziers in the mid-thirteenth century. Notables of Béziers asked him to translate works from Arabic. He rendered them into Hebrew for Jewish readers there.

He translated Maimonides' Sefer ha-Mizwot into Hebrew. He also translated Averroes on Aristotle's De Coelo. A medical poem by Avicenna was another of his translations. He wrote an original medical work on hemorrhoids as well. That work is called Ma'amar ba-Tehorim. It survives in a Paris manuscript to this day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-strakosch-morit:
Moritz Strakosch was an Austrian pianist, singer, and impresario born at Brünn in 1825. Isidore Singer and Joseph Sohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. At age eleven he played a Hummel concerto in public. His success won his father's leave for an artistic career. He died at Paris on October 9, 1887.

Strakosch toured Germany, then studied singing in Italy. Around 1848 he crossed to America and met Salvator Patti. In 1850 he married Amelia Patti, sister of Adelina. Young Adelina Patti toured and sang under his care. In 1859 he ran Italian opera in New York. He arranged Patti's New York debut that November. He later brought Christine Nilsson to American concert stages. The entry profiles the manager behind two famous sopranos.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-synod-of-usha-1:
The Synod of Usha was a rabbinic council held in Galilee. Wilhelm Bacher and Samuel Krauss wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Usha sat near Shefar'am, Tiberias, and Sepphoris. The Sanhedrin sometimes met in that small city. Rabbi Judah ben Baba ordained disciples there.

The council met in the middle of the second century. Persecution under Hadrian drove the court from place to place. Antoninus Pius lifted Hadrian's anti-Jewish laws about 140. After that repeal the synod gathered openly with festivities. Judah ben Baba had died a martyr for his ordinations. So the open meeting must postdate the repeal. Rabbinic sources give mixed accounts of the event. The entry dates the gathering by that careful logic.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-therapeut-greek:
The Therapeutae were Jewish ascetics living near Alexandria on Lake Mareotis. Kaufmann Kohler wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Philo alone recorded their life, in his work on the contemplative life. Eusebius later claimed they were Christian monks. Some scholars even doubted Philo's book itself.

Recent experts defended both Philo and the group's Jewish character. The name means worshipers of God. It matched titles used by Jewish religious guilds. The group seems to branch from the Essene brotherhood. Diaspora Judaism bred many such ways of life. Some of them later helped shape the Christian Church. The article weighs the long scholarly fight in detail.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tower-hebr-1446:
Towers in the Bible served as watch posts, defenses, and symbols of strength. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Vineyards held round watch-towers for their guards. Such towers still stand in the fields of Judea. Shepherds built towers for flocks in the desert.

King Uzziah raised desert towers for his great herds. Dwellings gathered around towers and grew into settlements. City walls carried towers at gates and corners. Jerusalem's walls were rich in such defenses. The tower of Phasael survives in the modern citadel. A citadel tower, the migdol, stood at a city's highest point. It was the last refuge when walls were stormed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-veneziani-emman:
Emmanuel Felix Veneziani was a French philanthropist. He was born at Leghorn in 1825 and died at Paris in 1889. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. Veneziani first worked at Constantinople. There he managed the Banque Camondo. He also led the local Alliance Israélite Universelle committee.

After 1870 Veneziani worked in Paris with Baron Maurice de Hirsch. In 1877 he traveled through Turkey and Bulgaria. He brought relief to war victims of all faiths. In 1878 he pled for religious liberty at the Berlin Congress. He later helped Russian Jews emigrate from Brody. He also toured the Jewish colonies of Palestine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wertheimer-john:
John Wertheimer was an English printer. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in London late in the seventeen hundreds. He died there on December 18, 1883. He headed the firm of Wertheimer, Lea and Company. From 1820 he worked as a printer until his death.

His press issued many weighty books. They covered education, medicine, and language study. Most works needing Hebrew type came from his shop. Commercial reports also bore his firm's name. The Jewish Chronicle was printed there as well. The brief entry honors a tradesman behind many books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wodianer-philip:
Philip Wodianer was a Hungarian lay leader who headed the Jewish town group at Szegedin. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He held that post from 1793 to 1809. He gave the town group the land for its first synagogue.

He also gave silver vessels for use by the burial society. The entry then turns to his son Cosman. Cosman trained as a Talmud scholar in three towns. At Gyor-Sziget he ran his own school of forty to fifty boys. His notes on the Talmud stayed in draft for years. His son Arnold later brought them out in two books in 1890. So one entry holds three generations of one family.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yaroslav-jarosl:
Yaroslav is a town in Galicia known for a great fair. Herman Rosenthal and M. Seligsohn wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The fair drew the Council of Four Lands each year. That council ruled the Jews of Poland in those days.

At the fair the council judged the needs of the towns. Heads of schools met there to trade views on the Talmud. By the late 1600s Yaroslav led all towns in this role. The council met there once in three years at least. In 1671 fear drove the meet to a safer spot. That move was soon undone by the council itself. At that fair the council judged a famed feud of two rabbis. It gave its leave for new books at the same fair.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yemen-13166:
Yemen is the southwest part of Arabia with a long Jewish past. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Tales trace its Jews back to the days of Solomon. One tale says they came forty-two years before the First Temple fell.

A second tale sends a vast host there with Jeremiah. It says Ezra banned them when they would not return. The entry calls that tale a myth with no base in fact. True moves of Jews there start near the year 100. They thrived till the 500s by one good source. The long entry then tracks their kings, faith, and crafts. It is a full past of a far and lone Jewish world.
kardec-evangile-selon-le-spiritisme-1866:
Allan Kardec made L'Evangile selon le spiritisme the third book of his Spiritist canon in 1866. The text here is the Paris third edition of that year, revised and corrected. Kardec reads the moral maxims of Christ through Spiritism, his system of spirit teaching. Each saying receives an explanation drawn from mediums' messages.

Charity, forgiveness, and humility form the core of the teaching. Kardec presents the book as moral guidance for daily life. No nineteenth century English translation exists, the first coming only in 1987. The French text therefore stands as a documentary edition. Spiritists still treat this volume as their gospel companion. Its order is calm and didactic.
king-lear-pg2266:
Shakespeare's King Lear turns, in this passage, on a letter shown to Gloucester. The Bastard hands it over with care, saying he must not detain it. He claims he found it thrown in at his closet window. He hopes his brother's heart is not in its contents.

Gloucester reads a plot against fathers who hold back sons' fortunes. The letter says a father should sleep until his son wakes him. Then the son would enjoy half the father's revenue forever. Gloucester calls the writer an abhorred, unnatural, and brutish villain at once. He asks when the letter came and who brought it here. The Bastard urges him to suspend anger until better proof appears.
lafontaine-memoires-magnetiseur-vol1-186:
Charles Lafontaine tells his own story in Memoirs of a Magnetizer, Volume One, in French from 1866. The celebrated stage magnetizer tours towns and courts with his trances. Cases, triumphs, and quarrels with doctors crowd his lively account of a life spent proving the power of the magnetic sleep.

Lafontaine's shows helped bring mesmerism to Manchester and beyond in Britain. He writes as showman and healer in one flamboyant voice. Public wonder and private method mix on every page he gives. The volume opens the heroic age of mesmerism in the first person, told by one of its stars at the height of his fame.
lafontaine-memoires-magnetiseur-vol2-186:
