Lafontaine closes his life story in the second volume of his Memoirs of a Magnetizer, in French from 1866. More strange cases and triumphant tours fill the later chapters. Quarrels with the doctors run beside cures he claims for the trance, as the showman-healer looks back over a long and contested career.

He defends his art against science, church, and stage rivals alike. Old triumphs are polished and old scores settled in print at last. The tone stays bold, vain, and hard to resist throughout. Both volumes together give mesmerism's heroic age a human face, in the words of a man who lived it nightly.
lessing-laocoon-1766:
Gotthold Ephraim Lessing published Laocoon in 1766, and Ellen Frothingham translated it into English in 1873. The essay takes its name from the famous statue of the priest Laocoon and his sons in the grip of sea serpents. Lessing asks why the statue's pain looks so different from pain in poetry.

His answer draws a famous line: painting and sculpture work in space, poetry works in time. Each art, he argues, fails when it tries to do the other's job. The argument reshaped how critics in Europe judged both arts. Laocoon became the founding text of modern aesthetics, the study of how art works. Its clear reasoning still anchors debates about image and word.
lippe-text-book-of-materia-medica-1866:
Adolph Lippe stood for the strictest reading of Hahnemann, and his Text Book of Materia Medica of 1866 shows that stance on every page. Lippe listed the drugs homeopaths used, with the signs that point to each one. He trusted the proving record and little else.

For each remedy he stresses the characteristic symptoms, the odd, clear signs that mark it off from all others. His practice used one remedy at a time, often in very high potencies. Students of the strict Hahnemann school still read Lippe as the purest guide to that way of prescribing.
mahhabone-1766:
Mahhabone, printed in London in 1766, promises to open the Grand Lodge door. The anonymous exposé covers the three Craft degrees and adds the Royal Arch beside them. That addition gives the pamphlet its scholarly weight today, as early printed evidence for how the Royal Arch degree was worked in the 1760s.

The title is itself one of the Craft's guarded words, printed for every reader to see. Ritual questions and answers carry the candidate through each degree. Exposés like this one sold because lodges would not speak for themselves. Mahhabone preserves forms that official Masonry left unrecorded. Historians of the Royal Arch treat the little book as a key witness.
mark-twain-a-biography-volume-i-part-1-1:
Volume one, part one of Paine's biography covers the years 1835 to 1866. Albert Bigelow Paine wrote it with the Clemens family's blessing. The dedication honors Clara Clemens for upholding history over eulogy. An acknowledgment thanks the old friends who shared their memories.

These chapters tell of a Missouri childhood in Hannibal on the river. Young Sam Clemens sets type, dreams, and runs to the river. He pilots steamboats, then loses that world to war. West he goes, to mining camps and newspaper desks. By 1866 the humorist 'Mark Twain' stands nearly formed. Paine tells the making of him with love and fullness.
mark-twain-s-letters-volume-1-1853-1866:
Volume one of Mark Twain's Letters covers 1853 to 1866. Albert Bigelow Paine arranged the letters with his own comment. His foreword praises letters written with no idea of print. Such letters, he says, reflect the soul of the writer.

The writer here is young Sam Clemens, still becoming Mark Twain. Letters home tell of printing offices, river towns, and the far West. He jokes with his mother and brother through every change of luck. Steamboats, mining camps, and raw newspaper work fill the years. The voice is already his: restless, funny, and confiding. Readers watch a great American humorist invent himself.
memoires-d-un-magnetiseur-suivis-de-l-ex: Charles Lafontaine wrote Memoires d'un Magnetiseur, printed in 1866. He also wrote L'Art de Magnetiser and ran a journal on the art. A phrenological study of him, by Doctor Castel, follows the memoirs. Germer-Bailliere sold the book in Paris, and Lafontaine sold it in Geneva. The hosted sample preserves the title page only, in French. No readable chapter text appears in it, so this note stays with those front page facts.
memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-and-o:
Volume seven of Saint-Simon's memoirs opens at chapter forty seven. The death of D'Avaux, past envoy to Holland, starts the year 1709. D'Avaux first warned the King of William of Orange's plan on England.

Barillon, envoy in England, was believed instead, and the warning was mocked. Then Saint-Simon tells of Louvois and a window at the Trianon. The King saw one window was too narrow, and Louvois would not yield. Le Notre was made to measure it, with the King and minister at odds. The King forced the test, and the tale turns on one window's width. Court anecdote here doubles as a study of stubborn power.
openalex-w1916572066:
Martina Crispo, Alejo Menchaca, and co-authors ran this gene editing study. It appeared in PLoS ONE in August 2015. Myostatin is a gene that limits muscle growth in animals. Turning it off should promote muscle and body growth. Farm animals had seen little CRISPR editing work before.

The team made CRISPR guides matched to the sheep gene. They injected the guides into sheep zygote cells. More than two hundred injected zygotes were tracked in development. Their growth was compared with uninjected control embryos. The study aimed to create myostatin knock-out sheep efficiently. It brought precise gene editing closer to livestock breeding.
openalex-w1931066666:
G. Aad and the ATLAS team at CERN wrote this paper. It came out in a European physics journal in 2012. ATLAS must spot electrons well to do its work at the LHC. Rare signals, like the Higgs, hide in a sea of jets. The team checked the tool with data from 2010.

Decays of known particles gave clean tests of the tool. The team set how well it finds and grades electrons. They checked its scale, its sharpness, and its hit rate. They also checked how often it swaps a charge by mistake. Parts of the tool were lined up with care. These checks ground all later ATLAS work.
openalex-w2097847166:
Rami Kantor, David Katzenstein, Brad Efron and colleagues ran a global study of HIV drug resistance patterns. Their paper appeared in PLoS Medicine in 2005. HIV comes in several subtypes worldwide. Most drug knowledge came from one subtype. Treatment was expanding into regions with other subtypes. Genetic differences could affect resistance routes.

The collaboration pooled virus gene data worldwide. They studied two key virus enzymes that drugs target. Patterns in treated and untreated patients were compared. Subtype and treatment history both shaped the patterns. Some resistance mutations appeared more in certain subtypes. Surveillance must account for subtype diversity, they argue. The findings guide resistance testing as treatment expands.
openalex-w2253274866:
Carlos Falcón-Rodríguez, Álvaro Osornio-Vargas, Isabel Sada-Ovalle, and Patricia Segura-Medina published this review in Frontiers in Immunology in 2016. They examine aeroparticles, the mix of tiny solids and droplets floating in air, and their links to lung disease. Urban air pollution is a serious problem worldwide, and particle makeup decides much of the harm.

Particles arise naturally from sea spray, volcanoes, wildfires, and soil erosion. Human sources add traffic, industry, power generation, mining, and fuel burning. Some particles are emitted directly, while others form in the air from gases. The review follows how particles nucleate, condense, and clump into larger sizes, and how their composition shapes respiratory effects.
openalex-w2738161666:
Catherine L. Moyes, John G. Vontas, and Ademir Jesus Martins lead a large team reviewing insecticide resistance in PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2017. Their subject is the two Aedes mosquitoes that spread dengue, Zika, yellow fever, chikungunya, and Rift Valley fever. Spraying insecticides and removing larval habitats remain the main defenses against these viruses. Resistance threatens both tools.

The authors mapped resistance evidence for the four main insecticide classes across the world. Emerging resistance to all four classes appears in the Americas, Africa, and Asia. Both target-site mutations and faster detoxification drive resistance in the two species. Many regions still lack any resistance data, and test methods vary between studies. The authors call for wider sampling with standard methods and shared diagnostic doses. Without that, control programs may keep spraying chemicals their local mosquitoes already shrug off.
openalex-w2765824866:
André Coelho da Silva reviewed the book Becoming Critical in Educar em Revista in 2017, writing in Portuguese. The book, by Australian educators Wilfred Carr and Stephen Kemmis, came out in 1986. Over thirty years it became a landmark in education research. It shaped later work on action research and group inquiry in schools.

Carr and Kemmis wrote from three convictions, the review explains. They disliked how studies of schooling ignored the field's historical and philosophical roots. They rejected treating classroom practice as mere application of theory made elsewhere. And they wanted research that develops teachers professionally as it proceeds. The book attacks borrowing natural-science laws for human behavior as misguided. Its alternative reads actions through the meanings actors themselves give them. Silva's review introduces this classic to a new generation of Brazilian education researchers.
openalex-w2789006266: Timothy Richard Rebbeck, Tara M. Friebel, and Eitan Friedman lead the author list on this 2018 study in Human Mutation. Its title announces a worldwide survey of the mutation spectrum in 29,700 families carrying BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations. Those genes strongly affect breast and ovarian cancer risk. The preserved sample contains only a repository citation page and the long author list. No abstract or results survive in the sample, so the study's specific findings cannot be stated from the evidence kept here.
openalex-w2922904366:
Pablo Fresia, Verónica Antelo, Cecilia Salazar, and colleagues published this study in Microbiome in 2019. It reads all the DNA in water samples to survey the microbes living in beach water and sewage around Montevideo, the capital of Uruguay. Such waters can hold germs that resist drugs and threaten human health.

The team took samples from twenty coastal sites, covering both beaches and sewage outflows. Beach and sewage waters held clearly unlike sets of microbes, as expected. Sewage carried more genes, and more kinds of genes, linked to drug resistance and to causing harm. Many came from familiar gut germs and matched genes behind serious hospital infections reported in Montevideo. The team also found disease-causing strains known across the world.
openalex-w3005664566:
Aziz Bousfiha, Leïla Jeddane, Capucine Picard, and colleagues present the 2019 phenotypical classification of inborn errors of immunity in the Journal of Clinical Immunology in 2020. It is the bedside companion to the gene-based classification from the same expert committee of the International Union of Immunological Societies.

Since 2013 the committee has published this clinical version, grouping disorders by the signs and lab results a doctor can see. It now covers four hundred thirty single-gene disorders, including sixty-five new ones. Their outward forms range across infection, cancer, allergy, autoimmunity, and self-inflammation. For each of ten broad groups, the paper gives diagnostic flow charts built from clinical and lab features.
openalex-w3021969666:
Mark Roelfsema, Heleen van Soest, Mathijs Harmsen, and colleagues published this study in Nature Communications in 2020. It takes stock of national climate policies to judge how the Paris Agreement is being carried out. Under that pact, countries pledged their own emission cuts, called Nationally Determined Contributions.

The team built on a public policy database and ran a multi-model scenario analysis. For each large economy, they picked around ten adopted policies with the biggest expected effect on emissions. Together the modeled economies produce about two thirds of global emissions. If no action beyond current policies is taken, they project emissions will still rise substantially by 2030, though the policies do trim that rise.
openalex-w4410722266:
Riku Matsubayashi, Shiki Ogata, Taishi Ihara, and colleagues measure spin behaviour in the superconductor LaRu4P12. Their paper appeared in the Journal of the Physical Society of Japan in 2025. The material is a conventional s-wave superconductor with an even energy gap. How its spin susceptibility changes with magnetic field was unclear.

Theory expects the susceptibility to grow in step with the applied field. Testing that is hard, because the signal mixes with other effects. The team uses nuclear magnetic resonance on phosphorus and lanthanum nuclei. Those nuclei act as tiny local probes inside the material. The measurements clarify how spins respond in an ordinary superconductor, a baseline for judging stranger ones.
openalex-w7128963966:
Hiroki Nakano, Tôru Sakai, and Yuko Hosokoshi map phase boundaries for a spin-2 antiferromagnet on the orthogonal dimer lattice. Their paper appeared in the Journal of the Physical Society of Japan in 2026. The lattice is the Shastry-Sutherland model, a classic frustrated magnet. Almost all earlier work treated spin one-half.

In that case, strong dimer bonds give an exact paired ground state. Strong square-lattice bonds instead give simple Néel order. Between them lie exotic phases still debated. For spin two, research has been scarce. The authors use numerical diagonalisation on finite clusters. They trace where each phase wins as the bond ratio changes. The map guides future experiments on real spin-2 materials.
openalex-w7163065466:
Koichi Mitsudo, of Okayama University, led a 2026 chemistry study reporting a new way to make boranils, glowing boron-containing compounds built from an imine and a phenoxy part. The team's method uses an iodide promoter to strip a methyl group during boron attachment, a step they call demethylative borylation. With the right amounts of three common reagents, the synthesis ran highly efficiently.

The method also produced boranils carrying heteroaromatic rings and larger, extended versions with wide pi systems, the electron clouds that govern color and light behavior. The authors then studied the physical properties of the compounds they made. Efficient routes to such boron complexes matter because these molecules are candidates for light-emitting and sensing materials.
openalex-w7204793266:
Felipe Teles Bahia and Jaqueline Santos Teles Bahia released a Portuguese-language review in Brazil in 2026 on music therapy as an added intervention for Alzheimer's disease symptoms. Alzheimer's is the leading cause of dementia in older people, with cognitive decline, memory loss, and severe behavior and mood changes, and standard drug treatment cannot reverse neuronal death. The review covers studies from the last two decades.

Musical intervention acts on brain chemistry, the authors report, boosting dopamine and serotonin release and lowering cortisol levels. Music also encourages neuronal plasticity, works as a nonverbal channel of communication, and helps recover memories, greatly reducing anxiety, depression, and anger. They conclude that music therapy is a low-cost, side-effect-free, highly effective adjunct for symptom control and quality of life.
openalex-w7212071566:
Jeiciane Gleicilene Silva leads a team reviewing one class of immune cells and their role in lung cancer. The cells are myeloid-derived suppressor cells. As their name says, they hold down the immune response. Lung cancer still ranks among the top causes of cancer death in the world. Two forces drive its growth: the tumor hides from immune attack, and the tissue stays inflamed for years.

The team read recent studies on what these cells do in lung tumors. They tracked how the cells act, and what that means for care. A tumor that can switch off its attackers gains room to grow. It also gains cover against drugs that rely on the immune system. Work of this kind maps a target that new care may one day strike. It also warns why some strong drugs fail in the lung.
openalex-w7213106566:
Mariana Prieto Barbosa leads a team that sets two ways to take out the gall sac side by side. The old way uses small cuts and a scope; it is the gold norm for gall sac ills. The new way sends a robot's arms through the cuts. The team read strict trials from 2010 to 2025; eleven made the cut.

The two ways, they find, tie on safety. Harm, death, switch to open cuts, and ward time all match. The robot wins small points: less pain at first in some reads, less strong dope used, and a calmer load on the surgeon's frame. But its runs can take more time, and its cost towers. Their close leaves the scope on top for most, with the robot a rich tool for set cases.
openalex-w7213394766:
Alva Valéria Moro Labs, with the same co-authors, examines new teaching methods for special education students in Brazil. Their 2026 article brings together assistive technology and universal design for learning. It reviews public policy, teacher practice, and the role of technology in promoting fairness.

The study contrasts segregated and integrated views with a curriculum built for access and autonomy. It draws on historical-cultural theory, the social model of disability, and current universal design guidance. Brazilian laws and curriculum rules are set beside specialist support and regular classroom teaching. Real innovation, the authors conclude, comes from rethinking methods and attitudes, not from digital tools alone.
openalex-w7213408366:
Carlos Eduardo Cruz Lustosa and co-authors compare feed additives for finishing beef cattle in feedlots. Their 2026 narrative review sets ionophores against newer alternatives in the Brazilian context. Twelve studies and reviews from 2012 to 2026, plus classic sources, form the base.

Monensin remains the additive with the strongest evidence, improving feed efficiency by a modest average amount. Nearly all Brazilian feedlots use some ionophore, the authors note. Essential oils, plant blends, and probiotics matched or beat it on some outcomes, such as intake and rumen health. Evidence on weight gain was mixed. Alternatives look promising as a complement, not yet as a consistent replacement.
openalex-w7213663466:
Roberta Moraes Sá Lima and co-authors review what is known about empathy and school bullying. Their 2026 qualitative study searched Google Scholar, SciELO, and a health library for 2017 to 2026. Thirteen articles on empathy and bullying formed the final corpus, studied by content analysis.

Four themes emerged: empathy as a many-sided capacity, factors tied to bullying, empathy in prevention, and permanent school intervention. Empathy alone cannot stop violence, the authors stress. It works through perspective taking, emotional response, and the quality of relationships. Its contribution grows when joined to teacher training, inclusion, family participation, and conflict mediation. A school culture of protection is the wider goal.
openalex-w7214121466:
Maria Luize Leite Gois, as spelled in the sample, leads a review on the kangaroo method in neonatal intensive care. Prematurity is a global public health challenge, they note, with immature breathing, nerve, and immune systems driving intensive care admission. Nursing carries much of the daily care in that setting.

Their 2026 integrative review covers the last five years of literature. It asks how the standardized three phases of kangaroo care affect humanized assistance, clinical outcomes, and the premature newborn's development. Parental autonomy after hospital discharge is also assessed as an outcome. Skin-to-skin care is thus treated as a clinical and family intervention at once, not a comfort extra.
openalex-w7214149066:
Carla Carolyne da Silva Santos and Ariane Loudemila Silva de Albuquerque analyse a 2026 Brazil law against organized crime, with a critical eye. Their 2026 library and court study reads the law as a new legal landmark in that fight. Penal efficiency and penal populism in current security policy frame the critique.

Several tools are examined for straining constitutional limits. Preventive detention tied to listed crimes, voting limits for people held before trial, and an official presumption of criminal link all come under scrutiny. Unlimited civil asset loss actions and benefit bans are also questioned. Fighting complex crime does not legitimate dropping constitutional safeguards, they conclude. Courts must run constitutional and treaty-based control checks.
openalex-w7214607666:
Priscila Castro Cordeiro Fernandes led a second 2026 study from Uberlândia, Brazil, this one on breastfeeding and child health indicators during 2023 and 2024. More than three hundred caregivers of children under two, registered at basic health units, were interviewed. The team compared how long babies were exclusively breastfed with prenatal care, birth timing, well-child visit attendance, and use of urgent care services.

Longer exclusive breastfeeding lined up with completed prenatal care, births at a fuller term, and regular attendance at child health visits. Children breastfed exclusively for a shorter time used urgent care services more often. Taken together, the findings link shorter exclusive breastfeeding with poorer child health indicators. The authors reinforce the case for promoting and supporting breastfeeding inside primary care, where these families are already followed.
openalex-w7214621666:
Néfi Wilson Martins Santos led a team report, published in 2026, on a university outreach project that used play to teach young children about emotions. The project, called The Colors of Emotions, worked with a first-grade class of about thirty-five children at a public school in Manaus, Brazil, over four visits. Activities drew on familiar animated characters, a traffic-light tool for naming feelings, storytelling, and an emotions dance.

Observers recorded active participation, better organization during activities, and later use of the emotion traffic light in the class routine. One story session also addressed preventing sexual violence in childhood. For the university students running the project, the experience built skills in communication, planning, teamwork, and health education. The authors value playful strategies for opening talk about feelings, while noting that without standard measures or long follow-up, lasting change cannot be proven.
openalex-w7221007566:
Ana Maria Barboza dos Santos and four co-authors reviewed research on early menopause and Alzheimer's disease, publishing an integrative review in 2026. Alzheimer's affects women disproportionately, and the authors examine whether losing estrogen early, when menopause comes ahead of time, speeds the brain changes behind dementia.

From more than a hundred and fifty studies found, eleven original papers formed their final synthesis. Those papers link early estrogen loss to a weaker blood-brain barrier, brain inflammation, and reduced growth of new neurons in the hippocampus. That window of vulnerability favors the amyloid plaques and tau tangles of Alzheimer's. The authors propose reproductive history as a clinical warning sign worth acting on early.
openalex-w7221160366:
Altino Dias Sacawe, writing from Angola, examined how information and communication technologies can prevent the non-consensual sharing of intimate images on social media, in a 2026 article. Set in Luanda province, the study links digital security to human dignity, treating leaked intimate content as a form of digital violence.

Reviewing research, institutional documents, and legal instruments, Sacawe describes a problem fed by personal vulnerability, social habits, platform design, and weak institutions together. Digital literacy helps people protect themselves, but it cannot replace reporting channels, institutional response, and accountability for those who share the material. The article offers grounding for public policy and literacy programs in Angola.
petofi-translations-from-alexander-petof:
Sandor Petofi, Hungary's national poet, sings of love, wine, and freedom in these poems, Englished by John Bowring in 1866. Petofi died at twenty-six in the rising of 1848. His short life made him a hero as well as a poet to his people.

Bowring's versions carried the Magyar poet to English readers for the first time. Folk song rhythms and bold, plain speech mark the lyrics throughout. Joy and defiance stand side by side in his lines. Readers meet the voice that helped rouse a nation, in the dress that first brought him across the language border.
plos-pbio-0020366:
Susan R. Schwab, Jessica A. Shugart, Tiffany Horng, and their team found an odd source of immune targets in PLOS Biology in 2004. The immune system attacks cells that display foreign protein pieces, called antigens. Proteins are normally read starting from an AUG code in the RNA. The team showed some antigens start instead at CUG, with the amino acid leucine.

That nonstandard start means cells display more kinds of pieces than expected. Hidden starts could help explain how the immune system spots some infected or cancerous cells that lack obvious foreign proteins. They also widen the search space for vaccine design. The work is a reminder that the rules for reading genes have more exceptions than textbooks suggest.
plos-pone-0000066:
Ana Carmena, Stephan Speicher, and Mary Baylies studied a linker protein in the fruit fly in PLOS ONE in 2006. The protein, Canoe, also called AF-6, has a PDZ domain, a common docking module. The authors show Canoe binds a key protein in the Ras-MAPK pathway and ties three major signal routes together.

Ras-MAPK, Notch, and Wingless/Wnt signals each guide growth and pattern in embryos. A protein that touches all three can coordinate their timing. That kind of coordination is how embryos keep many instructions from clashing. The work adds Canoe to the list of hub proteins worth watching in development and in cancers where Ras signals run hot.
plos-pone-0000166:
Pierre Krystkowiak, Véronique Gaura, Myriam Labalette, and colleagues published this clinical study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Patients with Huntington's disease received grafts of foetal neural tissue into the brain, an experimental attempt to replace lost neurons. The authors report that some patients became immunized against donor antigens, leading to immune rejection of the grafts.

The brain was long thought to be partly sheltered from immune attack, but these results show rejection can still happen. The paper documents alloimmunisation in graft recipients and its consequences. For cell transplant therapies in the brain, it underlines that immune matching and monitoring cannot be skipped.
plos-pone-0000266:
Joseph J. Gillespie, Magda S. Beier, M. Sayeedur Rahman, and colleagues published this genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Rickettsia are bacteria that live inside host cells and cause diseases like typhus. The authors use plasmids, small DNA circles, from Rickettsia felis to gain insight into how the whole group evolved.

Plasmids move between bacteria and carry genes that can reshape a genome. Finding them in Rickettsia, long thought to lack them, changes the group's evolutionary story. The paper traces how plasmid genes fit into rickettsial history, with implications for how these pathogens gain new traits.
plos-pone-0000366:
Amir Ali Abbasi and colleagues wrote a 2007 PLOS ONE paper on the human GLI3 gene. The gene helps guide how body parts form as an embryo grows. Much of the DNA inside the gene does not code for protein. The team asked whether some of these stretches act as switches. Those switches would turn genes on in specific tissues.

Their study reports that conserved non-coding stretches inside GLI3 work as enhancers. Enhancers are DNA elements that boost gene activity. These ones act in certain tissues rather than everywhere. Results like these help map the hidden control layer of the genome, where small changes can alter development even when the protein itself is unchanged.
plos-pone-0000466:
Linley E. Watson and colleagues showed how anthrax toxins can cause shock, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Anthrax's deadliest phase often involves a sudden collapse of circulation. Working with rats, the team found that anthrax toxins induce shock by depressing cardiac ventricular function, weakening the heart's main pumping chambers.

If the collapse is driven by the heart rather than only by blood vessels, treatment thinking changes. Supporting heart function becomes part of countering the toxin. Mechanistic findings like this matter for biodefense medicine, where the goal is to keep patients alive after exposure long enough for antibiotics to work.
plos-pone-0000566:
Blanca Amengual and colleagues tracked a bat rabies relative through natural colonies over time, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. European bat lyssavirus type 1 is related to rabies and infects bats across Europe. The team studied its temporal dynamics and the survival of Myotis myotis bats in natural colonies.

How a virus persists in a colony without killing it off decides the long-term risk to people and livestock. Following real colonies across seasons shows whether the virus flares, fades, or smolders. Such ecology is the basis for bat conservation that also manages disease risk, rather than reflexive culling.
plos-pone-0000666:
Debbie A. Lawlor, Susan Morton, G. David Batty and colleagues asked whether a doctor's judgment in pregnancy echoes decades later. Their 2007 PLOS ONE study used a birth cohort of 11,106 people, followed for 245,000 person-years in total. Obstetricians had assessed each mother's physical health at the time of pregnancy. The outcome tracked was the children's cardiovascular disease risk as adults.

The title gives the result: the obstetrician's assessment predicts offspring future health. A simple clinical judgment, recorded once, carried signal about the next generation. That raises questions about what such assessments capture, from the mother's condition to her circumstances, and how far their reach extends.
plos-pone-0000766:
Sven Heinicke, Michael S. Livstone, Charles Lu and co-authors built a web database that matches genes across species. Many such databases were already online in 2007. To the authors' knowledge, none of them mixed results from several matching methods with facts checked by hand. Their tool is called P-POD, the Princeton Protein Orthology Database, and it appeared in PLOS ONE in 2007.

Orthology means genes in two species that descend from one gene in a shared ancestor. If a mouse gene is the match of a human gene, what is known in mice may apply to us. P-POD was made for working biologists, not just computer experts. Good matches, backed by hand checks, make cross-species claims safer to use.
plos-pone-0000866:
Najmus Mahfooz, Nataliya Turchyn, Michelle Mihajlovic and co-authors looked at why insect hind legs grow so much larger than other legs, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Big hind legs are a hallmark of insect history, yet the steps behind that growth were not known. The team studied the milkweed bug, a species where the third pair of legs is clearly enlarged.

Their work centers on Ubx, a gene that helps give body parts their identity. They trace how Ubx shapes both the extra growth and the varied forms of hind legs. The study links a single gene to a trait seen across many insect groups.
plos-pone-0000966:
Wai-Ming Lee, Christin Kiesner, Tressa Pappas and colleagues identified a set of unrecognized rhinoviruses in sick infants, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Human rhinoviruses are the most common human pathogens and the usual cause of colds. At the time, one hundred and one types were classed into groups A and B by their sequences.

The team found a diverse group outside that scheme, and show these viruses commonly cause respiratory illness in infants. Illness from rhinoviruses ranges from no symptoms to severe lower airway disease. A missed branch of the family tree means tests built on the old groups may overlook real cases.
plos-pone-0001066:
Daciana Margineantu, Christine Emerson, Dolores Diaz and colleagues found that blocking Hsp90 slows mitochondrial protein turnover, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Drugs that inhibit Hsp90, a major chaperone, change cells in many ways. Treated cells expand their mitochondrial compartment, the mitochondria fragment and condense, and in time their integrity fails and the cell dies.

The team focus on protein turnover inside mitochondria under that treatment. A slower turnover could explain the buildup and odd shapes. Hsp90 inhibitors are cancer drug candidates, so their full effects on the cell's power plants matter. Mitochondrial damage may be part of how they kill tumor cells.
plos-pone-0001166:
Malaria in pregnancy is dangerous for mother and child, and drug resistance in Africa has shrunk the treatment options. Linda Kalilani and colleagues ran a pilot trial in Blantyre, Malawi, reported in 2007 in PLOS ONE. They added either azithromycin, an antibiotic, or artesunate, a fast malaria drug, to the standard sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine.

The randomized controlled trial tested the safety and the benefit of the two combinations in pregnant women. New regimens are badly needed across sub-Saharan Africa as resistance grows. A pilot trial like this one checks whether a fuller trial is worth doing and how it should be run.
plos-pone-0001266:
Whether scientists disclose their financial ties affects public trust in research. Daniel Cook and colleagues checked how newspapers handle those disclosures, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They searched a news database for the top science stories published in 2004 and 2005 and conducted a content analysis. The database they searched was Lexis/Nexis Academic News.

The authors examined how often the lay press reported conflicts of interest behind the science it covered. Forthright reporting of financial ties is associated with public trust in the scientific enterprise, they note. Their audit measures how far short of that standard popular coverage fell.
plos-pone-0001366:
Corinne Rodgers and her co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2007 on waves of low nerve activity in the locust brain. These waves, called spreading depression, also occur in people. In humans they are linked to stroke, seizures, and migraine. The team asked whether stress before a wave could change how the wave acts.

The authors describe waves like these in a simple model, the nerve cord of the locust. They test how brief stress first changes later waves. The work gives a cheap and clear way to study a brain event that is hard to watch in people. It may help explain why some brains cope with such waves better than others.
plos-pone-0001466:
Gwenn Le Mée and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on toxic RNA repeats in fruit flies. Some human ills grow from RNA with a repeated stretch that turns toxic. One such ill weakens muscle and is tied to harm from these repeats. The team used fly models to test what drives that harm.

They varied both the length of the repeat and how much RNA the flies made. Neither trait alone proved to be the main driver of harm in their tests. That result shifts focus to other traits of the toxic RNA. It refines how labs should model this class of disease in flies.
plos-pone-0001566:
Torsten Ochsenreiter, Michael Cipriano, and Stephen Hajduk published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on RNA editing in trypanosomes. These parasites rewrite their power unit messages by adding or cutting letters. The edits are guided by small RNAs and are vital for the cell's energy work. Most known edits were of the deep, standard kind.

The team found a second, more varied kind of edit is wide spread too. These edits may add to the range of proteins the power units can make. A wider edit map changes the count of what these parasites can do with few genes. It also hints at how RNA editing first arose.
plos-pone-0001666:
Kenichi Yamahara and co-authors tested a combined cell transplant to restore blood flow in legs, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. In earlier work, the group had grown vascular progenitor cells from embryonic stem cells. Those cells could become both endothelial cells, which line vessels, and mural cells, which wrap and support them.

For this study they derived the matching human cells and transplanted both types together into limbs with poor blood flow, a condition called hindlimb ischemia. The full text gives the cell preparation, the transplant results, and the new vessel growth they measured. Using both cell types at once mimics how vessels form in the body. The approach may one day help patients whose limbs are starved of blood.
plos-pone-0001766:
Xavier Roux, Catherine Dubuquoy, Guillaume Durand, and their co-authors built a nasal vaccine candidate against a baby-threatening virus in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Respiratory syncytial virus causes bronchiolitis in children under two and is a growing public health concern. No safe, effective vaccine existed. The virus's nucleoprotein, a core component, had performed poorly as a vaccine part on its own.

The team packaged the nucleoprotein into sub-nucleocapsid nanoparticles and delivered them through the nose. The full text gives the particle design and the immune results. Nasal delivery suits a virus that enters through airways, and particle packaging can turn a weak antigen into a workable vaccine.
plos-pone-0001866:
Vera Rocha-Perugini, Claire Montpellier, David Delgrange, and their co-authors studied a protein that blocks hepatitis C virus entry in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Two to three percent of the world's population is chronically infected with HCV and at risk of liver cancer. The precise mechanisms regulating HCV entry into liver cells were still unknown, though several cell surface proteins had been identified as needed.

The team reports that EWI-2wint, a partner of the CD81 surface protein, inhibits hepatitis C virus entry. The full text gives the cell infection assays. Entry blockers are attractive drugs because they act before the virus is inside, and each new entry factor refines the target list.
plos-pone-0001966:
Mahan Azadpour and Evan Balaban tested how the brain hears speech-like sounds that are not speech, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Brain scans of speech often use fake speech sounds, and whether each sound counts as speech is set by what listeners say they hear. Brain results are then read through those labels, which can bias the science.

The pair asked whether the brain uses sound patterns from speech, called phonological patterns, without a person being aware of it. They tested this with complex signals that are not speech. If it does, labels based on reports alone are shaky. The study urges more care in how speech scans are designed.
plos-pone-0002066:
Giacomo Donati and co-authors studied a switch that flips gene tags from on to off, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Histone tails carry many chemical tags, placed in unlike ways in open and closed parts of the genome. Two tags mark early active chromatin, and a third marks inactive chromatin, setting up the split between used and unused genes.

The switch centers on NF-Y, a protein bound to promoters with a CCAAT motif. The team report that NF-Y drives a change from positive to negative histone methyl marks on those promoters. Such a flip could be how genes are shut for the long term.
plos-pone-0002166:
Yanjun Li, Erhei Dai, Yujun Cui, and co-authors refined a DNA typing method for the plague bacterium, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Yersinia pestis, the germ that causes plague, still circulates in parts of China. The team's method, called different region analysis, sorts strains by which chunks of DNA they carry or lack.

Here they widened the method to 23 such regions and applied it to 909 Chinese strains of the bacterium. The larger test checked whether the typing scheme holds up and what it reveals about how local strains adapt. Reliable typing helps track where plague strains come from and how they move.
plos-pone-0002266:
Olivier Hermine, Olivier Lortholary, Phillip Leventhal, and co-authors surveyed patients with mastocytosis about how the disease disables daily life, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Mastocytosis is a rare disease where mast cells build up in tissues. Its mild forms make up over 90 percent of cases, yet how its symptoms affect quality of life had not been well studied.

The team ran a case-control study comparing patients' self-reported disability with that of healthy people. They mapped which symptoms hurt most and how deep the impact runs. For a disease often called mild on paper, measured patient experience gives doctors and regulators a truer picture of its burden.
plos-pone-0002366:
Giovanna Ponti, Paolo Peretto, and Luca Bonfanti looked for new neuron production in the rabbit cerebellum, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In adult mammals, the birth of new neurons is restricted to a few brain regions, unlike in other vertebrates where it is widespread. In the mammalian cerebellum, new neurons were thought to appear only in the earliest postnatal days.

The team studied peripuberal and adult rabbits, whose cerebellum keeps growing late. They document the genesis of neuronal and glial progenitors in the cerebellar cortex at those ages. A late window of cell birth in a motor center revises the map of where adult brains can still build.
plos-pone-0002466:
In 2008, Skov and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Vibe Skov, Dorte Glintborg, Steen Knudsen, and others. Its subject is pioglitazone Enhances Mitochondrial Biogenesis and Ribosomal Protein Biosynthesis in Skeletal Muscle in Polycystic Ovary Syndrome. Insulin resistance is a common metabolic abnormality in women with PCOS and leads to an elevated risk of type 2 diabetes.

Studies have shown that thiazolidinediones (TZDs) improve metabolic disturbances in PCOS patients. Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002566:
A research team led by Wu reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Dongying Wu, Amber Hartman, Naomi Ward, and others. Its subject is an Automated Phylogenetic Tree-Based S mall Subunit rRNA T axonomy and A lignment P ipeline (STAP). Comparing small-subunit ribosomal RNA gene sequences underpins much of what is known about microbial diversity.

That holds for both cultured microbes and microbes that have never been grown in a lab. Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002666:
Min Zhao led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was amelioration of Streptozotocin-Induced diabetes in mice with cells derived from human marrow stromal cells. Authorship is credited in the record to Min Zhao and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Pluri-potent bone marrow stromal cells (MSCs) provide an attractive opportunity to generate unlimited glucose-responsive insulin-producing cells for the treatment of diabetes. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002766:
Asma Khalil led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was effect of antihypertensive therapy with alpha methyldopa on levels of angiogenic factors in pregnancies with hypertensive disorders. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Asma Khalil, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Antihypertensive drugs are believed to lower blood pressure in pre-eclampsia by direct or central vasodilatory mechanisms. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002866:
Published in PLOS ONE in 2008, research by Martin Voss and colleagues addresses mere expectation to move causes attenuation of sensory signals. The catalog record names Martin Voss first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. When a part of the body moves, the sensation evoked by a probe stimulus to that body part is attenuated. The summary also notes a further point. Two mechanisms have been proposed to explain this robust and general effect. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002966:
Vincent Plagnol, Elif Uz, Chris Wallace and co-authors warned in 2008 that many lymphoblastoid cell lines are far less mixed than assumed. These lab-grown lines from blood cells are used widely to study gene expression, including allele-specific work. Earlier results hinted a tenth of human genes show random monoallelic expression.

Extreme clonality means a line descends from very few starting cells, which can skew expression results. The PLOS ONE paper sets out the scale of the problem and its implications. Geneticists using these lines for expression assays need to account for it or risk false patterns.
plos-pone-0003066:
Daouda Sissoko, Amrat Moendandze, Denis Malvy and co-authors surveyed chikungunya infection on Mayotte for 2005 to 2006. Since 2006 the virus had re-emerged as a pathogen of global concern. Individual and household factors behind infection, and the scale of silent infections, remained poorly understood.

Their population-based survey measured seroprevalence, the share with antibodies, and risk factors on the island. Published in PLOS ONE, knowing how many infections passed silently changes outbreak counts and control plans. Household data show where transmission concentrates. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003166:
Joseph Donroe, Monica Tincopa, Robert H. Gilman and colleagues study child pedestrian injuries in urban Peru in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Road traffic injuries to child pedestrians are an important cause of death and disability in poorer nations. Yet prevention there largely draws on studies from wealthier countries, which may not fit local streets and habits.

Using case-control analyses, the team investigate personal and environmental risk factors for these injuries in children and adolescents. Readers get evidence gathered where the burden actually falls. Local data like this can shape safer routes, traffic rules, and school area design that imported advice might miss.
plos-pone-0003266:
Junya Hirokawa, Akiya Watakabe, Sonoko Ohsawa and colleagues map gene patterns across rat cortex in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The mammalian neocortex is subdivided into many areas, each of which exhibits distinctive lamina architecture. To investigate such area differences in detail, the team chose three genes for comparative analyses, namely RORbeta, ER81 and Nurr1, whose messages had been reported as area markers.

Using double in situ hybridization and a cortical box method, they analyse area-specific expression patterns. Readers get a finer map of how cortex areas differ in gene use. Such maps help link anatomy to function in the brain's outer layer.
plos-pone-0003366:
Rosalynn L. Ord, Adriana Tami and Colin J. Sutherland compare malaria parasite genes in Venezuela in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The authors present the first population genetic analysis of homologous loci. The loci come from two sympatric human malaria parasite groups sharing the same human hosts. They use full-length sequences of ama1 genes from Plasmodium vivax and P. falciparum. The samples were collected in the Venezuelan Amazon.

The title reports ama1 genes of the two species differ sharply in genetic diversity and recombination rate. Readers see two parasites in one place evolve by different rules. The ama1 gene is a vaccine candidate, so its diversity directly affects vaccine design.
plos-pone-0003466:
Borja Guerra and co-authors compared hunger signaling in men's and women's muscles in this 2008 study. Leptin is a hormone that reports body fat stores to tissues. It docks at receptors found on skeletal muscle. The team measured receptor forms, blood leptin, and insulin sensitivity by sex.

They also checked a brake protein called SOCS3 in the muscle. Levels differed between men and women in several of these measures. Such sex gaps may help explain unlike patterns of metabolism. They could also bear on why diabetes risk differs by sex. Muscle is a major user of blood sugar, so these gaps carry real weight.
plos-pone-0003566:
Marie Forgeard and co-authors linked childhood music practice to wider skills in this 2008 study. They asked whether instrumental training in childhood relates to other abilities. Some outcomes sit close to music, others far from it. Children with at least three years of training were studied.

That trained group outperformed peers on verbal ability tests. They also scored higher on nonverbal reasoning. The average training length was about 4.6 years. Sustained practice may sharpen powers well beyond music itself. Music training is common in childhood, so wide effects would touch many lives.
plos-pone-0003666:
Joan Y. Chiao, Nicholas E. Bowman, and Harleen Gill published this psychology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Men hold most top political posts, even where any elected person may serve. The team asked whether quick judgments from candidates' faces feed that gap.

Voters' snap reads of faces predicted how they voted in the study. Those same reads tilted by the candidate's gender, favoring some looks in men and others in women. The study shows a facial bias in voting that may help keep political power uneven between the sexes. The work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008.
plos-pone-0003766:
Alexander Vogt, Cecilia D'Angelo, Franz Oswald, and colleagues published this protein study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Fluorescent proteins from sea creatures are standard markers for filming living cells. Demand for better imaging keeps driving the search for new ones with fresh properties. The team found one in the deep sea.

Their green fluorescent protein can be switched on and off with light. That photoswitchable emission lets researchers highlight and track chosen molecules in a cell. The marker gives cell biologists a sharper tool for live imaging than always-on proteins allow.
plos-pone-0003866:
Eva Terzibasi, Dario Riccardo Valenzano, Mauro Benedetti, and colleagues published this aging study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The annual fish Nothobranchius furzeri lives fast and dies young, making it a handy model for aging research. One inbred lab strain shows exceptionally short life and fast-rising age markers.

The team analyzed new wild-derived lines of the species in captivity. They characterized survival and age-related traits in each line. Large differences in aging phenotype appeared between strains, a range that turns this tiny fish into a sharper tool for studying why organisms age.
plos-pone-0003966:
Lihua Tan, Paul Schedl, Ho-Juhn Song, and co-authors used fruit flies to trace Alzheimer's damage in 2008. Alzheimer's disease slowly destroys memory in many older people. A short protein piece called Abeta42 is directly implicated in it. Which genes and paths carry its harm stayed unclear.

Their PLOS ONE article reports the Toll to NF-kappaB path carries that harm in flies. That path is better known for fighting infection in the body. Finding it in brain damage links immunity and Alzheimer's in a new way. Fly results can guide which paths to check in human tissue.
plos-pone-0004066:
Solène Mine, Nicolas O. Fortunel, Hervé Pageon, and co-authors compared two skin cell types across aging in 2008. Skin strength rests on the dermis, the layer under the surface. The dermis holds two fibroblast types, papillary and reticular. Their separate roles in aging were poorly understood.

Their PLOS ONE article used matched cell pairs from the same donors. Aging changed papillary fibroblasts in function, but not reticular ones. That split view revises how skin aging is described. Treatments may need to target one layer's cells, not skin as a whole. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004166:
Harry Courtney and colleagues published this microbiology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Streptococcus pyogenes is a bacterium that causes strep throat and more serious infections. Its surface is water-repelling, a trait that helps it stick to surfaces and form biofilms. That trait comes mainly from lipoteichoic acid held on the cell surface.

How that acid stays anchored was not well understood. The team tested how the family of M proteins relates to this acid and to biofilm growth. M proteins are key surface proteins of the bacterium. Their findings tie the bacterium's grip and film-forming habits to specific surface parts.
plos-pone-0004366:
Philip Gingerich and colleagues published this fossil whale study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Protocetids are middle Eocene archaeocetes, predators ancestral to later whales, living 49 to 37 million years ago. They are found in marine rocks but retain four legs and were not yet fully aquatic. They are interpreted as amphibious animals that fed in the sea but returned to land, perhaps to rest and give birth.

The team describe a new protocetid whale from the middle Eocene of Pakistan. Their evidence covers birth on land, precocial development, and sexual dimorphism. The fossil fills a step in the whale's long route from land back to sea.
plos-pone-0004466:
Losing a gene called yata wrecks nerve tissue and shortens life in fruit flies, report Masaki Sone, Atsuko Uchida, Ayumi Komatsu, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cells keep tight control over where their proteins sit, using tiny internal sacs to move them around. Two proteins that ride this system in flies are APPL, a relative of a human Alzheimer's protein, and HIG.

The team found yata is a new gene that controls where APPL ends up inside the cell. Without it, neural tissues fall apart and the flies die early. The result ties a traffic-control gene to brain health and lifespan. It also gives Alzheimer's research a simple animal in which protein placement goes visibly wrong.
plos-pone-0004566:
A single antibody test that could detect bird flu infection in any person is developed by Mookkan Prabakaran, Hui-Ting Ho, Nayana Prabhu, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Human infections with the highly pathogenic H5N1 avian influenza virus were usually confirmed by amplifying the virus's genes or by growing it in culture. Blood-based surveillance has advantages, but rapid and specific antibody tests had been lacking.

The team built an epitope-blocking ELISA, a test in which patient antibodies block a known marker antibody if they target the same spot. A universal test of this kind could survey whole communities for past H5N1 exposure. That would show how often the virus silently infects people, a number that shapes pandemic planning.
plos-pone-0004666:
One small region of a body protein is the trigger point for rheumatic fever after strep infection, show Katrin Dinkla, Susanne Talay, Matthias Morgelin, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease are serious autoimmune consequences of infection with Streptococcus pyogenes, the strep throat bacterium. The bacterium's M proteins have been implicated in causing the disease.

M proteins interact with collagen type IV, a structural protein in tissues. That interaction is a triggering step that induces the autoimmune attack. The team pinpoints the CB3 region of collagen IV as crucial in this process, called PARF-induced acute rheumatic fever. A precise trigger point gives vaccine designers something to avoid, and may explain why only some strep infections turn dangerous.
plos-pone-0004766:
Caroline Dahlberg and colleagues studied how a kinase family picks its targets among distinct pathways, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The Casein Kinase I family adds phosphate tags and controls many cell pathways. Humans have seven forms with a shared core but distinct ends that may steer each form to its own jobs.

All forms prefer a like target pattern, so choice rules were unclear. The team compared how one form handles two targets from unlike pathways. Their work shows how subtle contacts grant specificity. That helps predict kinase action and design selective drugs. The results give future studies a clearer base for comparison and follow up.
plos-pone-0004866:
Stefan Spring led a team that described a new marine bacterium and its light harvesting gear for PLOS ONE in 2009. The bacterium, named Congregibacter litoralis, lives in coastal water. It can make energy from light with a pigment like the one plants use, yet it does not release oxygen. Such bacteria are now known to be common in the sea and may take up a large share of sun light there.

The team laid out how the light gear is built and how the cell controls it. They also asked how light use fits with the cell food and carbon use. The answers help show how these common bacteria shape carbon flow in the sea.
plos-pone-0004966:
Electrical impulses coordinate movement, secretion and sensing in animals. Many of those signals are fast action potentials based on sodium. Alison Taylor reported an unexpected case in PLOS ONE in 2009. She studied a marine diatom, a single-celled alga. The diatom fired fast electrical spikes of its own.

The diatom's action potential is based on sodium and calcium together. That makes it much like an animal nerve impulse. Finding it in plankton pushes the roots of electrical signaling deep into evolution. Excitability is not an animal invention. Even a drifting alga can spark, which raises new questions about what such spikes do for the cell.
plos-pone-0005066:
Soybeans battle a water mold called Phytophthora sojae. The mold attacks roots and ruins harvests. Dinah Qutob and colleagues studied two of its weapon genes. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The genes are Avr1a and Avr3a. Plants can recognize these genes' products and resist. The mold evolves to escape recognition.

The study found copy number variation in both genes. The mold duplicates or drops copies to dodge plant defenses. It also varies how strongly the genes are transcribed. That double game reveals an arms race at the DNA level. Breeders can use the knowledge. Knowing how the mold escapes helps them design resistance that lasts longer.
plos-pone-0005166:
Many pregnant women in the United States skip HIV testing. Shorter pre-test counseling had raised testing uptake. Deborah Cohan and colleagues compared the two counseling styles in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their trial ran in the prenatal setting. It was randomized and designed as a non-inferiority test. Patient perspectives were the focus.

Abbreviated counseling held its own against standard counseling. Patients' decision-making and satisfaction were measured. Shorter sessions did not leave women worse informed. That supports simpler counseling to get more mothers tested. Testing in pregnancy prevents transmission to babies. Removing friction from testing saves lives. The study checks that simplification does not cost patients anything important.
plos-pone-0005266:
Smell begins in tiny cilia where odor signals flood the cell with calcium. That calcium must be cleared fast, before it reaches toxic levels. Kleene studied the pump that does the clearing in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The pump, called the plasma membrane calcium ATPase, moves calcium out of the olfactory cilium. The study probed the limits of how much calcium it can clear. Knowing the ceiling explains how smell cells reset after each sniff and where that reset can fail. Smell fades when this pump can no longer keep up, so the limits found here may help explain some losses of smell that come with age or illness.
plos-pone-0005366:
Streptococcus pyogenes, the strep throat bacterium, coats its wall with a component that carries D-alanine. Mutations in the dlt machinery change that coating and reduce virulence in many species. Cox and colleagues switched off the DltA gene in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Inactivating DltA modulated how the bacterium expresses its virulence factors, as the title states. The wall change was thought to work by exposing the germ to antimicrobial peptides. Showing wider effects on virulence genes reframes how this surface tweak tames the pathogen. The wall of this germ is its first touch with the throat, so a change there shifts each step that comes next. From sticking to the wall to the sore and fever a child feels at home.
plos-pone-0005466:
Yu Lei and co-authors studied a cell alarm protein in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. When a virus attacks, cells raise the alarm and make interferons that fight back. Some cells also choose to die, which stops the virus from spreading.

A protein called MAVS sits at the centre of the alarm and helps trigger both responses. The team showed that MAVS can also drive cell death, and that some viruses make proteins that block that move. The contest over MAVS helps explain why some virus infections are beaten off and others take hold.
plos-pone-0005566:
Swasti Raychaudhuri, Sucharita Dey, and Nitai Bhattacharyya studied loose-shaped proteins in brain diseases in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Some proteins have no fixed shape and flop between forms, yet they do vital jobs in cells. More and more of them are being tied to human disorders.

The team used computer prediction tools to survey such proteins among those linked to nerve diseases. They asked whether loose shape itself is part of why these proteins cause harm. The survey helps frame new tests in diseases like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's. Loose proteins are hard to study with standard tools, so surveys like this help choose which ones to test first.
plos-pone-0005666:
Noa Lamm and co-authors studied chromosome ends in a rare disorder in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Chromosomes end in telomeres, caps of repeated DNA that protect the ends. An enzyme builds those caps, and its activity is kept low in most human tissues, so caps shorten with age.

In Hoyeraal-Hreidarsson syndrome, a severe disorder of that system, the team found that the single-stranded overhang at the cap is unusually short. Short overhangs matched signs that the caps were failing. The measure may help diagnose and follow this rare disease.
plos-pone-0005766:
Rodrigo Vasquez-Del Carpio and co-authors solved in 2009 the shape of a DNA-copying enzyme caught in the act of a risky move. The lesion 8-oxoG forms when oxygen radicals scar a DNA base. It is highly mutagenic because it can pair two ways, fooling copying enzymes.

The team captured human DNA polymerase kappa inserting a base opposite the lesion. The structure shows how the enzyme handles, or mishandles, the damaged spot. That view explains mutation patterns seen in cells. It also guides work on how some polymerases protect the genome while others let errors through.
plos-pone-0005866:
Bassam Berry and co-authors showed in 2009 how viral weapons against gene silencing also blunt a fly's own small RNA systems. In insects, RNA interference is the main antiviral defense. Viruses fight back with suppressor proteins that jam that defense.

In Drosophila, those suppressors hindered not just the antiviral pathway but also the fly's internal small RNA routes. That collateral damage may cause some symptoms of infection itself. It also means virus and host small RNAs compete for shared machinery. The findings refine how researchers model viral infection in a favorite lab animal.
plos-pone-0005966:
HIV harms the antibody arm of the immune system early, and treatment does not fully repair it. Sandrine Peruchon, Nada Chaoul, Chantal Burelout and colleagues studied that early harm in 2009 using SIV, the monkey form of the virus. Their PLOS ONE paper follows B cells, the cells that make antibodies, in blood and in tissues during acute infection.

Memory B cells, which hold the record of past fights, were broadly lost, and the loss differed by tissue. Damage done this early may set the course of the whole disease. The work shows why the first weeks of infection deserve close study, and why a vaccine will need to guard B cells before the virus can thin their ranks.
plos-pone-0006066:
A fatty diet loads the liver with fat, and strangely also switches on fat-making genes there. Maaike Oosterveer, Theo van Dijk, Uwe Tietge and colleagues asked in 2009 whether those genes truly raise the flow of new fat. Their PLOS ONE paper feeds mice a high-fat diet and measures fatty acid elongation in the liver directly.

The title confirms real induction: the liver lengthens fatty acids more under the diet. Gene switches alone can mislead, so measuring the actual flux settles the paradox. The result matters for fatty liver disease, a growing burden, since it shows the liver under a fatty diet is not just storing fat but actively reshaping it.
plos-pone-0006166:
Fruit and nut trees need a dose of winter cold before they will bloom well in spring. Eike Luedeling, Minghua Zhang and Evan Girvetz mapped that dose across California, past and future, in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper tracks winter chill from 1950 to 2099 using two different chilling models, since chill defines where many tree crops can be grown.

Chill is declining across that span, the title reports, under both models. A tree planted for a thirty-year life may outlive the climate it was chosen for. The maps give growers and planners a hard basis for shifting crops and regions before orchards fail, rather than after.
plos-pone-0006266:
Guessing a protein's job from its letter sequence works for fewer than half of newly found proteins. Torgeir Hvidsten and colleagues tested shape as an alternative clue in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Structural genomics raised hopes that similar local shapes would imply similar functions.

The team ran a comprehensive analysis of structure and function based on local structure similarity. Comparing small shape patches can link distant proteins that sequences cannot. Better function guesses speed up genome annotation everywhere. The work weighs how far shape alone can carry those guesses. Readers gain a clear view of how shape can hint at what a protein does.
plos-pone-0006366:
When did the peoples of Africa first grow fast in number? Murray Cox and his team read DNA from foraging and farming groups south of the Sahara in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. One view ties growth to new tools made by hunters in the Late Stone Age; a later view ties it to the spread of farms.

The DNA bears signs of growth that reach back to the Late Stone Age, well before farms spread. Growth thus seems to have begun with Stone Age hunters, not with crops. That moves the start of the boom back by a long span. The work gives a firmer past for the peoples of the region.
plos-pone-0006466:
Maria Van Kerkhove and co-authors tracked poultry habits in rural Cambodia for PLOS ONE in 2009. Since 2004, Cambodia had confirmed many outbreaks of highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 in poultry and several human cases. Large education campaigns had run in the provinces where outbreaks occurred. The team asked whether those campaigns changed how people handle poultry and report dead birds.

Changes in daily practice are what turn campaign messages into real protection. Reporting of poultry deaths also feeds early warning of new outbreaks. The study checks both behavior and reporting on the ground. Its lessons apply wherever bird flu threatens farming communities.
plos-pone-0006566:
Tai On Yau and co-authors tested whether a liver cancer gene is essential in PLOS ONE in 2009. DLC2, deleted in liver cancer 2, is a Rho GTPase-activating protein. It was previously shown to be underexpressed in human hepatocellular carcinoma and to have tumor suppressor functions. The team deleted it in mice to test its importance.

Their title reports DLC2 was dispensable for development. Its deficiency did not aggravate hepatocarcinogenesis, liver cancer formation, either. A protein can be lost in tumors yet not drive them. That distinction saves research from chasing bystanders. It also highlights backup systems in development.
plos-pone-0006666:
Kok Keng Tee and co-authors isolated a working molecular clone of a recombinant HIV-1 form in PLOS ONE in 2009. A growing number of emerging HIV-1 recombinants classified as circulating recombinant forms have been identified in Southeast Asia in recent years. Recombinants arise when two viral strains mix in one person. The team established a molecular clone of one such form.

Their title reports the clone is replication-competent: it can copy itself in culture. A working clone lets labs study the recombinant's biology precisely. Regional HIV diversity matters for vaccine design and diagnostics. Southeast Asian forms are an important part of that picture.
plos-pone-0006766:
Fiona D. Barr and co-authors studied how arsenic switches off stress-hormone genes in PLOS ONE in 2009. Long-term exposure to inorganic arsenic is a worldwide health risk. It is linked to effects from cancer to diabetes. It also affects reproduction. The authors focused on genes controlled by the glucocorticoid receptor. That receptor manages stress and metabolism signals.

Arsenic disrupted histone modification at those genes' promoters. It also blocked recruitment of a partner protein called CARM1. Without those steps, transcription was repressed. The mechanism connects an environmental poison to gene control directly. It may explain several of arsenic's varied health effects at once.
plos-pone-0006866:
Johan Ursing and his team tracked drug-proof malaria germs through the year in PLOS ONE in 2009. A gene mark called pfcrt 76T flags proof against chloroquine. Germs with the mark are spread wide through Africa. In Guinea-Bissau, a double dose of chloroquine still beat a plain dose by far. The ask was if drug use piles up proof as the year turns.

The title gives the reply: no such pile-up was seen. Heavy use of the high dose did not stack proof through the seasons. That counts where chloroquine is still in use. Dose plans may keep a cheap drug of use for longer. Proof must still be watched as long as the drug is used.
plos-pone-0006966:
Flávia Mury, José Roberto da Silva, Ligia Ferreira, and colleagues studied blood digestion in a biting bug in PLOS ONE in 2009. Rhodnius prolixus feeds on blood and must handle large amounts of hemoglobin. Digestion frees heme, which is toxic in loose form. The bug detoxifies heme by packing it into crystals called hemozoin.

The team found an enzyme, alpha-glucosidase, helps form those crystals. They place the finding in an evolutionary story about blood feeders. Turning poison into inert crystal is a neat survival trick. Blocking it could one day offer a way to control this insect, which spreads Chagas disease.
plos-pone-0007066:
Ana Rivas-Caicedo, Gloria Soldevila, Teresa Fortoul, and colleagues studied an immune enzyme in PLOS ONE in 2009. Dendritic cells must mature and travel to lymph nodes to start immune responses. The signal receptor CCR7 guides that travel. The team had earlier shown the enzyme Jak3 helps CCR7 signaling in T lymphocytes.

Using mice that lack Jak3, they tested dendritic cells directly. Jak3 proved involved in both maturation and CCR7-driven migration. Without it, the cells' homing suffered. The finding ties a known immune defect gene to the cells that launch immune responses.
plos-pone-0007166:
Jung Hwan Kim, Min Ki Jee, So Young Lee, and colleagues studied stem-like genes in fat tissue cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Adipose tissue stromal cells are adult cells from fat. Oct4 is a transcription factor famous for marking embryonic stem cells. Whether it works in these adult fat cells was unclear. The team examined how Oct4 expression is controlled there.

They also tracked other embryonic genes in fully differentiated cells. Then they measured how endogenous Oct4 levels steer cell behavior. Even traces of this factor may keep adult cells more flexible. That flexibility is prized for regenerative medicine using a patient's own fat.
plos-pone-0007266:
Karine H. Hellemans, Jean-Claude Hannaert, Bart Denys, and colleagues studied how fatty acids harm insulin-producing cells in 2009. Chronically high fatty acid levels can kill pancreatic beta cells in the lab. Individual beta cells vary in how sensitive they are to that toxicity, even within the same culture.

Earlier rat work linked resistance to fat storage and mitochondrial handling. The authors examine a fat-regulating enzyme controlled by the LXR and PPARalpha pathways. They report that this enzyme regulates beta cell susceptibility to fatty acids. Their finding may guide efforts to protect beta cells in type 2 diabetes.
plos-pone-0007366:
Hossein Khiabanian, Vladimir Trifonov, and Raul Rabadan analyzed gene swapping in swine influenza viruses in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Three human influenza pandemics occurred in the twentieth century. Pandemic strains emerge from non-human reservoirs where humans have little or no immunity to the new virus combinations that form there.

At least two pandemic strains arose through reassortment, where viruses swap gene segments. The authors study reassortment patterns in swine influenza viruses. Pigs are a key mixing host for flu. Their patterns help scientists judge how new pandemic strains might assemble.
plos-pone-0007466:
Leticia Olvera and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how E. coli manages its core metabolism when sugar runs short. The bacterium normally imports glucose through a transport system called the PTS. A strain lacking that system grows slowly and must compensate. The team measured gene activity across central metabolism in this setting of carbon limitation.

They found changed expression in the genes that burn sugar and run the cell's energy economy. A stress regulator called sigma-38 appears to play a part in keeping those genes active. The picture is a cell rewiring itself around a broken food pipeline. Understanding that rewiring matters for industrial strains built from E. coli. It also shows how bacteria survive scarcity in the wild.
plos-pone-0007566:
Haoquan Wu and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 challenging a tidy assumption about microRNAs. These small RNAs silence genes, and each is cut from a longer precursor by an enzyme called Drosha. The standard view held that Drosha always cuts at the same place. That would give every mature microRNA a fixed start. The team examined the ends of mature microRNAs closely.

The cuts vary more than the textbook picture allows. Alternative processing by Drosha produces mature microRNAs with different 5-prime ends. A shifted start changes which genes the microRNA can target. So this variation is not noise; it widens the silencing repertoire. The finding makes the gene-regulation system look more flexible, and more subtle, than assumed. It also warns researchers to read microRNA sequences with care.
plos-pone-0007666:
Ginny Emerson and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the poxviruses native to North America. Orthopoxviruses include the smallpox virus and its many animal relatives. North America hosts its own endemic set, circulating in wildlife. Their evolutionary relationships and ecology were incompletely charted. The team reconstructed the group's phylogeny, its family tree, and reviewed how the viruses live in nature.

The tree clarifies which North American poxviruses are close kin and which are distant. Ecology explains where each one persists and in which hosts. Such natural history matters for both wildlife health and public health readiness. Poxviruses have surprised the world before. Knowing the local family's structure is basic preparation. The study gives the continent's poxviruses a proper genealogy.
plos-pone-0007766:
Yo-Ping Lai and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It clarifies how helper T cells boost killer T cells early in an immune response. Killer CD8 cells attack infected cells, but they do not expand well on their own. Signals plus antigen alone proved insufficient.

The missing help is IL-2, a growth signal made by activated CD4 helper cells. Given during early priming, IL-2 advances the CD8 response. The cells multiply more and gain stronger effector functions. The timing rule matters for vaccine design, where strong killer T cell responses are often the goal.
plos-pone-0007866:
Jacob Lowenstein and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It applies DNA barcoding to a practical problem: naming the tuna in sushi. A short standard DNA stretch can identify a species, like a barcode. The authors tested that idea on tuna sold for sushi, including the prized Thunnus maccoyii.

Seafood is often mislabeled, and tuna species look alike once sliced. Barcodes can expose swaps that cheat buyers and hide overfishing. The authors also contrast barcoding attributes with genetic distances. Their work supports DNA checks as a guard for consumers and for threatened fish stocks.
plos-pone-0007966:
Thomas Vernier and colleagues asked where electric pulses open the cell wall, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Pulses that briefly open pores, called electroporation, are a standard way to slip genes or drugs into cells. The team tested whether worn spots in the wall open first.

Their results say yes: fields strike places already harmed by oxidation before sound places. Stressed cells may thus take in more of what the pulse carries than healthy ones do. That bias matters for gene therapy and drug delivery, where the cells most in need may also be the most open.
plos-pone-0008066:
Weiguo Feng and colleagues mapped gene activity as the mouse face forms for PLOS ONE in 2009. The face grows from buds of tissue that swell, meet, and fuse. When fusion fails, cleft lip and palate result, among the most common birth defects.

The team read which genes were active, where, and when, as the buds grew and fused. The atlas shows the order of the building work in fine detail. It also gives a baseline: a gene active at the wrong place or time in this atlas is a prime suspect in facial birth defects.
plos-pone-0008166:
Devon Crawford and colleagues added borrowed temperature channels to rat brain cells and watched for side effects in PLOS ONE in 2009. The channels, TRPV1 and TRPM8, answer to heat and cold. Placed in chosen neurons, they promise remote control of cell firing for research.

Expressing the two channels in hippocampal neurons changed more than temperature response alone. The side effects differed between the two channels, which matters for picking the right tool. A control tool that quietly warps the cells it studies can mislead a whole line of research. The authors report those contrasts channel by channel.
plos-pone-0008266:
Gary Crameri and colleagues created bat cell lines in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Bats are suspected reservoirs for several dangerous emerging viruses.
