These include Nipah, Hendra, SARS-like coronaviruses, and Ebola. Studying such viruses safely requires bat cells that grow in the lab. Few suitable cell lines existed when the work began.

The team established, immortalised, and characterised lines from pteropid bats. Immortalised lines keep growing instead of dying after a few generations. With them, researchers can test how viruses enter and grow in bat cells. That supports work on preventing the next outbreak.
plos-pone-0008366:
Yun Wang and colleagues studied amyloid effects in rat brains in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Alzheimer's patients show changes in how neurons synchronize their firing. Synchronized network activity supports complex thinking, such as working memory. The mechanisms behind these changes are not understood. Amyloid-beta 42 is a protein fragment central to the disease.

Low and high doses of Aβ42 had opposite effects in the rat prefrontal cortex. Dose flipped the impact on network activity and neuronal excitability. Such a split warns that amount matters in Alzheimer's models. It helps explain conflicting results between studies.
plos-pone-0008466:
Michael Salvatore and co-authors link an enzyme change to movement in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The enzyme tyrosine hydroxylase controls how much dopamine the brain can make. Dopamine is a signal chemical needed for smooth movement. Its precursor, L-DOPA, is a main drug for Parkinson disease. The enzyme's activity shifts when phosphate tags are added. Tags at two sites, ser31 and ser40, play a role.

With aging, the ser31 tag in the nigra gains importance. The nigra is a brain area that loses cells in Parkinson disease. The team tie that tag to how active old animals are. The find helps explain age changes in movement.
plos-pone-0008566:
Laura Musazzi and co-authors test stress effects in rat brains in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Stress is a main risk factor for mental illness. Past work hints that brief stress raises excitatory signals in some brain areas. The team study the front part of the rat cortex. They measure release of glutamate, the main excitatory signal in the brain. Release is triggered by an electric stimulus in the lab tests.

Brief stress raises that glutamate release in the cortex. Drugs used for depression blunt the rise in their tests. A stress-driven surge of glutamate may add to risk of mental illness. Blunting it may be one way those drugs help.
plos-pone-0008666:
Claudine Benard and co-authors study a food additive in rats in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Carrageenan is a high molecular weight sulphated polysaccharide derived from red seaweeds. It is widely used to thicken foods. In rodents, its degraded forms can induce intestinal inflammation, or colitis. That inflammation involves macrophage recruitment and activation. The team analyze how degraded carrageenan acts on monocytes, macrophage precursors in blood.

They find it induces TNF secretion and ICAM-1 upregulation in monocytes through NF-kappaB activation. TNF is a potent inflammatory cytokine. Those effects show a direct path from additive to inflammation in their model. The work informs debate on carrageenan safety in food.
plos-pone-0008766:
Amanda Lorier, Gregory Funk, and John Greer studied how opioids quiet the tongue's nerve supply. Their rat study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tongue muscles keep the airway open during each breath. The hypoglossal nerve drives those muscles. Opioid painkillers depress that nerve and can endanger breathing. A drug class called ampakines boosts nerve signals elsewhere in the brain.

Opiates suppressed hypoglossal motoneuron activity in the rats. Ampakine treatment then restored much of that activity. Reviving tongue drive could protect the airway during opioid use. The result points toward safer pain treatment and overdose care.
plos-pone-0008866:
Veronica Ulici, Claudine James, Katie Hoenselaar, and colleagues listed genes steered by a growth signal in bone-forming cartilage. Their mouse study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Long bones grow at plates of cartilage near their ends. Cartilage cells first multiply, then swell into a mature form. The PI3K signaling pathway influences that sequence. Blocking it earlier had changed growth plate behavior.

The team profiled which genes PI3K controls in growth plate chondrocytes. Lists of responding genes map the pathway's reach in bone growth. Such maps help explain growth disorders of the skeleton. They also guide drugs that touch this common pathway.
plos-pone-0008966:
Khaled Alkhuder and co-authors found a potassium pump that a dangerous bacterium needs to spread, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Francisella tularensis causes tularemia, also called rabbit fever. It is highly infectious and lives part of its life inside immune cells. Between cells it must survive in body fluids low in potassium.

The team identified a gene, trkH, that builds the bacterium's potassium uptake protein. Mice infected with bacteria lacking trkH saw the germ spread through the body poorly. Without the pump, the bacterium could not thrive outside cells. The pump stands out as a possible weak point for new drugs.
plos-pone-0009066:
Yannis Guillemin and co-authors compared the membrane manners of cell-death proteins, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The BCL-2 family includes both killers and protectors of the body's cells. They act by opening or guarding pores in the mitochondrial membrane. How they meet that membrane decides whether a given cell lives or dies.

The team studied active fragments cut from family members of both camps. Pro-death and pro-life fragments behaved distinctly when they met membranes. Each camp's style of approach matched its job inside the cell. The split in membrane behaviour mirrors the family's deep split in function.
plos-pone-0009166:
Enrico Domenici and co-authors screened blood proteins for flags of mental illness, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Depression and schizophrenia are still diagnosed by talking about symptoms alone. No blood test backs up the doctor's judgement in the clinic today. Sound biological markers could make diagnosis and treatment checks much firmer.

The team profiled many blood proteins at once in sets of patients and controls. People with depression or schizophrenia were compared with healthy volunteers. Certain proteins in blood plasma set the patient groups measurably apart. Panels of proteins like these are first steps toward lab tests for psychiatry.
plos-pone-0009266:
Lawrence Sirovich, Mark Stoeckle, and Yu Zhang published this biodiversity study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Huge DNA databases now cover life from bacteria to humans. Hidden in those sequences may be a map of how species relate. The authors refined a method that turns DNA sequences into indicator vectors, simple numeric codes.

Plotting those codes reveals the structure of biodiversity in a visual form. Clusters and gaps in the plot reflect real divisions among life forms. The technique needs no family tree built in advance, so it stays open to surprises. It offers a fast way to survey the genetic shape of the living world.
plos-pone-0009366:
Eric Gamazon and co-authors published this genomics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Gene chips called exon arrays measure how genes are used across the genome. Such data feed studies linking genes to disease and drug response. But DNA variants inside the chip's probes can distort the readings.

The team surveyed the Affymetrix exon array against the 1000 Genomes dataset. They catalogued which probes overlap known SNPs, the single-letter variants people carry. A probe sitting on a variant can fake a change in gene activity. Their catalogue helps researchers clean their data before drawing conclusions.
plos-pone-0009466:
Brady Miller and John Stamatoyannopoulos combined many studies of a blood cancer in PLOS ONE in 2010. The cancer is acute myeloid leukemia. It is not one disease but many, and outcomes are often poor. Gene activity studies of patients had piled up in separate groups. Each study alone gave only part of the picture.

By merging the data sets into one large analysis, the authors could see which gene patterns hold up across all of them. Shared patterns are more likely to mark the disease itself. The combined view can sharpen diagnosis and forecasts for patients. It can also point to drug targets that single studies missed.
plos-pone-0009566:
Erich Bachler and colleagues tracked small migrating birds for a full year in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tiny songbirds cross the Sahara desert on migration. They are too small to carry satellite trackers. For over a century, ringed birds gave the only clues, and those were sparse. The team fitted birds with light level geolocators, small devices that record daylight to estimate position.

The devices revealed routes, stopover sites, and wintering grounds across the whole year. That fills a long standing gap in knowledge of these migrants. Knowing where the birds rest and winter shows where protection matters most. It also helps predict how climate change may shift their journeys.
plos-pone-0009666:
Joshua Ross, Thomas House, and Matt Keeling worked out epidemic math for households in PLOS ONE in 2010. Infections spread fast inside a home, where contact is close and long. They then leap between homes through work, school, and travel. Simple models that treat people as one mixed crowd miss that structure. The team developed methods to compute disease dynamics in a population built of households.

Their methods make household models fast enough to use in practice. Household structure changes how outbreaks start, peak, and fade. Policies such as isolating whole households can be tested in the model. Sharper forecasts follow when the math matches how people actually live.
plos-pone-0009766:
Gabriela D'Amico and co-authors published a cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The study asks whether Rac1, a protein that drives cell movement, is needed for tumors to grow new blood vessels. Work in dishes had implied that it was.

In adult mice, removing Rac1 from vessel cells had no effect on tumor growth or vessel growth, the team reports. Growth signals from VEGF also worked in a normal way. The need for Rac1 showed only when a partner grip protein was weak or missing. In that case, the extra tumor growth and vessel growth both hung on Rac1.
plos-pone-0009866:
Building muscle in the embryo means making some proteins and clearing others on schedule. Yvan Campos and colleagues found an enzyme that clears a fetal muscle protein at the right time. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Myosin is the protein that pulls muscle fibers tight.

The enzyme is Ozz-E3, a ubiquitin ligase that tags proteins for disposal. Its target is sarcomeric embryonic myosin heavy chain, a motor protein of young muscle. Tagging it during muscle development makes room for adult forms. The handoff shows how timed cleanup shapes growing tissue.
plos-pone-0009966:
During the 2009 pandemic, labs needed a test that could name the new flu virus fast. Martin Schulze and colleagues built a real-time PCR approach for exactly that. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The approach differentiates pandemic influenza A(H1N1)v from recent human influenza viruses. Real-time PCR counts viral genes as they multiply, giving answers in hours. A wrong call could mislead whole outbreak reports. Telling the pandemic strain from seasonal ones guided treatment and tracking. The method served labs while the pandemic was active. Hours, not days, decided care in the surge.
plos-pone-0010066:
The authors were Julia Arciero, G. Bard Ermentrout, Jeffrey Upperman, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE paper modeled a severe gut disease of premature babies. Necrotizing enterocolitis attacks the intestines of pre-term infants. It is thought to involve an immature gut and changed levels of normal gut bacteria.

Instead of lab animals, the team built a mathematical model of the disease. They used it to test how probiotics, helpful live bacteria, and inflammation interact. A working model lets doctors explore treatment ideas safely before trying them in fragile newborns. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.
plos-pone-0010166:
Clint Winkler, Alberto Ponce, and Albert Courey studied gene silencing in fruit flies in 2010. Their PLOS ONE paper covered Groucho, a corepressor that helps turn genes off. Groucho binds a partner enzyme, Rpd3, that removes acetyl tags from histones. Earlier cell studies suggested that binding was required for repression, but its role in living animals was less certain.

The team proposed that this partnership raises nucleosome density, packing DNA more tightly. Denser packing makes genes harder to read, reinforcing the off state. The work links a classic repressor to the physical layout of chromosomes.
plos-pone-0010266:
The authors were Germain Fernando, Xianfeng Chen, Tarl Prow, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study delivered flu vaccine through skin in mice. Over fourteen million people die yearly from infectious diseases despite wide vaccine use. Most vaccines still go in by needle into muscle, a device dating to 1853, though skin is rich in immune cells.

By micro-targeting vaccine precisely into skin, guided by probability models, they got potent immunity. Strong protection came from low doses that a needle might waste. Dose-sparing delivery could stretch vaccine supplies in a pandemic.
plos-pone-0010366:
John Nomellini and co-workers built a bacteria-based HIV blocker for PLOS ONE in 2010. Preventing HIV infection needs new tools, since early microbicide gels had mostly failed. Past gels acted in broad, non-specific ways. This team took a targeted route instead. They used a harmless water bacterium that coats itself in a protein layer.

The bacteria were engineered to display two human proteins on that outer layer. One, CD4, is the very handle HIV uses to enter cells. The other is a signal that can also interfere with the virus. Together they may trap or block HIV before it reaches real cells. A living, self-growing blocker would be cheap to make if it works.
plos-pone-0010466:
Simone Cardoso and colleagues simulated how bone changes radiation dose in small treatment fields for PLOS ONE in 2010. Planning radiotherapy for head lesions needs care, because tissue there is far from uniform. Bone next to soft tissue bends the dose pattern. Small beams make those effects sharper and harder to predict. The team used Monte Carlo simulation, which traces many virtual radiation paths.

They placed a bone-like block inside a soft tissue phantom and computed the dose inside. The results show where real dose departs from simple plans. Planners can use such checks to avoid under-treating tumors or harming healthy tissue. Head treatments leave little margin for error. Simulation, here, is a safety tool.
plos-pone-0010566:
Takashi Shimbo and colleagues proposed a blood antibody as a new marker for melanoma in PLOS ONE in 2010. Melanoma is among the most aggressive cancers. Once it spreads, treatment becomes very hard, so early detection saves lives. Reliable blood markers for early melanoma were lacking. The team measured antibodies against a protein called BPAG1 in patients' serum. These self-directed antibodies appeared tied to melanoma.

A blood test that flags melanoma early could change screening for high-risk people. Antibody markers are attractive because blood draws are simple and repeatable. The marker must still prove itself in larger, early-stage groups. This study introduces the candidate and its first evidence. It joins a long hunt for melanoma's early warning signs.
plos-pone-0010666:
Renata Cavalheiro and colleagues tested a heart-protecting compound in PLOS ONE in 2010. When blood returns to a starved heart, the return itself causes damage. The compound PD153035 was known as a growth signal blocker from cancer research.

Perfused rat hearts and heart cells both fared better with the compound. Injury after restored blood flow was smaller, and the cells' energy centers worked better. The protection ran through potassium channels inside mitochondria. Shielding those energy centers during a heart attack could limit lasting damage, which is why this side effect of a cancer compound deserves attention.
plos-pone-0010766:
Jianchang Yang and colleagues mapped a self-reinforcing loop that keeps stem cells young, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Two factors, SALL4 and OCT4, sit near the top of the stem cell control board. OCT4 was known to be switched on by SALL4. Both are required for embryonic stem cells to stay pluripotent and keep copying themselves.

The team showed the pair also regulate each other through a feedback network. Each helps hold the other's level steady. Loops like this make cell states stable: nudge one factor and the loop pulls it back. Knowing the loop's wiring helps scientists hold stem cells in the lab and, in cancer work, break similar loops.
plos-pone-0010866:
Nicholas Chia, Isaac Cann and Gary Olsen published this evolution study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Copying DNA takes a team of protein machines, including the PCNA clamp, the RFC loader, and the MCM complex. Archaea, single-celled microbes, and eukaryotes, the group that includes humans, use versions of these machines that look alike in structure.

The authors compared how the machines changed over evolution in the two groups. Each complex keeps a constant number of parts, but the parts vary: in some lineages they are identical copies, in others close relatives. Eukaryotes show no such variation, suggesting all their versions descend from one shared ancestor's set. Chia and colleagues use replication machinery as a fossil record, tracing how complex cells assembled their copying toolkit.
plos-pone-0010966:
Min Zeng, Hirotoshi Kikuchi, Maria Pino and co-authors published this colon cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2010. KRAS is a growth gene mutated in many tumors, but tumors without the mutation still activate it through signals. As tumors outgrow their blood supply they become oxygen-starved, and the authors asked whether low oxygen itself can switch KRAS on.

In colon cancer cell lines carrying the normal gene, low oxygen consistently raised the active, loaded form of the K-ras protein. That activation fed two survival programs: growing new blood vessels and resisting programmed cell death. Zeng and colleagues show the tumor environment can do what mutation usually does. Their finding widens the set of patients whose tumors might respond to drugs aimed at the KRAS pathway.
plos-pone-0011066:
Alice Li, Simon Waddell, Jason Hinds and co-authors published this tuberculosis study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Two famous laboratory strains of the TB bacterium descend from the same parent: H37Rv, fully virulent, and H37Ra, weakened. Comparing their gene activity inside macrophages, the cells where TB lives, offers a way to spot what virulence requires.

Profiled in broth and inside mouse bone-marrow macrophages, both strains switched on survival programs for life inside a cell, including iron-scavenging and fat metabolism genes. The virulent strain's response was stronger and broader, engaging many more genes than its weakened sibling. Li and colleagues use the contrast to shortlist the bacterial behaviors that matter during infection. Those differences are candidate weak points for drugs that work inside macrophages, where TB is hardest to kill.
plos-pone-0011166:
Lagana, Russo, Sismeiro and colleagues mapped fragile DNA sites in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some chromosome regions break easily, and genes plus small RNAs are not spread evenly across them. The team measured how often each element appears in these fragile zones.

They also tested how repeated DNA and certain marked islands shape that spread. The pattern they found adds to knowledge of genome layout and stability. Fragile sites are often altered in cancer, so their contents matter for cancer genetics. Knowing what sits in break prone zones helps interpret the damage found in tumor genomes.
plos-pone-0011266:
Almeida, Alfonso, Hankey and colleagues followed older men in PLOS ONE in 2010. The Health in Men Study let them examine links between depression, antidepressant use and death in later life. Depression in old age is common and often undertreated, so its effect on survival is a serious question.

The analysis revealed a link between depression and higher mortality in these men. That argues for treating late life depression as more than a quality of life issue. It may be a matter of years of life. The study gives doctors and families evidence to take low mood in older men seriously and seek care.
plos-pone-0011366:
Mimi Ghosh and co-authors measured natural HIV-blocking activity in samples from women in a 2010 study. The lining of the vagina and cervix produces germ-fighting substances, and those secretions can slow HIV in the lab. The team compared women with and without HIV to learn which natural defenses track with that blocking power.

Blocking activity rose alongside levels of innate antimicrobial substances and a class of antibodies in the secretions. That pairing suggests the body's own chemistry, plus antibody defense, jointly sets how hostile the local setting is to the virus. The finding matters for prevention research. Products that boost these natural defenses, rather than adding foreign drugs alone, might lower the chance of infection during exposure and could work with the body instead of against its balance.
plos-pone-0011466:
Richard Zhao and co-authors tested in 2010 an unlikely weapon against a stubborn childhood cancer. Neuroblastoma arises from nerve tissue in children, and tumors that resist the drug doxorubicin are nearly untreatable. The team turned to Vpr, a protein made by HIV-1, which is known to stress and kill the cells it enters, and aimed it at the resistant cancer cells.

The viral protein killed doxorubicin-resistant neuroblastoma cells in their tests, succeeding where the standard drug failed. Borrowing a villain's tool is provocative, but the logic is sound: resistance to one killer says nothing about another with a different method. Much work would be needed to deliver such a protein safely and only to tumors. Even so, the study widens the search for resistant-cancer treatments beyond the usual drug families.
plos-pone-0011566:
Ricardo Betancur-R and co-authors combined family trees and body shapes in 2010 to find an invisible border in the sea. A coastal fish of the southern Caribbean split into distinct populations where no ocean barrier, current break, or distance explains the divide. Phylogenetic analysis of its DNA and morphologic analysis of its form agreed on the split, so the team looked to the land for the cause.

They identified a marine biogeographic break of terrestrial origin: a land feature, such as a river's outflow or a past coastline, dividing sea life from the shore side. Geography sculpting ocean diversity from land is a reminder that the two realms share one history. Biogeographic maps drawn only from water will miss such borders. The finding also gives conservation a finer map of Caribbean populations that must be managed as separate stocks.
plos-pone-0011666:
Xiuchun Ge and co-authors developed a faster way to find vaccine targets on a mouth bacterium, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Streptococcus sanguinis normally lives in dental plaque but can also infect the heart. With full genome sequences available, researchers can hunt for surface proteins as vaccine candidates, yet testing them one by one is slow and costly.

Their method immunises with pooled proteins and reads out which surface antigens the immune system recognises. The pooled approach cuts time and animal use while still flagging promising targets. It offers a general shortcut for reverse vaccinology in other bacteria too.
plos-pone-0011766:
Emilie Sapin and co-authors counted brain cells active during excess dream sleep, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Using a staining method that marks recently active neurons, the team had found a massive population in the lower hypothalamus switched on during paradoxical, or REM, sleep hypersomnia. Some of those cells in the tuberal region used the calming transmitter GABA.

Their census shows a very large number of GABAergic neurons are activated there during the hypersomnia state. Mapping this dreaming circuitry in overdrive helps explain how the brain generates and sustains REM sleep, a state tied to memory and mood.
plos-pone-0011866:
Kaushik Ghosal, Andrea Stathopoulos, and Sanjay Pimplikar reported in 2010 on a piece of the Alzheimer's-linked protein APP. APP sits at the center of Alzheimer's research because fragments cut from it form the amyloid found in patients' brains. The team studied a different fragment, the part that stays inside the cell after cutting.

In mice engineered to produce this inner fragment, the birth of new neurons in the adult brain fell, and inflammation in the brain rose alongside. Adult-born neurons support memory, which fades early in Alzheimer's disease. Tying the fragment to inflammation and blocked neuron birth suggests a route of harm quite separate from the plaques that get most attention.
plos-pone-0011966:
Vivien Béziat and co-workers charted in 2010 the final maturation steps of natural killer cells, a front-line immune cell type. Mature NK cells must stay broadly ready for trouble while sparing healthy tissue, a balance taught during their education. Two receptor families, KIRs and NKG2A, carry much of that teaching.

Tracking both across development showed a stepwise pattern: NKG2A levels fall in a coordinated way as KIRs are acquired. That ordered handover gives immunologists a ruler for judging how mature a patient's NK cells are. It also sharpens thinking about NK cell therapies, where the maturation state of infused cells may decide how well they work.
plos-pone-0012066:
Sarrah Castillo and co-workers made in 2010 a first list of the immune gene forms found in raccoons, the chief land carrier of rabies in North America. The genes belong to the MHC set, which shows bits of germs to the immune system so it can learn them. The set's wide range of forms is kept up in part by germ pressure. Most wild-life work on these genes had passed this species by.

The team read two key parts of the raccoon's MHC genes and set down the forms they found. A base list of immune range in the top rabies host helps work on how rabies lasts and spreads in the wild. It also bears on why the bait vaccines dropped for raccoons work well in some places and poorly in others.
plos-pone-0012166:
Guillaume Dumas, Jacqueline Nadel, Robert Soussignan, and co-authors studied two brains working at once during social interaction, in PLOS ONE in 2010. When two people interact, each keeps adjusting to the other in real time, and a shared rhythm often emerges from that back-and-forth. Most brain studies look at one person alone, which misses the coupling that makes interaction what it is.

Recording both partners at once, the team found their brain activity can synchronize during the exchange. That coupling is a physical trace of mutual adaptation between people. It opens a way to study social difficulties, such as those in autism, as problems of coordination between brains rather than faults inside one brain alone.
plos-pone-0012266:
Smriti Mehra, Bapi Pahar, Noton Dutta, and co-authors read gene activity inside tuberculosis granulomas in monkeys, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A granuloma is the dense ball of cells the body builds to wall off tuberculosis bacteria in the lung. The wall should contain the infection, yet the bacteria have evolved ways to live inside it, sometimes for decades.

Profiling which host genes switch on or off inside these structures shows how the standoff is maintained, and where the bacteria gain the upper hand. Monkeys mirror human tuberculosis closely, so their granulomas speak to human disease. That knowledge guides vaccines and drugs meant to tip the balance toward the host.
plos-pone-0012366:
Thomas Riess, Maryline Achieng, Samuel Otieno and co-workers interviewed circumcised men in Kisumu, Kenya, for a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Trials had shown that circumcision cuts a man's risk of catching HIV through sex by more than half. Health experts worried that newly circumcised men might feel fully safe and take more risks, wiping out the gain.

Through interviews, the men described what they were taught during the rite and how their behavior changed after. Some did report riskier behavior, tied in part to beliefs about what circumcision protects against. The findings tell HIV programs to pair circumcision with strong counseling, so men keep using other protection as well.
plos-pone-0012466:
William Weldon, Bao-Zhong Wang, Maria Martin and colleagues strengthened a flu vaccine protein, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The swine-origin H1N1 pandemic showed how slowly egg-grown vaccines arrive. One faster route builds vaccines from the flu surface protein hemagglutinin alone, but the lone protein is a weak immune trigger, especially when it falls apart.

The team stabilized the protein in its three-part trimer form, the shape the immune system meets on real virus. The stabilized version provoked stronger immunity in their tests. Sturdier vaccine proteins could mean faster, egg-free flu vaccines when the next pandemic strain appears.
plos-pone-0012566:
Renee Ruhaak, Hae-Won Uh, Marian Beekman and colleagues hunted blood markers of healthy human aging, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Markers that reflect true health in old age, not just years lived, are extremely scarce yet valuable. Antibodies wear sugar coats whose patterns shift with age and disease, so the team read the sugar forms on IgG antibodies.

One form — IgG carrying a bisecting GlcNAc sugar — was notably lower in long-lived people. A sugar signature tied to longevity could help researchers measure whether lifestyle or drugs truly slow aging. It also links immune aging to the broader biology of the long-lived.
plos-pone-0012666:
Saisongkorh, Robert, La Scola and co-authors found gene swapping between bacteria that live inside amoebae. Bartonella bacteria live inside mammal blood cells, a tight and sheltered home. Computer scans of their genomes hinted that they still trade genes with other bacteria despite that shelter.

Their 2010 work gives evidence that type IV secretion genes passed between Bartonella and Rhizobium radiobacter inside amoebae. Shared amoeba homes may act as mixing vessels for bacterial genes. Such swaps can hand pathogens new tools, so tracking them matters for disease science and for watching how new traits spread.
plos-pone-0012766:
Gossens, Naus, Hollander and co-authors found that mice missing the protein ADAM8 grow an overfull thymus. The thymus trains T cells, and its work needs constant traffic between young T cells and the tissue around them. Proteases that trim the matrix and free signals help that traffic flow.

Their 2010 knockout mice ended up with far more thymus cells than normal. That surplus suggests ADAM8 normally reins in T cell growth or movement there. The result informs how the immune system's schoolhouse is kept in balance.  Cell counts made the difference large and easy to measure.
plos-pone-0327266:
John Baptist Asiimwe and five colleagues measure how widespread chronic diseases are among Kenyan men, in this 2026 PLOS ONE analysis of a national health survey. The data cover more than fourteen thousand men aged fifteen to fifty-four, interviewed in 2022. The diseases counted include high blood pressure, diabetes, heart and lung disease, arthritis, depression, anxiety, and cancer.

About one man in eleven reported at least one such condition, and roughly one in fifty lived with several at once. High blood pressure was the most common, followed by depression. Risk rose with age, wealth, region, and sedentary habits. The authors argue men's health checks in Kenya should look beyond infections to these slower, lasting illnesses.
plos-pone-0332566:
Ehud Herbst and colleagues describe a bacterial weapon that works outside the cell, a rarity among the defences bacteria aim at the viruses that infect them. A soil bacterium's secreted protein-chopping enzyme, brewed in a lab strain, cut down two related viruses even when only the used culture fluid was added to fresh virus, with no bacteria present. The fluid left many virus particles empty of their DNA.

Viruses could escape, but only by mutating a protein on their tails, the part that first grips a victim cell. Nearly all previously decoded bacterial defences act inside the cell, after invasion begins. An outside guard that damages virus particles in the open adds a new layer to the arms race, and the authors suggest such secreted guards may be common and simply overlooked.
plos-pone-0341766:
John Rong Hao Tay and seven colleagues describe this 2026 PLOS One paper on the creation of a large oral disease registry at Singapore's national dental center. The registry pulls together electronic health records to standardize information on dental and mouth diseases across the country's largest healthcare group. The authors explain how it was governed and built, and profile the patients recorded between 2013 and mid-2025.

The registry now holds records for well over two hundred thousand patients, roughly half women and half men, with an average age near fifty. Those records reveal a heavy burden of tooth loss and gum disease, including many advanced periodontitis cases. As Singapore's first resource of this scale for oral health, it gives researchers and planners real-world data for improving dental services.
plos-pone-0344266:
Quanlong Fan, Gang Xu, Yunge Wang, and Mengke Wu published this 2026 computer science paper on spotting real-world events in social media streams. Posts mix text, images, and video, and older detectors usually read only one source. Their framework links posts into a graph and uses graph neural networks with cross-modal attention to weigh words and pictures together.

Checked against news coverage from the same period, adding images and news to text improved how accurately events were found and classified. Fan offers the design for faster, fuller awareness during fast-moving public events.
plos-pone-0345766:
Song Fang and colleagues developed in 2026 a model for judging driving risk inside urban road tunnels. Tunnels concentrate several hazards at once: sudden changes in light at the entrances, narrow lanes with walls close by, and no room to escape a crash. A risk model gives engineers and tunnel operators a structured way to score how dangerous a tunnel or a driving situation is.

The authors build their model around the factors that drive tunnel accidents, so that risk can be assessed before crashes supply the data the hard way. Cities keep adding road tunnels as they grow, and traffic through them is heavy. A sound risk model supports decisions on speed limits, lighting, ventilation, and emergency planning.
plos-pone-0346366:
Paying one bundled price for a whole course of care sounds simple, but designing the contract is anything but. Sander Steenhuis, Jeroen van der Wolk, and Eric van der Hijden sorted the design decisions facing health insurers, in this 2026 PLOS One overview built from earlier literature.

Two reviewers independently pulled every stated choice from selected articles, then organized them across six stages of buying care. They found thirty-three decisions carrying one hundred ten possible options, from which treatments enter the bundle to how quality is checked. An expert panel tested the framework. The authors hope the map helps payers design bundles that reward value without inviting gaming.
plos-pone-0346466:
Varsha Bommineni led a team of five authors mapping gene activity in chickens with spotty liver disease, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The disease cuts egg production and costs the industry heavily. The team read the full set of active genes in the liver, the organ at the center of the illness.

Bommineni's gene-level picture shows how birds respond as the disease attacks, which defenses switch on and which pathways fail. That map points to where vaccines or breeding could help most. Poultry diseases spread fast in dense flocks, so molecular insight that arrives before an outbreak is worth far more than insight after. The study gives the egg industry a molecular baseline for this costly disease.
plos-pone-0346666:
Tomasz Piróg and colleagues analysed more than fifty-five thousand Polish-language posts on X, formerly Twitter, from the first year of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Poland took in huge numbers of Ukrainian refugees, and social media framed what the public made of them. The 2026 study combined frame analysis with stance detection, network mapping, and engagement measures.

Negative posts were the most numerous, at about sixty percent, yet positive posts spread furthest per post. Government supporters and the liberal opposition both leaned pro-Ukrainian, while a nationalist cluster criticised the arrivals but reached few people. A smaller mixed group stayed neutral. The authors show how framing and network structure together shape crisis debates.
plos-pone-0346766:
Grace Semabia Kpeli and seven colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One water study from Ghanaian towns flooded after the controlled spilling of the Akosombo and Kpong dams in late 2023. Ten months later, the team sampled rivers, ponds, wells, boreholes, and drains in four downstream communities and sequenced the bacterial DNA in each sample.

The water carried a wide cast of microbes, including organisms tied to gut infections and several hardy hospital-associated species known for drug resistance. Contamination varied sharply by place and water source, and even some groundwater sources carried high-risk organisms, with two towns worst affected. The authors say flood risk does not end when waters recede, and they call for targeted water safety work in the affected communities.
plos-pone-0347366:
Ihor Kendiukhov stress-tested a habit in gene science: trust that mouse gene wiring holds in humans. Labs match genes by descent and borrow the wiring, but no one had checked how often the loan pays off. The 2026 study built gene links from human and mouse lung cells apart, then set them side by side.

Links matched well when the organ was the same, far past chance. The sign of each link, boost or brake, matched for all the strongest ones. But the match was patchy. Links for cell-identity genes, which mark what a cell is, crossed species near intact. Links for signal genes barely crossed at all. Borrowed wiring is safe for identity, shaky for signals.
plos-pone-0347866:
Hamed Tabesh and co-authors built hybrid forecasters for the daily flood of patients into an emergency department, a number managers must predict to staff safely. Weather and calendar effects make arrivals bend in both straight-line and curved patterns. Their 2026 study blended a classic time-series method with a neural network in two architectures, then raced them against five rival approaches at several forecast horizons.

The second hybrid, which merged the two methods' forecasts, won overall, especially in the volatile middle horizon where single models stumbled. The extended statistical model did best at calm, long horizons. The authors offer emergency departments a practical recipe matched to forecast distance and turbulence.
plos-pone-0348066:
Madeleine I. R. Brodbeck and colleagues asked whether a brain region called Cluster N, linked to magnetic compass sensing in migrating birds, also switches on in zebra finches, which do not migrate. Finches searched for food in a maze under three magnetic conditions: one honest field pointing to the food, and two scrambled fields carrying no direction. Afterwards the team stained brains for a gene that marks recent activity.

Activity rose in both Cluster N and the hippocampus, the brain's map room, but equally under all three field conditions. That gives no firm proof Cluster N reads the compass here. Still, its presence and activation in a non-migrant hints the region serves broader orientation jobs.
plos-pone-0348266:
Salwa S Zghebi and co-authors evaluated England's national online diabetes self-management program, Healthy Living, in work published in 2026. The free program teaches people with type two diabetes about their condition and daily habits, but who signs up and whether it helps were unclear.

Linking program records with the national diabetes audit, the team compared people who registered with matched non users over a year. They mapped who joined, who stayed, and how health measures such as blood sugar changed. Large scale digital help only counts if people actually use it, and this check shows where the program reaches and where it falls short.
plos-pone-0348366:
Ayumu Kojima and colleagues fed Alaska pollock protein to animals and cells to learn why this fish protein builds fast-twitch muscle so well. Blood taken about ninety minutes after eating the protein made muscle cells in dishes grow larger and contract more strongly. Levels of a gut hormone rose at the same moment. That hinted that something circulating carries the effect.

Deep surveys of muscle found thousands of proteins and hundreds of fats reshaped, with a striking rise in membranes carrying a prized omega-three fat. The diet held almost none of it. The pattern partly resembled endurance training. Fat-burning enzymes in muscle also switched on. The authors conclude the protein itself, as a high-quality building source, drives growth while quietly rewiring fat metabolism.
plos-pone-0348566:
Qiu Jie and co-workers ask how social media use connects with exercise habits among older adults in China. Phones and apps now bring seniors health news and social contact. Their 2026 study surveys more than eleven hundred people aged sixty and over, measuring media use, coping style, felt support from others, and exercise habits in one snapshot.

Media use linked with more active coping and stronger felt support, and both of those linked with better exercise habits. The path ran in a chain: media use fed coping, coping fed felt support, and support helped lock in exercise. The authors suggest programs that use social platforms to build confidence and community could help older adults stay active.
plos-pone-0348766:
Woo Sub Kim and colleagues asked how ankle arthritis severity relates to how much people actually move. Activity protects the heart and metabolism, but a painful, arthritic ankle can quietly cut it off. The study reviewed two hundred sixty-two patients at a specialty foot and ankle clinic whose arthritis had reached at least a moderate stage on X-rays.

Patients reported their weekly activity on a standard questionnaire, converted into energy units, and rated their foot outcomes and pain. The analysis connected activity with arthritis stage while accounting for age, sex, body mass, and pain. If worse joints mean less movement, these patients face a double burden: joint damage plus the metabolic diseases that inactivity invites, which argues for activity support as part of ankle care.
plos-pone-0348866:
Leo Joskowicz and co-workers train deep learning models to spot inherited eye diseases from wide pictures of the retina. These diseases, passed through families, can be slow to diagnose. Their 2026 study uses records from an Israeli medical center covering just over four hundred patients, pairing two kinds of eye images with genetic test results.

Models given both image types did best at telling diseased eyes from healthy ones. They also sorted patients into groups of likely faulty genes with good accuracy. Results held up across repeated rounds of checking. Image-based screening of this kind could point patients toward the right genetic tests sooner, saving time in clinics that lack eye-genetics experts.
plos-pone-0349666:
Eva Messer and colleagues tracked a fat-regulating blood protein, ApoC3, across the stages of the common fatty liver disease now called MASLD. The protein helps govern triglycerides and is tied to heart risk, but its behavior as liver disease advances was unclear. Blood from a hundred ninety-seven patients, from simple fatty liver through scarring to liver cancer, was compared with samples from healthy donors.

ApoC3 did not simply climb with damage. It ran lower in the cirrhosis and cancer stages than in early disease or in controls, and low values traveled with other signs of advanced liver failure. That arc matters for drug developers, since new medicines aim to block this very protein: the stage of disease may decide whether lowering it further helps, harms, or misses the point entirely.
plos-pone-0350166:
Tom Moorhouse and five colleagues investigate this 2026 PLOS One study of conflict between people and elephants in villages along the edge of South Africa's Kruger National Park. Elephants that leave the park can endanger residents and crops, and some are killed under current policy. The team combined community surveys with social media accounts of one incident in the village of Matsulu, where an elephant died.

Both sources pointed the same way: some residents tampered with the park fence and lured elephants out, gaining meat and, for a few, money, while the wider community bore the costs. Most survey respondents still backed non-lethal ways of managing elephants. The authors recommend re-examining the policy that allows escaped elephants to be killed, since it may reward the very escapes it aims to handle.
plos-pone-0350266:
Rogelio A Coronado and co-authors interviewed emergency doctors in 2026 about non drug pain treatments, from heat and movement to complementary approaches. Such options are endorsed for pain yet rarely offered in emergency departments, and provider views gate any change.

Nine physicians at one academic centre spoke in depth about current practice and what helps or blocks new options. Six themes emerged, spanning hospital systems, professional beliefs, and patient factors, and were drawn into a working model for rollout. The study's use is practical: it tells implementers which doors to push first, in a setting ruled by minutes.
plos-pone-0350666:
Asmaa Ahmad and three colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One statistics paper on filling gaps in seasonal data without wrecking the season's pattern. Standard gap-filling tools often flatten the repeating cycles in series like temperature records. Their framework first extracts the statistically solid periodic components of a series using a specialized bootstrap method, then feeds those components as helper information into an established multiple-imputation program.

In simulated experiments on temperature data with realistic seasonal structure, adding the periodic information cut reconstruction errors roughly in half compared with the same imputation program working without it. The authors stress the method assists existing imputation rather than replacing it. They present it as a practical upgrade for health and climate datasets where cycles carry real meaning.
plos-pone-0351466:
A narrowed aortic valve once meant open-heart surgery for everyone. Now many patients receive a new valve through a leg artery. Anaïs Havet and colleagues traced how France used both options. They studied the years 2010 to 2022. Their data came from the national health system. The paper appeared in PLOS One in 2026.

More than two hundred fifty thousand procedures were counted. Tube-based replacement grew from about fourteen hundred cases a year. By 2022 it reached nearly seventeen thousand. Those patients were older than surgery patients. They also carried higher surgical risk scores. Surprisingly, famous trials and guideline updates showed no clear link to the growth.
plos-pone-0351666:
Worn knee cartilage involves many genes, and Jing-le Zhuge and colleagues combined several public gene datasets to find the ones most tied to osteoarthritis. Their 2026 PLOS One study merged five collections of cartilage cell data and kept a sixth aside for checking.

After cleaning batch differences, the team listed genes whose activity changed in disease. Three different machine learning methods then voted on the strongest candidates, each using a different logic. The winners were checked against the spare dataset and against which immune cells appear in diseased tissue. The authors hope the shortlist points toward new drug targets and diagnostic markers.
plos-pone-0351766:
Swedish children who struggle mentally often cannot get help until a formal diagnosis lands. Karin Törnbom and co-authors interviewed fourteen executives, clinicians, and parents in the Västra Götaland region about this bottleneck, in this 2026 PLOS One qualitative study.

Waiting for a diagnosis was the central complaint, especially in schools and primary care, where support rules hinge on labels. Children with mixed or unusual difficulties fell through the cracks entirely. Regional differences and weak cooperation between services made care uneven. Participants pointed to earlier, lower-threshold support as the main opportunity to fix the pathway.
plos-pone-0351966:
Donghao Zhang, Xiaodong Yan, and Feng Shen built a better way to map how extreme losses could jump between Chinese financial firms. Standard tools for tail risk, the rare bad days that cause crises, often fail their own accuracy tests. Their method blends a factor model with flexible dependence patterns and checks itself by backtesting, comparing predicted joint crashes with what the math says should happen.

The new model failed its backtests far less often than the rival versions, with rejection rates cut by roughly half against two of them. Applied to listed Chinese financial institutions, the risk network it drew lined up with real market stress events. Regulators watching for contagion get a network map that has passed stricter honesty checks, and a clearer view of which firms sit at the web's risky center.
plos-pone-0352166:
Singh and colleagues designed a gene edit for rohu, a major food fish, in a 2026 study. The target was a gene that slows muscle growth, so switching it off could one day yield bigger fish for farming. All of the work was done by design and computer checks, before any live fish would be changed.

The team built a short piece of donor DNA with one letter swapped to create an early stop signal in the gene. Lab checks confirmed the swap was in place, and computer models predicted the gene product would be cut short and lose its normal shape. Readers get a tested blueprint for a future breeding step, not a finished fish.
plos-pone-0352766:
Abdullah Alasmary presents this 2026 PLOS One corpus study of the words of contract law. The aim is a keyword list for students and lawyers from abroad who work in legal English. The words come from a set of contract law textbooks. Alasmary chose them by how often they appear, how widely they spread, and how distinct they are from general legal writing.

The final list holds more than seven hundred words. They make up a clear slice of textbook language. Nouns dominate, at nearly half the entries. Adjectives and verbs come next. The author argues that a focused list helps teachers build lessons around the words that truly carry contract law. Generic academic lists miss the field's habits and stock phrases.
plos-pone-0352866:
Robert Davis and seven colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS One primer explaining the daily temperature swing, the gap between a day's high and low, for health researchers. Large swings are often linked to illness and death, but the weather behind them is rarely explained. Using a detailed climate archive, the team mapped how the swing has changed across the mainland United States from 1950 through 2022.

The daily swing has shrunk over most of the country, because nights are warming faster than days as air grows more humid and cloudy. The most extreme swing days, those most tied to health effects, are also becoming rarer. The authors note this could mean falling risk if the swing itself causes harm, and they call for clinical evidence on why calm, dry, clear days might strain the body.
plos-pone-0352966:
Rana Ali Al-Qaari and seven colleagues build a questionnaire on folic acid. It had to work across two very different cultures. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Folic acid before pregnancy prevents serious birth defects. Yet awareness varies widely. Five hundred and thirty-eight women completed the new tool. They lived in Thailand and Yemen. The tool has eight knowledge questions and ten attitude questions. Experts helped develop it. It was tested twice for stability.

The attitude section performed strongly in both countries. Its structure held together well. Knowledge was patchier. Women knew food sources and timing best. They knew the underlying biology least. The Yemeni knowledge section held together less tightly. A shared tool lets health programmes compare barriers honestly across borders.
plos-pone-0353166:
La and colleagues, writing in 2026, introduce a new language resource for Vietnamese government work. Their team built a large set of labeled administrative texts, meant to teach computers to find named items in official papers. Older Vietnamese data sets drew mostly on news or health texts, which left a gap for formal state documents.

The new corpus holds a very large number of sentences marked for five kinds of items, such as agencies, legal papers, dates, and amounts. Human checkers agreed closely on the labels, which supports trust in the data. The authors also test a model that pairs a Vietnamese language model with a step that keeps labels in a sensible order. That model beat older methods on their tests, and the data set is shared in public for other teams to use.
plos-pone-0353266:
La and colleagues, in a 2026 survey, ask American health professionals what they know and do about RSV, a respiratory virus that can hospitalize older adults. Vaccines for adults are new, uptake is low, and doctors' own gaps may be part of the problem. Seven hundred clinicians, from primary care doctors to pharmacists, answered during the 2024-25 season.

Most said they were very familiar with the disease, yet real gaps showed on who the vaccines are approved for and what national advisers recommend. The most common barriers were patients refusing or hesitating, and patients simply never having heard of RSV. Only about a third of workplaces stocked the vaccine, though most clinicians said they recommend it to eligible patients. Recommendations, however, were not made consistently to everyone eligible. The authors point to education for clinicians and patients alike as the fastest lever.
plos-pone-0353466:
Muhammad Danyal and three colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One paper on teaching computers to write captions that describe what is happening in a picture. Many automatic caption systems match words without grasping how objects relate to each other, so their captions come out thin. The team combined an object-detection model with a text-generating transformer that also encodes where objects sit in the image.

Against two older approaches, the new system scored best on measures that reward meaning and object relationships, even though it trailed on one word-matching score. Human experts also rated its captions highly for accuracy across several hundred test images. The work points toward image descriptions that are more useful for search, accessibility, and content sorting.
plos-pone-0353666:
Ji Eun Song, Mi Yeon Lee, Chungkwon Yoo, and Joon Mo Kim published this 2026 study of eye pressure and women's reproductive history in South Korea. Using a national health survey, they analyzed more than eighteen hundred women past menopause. They related age at first period, age at menopause, and reproductive span to pressure inside the eye, split by whether the women had glaucoma.

Longer estrogen exposure tracked with higher eye pressure in women without glaucoma, but with lower pressure in women with glaucoma. Song calls estrogen's role context dependent, with possible use in judging glaucoma risk.
plos-pone-0353766:
David Madden analyses how countries' COVID-19 death tolls compare once their different age structures are handled fairly, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Older populations naturally suffer more in a pandemic, so crude comparisons mislead. Using a standard dataset of short-term mortality, Madden recalculated excess deaths with one shared age distribution, and also counted years of life lost, then related the results to national income and inequality.

The recalculations moved individual countries somewhat but barely shuffled the overall ranking. Richer countries generally fared better; inequality showed no clear link. Former planned economies of central and eastern Europe clustered together with poor outcomes. Rankings, he concludes, are sturdier than critics of excess-death statistics suggest.
plos-pone-0353866:
Andras Dobos and seven colleagues test a hormone-like drug against eye inflammation in mice, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The drug, maxadilan, activates a receptor that calms inflammation and swelling, and the team wanted to know whether it could protect the cornea. Mice were given a bacterial toxin that triggers eye inflammation, followed by the drug injected into the eye.

Scans showed less corneal swelling and better-preserved tissue in treated animals. Eye pressure dropped, fewer inflammatory cells gathered in the eye fluid, and several inflammatory signals fell. Microscope checks confirmed the cornea kept its normal structure. The authors propose this receptor as a promising target for treating inflamed eyes.
plos-pone-0353966:
Marcelo Bueno and eight colleagues ask whether a field's cropping history helps predict how much carbon its soil holds, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study of Peru's northern highlands. Andean soils are carbon-rich but threatened as farming expands. The team trained a satellite-based classifier on more than five hundred fields to reconstruct which crops rotated where between 2019 and 2022, then tested whether that history improved a soil-carbon model.

The full model explained about two thirds of the variation. Soil properties themselves mattered most, but among management signals, how often a field lay fallow was the strongest single clue. Dropping climate data hurt the model more than dropping rotation history — useful guidance for where to spend measurement effort.
plos-pone-0354266:
Xiang Feng and six colleagues piece together the molecular structure of a particular Chinese coal, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Knowing coal's exact structure helps engineers burn and convert it more cleanly. Their sample was a high-volatile bituminous coal from Inner Mongolia. Four laboratory techniques probed its elements, carbon skeleton, chemical groups, and nitrogen forms from different angles.

Combining the readings, they proposed a single large molecule with a stated formula, built from small aromatic rings linked by carbon and oxygen chains. Its oxygen sits mainly in phenol and ether groups, its nitrogen in ring structures. Simulated spectra matched the real measurements, supporting the model as a working picture of this coal.
plos-pone-0354366:
Shabnam Varmazyari and three colleagues compare how Iranian dentists and their patients feel about dentists counseling smokers to quit, in this 2026 two-phase survey. Dentists see smokers' mouths regularly, making the dental chair an underused front against tobacco. The study canvassed all dentists in Tehran province's comprehensive health centers and several hundred patients at city centers, a few years apart, asking about attitudes and what shapes them.

Non-smoking dentists held notably more positive attitudes toward offering cessation counseling, as did those working in the city itself. Among patients, non-smokers were more likely to judge such counseling effective, while patients with a smoker in the family were less convinced. Employed patients found oral symptoms a stronger motive to quit and were more willing to try quitting with dental support. The authors suggest mentoring for smoking dentists, remote training for rural ones, and workplace-based programs.
plos-pone-0354466:
Ruoyan Pei and colleagues present in 2026 a two stage detection system for finding road users in poor light, blending normal camera and heat images. Distant small objects give weak signals, and glare or darkness degrades each image type in its own way. The first stage fuses the two views with gated attention, and the second links candidate objects in a graph to reason about their layout.

Tests on two public datasets showed much stronger results across day and night, with the day to night gap shrinking dramatically. Small object detection improved a lot, and speed stayed fast enough for real time use. Self driving systems in hard conditions could benefit.
plos-pone-0354666:
Abdirisak Nur Yusuf is first author on a 2026 PLOS ONE survey of anemia in pregnant women in Garowe City, Somalia. Anemia, a shortage of healthy red blood cells, is common in pregnancy in poorer countries, but local data for Garowe were scarce. The team studied four hundred and twenty-two randomly chosen women at public clinics.

About thirty-nine percent had anemia, a moderate public health concern by world standards. Rural residence and having had several pregnancies raised the odds. So did missing nutrition counseling, testing positive for malaria, and not eating an extra daily meal. The authors urge better nutrition advice, extra meals, and malaria prevention in pregnancy.
plos-pone-0354966:
Luca Martino and co-authors propose a way to show uncertainty when choosing how complex a statistical model should be. Analysts often must pick a number of components, or how strongly to shrink a model toward simplicity. Their 2026 paper gives two procedures that return a plausible range instead of a single guessed value.

Both procedures read the shape of the error curve, so they need no probability model for the data. Tests on made-up and real datasets showed the ranges worked well in practice. The methods apply across regression, classification, clustering, and related tasks. Martino and colleagues also share MATLAB code, so other researchers can use the approach directly.
plos-pone-0355166:
Alaa Abdulelah Alansari and co-authors gauged smoke exposure in Saudi women with a urine test, not just with self-reports. Shame makes many women hide smoking, so surveys miss the truth. Their 2026 study took urine from one hundred thirty-three women who also filled forms on smoking and on smoke breathed from others.

The team proved out a fine lab method for cotinine, the stuff nicotine breaks down into, which stays in urine. The method was true and tight across the range they need. They set cut points fit for this group to split smokers from non-smokers. Alansari and colleagues say body tests should back up surveys where shame skews frank replies.
plos-pone-0355466:
Corinna Urmann and colleagues tackled a classic trap in hunting antiviral compounds in plants. One common chlorophyll breakdown product, pheophorbide A, blocks viruses so reliably that it drowns out every subtler candidate in a screening test. Their 2026 study built a leveling strategy. It measured each extract's pheophorbide content. It judged the extract's antiviral effect against what that content alone predicts.

Six of fifteen plant species cleared the bar and earned priority for deeper work. In cowslip fractions, the comparison plus chemical profiling pointed to additional candidate molecules beyond the usual suspect. The method generalizes. Any natural product screen haunted by one dominant compound can use the same accounting trick to find the quieter chemistry hiding behind it.
plos-pone-0355866:
Md Mahfuz Islam, Richard McLaughlin, and Joshua Heitman test whether mixing compost into construction-battered soil can help cities absorb stormwater, in this 2026 laboratory study. Building work compacts soil until rain runs off instead of soaking in. The team packed soil columns with two soil types and two compost recipes at four mixing rates, then ran water through them repeatedly over six months while tracking the soil's physical condition.

At the two higher rates, the soil grew lighter and more porous and held more plant-available water. Infiltration was fastest at the highest compost rate, roughly ten times the untreated soil, with middle rates close behind; gains steadied after about two months but lasted the full trial. Compost type made no difference. The authors suggest at least a thirty percent mix is needed for a real stormwater benefit.
plos-pone-0356066:
Rebecca Dudovitz and co-authors compared how families report adverse childhood experiences in clinic versus by telephone. Screening for childhood adversity can trigger help, but only if parents answer fully and honestly. Their 2026 study re-screened, by a community helpline's telephone service, families who had already completed the same screen at well-child visits.

Fifty-one families from three community health centres took part in the within-family comparison. The analysis asked whether scores shifted between settings and which family traits, including trust in healthcare, predicted any shift. Dudovitz and colleagues frame screening mode as a design choice with consequences: the same questions may harvest different truths depending on who asks, and where.
plos-pone-0356266:
Hanye Zhou and coauthors published a 2026 plant pathology paper in PLOS ONE on detecting a damaging passionfruit virus, East Asian Passiflora virus, with a new laboratory test. The virus spreads through China's passionfruit regions and cuts yields, so growers need fast, certain diagnosis. The team built a real-time fluorescence test targeting the virus's coat protein gene and tuned it carefully.

The assay proved highly specific, flagging only the target virus, and roughly a thousand times more sensitive than the older standard test, detecting very small amounts of viral material. It found the virus in deliberately infected plants and in leaves the infection reached on its own. In 2025, one hundred twenty suspect samples from Yunnan Province all tested positive, confirming how established the virus is there. The assay is offered as a surveillance tool for nurseries and regional monitoring programs.
plos-pone-0356366:
Farai Nyabadza modeled a dark side of prisons in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. Jailing people for petty crimes may increase later crime, if prison exposes minor offenders to harder criminal influence. Nyabadza built a model to quantify that criminogenic effect, the degree to which incarceration itself breeds crime.

The model's numbers put a measurable size on the school-of-crime effect that reformers have long warned about. Policymakers weighing short sentences for minor offenses gain a cost rarely shown in budgets: future victims and future prison load. Even readers who favor tough sentencing benefit from seeing the trade-off priced. Sentencing debates improve when both sides must answer the same arithmetic.
plos-pone-0356566:
Takuya Nishioka and colleagues tested a shortcut for profiling leg strength. Instead of pressing against many loads, use just two, one light and one heavy. The loads chart how force falls as speed rises. Their 2026 study had sixteen young men perform maximal leg presses on a pneumatic machine. Eleven loads were used. Full profiles were then compared against profiles computed from ten possible load pairs.

Pairs spanning a wide gap reproduced the full profile almost perfectly. The lightest load worked best against loads at roughly two and a half to three times body weight. Pairs with close-together loads degraded quickly. Coaches use these profiles to target training. A valid two-load test saves athletes a long, exhausting testing session, provided the two loads are chosen far apart.
plos-pone-0356766:
Un-Kon Lee reviewed five years of worldwide AI ethics principles. They came from governments, think tanks, and technology companies. His goal was to update South Korea's national set. His 2026 study combined thirty-seven prior reviews into seventeen candidate principles. It ranked their standing across the field. It tracked how rankings shifted around 2020, when most national sets appeared.

Three principles proved durable everywhere: transparency, robustness, and a ban on rights infringement. Five others rose or lagged in use and need fresh emphasis. They include responsibility, well-being, human rights, controllability, and sustainability. Lee proposes expanding Korea's ten principles to fourteen. His analysis also flags which ideals are both valued and well served, and which need governing machinery built urgently.
plos-pone-0357466:
José Luís Pimenta, João Carlos Paiva, and Maria João Fonseca published a museum education study from Portugal in PLOS ONE in 2026. They asked children in a program called Young Naturalists what they think of natural history museums. Adult planners often guess at what holds a child's interest; this team asked the children directly.

Pimenta and his colleagues gathered the children's own views on what draws them in and what leaves them cold. Answers like these help museum staff design visits that spark real curiosity instead of passive walking. For any museum trying to serve young visitors, the study is a reminder to build programs with children's voices in the room.
plos-pone-0357566: Vásquez-Arévalo and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on birds, fruit, and forest regrowth in southern Brazil. They mapped which birds eat fruit from which plants in two young Araucaria forests. These feeding webs show how seeds get carried to new ground. When key birds vanish, tree spread can stall. The maps help managers plan how to help damaged forests heal.
plos-pone-0357666:
Yuta Nemoto and co-authors ran a small pilot trial in Yokosuka, Japan, asking whether video game contests can help older adults stay sharp and active. Their 2026 program mixed health lessons, exercise, and organized gaming in weekly sessions over about three months. Adults aged sixty and over who had never played digital games took part, split between the program group and a comparison group.

No one was harmed, nearly everyone stayed, and all players said they enjoyed the sessions. Mood scores rose after each meeting, and walking speed and balance improved more in the gaming group than in the comparison group. Nemoto and colleagues stress that the trial was small and exploratory, so larger studies must confirm any real benefit.
plos-pone-0357966:
Shuting Cheng and colleagues published a 2026 gene study in PLOS ONE on how the heart adapts when oxygen stays low for a long time. Chronic low oxygen is a driver of cardiovascular disease, but its effects on heart tissue were tangled up with two other patterns: low oxygen before birth, and a shorter adult exposure. Using three public gene-expression datasets, the team compared the patterns side by side, with extensive permutation testing.

Each pattern produced its own distinct set of changed genes, with no overlap between the groups. The sustained pattern rewired the heart's daily clock network heavily: links between clock genes thinned by about two-thirds, while one gene, ASS1, became a central hub. Changed genes split into two camps, metabolic-immune versus clock pathways, with matching splits in linked diseases and drug targets. Long-term oxygen shortage, they say, reshapes heart biology along two separate tracks.
plos-pone-0358066:
Joseph Mwaka, Conrad Sserunjogi, and Jesca Natalayi catalogue the tumours found in patients at a specialized HIV centre in Kampala, in PLOS ONE in 2026. They reviewed two hundred nineteen tumour records at Mildmay Hospital, spanning 2017 into 2026. For each growth they noted whether it was malignant. They also recorded the patient's immune status and virus control at diagnosis, in the modern era of effective HIV treatment.

Nearly two thirds of the tumours were malignant, and Kaposi sarcoma alone supplied almost half of the cancers. Most patients had their virus suppressed at diagnosis, yet over half of those suppressed cases were still malignant. Cancer clustered in patients who had started treatment late: low immune cell counts, advanced disease stage, and fewer months on therapy before the tumour appeared. The authors caution these are unadjusted patterns, but they set a baseline for a planned prospective cancer cohort at the centre.
plos-pone-0358266:
Panthip Patrakunwiwat led a team of eight authors comparing two lifelines for newborn hearts, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Some babies are born with lung circulation that depends on a fetal vessel staying open. Doctors can keep flow with a stent in that vessel, or with a surgical shunt called a modified Blalock-Taussig shunt.

Patrakunwiwat's team compared how the lung arteries change after each approach. That growth matters because these babies later need full repair surgery, and vessel size shapes its success. Head-to-head results guide heart teams choosing the safer bridge for each fragile newborn. Both options save lives; the question is which grows better arteries with fewer problems.
plos-pone-0358366:
Hui Zeng leads a team of seven mapping the uncertainty that shadows women treated for gynecologic and breast cancers, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Not knowing what comes next corrodes mental health, especially where support is thin. Four hundred thirteen patients at a Beijing hospital completed scales for uncertainty, support, depression, and anxiety. Statistical profiling sorted the women by how uncertainty presented, and a structural model tested whether uncertainty links support to depression.

Three profiles emerged. A small group, about eight percent, combined low uncertainty with good adaptation. The largest, over half, lived with high uncertainty and a foggy grasp of their disease. Education, who provided care, time since diagnosis, support, and depression all separated the groups. The modeling placed uncertainty in the middle of the support to depression pathway. Screening for the fog itself could catch struggling patients that symptom checklists miss.
plos-pone-0358466:
Ya-Ling Hsieh, Chia-Jung Chiang, and Tsung Yu published a 2026 population study in PLOS ONE on childbirth after cancer among women in Taiwan. As survival improves, more women diagnosed during their reproductive years wonder whether they can still have children, but Asian population data were scarce. The authors linked Taiwan's cancer, birth, and death registries to follow tens of thousands of women diagnosed at age thirty-nine or younger.

About one survivor in ten had a live birth after diagnosis, and overall survivors had roughly half the births expected in the general population. Outcomes differed sharply by cancer type: thyroid and skin cancer survivors kept childbearing nearly intact, while cervical, uterine, breast, blood, and brain cancers cut it most. Older age at diagnosis and chemotherapy also lowered the chances. The authors press for early fertility counseling and better access to fertility-preserving care.
plos-pone-0358566:
Hala Alkhoury leads a team of six assembling the first large picture of gunshot wounds treated across the Palestinian West Bank, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Eight hospitals contributed records for three hundred ninety-two patients treated between 2020 and 2025. Nearly all were male, and the typical patient was a teenager or young man of about nineteen. The study maps where bullets struck, what surgery was needed, and how patients fared.

Limbs took most injuries, about two thirds, and broken bones were the commonest accompanying damage. Chest, belly, and blood vessel wounds were rarer but far more dangerous. Over half the patients needed surgery, most often bone fixation or vessel repair. One in five required intensive care, about three percent died in hospital, and more than half of survivors left with some dependence on others. A fast pulse and abdominal injury best predicted intensive care need.
plos-pone-0358866: Yang and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on software that finds flaws on steel surfaces. Their network, EMamba, adds a mixture-of-experts design to a state space model. The goal is sturdy detection even when lighting or steel type changes. Missed cracks in steel can fail later in bridges or machines, so reliable automated inspection has real safety value.
plos-pone-0358966:
Solomon Daniel Halilu leads a team of seven asking Nigerian medical students how they want to be taught, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The survey covered one hundred seventy-one students at Abubakar Tafawa Balewa University in Bauchi and mixed counted answers with written comments. Lectures, problem based learning, team learning, practical demonstrations, and digital tools were all on the table.

Practical demonstrations won, chosen by about a third, followed by small group activities at about a quarter. The biggest complaint was trouble retaining information, named by nearly half, with a smaller share feeling underprepared for clinical work. Students asked for teaching tied closely to real patients, lecturers who know their subjects deeply, and consultants who also mentor. The authors recommend more hands on and group learning, better clinical exposure, and stronger digital facilities in the curriculum.
plos-pone-0359066:
Ahmad Bishr Nasra leads a team of eight surveying whether patients in Syria care about their doctor's sex, in a 2026 PLOS ONE study. In conservative settings, comfort with a male or female physician can shape whether people seek care at all, especially for private examinations. Local evidence was thin, so the team questioned adults at major public teaching hospitals across several centers.

For everyday matters and most routine interactions, many respondents said they had no preference. The picture changed for intimate examinations, where patients strongly favored a doctor of their own sex. Women leaned toward female doctors for intimate and reproductive care, while men more often chose male doctors even for general examinations. The findings help hospitals think about staffing and scheduling where patient comfort decides attendance.
plos-pone-0359266: Landa and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE case study on water, sanitation, and hygiene guidance in Indonesia. The guidance aims to be climate-resilient and inclusive, so services hold up under floods and reach everyone. The team used mixed methods to study how the guidance was put into practice. Lessons from one country can help others adapt similar guidance to local risks.
plos-pone-0359566:
Yingzhe Wang and six colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on a medicinal plant, Eupatorium lindleyanum. Using multi-omics integration, several layers of molecular data combined, the authors reveal how sesquiterpenoids are made. These plant chemicals, thought to carry much of the plant's healing value, are made differently in different tissues.

Knowing which tissue makes which compound tells growers and chemists which plant parts to harvest and when. Tissue-specific production also hints at the genes worth breeding or engineering for stronger medicine. Researchers of healing plants and natural drug chemistry are the audience for this molecular map.
plos-pone-0359866:
Cartrine Anyango, Isabel Goicolea, and Fredinah Namatovu published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. Set in Sweden, it assesses whether formal service providers are ready to address intimate partner violence among women with disabilities. The analysis uses mixed methods, combining surveys with deeper qualitative material.
