Women with disabilities face high rates of partner violence and extra barriers when seeking help. Readiness covers whether police, health, and social services can recognize abuse and respond accessibly. Swedish service planners, and disability advocates pressing for safer services, are the readers for this readiness check.
plos-pone-0360066:
Peiyuan Liu, Tania Espinosa, Elham Samami, Bernard Mensah, and Hermine Poghosyan wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article. It studies adults in ten United States states and the link between economic instability and substance use. The work is population-based, drawing on a broad sample rather than a clinic group.

Economic instability covers insecure work, income swings, and trouble meeting basic costs. Tying that instability to substance use helps explain why addiction clusters where livelihoods are shaky. Public health officials designing prevention programs can use state-level evidence to argue for pairing treatment with economic support services.
pmc-13197166:
Gustavo Aguilar and colleagues report a 2026 gene study in fruit fly wings. Wing growth needs two borders that set top-bottom and front-back axes. One selector gene, apterous, switches on early in wing growth, and its control region must fire in the right place.

The team mutated that control region in place with gene editing tools. Faults shifted the top-bottom border and at times doubled front wing parts in mirror form. One binding site proved vital, since its loss left flies wingless. A silencing tool let them test when and where the region must act. Three helper factors proved needful for its work. The work maps how the gene first turns on.
pmc-13198466:
David Gaist and colleagues measured repeat stroke risk in England and Denmark in a 2026 records study. An ischemic stroke occurs when a clot blocks brain blood flow. Repeat strokes can strike even with standard prevention, so the team tracked first strokes not caused by heart rhythm faults.

More than fifty thousand English and sixty thousand Danish patients were followed for years. Repeat stroke rates were alike in both nations and highest in the first year. By five years, roughly one in six patients had a repeat event. In Denmark, repeat strokes were more often moderate or severe than first strokes. The authors call for stronger prevention after a first stroke, above all in year one.
pmc-13201266:
Gözde Tekin and co-authors present a 2026 case report about a rare complication of implanted chemotherapy ports. Their patient, a 63-year-old man with lung cancer, had a port catheter that fractured and migrated into his pulmonary arteries after compression between the clavicle and the first rib.

Clinicians first tried to retrieve the fragment through a vein using a snare, but the catheter was firmly stuck to the vessel wall. Imaging also showed serious coronary artery disease, so surgeons removed the catheter and performed coronary bypass grafting in one operation. The report shows why surgery can succeed when catheter retrieval fails.
pmc-13201866:
Tuberculosis can silently damage the fallopian tubes, and a 2026 case article from Maryam Hashemi presents two women whose infertility workups uncovered pelvic tuberculosis. The article describes both cases and reviews how this rare, often forgotten diagnosis presents and should be managed.

In both women, the infection centered on the fallopian tubes, the site most often affected in genital tuberculosis. Care combined surgery with medical therapy, since confirming the diagnosis often needs laparoscopy and biopsy rather than imaging alone. The authors urge clinicians to consider tuberculosis in infertility patients from regions where the disease is common, because drug treatment follows a four-drug regimen.
pmc-13202666:
Collegiate dancers train hard on little food, and a 2026 study authored by Samantha Brooks audits their micronutrient intake against recommended levels. The research article assesses thirty female dancers from three United States university programs using a detailed diet history questionnaire covering food and supplements.

Most dancers fell below recommended intakes for calcium, iron, vitamin D, omega-3 fats, and folate, while majorities met targets for vitamins B12 and C. Against stricter sports nutrition guidance, shortfalls grew even wider for several nutrients in the group. Supplement use was linked to meeting targets for iron and folate, and total energy intake predicted adequacy, underlining fueling as the core problem.
pmc-13211866:
Young heart patients who can handle online health information may live better with their disease, and a 2026 cross-sectional study by Puteri Sofia Nadira Megat Kamaruddin tests that chain in Malaysia. The survey recruited 136 young patients with ischemic heart disease at two hospital cardiology clinics and modeled links among health consciousness, eHealth literacy, adherence, and quality of life.

Structural equation modeling found digital health literacy carried the strongest direct association with quality of life among the factors studied. Treatment adherence and health consciousness also contributed positively in the fitted models. Consciousness reached quality of life partly through both mediators working side by side, a parallel pathway the authors judged the best-fitting explanation of their data.
pmc-13238666:
Catalase, a food enzyme from a natural fungus strain, returns for a revised safety verdict from the EFSA Panel on Food Enzymes. It is made by an Aspergillus niger strain for Shin Nihon Chemical in Japan, and an earlier panel had left its safety in doubt. Food makers use catalase to break down hydrogen peroxide left over from processes such as cheese making and egg treatment.

In the earlier check, the panel could not rule out safety worries because the margin of exposure was too small. This revised evaluation re-examines the data and the exposure estimates behind that gap. Updated verdicts like this are how food law adapts: an ingredient is neither banned forever nor waved through, but retested as figures improve.
pmc-13238966:
Nisar and colleagues test how usable a best-practice phone platform feels to the hospital staff meant to use it. The platform, C8 Health, pushes proven clinical routines into daily workflow. It was deployed in the anaesthesiology department at MetroHealth in 2024, and this study surveys the people who worked with it there.

Mobile health tools live or die on usability: a clunky app is quietly abandoned, however sound its content. The survey measures how easily staff could find, trust, and act on guidance in real shifts. Results like these tell builders whether the barrier to better practice is the evidence, the software, or the fit with a busy department's day.
pmc-13240966:
Firth and a Nepal-UK team spoke with parents whose children joined a vaccine schedule trial in the Kathmandu Valley. 33 parents from the OptImms study described their choices in Nepali. The trial compared other schedules for the diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis vaccine. Talks were translated and sorted by theme.

Trust in health workers and research groups anchored nearly every sign-up. Family talks mattered too, mainly comfort from kin in healthcare jobs. Smooth scheduling, extra care access, and travel pay-back helped families stay in. Time pressure, distance, and dread of blood draws were the main barriers.
pmc-13242666:
Mai Elbatanony and co-authors tested whether children's multivitamins damage the materials dentists use to fill young teeth. Their laboratory study appeared in BMC Oral Health in 2026. Gummy and chewable vitamins carry citric and ascorbic acids strong enough to erode dental materials in principle. The team soaked 135 specimens of three restorative materials in dissolved gummies, dissolved chewable tablets, or artificial saliva, repeating the exposure daily for six months.

Every material suffered some loss of hardness, smoothness, or color stability, but the pattern depended on both material and vitamin form. The gummy preparation proved more erosive than the chewable tablets for most combinations. Glass ionomer cement and the composites reacted differently, which matters when dentists choose materials for children who take daily vitamins. The authors caution that the soaking model only simulates mouth conditions. Even so, the results give pediatric dentistry a concrete reason to ask about supplements.
pmc-13242866:
Hatice Betigül Meral and colleagues compared sexual function in women with lipedema against matched healthy women. Their cross-sectional study appeared in Sexual Medicine in 2026. Lipedema causes painful, heavy fat buildup in the legs and limits movement, but its effect on sexual health is rarely studied. Fifty patients and fifty controls of similar age and body mass completed standard questionnaires on sexual function, anxiety, depression, leg function, pain, and quality of life.

Women with lipedema scored far lower on sexual function overall and on every subscale. Three-quarters of patients fell below the clinical cut-off for dysfunction, compared with about a third of controls. Within the patient group, scores tracked with age and pain intensity among other factors. The authors argue the condition's burden reaches well past appearance and mobility into intimate life and well-being. They urge clinicians not to overlook sexual health when treating lipedema.
pmc-13243166:
Ankita Wal and co-authors reviewed smart nanogels, soft particles that hold cancer drugs and release them only where tumors lurk. Their review appeared in Discover Nano in 2026. Nanogels are water-rich networks of cross-linked polymers that can be built to react to acidity, heat, or the chemical mood inside cells. Tumors offer all these triggers: they run acidic, hoard glutathione, and overproduce certain enzymes.

The article sorts nanogels by trigger type, including designs that answer to several signals or to magnets, and compares how they are made and measured. Standard chemotherapy drugs from doxorubicin to docetaxel have been loaded into them with good uptake by cancer cells. Targeting tags such as folic acid steer the particles into tumors, sparing healthy tissue and cutting side effects. Release inside the cell rises while exposure elsewhere falls. The authors judge the platform promising but still preclinical in most forms.
pmc-13243866:
Alireza Babajani and colleagues report a woman treated for a foreign body that had sat in her cervix for four years. Their case report appeared in Case Reports in Obstetrics and Gynecology in 2026. The thirty-nine-year-old mother of three came to hospital in January 2024 with heavy vaginal discharge and fever. Examination found a woolen object lodged in the cervix, placed there years earlier as a traditional method meant to influence a baby's sex.

Ultrasound showed a spongy mass filling the vaginal canal. Under anesthesia, camera inspection of the vagina and uterus let the team extract a foul-smelling wool mass that had burrowed five millimeters into the cervical tissue. Biopsies showed foreign body reaction with mixed acute and chronic inflammation, and no spread to bladder or womb. Three days of antibiotics completed her recovery. The authors warn about retained objects and unproven traditional practices.
pmc-13245766:
Zuriegat, Itani, and Abu Hammour reviewed diabetic foot infections at a Jordanian tertiary hospital in this 2026 PLOS One study, asking what keeps patients in hospital longest. The team examined two hundred thirty-four cases, cataloguing the infecting bacteria, their drug resistance, and whether the first antibiotics chosen, before culture results, actually covered the organisms found.

Staphylococcus aureus caused half the infections, and two thirds of cases involved multidrug-resistant organisms. The initial therapy was judged appropriate in under half the patients. Surprisingly, neither resistance nor inappropriate first therapy significantly predicted longer stays once other factors were weighed; infection severity was the one clear predictor. The authors stress early severity assessment, empiric choices guided by local resistance patterns, and strong antibiotic stewardship.
pmc-13246466:
Awan and Raza argue a safety point about remote monitoring of children's implanted heart devices, in this 2026 letter in Clinical Case Reports. Daily remote checks of pacemakers and defibrillators can catch rhythm problems early, and studies often report that detection success. The authors say detection is only half of a safe system.

What matters just as much, they argue, is the response pathway: how many alerts arrive and how many are false alarms. It also covers how fast a human reviews each alert, how quickly families are contacted, and what escalation steps follow. They call on future reports to publish those operational numbers, so readers can judge whether a monitoring program is truly safe and workable at scale.
pmc-13248966:
Yang and colleagues reviewed a combined blood index across many chronic diseases, in a 2026 narrative review. The index, called CTI, joins C-reactive protein, a marker of inflammation, with a triglyceride-glucose score tied to insulin resistance. It was first proposed in 2022, and the team searched the literature through January 2026 for what it predicts.

Higher CTI tracked consistently with worse risk and outcomes in heart disease, stroke, diabetes, and a combined heart-kidney-metabolic syndrome. Early work also links it to weaker bones, especially in type 2 diabetes. Cut-off values still vary by study, so the authors position CTI as a supporting risk tool, not a diagnosis by itself.
pmc-13249066:
Guo and colleagues tested a metabolic score against leg artery disease in diabetes, in a 2026 study. The triglyceride-glucose index reflects insulin resistance, and versions of it fold in waist measures of central obesity. The team reviewed more than twenty-two hundred patients with type 2 diabetes at one hospital and checked their ankle-brachial readings and scans.

The plain index and its waist-based versions each tracked independently with peripheral artery disease. The version using waist-to-height ratio separated patients best, though still not well enough to screen alone. A version built on body mass index performed weakest. The authors cast the score as a supporting clue, not a stand-alone test.
pmc-13249266:
Maazalahi and Hosseini model botnet spread like an epidemic, in a 2026 PLOS One paper. Botnets are networks of hijacked devices used for coordinated attacks, and their growth in scale-free networks resembles disease transmission. The authors extend a standard epidemic model with exposed, improved, and vaccinated states, then ask whether an infection wave will grow or die out.

Alongside the model they built a detector mixing feature selection and a nearest-neighbor classifier tuned by two nature-inspired algorithms. Tested on three public datasets, it identified attacks with accuracy around ninety-three percent, with few missed or false alarms. In simulation, their combined approach cut the share of infected nodes and halted spread sooner than rival models.
pmc-13249966:
Killing and a multinational team taught a neural network to estimate lung function from chest X-rays, in a 2026 Communications Medicine study. Breathing tests called spirometry are the standard, but machines and trained staff are scarce in many clinics. The model adds a simple blow measurement and patient measurements to the X-ray, and reports its own uncertainty, refusing a verdict on the most doubtful cases.

Tested on nearly a thousand image-test pairs from tuberculosis patients in several countries, the system flagged moderate or severe impairment with strong accuracy, clearly beating earlier methods. Letting it abstain on ten percent of cases improved accuracy further. The authors propose it for places where spirometry simply is not available.
pmc-13250766:

pmc-13251866:

pmc-13252766:

pmc-13260566:

pmc-13262766:

pmc-13263366:

pmc-13263766:

pmc-13264566:

pmc-13269966:

pmc-13270866:

pmc-13271466:

pmc-13272866:

pmc-13273166:

pmc-13274566:

pmc-13274866:

pmc-13274966:

pmc-13280466:

pmc-13280566:

pmc-13288866:

pmc-13288966:

pmc-13289066:

pmc-13289266:

pmc-13289566:

Measurement tools are compared in depth, from wave-based scans such as optical and ultrasound elastography to probe methods such as rheology and atomic force microscopy. Future ideas include sensors inside microfluidic chips and machine learning for uneven stiffness maps.
pmc-13289766:
Darmayanti Darmayanti, Restuning Widiasih, Setiawan Hadi, and Tetti Solehati carried out a 2026 scoping review on digital aid tools in mother and baby care. Timely risk checks, early problem spotting, referral, and coordinated action decide outcomes for mothers. Three databases were searched for original work from 2011 to 2025 in English or Indonesian. Only twelve studies qualified for mapping. Four themes emerged: protocol and workflow effects, clinical accuracy, patient-centered outcomes, and barriers to lasting use. Several systems improved rule use, full histories, triage speed, staff trust, and early problem spotting. Teams need tools that fit busy ward life well.
pmc-13290166:
A single session of virtual reality exposure for contamination fears is piloted by Anna Caltabiano and colleagues in 2026. Exposure therapy is a first-line treatment for obsessive-compulsive disorder, yet many people with contamination concerns never reach it, and virtual reality might make the treatment easier to deliver.

Sixteen adults with raised contamination concerns but no formal diagnosis completed one laboratory session in a virtual public toilet, then a follow-up survey a month later. Anxiety climbed during the exposure tasks and dropped after virtual hand washing, showing the setup provoked the intended response. Contamination symptoms, however, did not change significantly by follow-up. Usability ratings were adequate, and the authors frame the protocol as feasible groundwork for larger trials.
pmc-13290866:
A many-sided self only weakly shields larger-bodied people from weight stigma's sting, Lukas Loreth and Julian Paffrath report in a pair of experiments from 2026. Self-complexity, holding many distinct self-aspects, might buffer the well-being hit when weight-based social identity threat is salient, and the authors tested that hope directly.

Both studies manipulated self-complexity with a trait sorting task and threat salience with mental imagery. In the first experiment, with 405 participants, exploratory results hinted that high positive self-complexity could blunt the threat's effect. The second, with 335 participants, did not replicate the hint. Loreth and Paffrath conclude the evidence for a buffering effect is limited, and they discuss whether the manipulation or sample differences explain the mismatch. The work tempers enthusiasm for self-complexity as a stigma defense.
pmc-13290966:
Competition between two mosquito species in Florida is modeled mathematically in a 2026 study by Canrong Tian, Lan Zou, and Shigui Ruan. The model places Aedes aegypti and the invading Aedes albopictus on a compact metric graph, where each species can live along edges and move along them.

Under strong competition from one side, the authors prove that solutions settle toward an outcome where only one species remains. Under weak competition on both sides, solutions instead move toward a shared outcome where both species persist together. pmc-13291066:
Blood tests for a thyroid cancer mutation are assessed by Elena Colombo and colleagues in 2026. The cancer is anaplastic thyroid cancer, a rare and fast type. About 40 percent of cases carry the BRAF V600E change. That change opens the door to targeted drugs.

Twenty-four patients were treated from 2018 to 2021. They split into groups with and without the change. Care ranged from chemotherapy to targeted drug pairs. Tissue and blood were checked with gene tests. Blood tests repeated over time in the mutant group. Blood and tissue results were compared head to head. Liquid biopsy may guide drug choice without fresh tissue.
pmc-13291266:
A blood marker may flag prostate cancer bound to spread. Erik Djusberg leads a 2026 study of pro-neuropeptide Y in plasma. The common PSA test is vague. New markers are needed to guide personal care. This protein had shown tissue links to poor outlook.

The link held apart from PSA scores. Levels fell back to normal after hormone therapy. The authors call for forward trials before clinic use. Biology behind the rise is still unknown.
pmc-13291566:
Two egg reserve tests disagree in women seeking fertility care in Ghana. Francis Jojo Moses Kwadzo Damalie leads a 2026 study in Kumasi. Clinics must pick a first test in low-resource settings. Blood hormone AMH and follicle counts are the two options.

Follicle counts flagged low reserve two years earlier. They also caught more low-reserve cases overall. The two tests agreed poorly on single women. Local cost and skill should guide the first pick.
pmc-13292066:
Huimin Zhao and co-authors survey a 2026 shift in gut cancer care: bispecific antibodies that grab two targets at once. Cancers of the gut and digestive organs carry a heavy global burden and often shrug off single-drug therapy. The review ranges over colorectal, gastric, pancreatic, biliary, esophageal, and liver cancers, naming key targets and lead candidates such as CEA-TCB and RG7802.

The authors also discuss how AI might predict targets and refine antibody structures. Harms such as cytokine release syndrome and off-tumor toxicity remain real obstacles, as does tumor diversity. Proposed fixes include affinity tuning, conditional activation, and biomarker-guided patient selection.
pmc-13292166:
Shuang Tang, Jean J Zhao, and Ada Hang-Heng Wong introduce a 2026 special issue devoted to precision cancer immunotherapy. Immunotherapy is now a pillar of cancer care, but lasting benefit stays uneven across tumors and patients. The editors frame precision as gaining time and place control over immune evasion while keeping anti-tumor responses active, directed, and durable.

Myeloid cell programs also get attention for deciding whether treatment works. The editors argue that mechanism, bioengineering, and translation are converging on controllable, sustained immune attack.
pmc-13292566: Natalia Musiuk and co-authors published a 2026 correction to their review of Bacillus thuringiensis as a factory for parasporin toxins with anticancer promise, published in Microbial Cell Factories. The notice explains that Figure 1 was repeated by mistake as Figure 3 in the original article. The proper Figure 3, showing how two families of parasporin precursor proteins are cut into active form, appears in the correction, with the truncation point marked by a dashed line. The publisher has corrected the source article. Only this short figure fix is available here.
pmc-13293366:
Hyunmi Son and co-authors pilot, in a 2026 study, a metaverse program to keep teens from starting e-cigarettes. Teens often see vaping as low harm and fun to try, so standard anti-smoking lessons may miss the mark.

Surveys before and after showed a clear rise in confidence to resist vaping, while plans and attitudes barely moved. Talks with 10 teens found the virtual world made risks feel real and sparked peer debate. The authors note the short run limits what can be claimed.
pmc-13293566:
Matteo Pinna and co-authors test, in a 2026 feasibility study, a generative artificial intelligence chatbot called Safespace that supports student mental health by phone. Such bots could offer personal help at scale when counselors are hard to reach.

Forty-two university students joined, and 20 used the chatbot actively over two to four weeks, creating 286 exchanges in all. Most expected it to help, and nearly all trusted its privacy safeguards. Use peaked in early morning and late-night hours, when other support is scarce. Students valued it for reflection between counseling sessions, while naming technical snags that hurt ongoing use.
pmc-13293766:
Hein Thu and colleagues study, in a 2026 survey analysis, how digital access relates to social well-being in Myanmar during years of conflict, economic collapse, and surveillance since 2021. National proof on this link in an active crisis setting has been scarce.

Over half lacked regular internet access, and computer ownership was rare, with access varying fivefold between regions. Patchy internet use linked to greater loneliness and friend conflict, while steady access looked protective in the authors' models. Device crowding also tied to loneliness.
pmc-13293866:
Weihao Kong leads a 2026 multicenter study that builds a simple survival score for gastric cancer from routine blood electrolytes measured before surgery. Data came from 1,371 patients in two cohorts, a training group of 1,085 and a validation group of 286. Seven electrolytes were tested with survival models to find which ones predicted outcome on their own.

Only sodium and calcium held up as independent factors, and higher levels of each went with better survival. The combined score alone separated patients weakly, yet it split both cohorts into clearly different risk groups. The authors present it as a cheap add-on for sorting patients, not a stand-alone test.
pmc-13294066:
Kiran Kunwar and coauthors extend polygenic scores in a 2026 UK Biobank study to cover both trait level and trait spread. Standard scores predict the average value of a trait, yet genes can also make values more or less variable, hinting at hidden gene-environment interplay. A boosting method for location-scale models was applied to body mass index plus 30 blood and urine markers.

The tool builds sparse dual models, one part for the mean and one for the variance, by picking variant batches tied to current residuals. Some loci governed level, while others mainly governed variability. A fuller genetic picture could sharpen risk work for traits shaped by genes, diet, and daily habits.
pmc-13294166:
Grace Njeri Muriithi, Robert Arasa, and Theresia Mueni Mutetei study uptake of Kenya's electronic community health system in a 2026 cross-sectional survey. The mobile tool scaled nationally to community health workers from 2023, with uneven adoption. Five counties supplied 310 workers, including 40 assistants and 270 promoters, who answered a questionnaire blending acceptance and normalization measures.

How rollout was handled strongly shaped acceptance. Joining in early, grasping the purpose, and reviewing progress each tied to seeing the tool as useful or easy. Training gaps, thin funding, and weak technical and management support were the top barriers. Stronger rollout support, not just software, decides success.
pmc-13294366:
Geerthy Thambiraj and Antonis A Armoundas write a 2026 primer on bias in clinical research for mixed clinical and data science readers. Bias means a steady gap between measured and true values that endless data cannot fix. Big datasets and artificial intelligence now spread old errors faster and add new ones, so a shared map helps teams spot trouble early.

Three families organize the guide: selection bias in who enters, information bias in what gets recorded, and confounding plus analysis bias in how results are computed. Examples run from classic trials to data-heavy studies, across design, conduct, analysis, reporting, and sharing. Plain reporting of risks is urged.
pmc-13294466:
Liping Zhang and coauthors link ultrasound pelvic floor measures to daily trouble in gynecologic cancer survivors for a 2026 retrospective study. One hundred fifty survivors of cervical, endometrial, and ovarian cancer were grouped by treatment type. Muscle thickness and movement plus organ descent were measured by standard ultrasound, while a 20-item distress inventory scored symptoms.

Radiation thinned and stiffened pelvic muscles and let organs sag more. Radiation survivors also scored far worse on distress than surgery-only peers. Thinner muscles and greater descent each independently tracked worse function in adjusted models. Ultrasound numbers could flag who needs pelvic rehab most, without relying on symptoms alone.
pmc-13295066:
En-Shao Liu, Chien-Liang Chen, and Ming-Ting Wu study heart-area fat changes after parathyroid surgery in dialysis patients in a 2026 article. Overactive parathyroid glands harm bones, vessels, and metabolism during long-term dialysis. Removing the glands might also reshape fat around the heart, a marker of wider risk.

Patients who had surgery were compared with others on standard medical care over six months. After surgery, heart-area fat grew larger but less dense, suggesting calmer, more fat-rich tissue, while bone density and body fat rose. Calcium build-up in heart arteries also advanced more slowly than in controls, hinting at broad cardiometabolic gains worth confirming.
pmc-13295866:
Leanne Burton and colleagues review peer support after miscarriage in 2026, asking whether help from others with shared experience improves mental health. Such support is entering new maternal services in England, even though care after early pregnancy loss is often overlooked.

Searching nine databases in June 2025, the team screened thousands of records and found only a handful of trials, most of which did not test truly peer-led help. Evidence for benefit therefore stays weak and patchy. The authors call for well-designed trials before services treat peer support after miscarriage as proven.
pmc-13296566:
Printed scaffolds for regrowing the tooth support lost to gum disease, namely bone, ligament and root coating together, are reviewed in 2026 by Angeliki Tsantiri and co-authors. Rebuilding all three in their natural arrangement is hard, and standard graft surgery has limits in strength and shape.

Three-dimensional bioprinting can now lay down custom scaffolds with exact structure, and nano-scale additives boost strength, cell friendliness and breakdown control. Such scaffolds can release growth signals, germ fighters and stem cells in place. The authors weigh these designs against established care and judge them a promising route to fuller repair.
pmc-13296766:
Leandro Rodrigues-Freitas, Luísa Pinto and Teresa Canedo review, in 2026, sex differences in depression, centring on new cell birth in the adult hippocampus. Depression risk, symptoms and treatment response differ by sex, and many biological threads meet in this memory region.

Chromosomes, hormones, stress systems and brain wiring all contribute, and birth of neurons and support cells shifts under stress in sex-specific ways. The authors argue treating sex as a core variable can sharpen diagnosis and care. Tuning hippocampal cell birth, they suggest, opens a route to sex-tailored, precision treatments.
pmc-13297266:
Varun Iyengar, Kishan Patel and Alison Moskowitz review, in 2026, drug treatment for advanced Hodgkin lymphoma, one of modern cancer care's great success stories. Most patients are now cured up front, so the field balances cure against lasting harm.

The review traces combination chemotherapy, intensified regimens and scan-guided plans that adjust strength to early response. Targeted and immune drugs now join the mix. Blood markers and circulating tumour DNA may soon sort who needs more or safely gets less. The authors frame personalisation as the next frontier in advanced disease.
pmc-13298066:
Excess weight and abnormal blood fats are already common among Seri Indigenous children in Mexico, document Yazmín Hugues Ayala and co-authors in a 2026 cross-sectional study. They assessed 154 Comcáac children aged 3 to 11, measuring body mass, and blood lipids in the school-age group.

Higher child weight tracked with maternal weight, household modernity, and being male, and ran opposite to food insecurity and sleep time. Dyslipidemia affected 46.1% of school-age children and linked to maternal body mass and ultra-processed food intake. The authors offer the data to guide health strategies for vulnerable communities.
pmc-13298566:
Dental care leaves a large mark on the earth, and Thomas Gerhard Wolf and his team ask what can shrink it in a 2026 review. They searched five data banks with no bar on tongue. From more than two thousand hits, 51 studies made the cut.

The work spans life-cycle checks of dental goods, greener ways to run a clinic, and ways to teach the theme. Reused safety gear and water-saving tools showed clear scope to cut waste and harm. Dentists and patients, for the most part, backed greener care. Cost and thin know-how held change back. The team urge schools to teach the theme and funds and rules that make green picks pay.
pmc-13300766:
A helpful fungus that fights root-knot nematodes finally has a genetic toolkit, Ning Luo and colleagues announce in a 2026 study of Trichoderma longibrachiatum strain 40418. Without a way to insert genes, the biocontrol strain's inner workings stayed obscure. The optimized recipe yielded about 2.05 × 10^7 protoplasts per gram. Tomato plants treated with the labeled strain suffered 47.6 percent less root galling from Meloidogyne incognita. Defense enzymes climbed, and the resistance gene PR2 rose nearly thirty-fold over controls. The platform now lets researchers probe which fungal genes drive the protection.
pmc-13303066:
Five percent tantalum hits the sweet spot in a magnetic alloy that must also bear load, Shizhan Zhang and colleagues report in a 2026 study. pmc-13304866:
Johannes Gröne and co-authors test whether tea compounds that form as green tea's main polyphenol breaks down carry its cell effects in a 2026 study. The parent compound, EGCG, falls apart quickly in mildly basic lab fluids.

Liver cancer cells were exposed to the parent and to three stable breakdown products. Gene patterns for cell death differed by compound, and killer enzyme activity shifted unevenly. In extracted cell nuclei the breakdown products cut a gene-silencing enzyme's activity, though whole-cell tests did not mirror that result. Protein scans flagged ribosome parts as further targets.
pmc-13305366:
Banhi Biswas leads a 2026 study of a remdesivir parent compound against a virus tool that strips a host defense tag. Coronaviruses use this macrodomain part to dodge immune attack, making it a tempting drug target.

The compound, GS-441524, blocked the SARS-CoV-2 version of the tool while sparing a similar human protein, and it engaged the target inside living cells. A related MERS virus version was not engaged. pmc-13305666:
Adam D. Walsh ran a 2026 prospective study asking whether bedside oxygen measures could guide clot removal for pulmonary embolism. Twenty-seven patients having large-bore mechanical thrombectomy for intermediate-high risk disease gave blood samples just before and just after the procedure.

The gap between alveolar and arterial oxygen narrowed after treatment, reaching clear significance once implausible outliers were removed from analysis. Mixed venous oxygen fell slightly in most patients, alongside a small drop in estimated cardiac output, while breathlessness scores mostly improved. The authors suggest these mixed signals reflect changed oxygen extraction and may complement existing procedural endpoints.
pmc-13305866:
Aleksander Szpakiewicz-Szatan reported in 2026 on glass-ceramic composites holding a fast ion-moving phase of bismuth oxide. Grains of the delta-like phase sit inside an aluminosilicate glass after heat treatment and pressing above 750 MPa.

Total oxygen conductivity reached 4.5 × 10−4 S/cm at 600 °C in the reported tests, while conductivity inside grains alone was higher still. Two energy barriers appeared across temperature, likely tied to ordering changes among moving oxygen ions. The authors present the material as promising for electrochemical devices that run in a middle heat range of roughly 300 to 600 °C.
pmc-13306566:
Yusuke Ishii used the inner gaps of layered oxysulfide crystals as reaction sites for making hydrogen in a 2026 study. New solid-state cooking gave submicrometer particles of five lanthanoid variants, small enough for inner layers to take part.

Nickel swapped into the gaps in place of sodium ions lifted hydrogen output well above surface-loaded versions in reported tests. Electrons made by light were used more fully inside each particle in the authors' account. The result offers a fresh design route for visible-light water splitting with layered materials. Such inner space use may lift yield in sun driven fuel making as a whole.
pmc-13307066:
Antonio J. Santos coated glass with niobium-doped vanadium dioxide for smart windows in a 2026 study. Films at 3, 4.5 and 6 percent niobium were laid on soda-lime and borosilicate glass, then rapidly heated to set their heat-switching behaviour.

Niobium spread unevenly, causing stepwise switching on that glass, while borosilicate gave larger grains and steadier doping. The authors define a practical switching temperature to compare glazing performance fairly. The work sets a fair way to rank films for real world window use.
pmc-13307166:
Rodrigo Valle programmed printed lattice materials to collapse safely instead of shattering in a 2026 study. Auxetic and honeycomb cells printed in ABS or glass-filled polyamide were tested plain and filled with elastic polyurea.

Compression, bending and impact trials showed cell shape ruled stiffness and energy uptake, with the plain auxetic build strongest in reported results. Polyurea barely changed stiffness yet steadied post-yield behaviour, giving 96.6% elastic recovery in one glass-filled auxetic build. pmc-13309366:
Gianmarco Valenti and co-authors chart in 2026 which genes switch on as the Mediterranean seagrass Posidonia oceanica grows, across roots, leaves, and seeds at four early life stages. Seeds stayed live and primed, with sugar split enzymes that hint at a quick start when sprouting begins. Web maps of co timed genes named hub switches for each part. pmc-13309466: Priscila dos Santos Ribas is first named on a short 2026 correction notice in Veterinary Research Communications, tied to a study of reflux during dog surgery. Corrected here is only the way her given and family names were structured; the notice states the name appeared correctly in all versions at publication. Readers get no new data, methods, or findings, since the item exists solely to fix that name display.
pmc-13309666:
Shanshan Li and co-authors present two cases of gas in the liver vein system after brain surgery in a 2026 report. The finding, hepatic portal venous gas, is uncommon and rare in brain critical care. Both patients became gravely ill with belly swelling, silent bowels, and septic shock after their operations.

Scans confirmed gas in the portal vein system in both cases, alongside the belly signs. One case involved a woman near 40 treated for a tumor at the base of the skull. pmc-13310366:
Betelhem Tefera and co-authors measure heavy metals in Swiss chard grown along river banks in Addis Ababa in a 2026 study. Leafy greens can pick up metals from soil and irrigation water in fast-growing cities. Chard from three areas near the city was tested for food safety.

The authors urge cleaner irrigation as a first safety step.
pmc-13311166:
Ethan J Rowin and a large team study pouch size and risk in thick heart muscle disease in a 2026 cohort paper. Patients totaled 510 in number, followed a median of 4.1 years in total. Sudden death event rates rose step by step with pouch size, from tiny rates in small pouches to the highest in very large ones. Clot or spread events also rose with size. Size alone held as a risk factor after full adjustment.
pmc-13311366:
Juan F Poyatos presents a 2026 study using a transformer language model, named Zebraformer, to probe how zebrafish embryos develop. The model learned from single-cell gene data across early growth.

The work tests the hourglass idea that mid-development is the most tightly held stage. Attention-based gene networks, though, tightened into neat modules at the middle stage, with fewer links between modules. The author argues that constraint at that stage lives in network layout, not in single-gene behavior.
pmc-13311466:
Joanna M Fiszdon and co-authors in 2026 report a trial of a social skills program called Understanding Social Situations for people with psychosis. Poor social function in psychosis links to weak social and general thinking skills.

Social function, social skills role play, and phone-based momentary surveys were tracked. The new program group improved on a clinician-aided self-report of social function, though not more than the control group. Comfort during social contact rose within the program group.
pmc-13311566:
Areesha Rashid and colleagues, in 2026, describe a cohort of patients with cleft lip and palate treated at a specialist center in Pakistan. Data on the range of cleft types in Pakistan remain scarce.

The cross-sectional study enrolled 503 patients at a tertiary hospital in Faisalabad from September 2023 to March 2024. Cleft lip alone made up 26 percent, cleft palate 36 percent, and both together 38 percent of cases in this group. Parents were related by blood in 77 percent of cases, and only 27 percent of patients had had surgery. Few mothers reported folic acid use, pointing to gaps in prevention and care.
pmc-13311966:
Luke AR Farmkiss and colleagues, in 2026, analyze a decade of British quality assessment data for mismatch repair protein staining in tumors. The stain guides Lynch syndrome detection, variant reading, and immunotherapy choices.

Between 2011 and 2022 the scheme ran 38 assessment rounds, averaging about 45 submissions per antigen per round. Participation grew steeply over the decade. Average scores edged up slightly, with tighter agreement in the second half. The report names the best-scoring antibody clones for each of the four proteins, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, and PMS2. Labs can use the rankings to pick reagents that stain most reliably.
pmc-13312266:
Chandrashekhar T. Current smoking stood at 28.6 percent of respondents, and awareness of e-cigarettes was nearly universal at 92.4 percent, with daily and non-daily vaping both common.

pmc-13313266:
Jing Bai and co-workers search blood for signs that predict who gains from immune therapy for cervical cancer, in a study from 2026. They focused on advanced or returned disease, where first-line care now pairs immune drugs with chemotherapy or radiation.

The team compared 36 responders with 14 non-responders and tracked 26 patients whose disease grew or who died. Response tied to the starting share of CD4 T cells and to post-treatment levels of CA125, SCCA, CD8 T cells, and PD-1 on T cells, all at set statistical strength. The blood panel could help doctors pick patients for this care and spot poor outlook early.
pmc-13314766:

pmc-13315666:
Nikita Chanana and colleagues looked in 2026 for hidden heart relaxation problems in adults with extra weight but normal pumping strength. Extra fat strains the heart through blood flow, metabolic, and inflammatory routes, and South Asian adults face risk at lower body weight levels, yet data in otherwise healthy adults were thin.

In a hospital study of 72 adults with body mass index at or above 23 and no known heart disease, ultrasound checks found grade I relaxation problems in 29 people, or 40.3 percent, with no worse grades. Affected adults were older and had slightly higher blood sugar and LDL cholesterol measures than unaffected peers.
pmc-13315766:
Zhi-Fang Liu and colleagues turned peony seed meal, a farm leftover, into healing carbon dots in 2026 through a simple heated water process. The tiny nitrogen and oxygen doped particles mimic a protective enzyme, with surface carbonyl groups driving that activity.

They cleared harmful reactive oxygen and calmed the NF-kappaB and NLRP3 inflammatory axis, while a ROS and HIF-1 signal path encouraged new red cell making. Safety looked strong. The work offers a waste-to-therapeutics route that links greener farming with nanomedicine.
pmc-13315966:
Arnav Joshi, Ross C. Larue, and Rajgopal Govindarajan show in 2026 that a lysosomal transporter helps cells clear HIV particles from inside. The transporter, SLC29A3 or ENT3, moves nucleosides within endolysosomes, and losing it made host cells more open to HIV-1 infection and genome integration.

pmc-13316366:
Robin Herbrechter and colleagues present a 2026 method for tracking where medical graduates end up working, tested on alumni of the University of Witten/Herdecke in Germany. With doctor shortages biting hardest in rural areas, schools need ways to judge whether their teaching keeps graduates nearby.

The team traced 333 graduates through online research and mapped their jobs with geographic software. Nearly half worked in outpatient care, helped by self-employment rates well above the national norm. Alumni density near the university ran 207 times the background level within 6 km of campus, and the pull still showed at about 30 km out in the reported figures. The authors offer the method as a blueprint other new faculties can use.
pmc-13316566:
Thierry Roland Njille Ehawa and colleagues ran a 2026 national screening study of inner capacity in older adults living at home in Cameroon.
