From January to June 2024, 597 adults aged 60 or more joined across all ten regions. Almost everyone, 96.8 percent of those screened, showed weakness in at least one domain, and counts spread up to all six domains in a small share. Checks against standard nutrition and disability scores supported the tool's cutoffs for eating and movement. The findings press for routine screening in primary care.
pmc-13316666:
Chao Ai and a large team fashioned, in a 2026 study, a tiny carrier for tea polyphenols, health compounds that break down fast in light, heat, and the gut. Their carrier joins a treated chitosan with extract from pomelo peel, turning fruit waste into a useful shell.

The peel extract proved to be a protein and pectin mix, and at mildly acid levels it locked with the chitosan into stable particles that held 39.6 percent of the loaded compound in the reported tests. After stomach-like and gut-like digestion steps, far more of the compound survived inside carriers than free, and light exposure also spared it. The design offers food makers a greener way to deliver fragile plant compounds.
pmc-13317066:
Jianwen Guo and colleagues surveyed, in a 2026 study, nearly four thousand school teachers across China on how support from their schools shapes the feeling of being valued as professionals. Many teachers feel overlooked, and surface-level support does little, so the team mapped the inner routes.

Questionnaire data from 3,983 primary and secondary teachers showed support raised recognition directly, and also through two side paths: stronger self-driven learning and stronger teaching skill. Support that helps teachers study on their own and design better lessons feeds pride in the profession, while empty gestures do not. The model joins organization-level and person-level thinking, giving school leaders concrete levers: fund learning time, coaching, and growth that teachers can feel.
pmc-13318666:
Pengfei Wang and a large team present a 2026 multilevel meta-analysis of exercise and self-control. Their population is children and teenagers living with overweight or obesity. Such young people often show weaker inhibitory control. The authors also hunt for the best exercise dose.

Searches across five databases found 11 studies from four countries. Together they covered 787 young people aged about 9 to 14 years. Exercise improved inhibitory control in the pooled results. The three-level model gave an effect size of 0.41 for that gain. Dose analysis suggested an optimum near 49 sessions of about 48 minutes each. Heavier body mass slightly weakened the benefit. The authors stress the evidence certainty is very low, so the dose is tentative.
pmc-13318766:
Roberta Scairati and colleagues present a 2026 cross-sectional study of sexual function in pregnancy. Most earlier work reports a simple overall decline. These authors instead look for distinct patterns across function domains. They also test whether gestational diabetes explains poorer function.

Eighty-three women completed a standard function index during diabetes screening at weeks 24 to 28. Dysfunction appeared in 51 women, or 61.4 percent of the sample. Clustering found three patterns: preserved function, global impairment, and a desire-satisfaction split. Older age and lower pre-pregnancy weight linked independently to global impairment. Diabetes itself showed no link to scores, dysfunction rates, or pattern membership. The authors back pattern-based profiling over simple yes-or-no labels.
pmc-13318966:
Linghao Li and colleagues present a 2026 modelling study judging instability in unruptured brain aneurysms from vessel wall MRI. Patients were screened between January 2022 and January 2024 at their centre. After exclusions, 293 patients with 312 aneurysms remained. Of these, 197 aneurysms were stable and 115 were unstable.

Each aneurysm was split into three habitat subregions by clustering. A Transformer model then fused habitat image features, deep learning features, and clinical data. It reached a validation AUC of 0.844 for instability in their testing. That beat the best habitat-only model at 0.721 and the best deep model at 0.816 in the same comparison. Reclassification also improved clearly. The authors present the tool as exploratory decision support.
pmc-13319066:
Longhua Zhang and co-authors present a 2026 retrospective study of bundled care for high-risk pregnancies with blood pressure disorders. The cohort held 103 women treated between January 2024 and February 2025. Fifty-five received cluster management: early aspirin, shifting pressure thresholds, and careful fluid control. Forty-eight received routine care.

The bundled group started heavier, yet fared better. Protein in urine appeared later, at about 34.7 weeks versus 31.5 weeks on average. Fluid build-up in chest or abdomen fell to 25.5 percent, against 52.1 percent under routine care. Delivery came near 37.5 weeks rather than 34.6 weeks on average. Newborn intensive care admissions dropped to 52.7 percent from 85.1 percent in the comparison. Hospital costs were lower too, supporting bundle-style care.
pmc-13319366:
Emily Sattora and co-authors assess teaching on climate and health across a large public university system in a 2026 study. The State University of New York runs 64 campuses, the most of any such system in the country. Health staff are now expected to deal with heat, storms, and other climate linked harms, yet class options remain scarce.

Listings for all campuses were checked and sorted by type and place. Of 225 climate linked programs and classes found, only 30 dealt with health at all, and most sat at just three sites. Rural sites and two year colleges offered the least. More staff training and shared online units are urged to close the gap.
pmc-13319866:
Jocielle Santos de Miranda leads a team study from 2026 on a scan based symmetry score after repair of a rare hernia from injury. A tear in the lower back wall is hard to fix, and bulge or uneven shape can linger even when the repair itself holds. A side to side scan ratio was tested as a plain way to grade shape after surgery.

Records covered 25 people who had open repair with a double mesh layer plus 25 peers with no wall disease, treated or seen at one center. Scans gave the score before and after repair for the hernia group and once for peers. No hernia came back in follow up. A plain score like this could help grade repair shape beyond a yes or no on return.
pmc-13320266:
Akua Adeneke McLeod and co-authors compare four learning models for sorting power faults in home meter data in a 2026 study with a policy lens. Power firms increasingly lean on such models to plan grid spending, yet a model can score well and still steer cash toward the wrong towns. Four model types were trained on the same home meter records and set side by side.

One tree based model beat a plain math model and edged the other two across most scores. Still, counts of fault length and rate built from each model pointed spending toward unlike towns. Up to 36 towns, holding more than 100000 homes, flipped priority with model choice in the counts reported. Fair and clear models matter as much as raw scores.
pmc-13320366:
Klinger Soares Faico-Filho and Nancy Bellei wrote a letter to the editor in 2026 on a missed deadly lung illness in Brazil. A rodent borne virus causes a lung and heart syndrome that kills about a third of its cases, and Brazil carries the largest load of it in the Americas through rodent contact. A world alert in May 2026 over a ship linked cluster drew eyes to a rare person to person route, not to this steady home toll.

Post COVID triage in Brazil now tests at once for flu, a child lung virus, and COVID, yet the rodent virus rarely enters the first round of thought. Its early clues, low platelet counts with thickened blood, need an active ask about rural or rodent contact. Late calls, not exotic spread, cost the most lives, the letter argues.
pmc-13320666:
Ian M. Power and co-authors argue in a 2026 perspective that spreading crushed rock on farms helps farming more than it helps the climate. Enhanced rock weathering speeds a natural process that draws carbon dioxide from the air, and it can stand in for the lime farmers already spread to cut soil acidity. Capital needs are low next to many removal plans.

Scaling the method still faces steep hurdles, since billions of tons of rock powder would be needed from new mines or waste piles, along with wide farmer uptake. Global removal by 2050 is put at 0.5 to 2 gigatons a year in cited work. The authors judge soil and crop gains the firmer promise.
pmc-13321766:
Emmanuelle Simo Yimgoua and co-authors study combined liver harm from a parasite and alcohol in Cameroon in a 2026 field study. Schistosoma mansoni infection and heavy drinking both strike the liver, yet their joint effects were poorly mapped. The cross-sectional study enrolled 310 adults in Makenéné and grouped them by infection and drinking level.

Infection was checked by stool and antigen tests and drinking by a standard audit scale. People with both exposures showed lower red cell and platelet counts and higher liver enzyme activity than those with drinking alone. Against infection alone, several liver enzymes also ran higher in the combined group. The pairing appears to deepen liver strain.
pmc-13323566:
Jiashuo Yang and co-authors chart stroke burden tied to high fasting blood sugar in young adults, in a 2026 Global Burden of Disease analysis covering 1990 to 2023 with projections to 2050. Adults aged 20 to 44 years form the focus, split by sex, age band and development level.

Total deaths and disability years rose across the period even as age-standardised rates fell, and ischaemic stroke grew much faster than bleeding stroke. Richer regions cut their rates clearly, while middle and lower development regions held steady or rose and took the largest death increases. Projections show total disability years climbing steeply by 2050, led by ischaemic stroke. The authors press for earlier glucose control in younger adults.
pmc-13325166:
Diana E. Rodríguez-Sánchez and co-authors simulate tube layouts inside a solar reactor that splits water for hydrogen in a 2026 study. Concentrated sunlight drives the chemistry in a 1.5 MW thermal tower plant, and heat layout decides success.

Six arrangements of 80 tubes were modeled inside a single cavity receiver. Several layouts pushed tubes past the 1300 °C mark needed for the reduction step of the cycle. A tight single-layer layout gave the most even temperatures across the chamber. Even heating matters because patchy heat leaves parts of the reactor underused. The study shows internal geometry alone can tame the thermal field and offers workable layouts for solar hydrogen.
pmc-13327866:
Gayatri Mishra and co-authors test biochar and compost mixes on specialty crops in a 2026 study. Both soil additions can help crops, but results swing widely with crop type and recipe, and few trials compare several pairings at once. The team ran greenhouse and field trials with raw biochar, biochar composted together with compost, and simple blends.

Adding compost, co-composted biochar, or blends raised output in sweet basil and strawberries, though the best mix depended on compost type, biochar, and crop. Co-composted biochar lifted basil growth in both settings, one basil type gaining more than the other, which hints at a genetic side to the response. Basil chemistry stayed largely unchanged, so quality held while yield rose.
pmc-13328266:
Ashraf F Hefny and co-authors compare blunt chest trauma in older and younger adults in the United Arab Emirates in a 2026 study. Most older-adult evidence comes from Western settings, so regional patterns were missing. Records covered patients admitted to one community hospital from 2014 to 2020.

Of 861 patients assessed, 73, or 8.5 percent, were aged 60 or more, and road crashes caused 69.9 percent of their injuries, ahead of low falls at 13.7 percent in that group. Multiple rib fractures were the commonest chest injury, at 34.2 percent, while lung bruising ran less common in older patients than younger ones. Low falls, though gentle, struck older patients far more often, marking a prevention target.
pmc-13328366:
Kirstine Kløve-Mogensen and co-authors track natural swings in blood extracellular vesicles in a 2026 study. These tiny parcels are hot biomarker candidates, yet healthy day-to-day variation was barely mapped. Four healthy women gave blood over five straight days and across six weeks, and three measurement platforms profiled their vesicles.

Vesicle counts and surface markers varied notably within and between donors, and longer gaps varied more than short ones. CD9-marked vesicles stayed the most abundant across both antibody methods, while CD63 and CD81 signals ran lower and jumpier. Without shared reference ranges, the authors warn, vesicle biomarker claims risk reading noise as disease.
pmc-13328466:
Xiangming Meng and Mingjing Cai link weather to fungal ear infections in a 2026 time-series study from Wuxi, China. Fungal otitis externa is thought to love warmth and damp, but day-by-day proof was thin. Outpatient records from one hospital ran from 2014 through 2025 and were matched to daily weather data.

In total 6,260 visits fell across 4,383 days, averaging 1.43 a day and bunching from July to October. Relative humidity and rainfall showed the steadiest cumulative links: at the 90th percentile of humidity, cumulative risk reached 1.236 against the median day in their model. Clinics in humid spells may brace for more itchy, discharging ears, the authors suggest.
pmc-13329666:
Sylvia C L Durian and co-authors ask how the eye keeps useful signals when many inputs squeeze into fewer outputs in a 2026 study. Retinal ganglion cells pass visual data onward through a narrow link. The team compared squeezing methods that aim to keep future-predicting data with common methods that ignore prediction as a goal.

Across natural scenes, prediction-tuned squeezing let later cells predict what comes next almost as well as possible, the authors report. Generic methods kept fair amounts of future data but missed patterns that work across all scenes. The result hints that wiring in the eye may be shaped to keep predictive data first. The frame could guide work in other senses too.
pmc-13330766:
Natasha J. Williams and a large team study what drove county pandemic policy choices in the United States in a 2026 article. Local rules varied widely during COVID-19, yet drivers of that spread were little known. Data from a county policy database covered 309 counties across 50 states over 2020 and 2021.

Policy breadth was scored overall and in three areas: closures, economic support, and public health steps. City-like character tied to more public health policies in the reported models. Higher Democratic voter share tied to more policies of every kind. Warmer average temperature tied to fewer policies overall. Knowing such drivers can aid fair crisis planning, the authors argue.
pmc-13331166:
Keisuke Onoda and colleagues assess internal neurolysis for facial nerve pain without vessel compression in older patients in a 2026 study. Records covered 22 patients split evenly at age 70 into older and younger groups of 11 each. Pain type, recurrence, and nerve signals during surgery were compared, with good outcome set as top grades on a standard pain scale.

Good pain control came to 19 of 22 patients overall, a rate of 86.4 percent in the reported counts. Older patients matched younger ones closely. Typical pain in older patients fared better than atypical pain in that small subgroup. Brief facial numbness arose in three patients and cleared. Nerve signal shifts during surgery tracked with good outcomes.
pmc-13331766:
Juhan Lee and co-authors analyze United States survey data from 2026 on how many substances adults used in the past month, split by HIV status. Earlier work showed people with HIV use single substances more often, but whether they combine several at once was less clear.

Pooling the National Survey of Drug Use and Health for 2021 to 2024 gave 186,823 adults. After adjusting for other factors, people with HIV reported about 1.60 times as many substances as adults without HIV, and the gap held among users and among those using two or more substances. Among people with HIV, the most common mixes were alcohol alone, alcohol with tobacco, and alcohol with tobacco and cannabis. The authors argue substance screening and treatment referrals belong inside routine HIV care.
pmc-13333366:
Sophie C Hagenaars and colleagues tested whether a simple slide measure, the share of supporting stroma inside a breast tumor, sharpens a widely used survival calculator, in a 2026 study. The tumor-stroma ratio already predicts outcomes on its own, but whether it adds anything to the established PREDICT model was untested.

Drawing on 1,770 patients from the Nottingham Breast Cancer Series, the team added the ratio to PREDICT and checked accuracy for survival at 5, 10, and 15 years. Accuracy rose everywhere, but the clear gain landed in triple-negative disease. There, the 5-year AUC climbed from 63.9 points to 70.9 points, with a hazard ratio of 2.58 for the ratio, and 15-year accuracy rose from 64.6 points to 71.6 points with a hazard ratio of 2.02 at that horizon. The authors conclude the cheap tissue measure earns its place in prediction, above all for the hardest subtype.
pmc-13333466:
Ke Wang and co-authors trained machine learning models in 2026 to flag infertile men whose sperm carries heavily fragmented DNA. They used routine semen measures and lifestyle answers instead of a dedicated DNA test. The fragmentation index informs fertility judgment and assisted reproduction choices, but the specialist assay is not run on everyone.

Data came from two Shanghai centers between March 2023 and March 2024: 1,037 men built the models and 290 others served as an outside test set. Of six algorithms, random forest performed best, reaching an AUC of 0.979 in cross-validation and 0.945 on the external set. Screening distilled prediction to eight features, sperm movement, count and viability plus daily exercise, smoking, drinking, stress, and insomnia, and the team published an online calculator. The authors are candid about a catch: outside predictions skewed too high, with a calibration slope of 2.196, so they urge caution until more testing is done.
pmc-13333766:
Xuezhi Zhao and co-authors examined parental age, the age gap between parents, and newborn health in eastern China in a 2026 retrospective cohort study. The question matters for counseling couples who delay childbearing.

The study analyzed 15,762 mother-infant pairs from Zhejiang University's Women's Hospital, covering deliveries between January 2016 and December 2022. Pairs where the father was older and pairs where the mother was older both showed higher odds of newborn disease than equal-age pairs. After adjusting for each parent's own age, the father-older link faded, while rising maternal and paternal ages each remained independent risk factors on their own. Flexible curve analysis probed nonlinear patterns. The results support age-aware risk checks before and during pregnancy.
pmc-13336866:
Luyuan Ning, Lu Lu, Sophie Leanza, and Ruike Renee Zhao teach a neural network the physics of ring origami in a 2026 study. Closed loops of elastic rods can snap between flat and three-dimensional shapes, suiting deployable structures and soft robots. Predicting those shapes, and designing loops for a wanted shape, is mathematically hard.

Their framework blends Kirchhoff rod theory with a learning model that respects physics. It finds stable states for square and hexagonal segmented rings with set or varying natural curve. A shape-matching term also works backward, finding the curve profile a ring needs to fit a target space or surface. The method extends to three-dimensional rod systems, aiding programmable shape-shifting design.
pmc-13337066:
Chrysanthi-Maria Moysidou leads a 2026 team training lab-grown neuromuscular tissue with electric pulses. Organoids from human stem cells model development well, yet their cells stay immature, weakening studies of adult disease. Gentle low-frequency pulse training began early in growth and continued for several weeks.

Trained organoids contracted more strongly and more often, and the gains persisted after stimulation stopped. Imaging and gene data showed better muscle and nerve structure, matched maturation markers, and tissue that was stiffer with faster relaxation. Those traits signal stronger force production and coupling. Non-invasive electrical training could mature many organoid systems, making late-onset disease easier to study in the dish.
pmc-13337366:
Heran Cao and co-authors chart chemical tags on sperm proteins in men with varicocele-linked weak sperm movement in a 2026 study. Varicocele is a leading cause of male infertility, but how it slows sperm was unclear. Paired sperm samples taken before and after treatment underwent deep mass spectrometry of lactylation, a tag derived from lactate.

Lactate handling was off balance, with less lactate inside sperm and more in seminal fluid, and tagging fell overall, especially in the sperm midpiece and tail. Profiling found 2,699 tag sites on 1,216 proteins, with 133 proteins changing after treatment in the analysis. Changed proteins cluster in energy and tail-structure pathways, and several key tail proteins lost tags. The lactate-tag axis may explain lost motility.
pmc-13337666:
Li He and Yang Ye present a 2026 narrative review on how metabolic problems affect lung infection in children with asthma. Asthma is the most common long-term airway disease of childhood, marked by inflamed airways and sharp reactions to triggers. Infections both follow from asthma and can set off acute attacks.

Metabolic syndrome in children is already tied to diabetes and heart disease risk. The review gathers evidence that faulty metabolism brings steady inflammation and changes gut microbes. Those changes can weaken lung function, make infection more likely, and worsen asthma control. The synthesis helps explain why weight and metabolic care may matter in pediatric asthma plans.
pmc-13337866:
Liping Li and a large team present TIC-XNet, a system for spotting tic events in children, in a 2026 study. The tool reads video together with heart rate and skin signals. Unlike a black box, it turns each decision into structured, time-aligned evidence clinicians can inspect.

Recordings came from 417 children during clinic tasks and home observation. Against a plain prediction model and a post-hoc explainer, TIC-XNet scored best on the shared test set with an AUC of 0.915 in the reported results. It missed fewer events and answered faster after buffering. Its evidence matched expert timing more closely and tracked tic severity.
pmc-13339766:
Caroline Desgranges and Jerome Delhommelle speed up simulation of gas mixtures in porous materials in a 2026 study. Screening adsorbents for storage and separation needs phase behavior under confinement, yet standard simulations stall near phase changes. Their adiabatic Monte Carlo method varies temperature broadly instead.

Argon-krypton mixtures in bulk and inside MCM-41 pores tested accuracy against standard runs. Adiabatic runs matched results while converging up to a hundred times faster in the reported comparisons, as large temperature swings crossed barriers quickly. Faster sampling could let screening cover far more porous candidates for gas capture and storage.
pmc-13340066:
Sem E. H. Vellema and colleagues validate a test for living gonorrhea bacteria in a 2026 study. Standard DNA tests cannot tell live from dead bacteria, and culture is finicky for this fragile organism. A dye that blocks dead-cell DNA enabled viability PCR.

Mixtures of live and heat-killed bacteria tested the method, followed by throat, rectal, and genital patient samples versus culture. The method erased 99.998 percent of dead-cell DNA as reported, with tight tracking across dilutions. Culture-positive samples carried far higher living loads than negative ones in the reported medians. Viability testing could judge cure and resistance risk better.
pmc-13341466:
Saliva proteins that betray early colorectal cancer are sought by Sama Rezasoltani and research partners in a 2026 proteomics study from Tehran. The case-control project collected 104 saliva samples from screening patients, including stage I cancer cases and non-cancer controls.

Mass spectrometry identified 2,456 salivary proteins, of which 181 differed significantly between groups. Members of the small proline-rich protein family stood out as consistent markers, joined by immune and metabolism proteins. Clustering partly separated cancer from control samples, though age, sex, and smoking also shaped profiles. A spit test for early cancer would be far easier than current screening routes.
pmc-13343166:
Anhui Liu and co-authors review heart and vessel damage in Long COVID in 2026, arguing that immune disorder and lasting inflammation drive much of the harm. Lasting symptoms after SARS-CoV-2 infection reach well past fatigue and breathlessness, touching the heart in forms from myocarditis and heart failure to clots and rhythm trouble.

Sustained firing of innate and adaptive immune pathways, the authors contend, injures vessel linings, fuels clot-linked inflammation, and remodels heart muscle for the worse. The review gathers clinical and lab evidence for those pathways and weighs treatments aimed at calming inflammation and immune misfiring. Targeting immune drivers, rather than symptoms alone, may guide future Long COVID heart care.
pmc-13347366:
Armanda A. Júlio and co-authors review turning plant biomass into both platform chemicals and useful carbon materials, in a review from 2026. Furfural and a second sugar-derived building block called HMF anchor the chemical side. With catalyst types compared for yield and reuse, including catalysts made from biomass itself that passed 90 percent yield in highlighted cases.

Heat routes such as pyrolysis and wet carbon treatment form the materials side, with added sulfonic, amino, and phosphate groups tailoring carbons for catalysis, energy devices, and pollutant capture. Using biomass as both feed and catalyst source closes the loop, though catalyst wear and scale-up still block wide factory use.
pmc-13348166:
Sharon D. Janssen and colleagues unite scattered harm measures into one global framework for land plant loss, in a methods study from 2026. Life cycle tools score each pressure alone at mixed scales. So the new frame scales local loss up to global extinction risk using area curves and endemism, covering land use, nitrogen fall, and greenhouse gases together.

Factors for 250 gases were set at two time spans, land factors swung across seven orders of size by region. Nitrogen factors swung across two orders in the reported set. Region drove nearly all land variation, while place and compound split nitrogen variation, giving product scorers a fairer global yardstick.
pmc-13348366:
Erna Karic, Amanda L. Haeberle, and Julia L. E. Willett report draft genomes for three soil isolates of an understudied gut-related bacterium, in an announcement published in 2026. Soil gathered in October 2023 near the University of Minnesota after rain, from under a large mushroom, grew dark colonies on selective plates. Yellow colour plus stillness marked the picks as Enterococcus mundtii.

Close kin gut species cause infections and resist drugs, yet this species is rarely studied despite colour and movement quirks that set it apart in the group portrait. Public drafts for three near-identical soil strains give researchers fresh material for tracing how harmless soil kinds relate to clinic troublemakers.
pmc-13349766:
Lawrence Merle Nelson proposes Clinical Coherence as a frame for holding patient knowledge together, in a conceptual paper issued in 2026. Modern systems store vast biology data yet scatter meaning across visits, specialties, firms, and software, causing late diagnoses and care that misses life context. So coherence is defined as keeping one steady picture of a patient over time.

Three strands must merge, covering biology, lived experience data such as symptoms, function, family, and spiritual concerns, and clinician judgement in the frame set out. Coherence is cast as a system trait, guarded by a duty-of-care structure that senses, assigns, escalates, and feeds back, drawing on quality and narrative traditions.
pmc-13351466:
Arjun Mohan and co-authors analysed in 2026 whether starting biologic drugs sooner after severe asthma begins improves their effect. Long uncontrolled inflammation scars and remodels airways, causing damage that later treatment cannot undo.

The analysis drew on a United States observational study of adults under specialist care for severe asthma. Among 244 patients starting a biologic with full data, flare rates in the year before treatment were compared with the year after, and factors tied to remaining flares were modelled. Earlier initiation was linked with greater benefit, supporting quicker escalation when standard inhalers fail rather than years of waiting.
pmc-13353766:
Misha K Rowell and Tasmin L Rymer test whether mother care or mother cognition shapes offspring thinking in a wild-derived rat in 2026. The fawn-footed mosaic-tailed rat, Melomys cervinipes, is little studied outside lab strains. Mothers' care amounts were recorded, then mothers and adult offspring each took three tests: associative memory, novel object recognition, and a food extraction lever task.

Offspring receiving more indirect care were likelier to learn the lever task, perhaps because it demanded heavier brain processing than the other tests. No other care measure mattered clearly, and earlier work found no maternal effect on problem solving. Parent-offspring comparisons probed whether thinking skills carry a heritable part in this species.
pmc-13354566:
Xi Wang and co-authors tested how well labs can count brand new gene changes in a 2026 study of flat-headed loaches. They used parent and young fish trios, long and short DNA reads, and seven ways of sorting the data. Each set of results was checked against lab tests that confirmed real changes.

Even the best method missed some real changes and flagged some false ones, with error rates that varied by method. Long reads gave lower counts than short reads, and deeper reads missed fewer real changes. The authors warn that many past counts in wild species may be off, and that extra lab checks matter before results are trusted.
pmc-13354666:
Avia Merenlender Wagner and co-authors report a 2026 early-stage trial of TV-46000, a long-acting shot form of risperidone given under the skin. The drug is used for schizophrenia and bipolar I disorder and can be given once a month or every two months. The trial tested single and repeated doses in people with schizophrenia or a related illness.

Ninety-nine people took part, and most side effects were mild shot-site reactions, weight gain, or lab changes. Blood levels reached a useful range within a day and stayed there for four to eight weeks, based on dose. The authors found no new safety concerns and support the shot for longer trials.
pmc-13355166:
Brandon Itson-Zoske and co-authors report 2026 early work on a gene therapy for long-term nerve pain. The therapy uses a harmless virus to deliver a peptide that blocks several sodium channels in pain-sensing nerves at once. The team removed a marker gene and doubled the peptide copy to strengthen its grip.

In rats with nerve injury, a shot into the sciatic nerve eased pain for three to four months, in both males and females. The virus stayed in the peripheral nerves, and the peptide also calmed human nerve cells in the lab. The authors see a path to pain relief that avoids the brain and heart side effects of many drugs.
pmc-13357066:
Dejin Li and co-authors used a large United States cancer registry in 2026. They asked whether tumor traits shape the risk of dying from heart and vessel disease in lung cancer patients treated with chemo or radiation. Earlier work focused on classic risk factors and drug harm to the heart. The study covered 59,726 patients treated between 2002 and 2017.

Non-small cell lung cancer carried higher heart-disease death risk than small cell types. Patients with local or regional stage disease also faced much higher risk than those with distant spread, likely because they live longer. A prediction chart sorted patients moderately well. The authors urge tailored heart monitoring for these groups.
pmc-13358666:
Bezares and co-authors trace the travels of a rare plant in a 2026 study. Diplotaxis ibicensis grows only on the Balearic Islands and a small patch of the Spanish mainland, with sea gaps between its homes. The plant has no clear way to cross water, yet it clearly did. The team used gene data to work out how and when.

They sampled all 16 known populations and built family trees from two kinds of gene data. The trees suggest the plant crossed the sea more than once, and quite fast in plant terms, long after the Mediterranean refilled. The case shows that rare long jumps, not slow spread, can shape where island plants live.
pmc-13360866:
Ana Garcia-Megias and Diego Diaz-Milanes mapped five decades of beer and health research in a 2026 analysis. Beer is drunk worldwide, so its health effects draw steady scientific interest. The pair searched a major database for work from 1974 to 2024 and screened the results with care. In the end, 2,609 documents formed the base for their map of the field.

Publication grew steadily and sped up after the year 2000. The United States and the United Kingdom stood out as leading sources. The map names the top journals, authors, and institutions, and traces how research teams link up. Two broad themes rule the field: one on body and nutrition effects, one on social and population patterns. The study gives newcomers a clear view of where beer research stands.
pmc-13361266:
Piet J M Swinkels and co-authors present a chemical computer you can rebuild on the fly in a 2026 paper. Chemical computing promises to process information where electronics cannot go, but most setups are frozen once built. The team printed soft gel walls inside a microfluidic chip and erased them at will. That makes the chip's shape itself a program the user can rewrite.

By reshaping the channels, they flipped DNA logic gates between AND and OR behavior. The chemical recipe stayed the same; only the layout changed. They also ran a restless reaction network that never settles, a step toward richer computing. Treating hardware as flowing as software could make chemical processors far more flexible and useful.
pmc-13362066:
Sami ur Rehman and co-authors review how durum wheat handles the toxic metal cadmium in a 2026 paper. Cadmium pollution hurts crop yields and grain quality. Durum wheat, the pasta wheat eaten worldwide, can load the metal into its edible grain, putting human health at risk. Cadmium control has been studied in bread wheat, but the durum story lacked a full review.

The authors gather what is known about how durum wheat takes up, moves, and detoxifies the metal at the molecular level. Special transporter protein families that shuttle or lock away cadmium get close attention. Knowing these pathways can guide breeding of varieties that keep cadmium out of the grain. Safe pasta starts in the field, and this review maps the genetics of that safety.
pmc-13362266:
Ion Costel Epuraș and co-authors map how patient voice is measured after laryngeal cancer treatment in a 2026 scoping review. The dataset contains 635 articles in structured files, one per paper, drawn from more than 580 journals and conferences. Persian papers form the majority, with English and Arabic splitting the rest almost evenly. Ten annotators spent over a year labeling seven header fields, from title and authors to the digital identifier. They also labeled full reference sections in 621 of the articles, totaling 17,832 individual reference strings annotated across twelve fields. Every file was checked against its source document, and each file stands alone, storing the labeled text spans so the original papers are not needed.

pmc-2815666:
Kabsch explains the working principles behind key steps in processing X-ray rotation data, as carried out by his program XDS. Rotation data come from turning a crystal in an X-ray beam and recording diffraction images as it moves. Each image must be merged into one consistent dataset.

The paper walks through integration, scaling, space-group assignment, and post-refinement: turning spots on images into measured intensities, correcting differences between images, and fixing the crystal's symmetry. Clear accounts of these steps help crystallographers judge data quality before building atomic models.  Post-refinement then polishes the merged data before structure solution begins in earnest.
pmc-3552766:
Tong, Flemming, McInnes, and co-authors develop ENTREQ, guidance for reporting syntheses of qualitative research. Combining findings across qualitative studies can reveal patterns across contexts, build new models, and expose research gaps. Such syntheses also inform the development and evaluation of health interventions.

Without transparent reporting, readers cannot judge how a synthesis was done. ENTREQ lists what authors should disclose about searching, appraising, and combining studies. The statement raised standards in a growing field, helping decision makers use patients' experiences with the same rigour as trial data.  Review teams in nursing and psychology adapted the checklist for their fields.
pmc-4174766:
Kawasaki and Kawai reviewed Toll-like receptor signaling in 2014. Toll-like receptors, or TLRs, are key sensors of the innate immune system, the body's first line of defense. They detect patterns that are typical of microbes and not found in human cells.

Once a receptor spots such a pattern, it recruits adaptor molecules inside the cell. That chain switches on transcription factors, including one known as NF-kappaB, which turn on defense genes. The review maps these pathways step by step for each receptor type. Knowing the routes helps explain infections and inflammation, and guides drugs that tune the immune response.
pmc-4283466:
Sheldrick presented SHELXT in 2015, a computer program for solving crystal structures. Crystallographers measure reflections from a single crystal and must solve the phase problem to recover the structure. SHELXT uses a new dual-space algorithm to do this, working from data expanded into a simple space group.

The program takes missing data into account and extends resolution when needed. It also works out the true space group as part of the same run. That integration saves steps that once took separate programs and expert judgment. SHELXT became a first tool many labs run when a new crystal yields fresh diffraction data.
pmc-7190266:
Mhairi Campbell, Joanne McKenzie, Amanda Sowden, and coauthors wrote the SWiM reporting guideline in 2020. Some systematic reviews cannot pool results in a meta-analysis. Authors then synthesize findings in words or tables, often with little method detail.

SWiM, short for synthesis without meta-analysis, sets nine items such reviews should report. They cover how studies were grouped, how effects were compared, and how certainty was judged. Clearer reporting lets readers check whether the summary is fair. Journals began asking authors to follow the guideline soon after it appeared. A checklist version of the guideline is provided for authors and journal editors.
pmc-8476166:
Mosè Manni and co-authors updated BUSCO in 2021, a widely used method for scoring how complete a genome assembly is. BUSCO judges data by looking for genes expected to appear exactly once in nearly every species of a group. Finding most of them suggests a complete assembly, while duplicates hint at errors or contamination.

The update adds streamlined workflows and extends coverage across eukaryotes, prokaryotes, and viruses, so more kinds of data can be scored the same way. The authors describe the new gene sets and how the scoring runs. Because nearly every genome project reports a BUSCO score, changes to this tool ripple through the whole field's quality standards.
stowe-chimney-corner-1866:
Fireside talk shapes The Chimney-Corner, Stowe's book of essays and sketches from 1866. She gathers readers near the hearth to mull over children, neighbors, and housekeeping. Grief and faith enter the talk as well, in a plain and friendly voice.

Many pieces were written during and just after the Civil War. They carry a mother's seasoned wisdom and a tired nation's mood. Small moral dramas of daily life matter more here than grand events. For readers who loved the warmth of her novels, the book feels like Stowe thinking aloud, close and unhurried, with no need to preach.
swinburne-poems-ballads-1866:
Algernon Charles Swinburne published Poems and Ballads in 1866, a year after Atalanta in Calydon made his name. The new book scandalized Victorian England. Reviewers attacked its passion and paganism so fiercely that the first publisher withdrew it, and another quickly took it up.

Dolores, a hymn to a cruel goddess of pain, leads the notorious pieces. The Garden of Proserpine imagines death as peaceful sleep beyond love and weariness. Other poems praise Sappho, freedom, and the sea in rushing, musical lines. Swinburne's technique dazzled even his enemies. The volume, complete in its first series here, made him the wild star of late Victorian poetry.
the-book-of-quinte-essence-or-the-fifth-: The Book of Quinte Essence, 1866. The fifth essence. This book preserves that work. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
the-cloister-and-the-hearth-pg1366: Charles Reade's 1861 historical novel about the parents of Erasmus: a young Dutchman torn between love and the church in the 15th century. Richly researched and passionately told, it brings medieval Europe to life. A great Victorian historical novel, too little read today.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing: Volume sixteen of Casanova's memoirs: the wanderer wanders on. Europe's courts and prisons. A life without pause. Sixteenth volume: courts and prisons, the wanderer never rests, Europe's courts and prisons, courts and prisons of Europe.
the-path-of-the-king-pg1966: John Buchan's 1921 episodic novel tracing the path of the king: from a Viking wanderer to Abraham Lincoln. The idea of leadership through the ages, told with his narrative gift. An unusual and fascinating Buchan. Buchan's kings are leaders in every age.
thoreau-yankee-in-canada-1866:
Henry David Thoreau's A Yankee in Canada saw print in 1866, after his death, a posthumous collection. The volume joins the Canada travel tale with his Anti-Slavery and Reform Papers in one last book. Slavery in Massachusetts, Life Without Principle, and Wendell Phillips stand among its fierce reform pieces in print.

Thoreau toured Quebec in 1850 and found old French Canada quaint, priest-ridden, and unfree in its own way. The travelogue mixes soldier lore, cathedral visits, and St. Lawrence scenery with his Yankee skeptic's dry wit throughout. Slavery in Massachusetts, his angriest speech, damns his state for returning fugitives under federal law in 1854. Life Without Principle scorns the money chase and calls work a form of prayer when freely chosen. The set shows Thoreau the reformer beside Thoreau the walker, one pen, two fires.
tob-0166:
Bahá'u'lláh, founder of the Bahá'í Faith, wrote The Seven Valleys in Baghdad around 1860, in answer to a Sufi correspondent's questions. In luminous Persian prose, it maps the soul's journey to God through seven valleys: search, love, knowledge, unity, contentment, wonderment, and finally true poverty and absolute nothingness. A companion piece, The Four Valleys, accompanies it.

Each valley has its perils and its signposts, described through parable, poetry, and quotation from earlier mystics. The Seven Valleys is the Bahá'í faith's most beloved spiritual text, read devotionally far beyond its original Sufi setting. English readers meet Persian mysticism at its most concentrated, in a short book meant for a lifetime.
tob-10066:
Christian D. Ginsburg, a Christian scholar of Hebrew, wrote an early English study of the Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition connected with the Zohar. His subject had few reliable guides in English when he wrote. He set out to explain its doctrines, trace its development, and survey its literature.

Readers learn what Kabbalah teaches about God and creation, how its ideas grew through the Middle Ages, and which books and teachers matter most. V1 evidence notes the study served for decades as the main English guide to a difficult subject. It remains useful as both an introduction and a record of nineteenth-century scholarship.
tob-10266:
Eliphas Levi, whose real name was Alphonse Louis Constant, published Dogme et Rituel de la Haute Magie in French in 1854. He wrote the work in two parts, doctrine first and ritual second. Most later occult writers drew on it, knowingly or not.

Levi ties magic to the tarot, the Kabbalah, and a force he calls the astral light, which trained will can direct. He gives rules, symbols, and rites for high magic while warning against fraud and black magic. Read in the original French, the book shows the style that made Levi the father of modern occultism.
tob-10466:
Volume two of Calvin's Institutes carries his system forward from Christ the Redeemer through the work of the Holy Spirit to the church and its sacraments. Where the first volume founded the doctrine of God and Scripture, this one asks how salvation reaches actual people. Prayer, providence, and the Christian life receive extended treatment.

Calvin explains the church's ministry, baptism, and the Lord's Supper, and closes with civil government and the hope of resurrection. His famous teachings stand in argued form, not slogans. Together the two volumes form Protestantism's most influential theological work, still read by students tracing how Reformed belief was built.
tob-12966:
James Legge, the Scottish missionary and scholar, spent decades translating China's classic books. His Chinese Classics series gives the Chinese text, an English translation, long notes, and full introductions for each work. The volume described by its evidence covers the Great Learning and the Doctrine of the Mean, two short Confucian treatises.

The Great Learning traces a path from ordering one's own thoughts to governing a state in peace. The Doctrine of the Mean praises balance, sincerity, and holding to the middle way. Legge's notes explain hard passages line by line. His series set the standard for all later English work on Confucian texts.
tob-4066:
Max Muller devoted much of his life to the Rig-Veda, the oldest religious text of India. His Rig-Veda-Sanhita presents the collection of 1,028 Sanskrit hymns with the learning of the age's leading orientalist. Verified from the 1919 public-domain edition, the work anchored Western study of the Veda.

Fire god Agni, storm god Indra, and Ushas the dawn receive hymn after hymn of praise, prayer, and myth. Sacrifices, battles, weddings, and riddles all enter the songs. Muller's edition, with its vast labor of editing and translation, made the hymns a subject scholars everywhere could share. The book remains a monument of Victorian Oriental scholarship.
tob-4166:
Andrew Lang, the Scottish folklorist and man of letters, published Myth, Ritual, and Religion in 1887 as his manifesto in the science of religion. Lang opposed Max Muller's school, which read all myth as a disease of language about the sun. He argued from custom instead.

Lang holds that the savage rites and beliefs of living peoples explain the strange, irrational parts of Greek and other myths: the myths are fossils of ritual ages. He ranges over totemism, sacrifice, and the making of gods. The book is the anthropological school's classic statement, complete, and a model of learned argument written with a storyteller's ease.
ufo-hearings-house-1966:
Congress called the Air Force to account on UFOs in the spring of 1966. The House Committee on Armed Services held its hearing on April 5, with the public and press at full attention. A wave of sightings over Michigan that March had forced the issue.

The astronomer Allen Hynek, the Air Force's own adviser, told the panel the subject deserved true science at last. Generals laid out the Blue Book files and held that most cases had plain causes. The hearing pushed the Air Force to seek an outside study. From that push came the Condon study and the end of Blue Book.
un-ga-res-a-69-66:
Half the world has already banned nuclear arms from its soil, and Resolution A/69/66, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session, marks that fact. Any group of states may make a pact to keep such arms out of its lands in full. That right stands in the 1968 pact against the spread of nuclear arms. Five zone pacts are named with praise, from Latin America to Africa and the Pacific.

With the Antarctic Treaty, those pacts have freed the whole southern half of the world, and the seas beside it, from nuclear arms. Mongolia's own lone-state free status is recalled as well. Till such arms end for good, the text holds, zones of this kind are a firm step toward that end.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: The General Assembly adopted Resolution 69/66 at its sixty-ninth session in 2014. It decides to convene the Third Conference of States Parties and Signatories to Treaties that Establish Nuclear-Weapon-Free Zones and Mongolia. The one-day conference is set for New York in 2015. Its purpose is to examine ways of strengthening cooperation among the zones and with Mongolia. The treaties' parties recognize Mongolia's single-state nuclear-weapon-free status alongside their own arrangements.
un-sc-res-1366:
Action on preventing armed conflict came with Resolution 1366, adopted on 30 August 2001. The Secretary-General had sent the Council a full report on prevention. Its lessons drew on failed efforts before the Rwanda genocide and the Srebrenica massacre. Small arms flows kept making wars worse and longer.

The Council vows to treat prevention as a core part of its work. It will watch danger spots closely and act early, with missions to tense regions where states agree. The Secretary-General should flag threats, rights abuses, and disputes that could turn violent. Peacekeeping mandates may add disarmament work and police for the peace that follows. Regional bodies, above all in Africa, need more capacity and funds.
un-sc-res-1466:
UNMEE was extended as demarcation approached on 14 March 2003. Prisoners of war had been freed and sent home by both sides. Crossings of the Temporary Security Zone's southern edge caused concern. The Boundary Commission's ruling of 13 April 2002 awaited marking on the ground. The peace process was about to enter its decisive phase, the Council noted.

The Council extended UNMEE to 15 September 2003, at the troop and observer levels set by resolution 1320 (2000). Both parties were urged to meet their Algiers duties and to work with the Red Cross on the questions left open. They had to work fully and swiftly with UNMEE and give it complete freedom of movement. Every limit on the mission had to go at once. The Council backed UNMEE's power to check the parties' conduct inside the zone. Mine action work by the mission was also praised.
un-sc-res-1566:
Terrorism's definition and reach were pressed forward on 8 October 2004. Beslan and other attacks had swollen the count of victims, children among them. The Council restated resolutions 1267 (1999), 1373 (2001), and 1540 (2004). It reminded states that every counter-terrorism step had to honor human rights, refugee, and humanitarian law. Its three counter-terrorism bodies were told to work more closely together.

The Council condemned all acts of terrorism in the strongest terms, whatever their motive, wherever and by whomsoever committed. It recalled that crimes meant to kill or maim civilians, or to take hostages in order to terrorize a public, can never be justified. States were called to join every anti-terrorism convention as a matter of urgency. They had to speed agreement on the draft comprehensive convention on terrorism. A working group was set up to weigh practical measures against groups and persons outside the Al-Qaida sanctions list.
un-sc-res-166:
Security Council Resolution 166, adopted on October 25, 1961, recommended Mongolia for membership in the United Nations. Mongolia had sought a seat since 1946, but Cold War bargaining kept its bid blocked for fifteen years. A package deal that year, which also cleared Mauritania, at last let the landlocked Asian state through the council.

The General Assembly admitted Mongolia two days later. The text follows the standard form for new members: the council finds the applicant peace-loving and able to carry out the Charter, then passes the choice to the Assembly. For Mongolia, the vote ended a long wait at the door of world politics.
un-sc-res-1666: Security Council Resolution 1666, issued in 2006, comes to the collection through the official record held by English Wikisource. Fifteen votes stand behind the text, five of them belonging to permanent members with veto power. The decision those votes produced is preserved whole here, ready to be read against the debates that surrounded it.
un-sc-res-1866: Resolution 1866, from 2009, is a formal Security Council decision preserved in official-record form via English Wikisource. Its number is its citation, the handle by which diplomats and scholars refer to it. The entry behind that handle is complete: findings, decisions, and the reporting duties that usually send the matter back for review.
un-sc-res-1966:
War crimes courts need an ending plan, and Resolution 1966, adopted in December 2010, created one. The tribunals for Yugoslavia and Rwanda were finishing their trials. The Council set up a residual mechanism to carry on their leftover duties for years afterward.

The new body tracks fugitives, protects witnesses, guards the archives, and can retry or refer cases as needed. It has branches in Arusha and The Hague, matching the two courts it serves. The text matters because justice for mass crimes does not end with the last big trial, and someone must keep the record.
un-sc-res-266: A formal decision of the United Nations Security Council, Resolution 266 is catalogued here under 1969. The Council's fifteen members vote on draft texts, and adopted ones enter the record as numbered resolutions. The library holds the complete text in the form transcribed for English Wikisource from the official UN record. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-366:
Namibia's occupier was given a deadline to declare itself on 17 December 1974. The General Assembly had ended South Africa's mandate in 1966 and set up a Council for Namibia. The World Court's 1971 opinion held that South Africa must withdraw. Pretoria still refused and ruled the territory by force. Its repression of Namibians and its racial laws drew the Council's anger.

The Council condemned the continued illegal occupation of Namibia. It condemned the racial and repressive laws South Africa applied there. South Africa had to make a solemn declaration that it would obey the United Nations decisions and the Court's opinion. It then had to take the steps needed to withdraw and hand power to the Namibian people. The Council would meet on or before 30 May 1975 to review South Africa's compliance and weigh the next steps.
un-sc-res-66:
Fighting broke out again in south Palestine in December 1948. The acting mediator sent word of the new clashes, which began on 22 December. On 29 December 1948 the Council called for a fast ceasefire. The governments had to use resolution 61 without more delay. That text told forces to pull back to their October lines. The mediator's orders under it also had to be obeyed.

United Nations observers needed full freedom to watch the truce on the ground. The Council wanted the truce checked in full. Its call came as talks on Rhodes were about to open. Those talks led to the 1949 truce deals. This text helped push the sides toward them.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Preventing wars before they start is the theme of Resolution 1366, adopted unanimously on 30 August 2001. The Council had before it the Secretary-General's report on the prevention of armed conflict, with ten principles and proposals for a system-wide strategy. It recalled the failures that preceded the Rwanda genocide and the Srebrenica massacre, and the threat from illicit small arms flows.

The Council declares conflict prevention an integral part of its core duty. It stresses that primary responsibility rests with national governments, with the UN in support. It promises prompt attention to early warnings from the Secretary-General under Article 99, more Council missions to tension areas, and preventive deployment with host consent. It backs fact-finding missions, regional prevention strategies, and stronger prevention capacity in bodies such as the OAU and ECOWAS. Peacekeeping mandates should include disarmament and child-soldier rehabilitation where fitting.

Resolution 1466, adopted on 14 March 2003, keeps the Ethiopia-Eritrea peace process moving toward marking the border. The Boundary Commission had issued its ruling on the line in April 2002, and both sides had accepted it as final. Prisoners of war had been sent home, and the UN Mission in Ethiopia and Eritrea, UNMEE, was in place as the marking phase drew near.

The Council extends UNMEE until 15 September 2003. It urges both countries to work with the Boundary Commission, follow its marking directions, and give its field staff safety on the ground. It voices worry about crossings into the Temporary Security Zone and new anti-tank mines there. It also demands full freedom of movement for UNMEE and notes drought and hunger pressing on both countries.

On 8 October 2004 the Council passed Resolution 1566 by a full vote. It hones the Council's words on terror. All states must fight terror by all means the Charter and world law allow, it says once more. It voices deep alarm at the growth in the slain, children among them. Hate and zealotry drive more and more of the attacks, in land after land. States were told to work in full with the Council's three anti-terror teams. Those teams, in turn, must work as one.

The text reached past the known foes as well. A team was set up to draft real bars, such as bans on trips and frozen funds, for terror-linked men and groups past Al-Qaida and the Taliban. Law binds this fight too, the Council stressed.

Mongolia's road to the UN took sixteen years of Cold War bargaining. The landlocked state had applied repeatedly since 1946. Great-power vetoes blocked it each time. A package deal finally cleared the way in 1961. Resolution 166 was adopted on 25 October 1961 by nine votes to none. The United States abstained.

The Council recommended the Mongolian People's Republic for admission. The Assembly seated Mongolia two days later. Mauritania entered in the same bargain. Washington disliked recognizing a Soviet ally. It let the vote pass anyway, swallowing its doubts. This resolution thus marks a rare Cold War compromise: two locked doors opened together, widening the UN toward true universality.

Georgia's observer mission, UNOMIG, is extended on 31 March 2006, and the terms for settling the Abkhazia conflict are restated. The work of the Secretary-General's Special Representative, helped by Russia as facilitator and by the Group of Friends, is backed. UNOMIG and the CIS peacekeeping force together kept the conflict zone stable.

Any settlement, the Council insists, must come by peaceful means within Georgia's recognized borders. Both sides are called on to finish a package of documents on non-use of force and refugee return without delay. Georgia is urged to take Abkhaz security concerns seriously, and the Abkhaz leadership to face the need for a dignified return of displaced people and respect for their rights.

Somalia's arms embargo Monitoring Group is extended on 23 July 2007. The group had been renewed in stages since 2003, most recently that February alongside the authorization of the African Union mission. The embargo's carve-out for supplies meant only to build Somalia's security sector is recalled in detail.

The group's mandate is extended for a further period so it can keep gathering evidence of embargo violations and report through the sanctions committee. Somalia's transitional institutions, it is stressed, must keep working toward effective national governance. The renewal kept independent eyes on arms flows into Somalia at a moment when a new regional force was deploying and the security picture was shifting fast.

Georgia's United Nations mission is extended on 13 February 2009, after the August 2008 war. A six-point agreement of 12 August 2008 and follow-up measures of 8 September had set the ceasefire terms. Geneva discussions between the sides had begun in October, and the Secretary-General's February report proposed a revised security regime for the conflict zones.

The August and September arrangements are recalled, and respect for the 1994 Moscow ceasefire's separation-of-forces rules is called for until a new security regime is agreed. Avoiding force and any ethnic discrimination is stressed, and free humanitarian access is demanded. The mission's mandate is extended for a new period, and the Secretary-General is asked to report on how the parties are carrying out the resolution.

The war crimes courts for the former Yugoslavia and for Rwanda were both winding down in 2010. On 22 December that year the Council adopted Resolution 1966. It created a new body, the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals. Some work would still remain after the two courts closed. Fugitive trials, appeals, and witness protection all needed a home.

The Mechanism was designed as a small, temporary body with two branches. The Rwanda branch would start work on 1 July 2012. The Yugoslavia branch would start on 1 July 2013. From those dates, the Mechanism would take over the courts' remaining duties and legal powers. The Council told both courts to finish all their remaining work by the end of 2014. They also had to prepare a smooth handover of files and tasks.

Cyprus's peacekeeping force was still needed in 1969, even though the island had grown calmer. The Secretary-General reported that recent improvements had held. Cyprus agreed that the force should stay beyond 15 June 1969. Resolution 266 was adopted unanimously on 10 June 1969.

The Council reaffirmed its earlier Cyprus resolutions. It urged the parties to act with the utmost restraint and to make good use of the calmer climate. The force's stay was extended for a further period ending on 15 December 1969. The Council expected that enough progress toward a final solution would be made by then. Such progress might allow the force to withdraw, or at least to be cut down.

Resolution 366, adopted unanimously on 17 December 1974, condemns South Africa's grip on Namibia in the bluntest terms yet. The Assembly had ended South Africa's mandate in 1966 and set up a UN council for the territory; the World Court ruled in 1971 that South Africa was obliged to withdraw. Pretoria answered with continued occupation, brutal repression of Namibians, and moves to break the territory's unity through ethnic homelands.

The Council condemned the illegal occupation and the persistent refusal to obey the Assembly, the Council, and the court's opinion. It condemned the repression and human rights violations as well. It demanded that South Africa withdraw its administration and stop carving up the territory, steps toward the free Namibia the UN had promised since the 1960s.

Fresh war broke out in south Palestine days before 1949. Shots had rung out on 22 December 1948. The stand-in mediator sent word of the clash. Resolution 66 passed on 29 December 1948 by eight votes to none. Three states held back, the two Soviet bloc teams and the United States among them.

Both sides had to call an instant halt to the guns. Old truce terms from November had to be put in force. UN men had to watch the truce in full, with free range. A Council team would meet at Lake Success on 7 January 1949. It would weigh how far each side had obeyed. Cuba and Norway would join the team from New Year. The new peace talks body, set up that month, was urged to start work fast.

Food for civilians sat inside the sanctions on Iraq in 1990, with one gate left open for cases of real need. The embargo of Resolution 661 covered food, except in humanitarian circumstances. Several member states had written to the sanctions committee about the food situation in Iraq and Kuwait. Resolution 666 set out how that need would be judged.

The Council decided that its sanctions committee would keep the food situation under constant review. Aid agencies had to report urgently on conditions. Children under fifteen, expectant mothers, the sick, and the elderly needed special attention. If the committee found an urgent humanitarian need, it would report to the Council at once. Food could then be supplied through the United Nations, working with the Red Cross or other aid bodies. The text also noted that medical supplies were not covered by the embargo.
walsh-examination-dorchester-1566:
John Walsh of Dorchester was called before a church court officer in 1566 to answer claims of sorcery. The Examination of John Walsh preserves that rare early session in print. Most later witch cases went to crown courts, but Walsh faced church discipline instead.

Question by question, the record shows how a lone man said to work magic was handled. The officers probe his books, his charms, and the help he gave his neighbors. No gallows waits at the end of this story, and that sets it apart. The pamphlet catches the years before the great witch panic took hold.
westcott-gospel-resurrection-1866:
Brooke Foss Westcott, the Cambridge scholar who later became bishop of Durham, published The Gospel of the Resurrection in 1866. The book began as essays on the meaning of Easter for faith and life. Westcott treats the resurrection not as one doctrine among many but as the center.

He argues that the risen life of Christ reshapes how believers read history, nature, and their own deaths. His method joins close Greek study to wide meditation on the church's worship across the ages. Victorian readers found in Westcott a learning that prayed, and the book shaped Cambridge theology for decades.
whittier-snow-bound-1866:
John Greenleaf Whittier published Snow-Bound in 1866, just after the Civil War, and it made him financially secure at last. Whittier set the long poem in his boyhood home in Haverhill, Massachusetts, remembering a great snowstorm that sealed the farmhouse for days. He dedicated it to the family circle it describes, most of them by then dead.

As the storm rises, the family gathers at the hearth: father, mother, uncle, aunt, brother, sisters, a schoolmaster boarder, and a storytelling guest. Each portrait is drawn with tender exactness, and the firelight holds off the cold and the reader's knowledge of loss. Whittier called it a winter idyll. It became the great American fireside poem and his most perfect work.
windsor-castle-pg2866: William Harrison Ainsworth's 1843 Windsor Castle: Henry VIII and Herne the Hunter. The great historical romance of old England. Tudor splendor and ghostly legend. Herne the Hunter haunts Tudor Windsor, ainsworth's pageant, Ainsworth's Tudor pageant and legend.
